News.title: Military training sites to be investigated following rape and abuse claims at Army college
News.content:
"Certainly when people go into phase one training, they are coming from a whole swathe of socio-economic backgrounds, and it's up to the MoD (Ministry of Defence) to bring those individuals up to the values and standards that would be expected in a modern armed forces - and that includes respect for women."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has previously said he wanted to lead cultural change in the UK military. "I expect every woman who serves to be treated with respect, with decency," he said.

The Armed Forces Commissioner is a newly-created role to provide independent oversight of the service complaints system. It also acts as a direct point of contact for serving personnel so they can raise problems that are impacting their lives and their ability to serve.

Miller-Perkins said she would aim to identify any systemic issues and make recommendations to the government to "ensure the welfare and safety of all personnel".

She said she plans to visit each of the 10 establishments in November and will speak to families, staff and recruits. She said the aim was to establish some early findings in the New Year.

The other locations are:

RAF Halton

RAF Cranwell

HMS Raleigh

CTC Lympstone

ATC Pirbright

ATR Winchester

ITC Catterick

"I'm interested in following the evidence, so we will go where the evidence leads us," she said. "This is independent - I think that's absolutely crucial. I am an independent voice and advocate of service people and their families."

However, one of the women the BBC spoke to as part of our investigation into the Army Foundation College said she had little confidence people would want to be honest about their experience with "another military person".

"It's easier for me to talk to you [a reporter] than it is to talk to someone who is an army or RAF person because they already are on the side of them.

"It's not easy to trust them because I know they're supposed to be independent but military life is ingrained in you - it's hard to step away from that and see the faults when it's what you've worked in for years."

Miller-Perkins said she "understands trust has to be earned" and expects to be judged on what her office delivers. She said she had been planning the review into training establishments since she began the job in the Spring.

"I would like to think if I put recommendations in front of the Secretary of State and the MoD, that they will take those very seriously because I certainly do."

The BBC investigation into the Army Foundation College also documented women making claims about inappropriate language and behaviour from some of the instructors, including marking young female recruits on their looks.

The Ministry of Defence said it welcomed independent scrutiny. A spokesman said: "We are committed to ensuring everyone beginning their military career receives the highest standards of training, welfare and support in a safe and professional environment."

In relation to the Army Foundation College allegations, it added: "Unacceptable and criminal behaviour has no place in the military, and it encourages anyone who has experienced such conduct to come forward. It said the college welcomes scrutiny and has received an outstanding report from Ofsted."

News.title: Battle of ideas looming in British politics, Badenoch to say
News.content:
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch will say there is a "battle of ideas" looming in British politics when she delivers a speech on the final day of her party's annual conference on Wednesday.

Badenoch is expected to tell delegates in Birmingham that the differences between her party and the Labour government go "to the very core of what kind of country we want to be".

This week the Tory leader has been seeking to re-frame the way the public views her party, which has yet to recover in the polls since the last election.

The party has already pledged Â£10bn for a UK air defence system, and proposed cuts to the rate of employer National Insurance contributions for those aged 21 to 24.

There is also speculation that Badenoch could propose changes to inheritance tax. According to the Times, external, Badenoch is due to announce a cut to the 40% rate of the tax.

That rate applies to a person's estate worth more than Â£325,000, or Â£500,000 if a home is left to children or grandchildren. Married or civil partners can also transfer assets between each other.

Asked if Badenoch would announce a new policy on the tax, Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart told BBC Breakfast: "Kemi has said she'd like to abolish inheritance tax but it's very important we can afford any announcement we can make.

"That is why she has asked Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, to see what is possible - when that work is finished we will make an announcement."

The Conservatives are trailing Labour and Reform UK in opinion polls and have yet to recover from their historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

During her main conference speech, Badenoch, whose personal poll ratings are higher than those of her party, will pitch the fight against Labour at the next general election as "a battle for the soul of this nation".

She will say there is now a clear distinction between the Conservatives and Labour under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

According to extracts released in advance, Badenoch will say Burnham's government wants to "wind back the clock to failed ideas of the past".

"They believe economic growth is created by politicians. They think government knows best.

"They think that your income, your pension and your savings are theirs to take and then hand out as they see fit."

Badenoch will add that Labour will "claim what they are doing is compassionate", but the result will be higher taxes and a poorer country caught in a "doom loop".

By contrast, Conservatives believe "what people earn belongs to them, not government", Badenoch will say - adding that growing the economy "will be the central organising principle of the next Conservative government".

Earlier this week, Labour said the Tories "completely failed at every turn" to grow the economy during their 14 years in power.

Chancellor John Healey said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" and the Budget on 28 October would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space".

News.title: The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope
News.content:
As US President Donald Trump hits the campaign trail in the final sprint to the midterm elections, he is launching an emphatic defence of America's economic performance, trying - as he often does - to bend reality to his will.

"We have the best economic numbers of any president in the history of our country, and yet people don't know about it because the press won't talk about it," he said last week.

While some economic indicators, including roaring stock market indexes and low US poverty rates, are indeed historic, the overall picture is not nearly as rosy.

Trump is often dismissive of concerns about aï¬ordability and the high cost of living in the US, describing them as "fake" and a Democrat-inspired "hoax".

The American public, however, sees it differently - and some key economic indicators provide ample evidence for their discontent. Inflation remains high at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth. The average cost of petrol has soared to $4.37 (Â£3.30) a gallon and beef prices are at a record high.

According to a YouGov survey, 63% of respondents believe the economy is "getting worse". An AP/NORC poll released last week found just 17% of adult Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Those polls also suggest that many of Trump's policies, including tariffs, aggressive immigration enforcement and the ongoing conflict with Iran, are widely unpopular.

"We ask our voters their motivation to turn out, and what we find is cost of living, cost of living, cost of living," said Avery James, the director of communications at the Republican-aligned polling company Echelon Insights. "That's the top issue."

News.title: Incredible or catastrophic? Jaguar unveils its polarising electric car
News.content:
Two years ago, JLR relaunched Jaguar into a blizzard of controversy. Its bizarre teaser ad was described as "woke" and its "Barbie pink" concept car was ridiculed.

Now, the first of its new models has appeared in public for the first time. The all-electric Type 01, unveiled in New York, represents a radical new direction for the classic brand.

The car itself is an imposing four-door "Grand Tourer", with a long bonnet that deliberately harks back to Jaguar's emblematic 1960s E-Type.

But it marks a gamble for JLR, which has invested billions reinventing Jaguar and is facing mixed reactions over the new car's design and the brand's all-electric strategy.

The new model's electric motors are potent, producing about 1000 horsepower and allowing it to accelerate from 0-62mph in 3.2 seconds. JLR says it has a range, at "sustained highway speed", of up to 320 miles.

The company describes it as the "most technically advanced, powerful and aerodynamic Jaguar ever engineered".

However, it comes at a hefty price tag, with a minimum cost of Â£130,000 ($172,426). In the US, the Type 01 has a starting price of $130,500.

Under normal circumstances, the launch of a car like this might generate few headlines. But in this case the attention has been much greater, and for good reason.

News.title: Three arrested after raid on gang accused of helping migrants pretend to be gay to get asylum
News.content:
It follows a BBC investigation earlier this year, which revealed that law firms and advisers were helping migrants pose as gay in an effort to get asylum.

Chris Foster, a regional lead for criminal investigations at the Home Office, said these separate fake claims were connected to a Bangladeshi community LGBT organisation called Apanjon, which is based in Whitechapel, east London.

He said asylum caseworkers had initially spotted patterns in suspicious claims, which raised concerns about the group, and that immigration officers had been investigating for several months.

"We've got some intelligence that they can provide fake letters and documents, and they could charge anywhere between Â£1,000 and Â£4,500," Foster said.

"It could be letters of support from Apanjon, it could be staged photographs, suggesting that these people are gay, it could be letters from people claiming to be in a friendship or a sexual relationship - [a] same-sex relationship - as the claimants."

More than 100 asylum claims linked to the criminal network are being reviewed by the Home Office. Foster said some of the fake asylum applications would have "undoubtedly" been granted.

Immigration judges have previously criticised evidence from Apanjon as unreliable or not credible and found that an applicant who claimed to have attended the group's events had submitted staged photographs.

The Home Office said the group would often vouch for men who claimed asylum on the basis they were gay only after having initially been refused on political grounds. In one case, a man didn't raise his sexuality until nine years after his original claim.

The group is accused of using the same tactics as those pushed by advisers exposed in the BBC's investigation earlier this year.

A Home Office spokesperson said it was continuing to review asylum claims linked to that reporting, which led to two arrests in May.

In the BBC report, published in April, an adviser called Tanisa Khan told an undercover reporter she could provide a "comprehensive package", including photographs at gay clubs and other supporting evidence.

She was linked to a community group called Worcester LGBT, which she told the reporter they should attend in order to add to evidence for his fake claim.

Men attending one of the group's events at a community centre in Beckton, east London, claimed they were not really gay. One said: "Nobody is a gay here. Not even 1% are gay. Not even 0.01% are gay."

The investigation also revealed how bogus medical conditions and fake news websites were being used to bolster fraudulent asylum claims.

Worcester LGBT has since closed. Its founder previously said the group did not create or support fabricated evidence in asylum claims and it was not up to the organisation to determine whether any individual was actually gay.

Khan blamed communication difficulties for a "misunderstanding" and denied advising the reporter to make a false claim or offering to create fabricated evidence.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said "those faking persecution are beneath contempt and mock real victims who need protection".

"To the gangs profiting from this disgraceful fraud: you will be prosecuted, stripped of your dirty money and shut down," she said.

"And to those cheating the system, your claim will be thrown out, and you will be removed from this country."

A conviction for asylum fraud carries a maximum sentence of up to 10 years in prison.

News.title: Green member behind Zionism motion named as 'close friend' of jailed al-Qaeda supporter in court
News.content:
The Green Party member behind a motion which declared Zionism to be racism was named in court documents as a "close friend" of a man who was jailed after being accused of plotting a suicide bomb attack at Heathrow Airport.

Lubna Speitan, a British-Palestinian artist, proposed the Green conference motion defining Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

Court documents from 2015 show she offered to testify as a defence witness in the trial of Minh Quang Pham, who was jailed for 40 years in the US after pleading guilty to supporting al-Qaeda. He denied planning a suicide attack.

The BBC has contacted Speitan for comment. The Green Party said she holds no official positions and the party "takes all allegations of this nature seriously".

The motion proposed by Speitan, which was passed on Sunday to become party policy, called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

In response, Israel banned Green leader Zack Polanski from entering the country, while Jewish groups described it as an "attack" on their community and some Labour and Lib Dem MPs reported the party to Great Britain's equality watchdog.

Speitan argued its backers wanted to voice opposition to "racist systems of oppression".

On Tuesday, it emerged she wrote a letter in 2016 to the New York judge in the Pham case describing him as "one of the kindest, honest, most sincere" people she had known.

The existence of the letter was first reported by the Jewish Chronicle, external and it has been seen by BBC News.

Pham, a Vietnamese-born British national who had lived in London, was arrested at Heathrow Airport in July 2011 after spending seven months in Yemen. He was found in possession of a live round of ammunition.

In 2015 he was extradited to the US and in 2016 sentenced to 40 years in prison after he admitted three counts based on his support for the group al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), an offshoot of al-Qaeda.

News.title: Man charged with GP's murder
News.content:
A man has been charged with the murder of a GP who was found dead at her home.

The man was arrested after the body of 45-year-old Dr Hannah Terry, also known as Hannah Cain, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday.

Norfolk Police said 45-year old Mark Cain, of Fern Hill, Dersingham, has been charged with her murder.

He was been remanded in custody ahead of an appearance at Norwich Magistrates' Court on Wednesday.

A notice on the website of Grimston Medical Centre, where Dr Terry is listed as a member of the NHS practice team, said it was "temporarily closed due to extremely difficult circumstances affecting our practice team".

Tributes have been left outside the centre, including a teddy bear and flowers on a bench. A card from two patients reads: "Dear Dr Hannah Terry. We are so shocked and saddened to hear such tragic news."

News.title: UK risks being 'uninvestable' if new oil and gas fields not approved, warns oil giant
News.content:
Rising energy prices have prompted renewed debate over the UK's energy security, with UK production forecast to halve by 2035.

The UK already relies on Norway for half of its gas needs, and the Norwegian government has continued to issue new licences for oil and gas exploration in its own North Sea waters.

Equinor has predicted production will remain at current levels until the middle of the next decade.

Opedal said he remained confident that Prime Minister Andy Burnham's talk of a "pragmatic approach to oil and gas" meant both projects would get approved but he said the current limbo was "an uncomfortable position to be in".

He said that the UK could produce more of its own oil and gas.

"It's a political choice," he said. "The North Sea oil and gas industry started on the UK side. We learned from the UK and it's actually the same geology on both sides of the border - several fields actually cross it."

Rosebank is the United Kingdom's largest undeveloped oil and gas field, located in the North Atlantic about 80 miles north-west of the Shetland Islands and is thought to hold up to 500 million barrels of oil and gas.

Opedal told the BBC the exploration licence for the site was originally granted 25 years ago. "The licence was awarded in 2001, the discovery was made in 2004 and the final investment decision in 2023," he said.

Both Rosebank and Jackdaw were initially given the go-ahead by the former Conservative government but were delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Following a public consultation on the sites, which closed in August, the final decision now rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between Equinor and Shell. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank.

Adura has previously said that if approval comes soon, Jackdaw could start delivering gas to UK homes by this winter as the construction is "99% complete".

News.title: 'Dad dragged me out of bed by my hair to work' – rural abuse victims want more support
News.content:
Warning: This story contains content that some readers might find distressing

Growing up on a farm, Tracy Lewis loved being around its animals but said the physical and emotional abuse from her farmer father was "torture".

When she was eight, she recalled her dad pulling her out of bed by her hair to go lambing as her battered mum told her "you have to get the lamb out or we're both going to die".

Tracy, now 48 and a farmer herself, and other domestic abuse survivors are calling on governments to better support victims in rural areas.

The UK government said it was working to address disparities while the Welsh government said challenges will be considered in its next national strategy.

For many people the idea of growing up in the mid-Wales countryside surrounded by trees and animals sounds idyllic, but Tracy says her dad was physically and emotionally abusive.

Tracy's family have given their permission to the BBC for her to share her story.

"I remember my father pulled me out of bed by my hair to go and lamb a ewe," she recalled.

"I walked past the bathroom and my mum's face had blood all over it and her nose was squashed, she'd been crying. She said to me, you have to get the lamb out or we're both going to die."

News.title: Asos confirms hackers sent 'unauthorised' notification to app users
News.content:
Asos says it is investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms it uses after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers.

Dozens of people told the BBC they received the strange "ASOS HACKED" message from the clothing and beauty store's app on Tuesday morning - with some saying it left them "scared" to open the app.

The notification was addressed to the company's data protection officer and IT teams in what cyber security experts said looked like a "brazen" extortion attempt.

Asos acknowledged the "unauthorised customer notification" on Tuesday afternoon, saying some "basic personal information" may have been accessed.

In an email to customers on Tuesday night, the company apologised and urged customers not to engage with the notification. And it said the website and app are "operating as usual" promising customers they can "shop with confidence" while it investigates the incident.

The company has not as of yet informed the UK's data watchdog, the Information Commission's Office (ICO), about any breach.

Exactly how many Asos customers received the notification on Tuesday remains unclear, but Google's Play store says the ASOS app has been downloaded to android devices more than 10 million times.

The British retailer has a substantial global footprint - serving around 17 million customers each year across more than 150 markets.

Some Asos app users in Australia, France, Sweden and the Republic of Ireland had also received the notification, according to local reports on Tuesday.

Hackers seeking to pile pressure on potential victims by informing their customers is rare, as most extortions happen in private, so this incident may go down as a significant moment in cyber-attack history.

Shares in the company fell by around a tenth on Tuesday.

Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point, called it a "deeply serious" and "brazen" attack whereby the hackers had apparently "turned Asos' own app into their ransom note".

But she told the BBC that Asos customers should not be "scared and frightened" - encouraging those worried to change their passwords, avoid clicking on the notification's link and be cautious about possible scam emails or texts.

News.title: Survivors 'betrayed' after rapist fled to Pakistan while on bail
News.content:
Three women who were sexually abused by a serial rapist have said they feel "betrayed" and "frustrated" after their attacker fled to Pakistan while on bail.

Amar Ilyas, 41, was convicted of 20 sexual offences against five girls in Sheffield and was sentenced, in his absence, to a minimum of 27 years in prison.

One of his victims told the BBC she had assumed his passport would automatically be surrendered after he was charged and said she was "so disappointed in the law."

The government said "decisions on bail restrictions are a mattter for the independent judiciary", while the National Crime Agency (NCA) said it was "making every effort to ensure Ilyas is brought before the court".

A woman who was sexually abused by Amar Ilyas when she was 13 said she had been "cheated" because she felt unable to go out and leave her home, yet her abuser had been able to leave the country.

"There is no justice is there really? He didn't take accountability. He's not getting any consequences for his actions," she said.

"We were told that he got to keep his passport because of his human rights but he wasn't humane towards other people.

"He didn't show any empathy so it was a really big insult when his human rights and feelings were taken into consideration."

Amar Ilyas was arrested in 2020 and charged in 2023, as part of the NCA's Operation Stovewood, investigating sexual abuse in South Yorkshire.

Sheffield Crown Court heard he had carried out the offences against girls as young as 12 in the Meersbrook and Sharrow areas of Sheffield between 2004 and 2007.

The BBC understands he was allowed to keep his passport after appearing in court and had previously travelled abroad while on court bail, but had returned to the UK.

He went to Pakistan in July 2025 and did not return for his trial in September of that year, despite being ordered to fly back to the UK by the judge.

His younger brothers are both currently in prison for sexual offences against one victim. Kamar Ilyas, 40, was jailed for 10 years and Kamran Ilyas, 39, was sentenced to three years.

News.title: Metal detectorist finds second Bronze Age hoard in Scottish Borders
News.content:
A metal detectorist has revealed his "quite extraordinary" discovery of a second Bronze Age hoard in the Scottish Borders.

Mariusz Stepien found his latest haul of 3,000-year-old treasure in 2022 at a spot seven miles from where he discovered the Peebles Hoard in 2020.

Dubbed the Blyth Hoard, the artefacts date from the Late Bronze Age between 1150BC to 850BC.

They feature two bronze axe-heads, and clay moulds potentially used to make some of the unique bronze fittings in the nearby Peebles Hoard - which was saved for the nation in 2024.

News.title: Puffin island on cusp of closure as it runs out of water
News.content:
Famed for its puffins, the picture-perfect island of Lundy attracts birdwatchers from all over. But the island is on the cusp of being evacuated as water levels drop to the lowest levels ever, forcing residents to take drastic measures to ensure supplies do not run out.

Located in the Bristol Channel off the north Devon coast, the 5km (3.1 mile) long island is not the first place you expect to be running out of water.

It is rich with wildlife including puffins and seals and its rugged landscape makes for breathtaking views.

But speak to the handful of residents here and they will tell you of the battle waged since summer to ensure the taps do not run dry.

Entirely self-sufficient, the National Trust-owned island relies on a combination of rainwater and boreholes drilled into the granite for supplies.

Severe water shortages in Lundy are not new, with islanders and visitors previously resorting to bottled water.

News.title: UK set for coldest night of autumn so far
News.content:
After a spell of unusually warm weather, temperatures across the UK are set to tumble with the coldest night of autumn so far arriving by midweek.

Wednesday night will bring the first frost of the season to some places, as colder air arrives from the Arctic.

In some areas, minimum temperatures could be just a degree or two above freezing by dawn on Thursday.

Along with the plummeting temperatures, some much-needed rainfall is on the way for England and Wales.

News.title: British national arrested in connection with RAF Fairford incident
News.content:
A 22-year-old British national has been arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident close to RAF Fairford, counter-terror police said.

He was arrested in Westminster, London, on Tuesday as part of the investigation into the incident near the airbase in Gloucestershire on 27 September.

It is the seventh arrest in connection to the incident but no one has been charged.

A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

Senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, Vicki Evans, said it "remains a live investigation" and police are continuing to "pursue multiple lines of enquiry".

Five men were arrested on 27 September near the base in connection with the incident and were subsequently released on police bail.

The men, aged between 23 and 25, were detained in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".

A sixth man, a 25-year-old dual Iranian-British national, was arrested on 1 October in Westminster and was also later released on bail.

RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford, has been used by the US Air Force for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for Fairford to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

On Sunday, it emerged the US had pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

US President Donald Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base without giving specific details.

While speaking to a group of reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump was asked if a "specific threat" had led the US to pull its bombers from the airbase.

He replied: "Yeah I think we can say that. They didn't fly out by accident.

"There were some threats. And rather than tempting the enemy, we'll capture the enemy and beat the enemy.

"But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit. Not very far."

Earlier, US Vice-President JD Vance said the bombers were moved "out of an abundance of caution".

The comments came after US media reports suggested the decision was made after intelligence suggested Iran was plotting a drone attack. The BBC has not verified those reports.

On Tuesday, a spokesperson for US European Command, which coordinated American military activity in Europe, said it would be "inappropriate to discuss matters of intelligence" but that the US would "continue to assess the threat environment" at bases.

The spokesperson added the US remains at the "highest state of readiness" and would take "appropriate actions to protect our people, our platforms, and the bases where our forces operate".

Prior to Trump's intervention on Monday, a No 10 spokesperson had insisted RAF Fairford was safe and pointed to his previous comments, where he praised the UK's "police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.

News.title: The English cities that are Neet hotspots as expert issues fresh warning
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Urban areas account for the majority of young people in England who are not in employment, education or training (Neet), new findings show.

A study by the Centre for Cities reveals that over a third of these people are concentrated within the nation's nine biggest cities.

Highlighting "stark differences" across regions, the research notes that youth in certain locations are over three times as likely to fall into this category compared to others.

London recorded the highest total figure at an estimated 117,100—representing one in six across England—with Birmingham and Manchester following at 45,000 and 37,700 respectively.

In terms of local proportions, Blackpool registered the highest share at 21 per cent, followed by Doncaster, Bradford, Middlesbrough and Barnsley, which all stood at 17 per cent.

Conversely, York recorded the lowest rate at 6 per cent, followed by Nottingham on 8 per cent, with Bristol, Brighton and Portsmouth each at 9 per cent.

open image in gallery London has around one in six of all Neets in England, according to the research ( PA Archive )

Rob Johnson, senior analyst at the Centre for Cities, said: “Getting young people into work or training is a national challenge that will be won or lost in England’s cities.

“In places like Birmingham, the scale of the problem is striking, with 45,000 out of education or training.

“In other places like Blackpool, the actual number is small but the proportion of young people affected is very high.

“This shows there can’t be a single national solution. Stronger local economies are essential.

“Interventions will only get us so far if areas lack jobs or training places.

“Mayors need the powers to tackle the barriers that young people face, whether that’s skills, training, or the ability to actually get to jobs and courses from where they live.”

open image in gallery London has the largest number of Neets, an estimated 117,100, or one in six of all Neets in England, said the report, followed by Birmingham (45,000) and Manchester (37,700) ( Getty )

The number of young considered Neet currently hovers around the one million mark, recording a slight fall between April and June from 1.01 million to 981,000.

The government has indicated that it will take further action to tackle the UK’s Neet crisis following the publication of a review into youth unemployment by Alan Milburn later this year.

Delivering his interim report earlier this year, the former Labour health minister said that young people were being “abandoned” to a life on welfare. The current system presents a “perverse choice” his report found, with those on health benefits able to find a “higher income, less hassle and lower risk” than if they took up work.

Reacting to his comments, several charities and campaigners have urged the government not to pursue changes to the welfare system which would see health benefits cut only for young claimants.

News.title: I led the controversial SAS Death on the Rock operation – this is what happened
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

One decision was based on an assessment of intelligence; the others were taken in a split second on the front line of an undeclared war. All led to the deaths of three unarmed members of the Irish Republican Army in Gibraltar.

Now, for the first time, the SAS commander who directed one of the most controversial operations of the Northern Ireland conflict reveals what that crucial intelligence assessment was - and how it proved to be wrong.

Daniel McCann, Mairéad Farrell and Seán Savage were shot dead by four undercover SAS soldiers on 6 March 1988 after British intelligence discovered that their team was preparing a car-bomb attack on British troops on the Rock.

Listen to the full second episode of SAS: The Shadow War here, or become an Independent Member for exclusive access to all eight episodes:

The killings became one of the defining controversies of the so-called “Troubles” - when in the later stages of the conflict British special forces were accused by some of a “shoot-to-kill” policy.

British intelligence had discovered plans for an IRA attack on the changing of the guard outside the Gibraltar governor’s residence. A school and an old people's home were nearby, and spectators regularly watched the ceremony.

“Whatever way you cut it,” Ed* says, there would have been the potential for civilian casualties.

But in his first detailed public account of Operation Flavius, Ed the SAS tactical commander responsible for the soldiers on the ground, insists that the primary mission was to arrest all three.

“The orders to us were absolutely as a priority to work in support of the police and arrest them if at all possible,” he says in an interview for SAS: The Shadow War, an eight-part audio podcast from Aurra and Independent Studios.

Lethal force was authorised only if there was an immediate threat to life and no other means of stopping it, he adds.

open image in gallery SAS operatives leave the scene where three IRA members were shot dead in Gibraltar, 1988, in Operation Flavius ( Supplied )

These are the same rules of engagement - known as the “Yellow Card” - for all soldiers operating on British territory, whether in Northern Ireland or Gibraltar.

But the decision to open fire, in self defence or the defence of others, depends not only on the perceived threat in the moment, but on a wider setting; the intelligence context.

British intelligence was confident about the identities of the IRA team and its intended military target in Gibraltar, and had tracked them to the Rock through Spain.

But they did not know how the bomb would be detonated, whether the three would be armed or whether the car Savage parked in Gibraltar actually contained explosives.

The assumption made about how the bomb would be triggered was based on a previous attack by the IRA at Enniskillen when, four months earlier, on Remembrance Sunday, an IRA bomb was detonated by a timer beside a memorial service, killing 11 people — ten civilians and an off-duty police officer.

Scores of civilians were also injured in the bomb, which caused revulsion and the IRA issued a swift, and very rare, apology for the atrocity it said had been intended to target soldiers.

open image in gallery The Enniskillen bomb blast in Co Fermanagh in 1987 claimed the lives of 11 people ( PA Archive )

In Gibraltar, British intelligence guessed that any new IRA bomb was unlikely to be controlled by a timer. Instead, they expected a radio-controlled device, enabling the IRA to choose the precise moment that soldiers of the Royal Anglian Regiment were passing and therefore concentrate the attack on its military target.

Ed says the assumption that the bomb would be radio-controlled “seemed to us… based on such sound logic that we would not question it”.

The soldiers were told one or more of the IRA members might be carrying the remote-control switch. They also believed Savage had parked the bomb itself close to the assembly area for the military parade.

“We had no reason to question what we'd been told about the basis for the operation,” Ed continues.

At a briefing shortly before midnight on 5 March, military intelligence, surveillance personnel, bomb-disposal experts, Gibraltar police and the SAS gathered to assess the available picture.

Ed identified three opportunities to arrest the IRA members: at the border; around the expected bombing site; or subsequently, while surveillance teams followed them.

“It was not an operation concocted and carried out purely by the military authority,” he says. The Gibraltar police ran the operation, handing over to the SAS only when they believed their officers did not have the training to grab the three known IRA militants.

At about 3pm on March 6, the suspects - closely tailed by intelligence agents - separated and set off on different routes through Gibraltar.

Two SAS soldiers approached McCann and Farrell near a Shell petrol station.

One soldier later testified that he was preparing to challenge them when McCann suddenly moved his hand across his body. Farrell appeared to reach towards her handbag.

Believing they might be reaching for weapons or the remote detonator, the soldiers fired.

Nearby, Savage heard the shots. He turned as another pair of SAS soldiers closed in on him. According to their evidence, he too made a movement they believed was him reaching for a gun, or a detonator. All three were dead within seconds.

open image in gallery The three IRA members who were shot dead in Gibraltar. (L-R) Sean Savage, Mairead Farrell and Danny McCann ( PA )

The assumptions made by the SAS team on the ground, that the IRA team were likely to have been armed - and at least one of them would be carrying the detonation button for the bomb, proved to be wrong.

They were unarmed. They had no detonating device. And when bomb-disposal officers examined Savage's car, they found no bomb.

But the IRA operation itself was real.

Spanish police subsequently found a car parked in Marbella, in neighbouring Spain. Inside was a bomb containing 64kg of Semtex, four detonators and approximately 200 rounds of ammunition packed around it as shrapnel. It was equipped with two timers, not a remote-control switch.

Investigations into the deaths in Gibraltar dragged on for years.

A 19-day inquest returned verdicts of lawful killing by nine votes to two. But seven years later, the European Court of Human Rights reached a more complicated judgment.

It rejected the allegation that the British state had deliberately sent the SAS to execute the three. It also accepted that the four soldiers themselves genuinely believed, on the information they had been given, that the suspects could detonate a bomb.

But by ten votes to nine, the court ruled that Britain had violated Article 2, the right to life, because the operation had not been planned and controlled with sufficient care to minimise the need for lethal force.

It questioned, among other things, why the suspects had not been arrested at the frontier and why assumptions about the bomb had been transmitted to soldiers facing split-second decisions.

open image in gallery SAS soldiers at the scene of the shooting of suspected IRA members Daniel Mccann, Sean Savage and Mairead Farrell ( Daily Mail/Shutterstock )

The argument was intensified by Thames Television's Death on the Rock, which challenged the official version of the shootings.

One witness, the TV show alleged, suggested Savage had been finished off while on the ground. They later withdrew that account, but other witnesses continued to dispute aspects of the military version.

What SAS Shadow War interview reveals is how worried the SAS itself became about the legal aftermath.

Ed says the regiment obtained its own lawyer because its interests and those of the British government might not necessarily remain the same if an inquest returned unlawful-killing verdicts.

“There was a concern that the intelligence picture… would not be set out,” he says. A senior intelligence officer eventually gave evidence explaining the information and assumptions behind the operation. Without that, Ed argues, the soldiers would have been required to justify what they did without explaining what they had been told before doing it.

He recalls feeling that the men might be “thrown under the bus” if the legal process went badly. Decades later, he argues that legal scrutiny should be timely and based on new evidence.

The operation in Gibraltar itself unleashed a lethal chain reaction.

Ten days afterwards, loyalist gunman Michael Stone attacked the funerals of McCann, Farrell and Savage at Milltown Cemetery in Belfast, killing three people.

Three days later, two plain-clothes British Army corporals, Derek Wood and David Howes, inadvertently drove into the funeral procession of one of Stone's victims. They were dragged from their car, beaten and shot dead by the IRA.

In just 13 days Gibraltar, Milltown and the corporals' killings had left eight people dead and dozens wounded, creating some of the most enduring television images of the Troubles.

open image in gallery During the funeral of the three IRA's members killed in Gibraltar by British secret agents, the crowd of mourners dives for cover as loyalist gunmen open fire ( AFP/Getty )

Nor did Gibraltar end there.

In September 1990, the IRA shot Sir Peter Terry, the former governor of Gibraltar, at his home in Staffordshire. He survived, but both he and his wife was injured. The IRA said the attack was retaliation for his role in Operation Flavius.

This helps explain why Ed is still speaking under a false name, with his voice disguised, almost four decades later. He says he remains concerned not only for himself but for his family.

Yet Ed, like many other SAS and operators from the even more secretive “Det”, then 14 Intelligence Company, has sympathy for the Republicans he spent much of his covert career fighting.

“The job of the military is not to use force to resolve a situation such as the Troubles,” he said. Its task, he argues, was “to hold the ring until a political solution can be found”.

In March 1988 that political settlement remained more than a decade away.

The killings on Gibraltar lasted only seconds. The arguments over the intelligence that led to them, the decisions made by the soldiers, and where responsibility ultimately lay have now lasted almost 40 years.

Listen to the first three instalments of SAS: The Shadow War now, or become an Independent Member for exclusive early access to the entire series. Available on Apple Podcasts and Spotify

News.title: What is the Plague? The deadly disease that killed up to 60% of Europe’s population
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

There have been conflicting reports about the death of an employee at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute in Russia, including the claim that she contracted the pneumonic plague.

Many of us have heard of bubonic plague and its telltale swellings known as buboes. However, pneumonic plague has also been recognised and feared by humans for centuries before the advent of modern antibiotic treatments.

When news breaks of a death by an infectious disease as infamous as plague, a measured, informed response includes understanding how past societies have thought and behaved during plague times.

What is plague?

The disease known as plague (from the Latin plangō, meaning “to strike”) is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis.

Plague is a rodent disease, rarely moving beyond its usual rodent “reservoir” to circulate among humans. But this does happen occasionally. Historically, the likely culprit was the vector of the black rat flea.

open image in gallery The plague was historically passed onto humans via the fleas on rodents such as rats. ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

The location of the plague infection in the human body dictates how the disease will manifest.

Bubonic plague attacks the lymph nodes, causing the infamous buboes one might typically associate with plague. Septicaemic plague occurs when the bacteria proliferate in the bloodstream, which can come as a later stage of bubonic plague. The rarest but most deadly form is pneumonic plague, which infects the lungs.

Untreated pneumonic plague kills the quickest, and the most consistently.

‘The most dangerous of all these terrible things’

We know of three significant historical pandemics, during which plague flared up in wave after wave:

the first plague pandemic of around 541–750

the second plague pandemic from the 14–18th centuries

the third plague pandemic from 1855–1960.

This final pandemic ended with the wide adoption of medical hygiene practices, quarantining, inoculation and antibiotics. The plague, however, still exists as an endemic disease in many parts of the world.

The Black Death (1346–58) was the most significant outbreak of the second plague pandemic.

We have known since 2011 that these historical outbreaks of plague were caused by ancestors of the Y. pestis strains circulating today.

Scientists were able to reconstruct the full Y. Pestis genome from ancient DNA extracted from the dental pulp of human skeletons buried between 1348 and 1350 in a known plague cemetery in East Smithfield, London.

open image in gallery A gravestone in Eyam village in Derbyshire, a village which famously voluntarily introduced a plague quarantine in 1665. ( Getty/iStock )

The Black Death struck vast swathes of Europe, Asia and Africa in the 14th century, killing an estimated 40–60% of the populations it struck.

Even during this medieval period, observers recognised the plague could have three distinct manifestations.

Monk and musician Louis Heyligen was with the papal court in Avignon when the Black Death arrived in Europe in 1347. In a letter dated April 27 1348, he wrote:

“It is said that the disease takes three forms. In the first people suffer an infection of the lungs, which leads to breathing difficulties. Whoever has this corruption or contamination to any extent cannot escape, but will die within two days. […] And this form is the most dangerous of all these terrible things, which is to say that it is the most contagious.”

Medieval responses to the plague varied.

Many people believed that the plague was God’s punishment of humankind for its sins, and turned to devotional acts like pilgrimage, procession and prayer as acts of contrition and to prepare their souls for the possibility of imminent death.

Others, like the Arab geographer Ibn al-Wardi, considered it a martyrdom, and criticised those who fled plague-affected areas.

Many turned to medicine, informed at this time by humoural theory. According to this ancient model, human health and temperament is determined by the balance of four distinct humours (black bile, yellow bile, blood and phlegm).

open image in gallery Plague doctors in the 17th century wore protective clothing with nosegays concealed in their masks and carried pomander canes. ( Public domain )

Medical treatments to “rebalnce” these humours included purging the body via bloodletting, emetics and laxatives, purifying or fumigating corrupted air, and applying poultices to buboes in an attempt to draw out the corrupted matter.

Physicians encouraged people to maintain a strict health regimen to avoid catching the plague.

Importantly, the ministrations of physicians were not considered antithetical to the belief that plague was God’s judgement.

As the Paris Medical Faculty noted in its plague report of October 1348:

“We must not overlook the fact that any pestilence proceeds from the divine will, and our advice can therefore only be to return humbly to God. But this does not mean forsaking doctors. For the Most High created earthly medicine, and although God alone cures the sick, he does so through the medicine which in his generosity he provided.”

About the author Beth Spacey is a Lecturer in Medieval History at The University of Queensland. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

Still, others looked to scapegoat particular communities, leading to the violent persecution of Europe’s Jews during plague times.

In some areas, early quarantine methods were developed, and restrictions were placed on the movement of goods and people. People perfumed the air and consumed particular food and drink, hoping to prevent corrupted, plague-causing miasma from entering their bodies.

Medieval people had various ideas about and responses to the plague. One thing they did not do, though, was don a beaked plague mask. This was an uncommon later phenomenon of the 17th century, where doctors would wear a mask filled with aromatics to protect them from the “miasma”.

News.title: Ted Lasso’s fourth season was a success. But there’s one thing still missing
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Late on Tuesday night (or early Wednesday morning, depending on your timezone) the footballing world came together in unison to bid farewell to an icon of the game. Some supporters argued the final whistle was long overdue, while others still cling to the hope that their hero might return to fight one last battle. As the curtain fell, we were left with a lasting image, both poetic in its narrative weight and overwhelming in its emotion: Lionel Messi sending the goalkeeper the wrong way from the spot to score one last goal for Argentina. Oh, also the Ted Lasso finale was on.

***SPOILERS FOR THE FINAL EPISODE OF TED LASSO SEASON 4 FOLLOW***

Strangely, if there’s one thing the fourth season of Ted Lasso lacked, it was football. As events in Buenos Aires proved last night, the real game is ripe with high drama. For a season of television that ostensibly set out to celebrate women’s football, Ted Lasso showed us precious little of it over its last ten episodes. In the finale, we cut away from the all-important, last match of the season before a ball was even kicked. Messi would never miss an open goal like that.

Instead, the show chose to focus on the relatively minor matter of life and death. There was a wake for the beloved pub landlady Mae Green (Annette Badland), and the pitter-patter of tiny football boots on the way for Roy Kent (Brett Goldstein) and Keeley Jones (Juno Temple).

As sad as many fans of the show understandably were about Mae’s abrupt demise, it did give the finale real weight as it stuck the landing in its most emotional moments: a moving performance of the folk song “The Parting Glass” and Badland’s wonderful reading of the Mary Oliver poem “When Death Comes.”

open image in gallery Coach Beard (Brendan Hunt) and Ted Lasso (Jason Sudeikis) ended season four of 'Ted Lasso' still without a major trophy. Could they return for a fifth season? ( Apple TV+ )

Still, you can’t help but think that Mae herself would have agreed with the legendary Liverpool manager Bill Shankly, who famously quipped: “Some people believe football is a matter of life and death. I am very disappointed with that attitude. I can assure you it is much, much more important than that.”

There had been a fair bit of trepidation about whether Ted Lasso would justify its return after three years away from our screens. The warmth and wit of the show’s first season arrived like a life-affirming balm in the pandemic-hit days of 2020, but by the time it ended its run after three seasons in 2023, its charms had curdled and become cloying. Earlier this year, the show returned for an unexpected fourth season, which saw Lasso (Jason Sudeikis) taking charge of AFC Richmond’s newly formed women’s team.

If the show’s comeback felt like a risk, it’s one that’s been justified by a largely endearing, funny and welcome run of new episodes. Not everything has worked. Coach Beard’s (Brendan Hunt) continued tangles with estranged wife Jane (Phoebe Walsh) have been mostly laugh-free and head-scratching at best, while the eccentric Zelda’s (Tracey Ullman) well-signposted and long-winded betrayal of club owner Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham) was another misfire. The show’s only true mystery remains why Sudeikis and Waddingham have shared so little screen time since the reboot.

open image in gallery Roy Kent (Brett Goldstein) learns he has a baby on the way — and a new job at Chelsea — as season four of 'Ted Lasso' comes to an end ( Apple TV+ )

But the gamble certainly paid off with audiences. According to recent data from Ampere Analysis, the fourth season pulled in 3.3 million views in the U.S. alone last month, making it Apple TV’s most-watched show or film in September. For context, in second place was the new Ryan Reynolds movie Mayday, trailing by some distance with 2.1 million views.

The question now is whether Lasso will return for a fifth and even sixth season. Apple has remained tight-lipped thus far, although Sudeikis has said that he and the show’s other creators do indeed have another two seasons sketched out. Back in July, an interview with Sudeikis and his collaborators in The Hollywood Reporter suggested that: “If all goes according to plan, the Lasso team will be back in the writers room in late August mapping out a not-yet-ordered season five.”

With fans still watching in droves, there seems to be little reason Apple would stand in their way. The finale of the fourth season tied up some plot threads neatly, but left plenty of questions unanswered and ambiguous. Coach Alice Chilton’s (Tanya Reynolds) elevation to lead the women’s team felt both fitting and inevitable, but the question of who will take over the men’s team now that Roy is off to Chelsea remains open.

open image in gallery Alice Chilton (played by Tanya Reynolds) was promoted to lead the AFC Richmond women’s team at the end of the fourth season ( Apple TV+ )

A cameo appearance from Nick Mohammed’s Nate Shelley suggests he could be welcomed back into the fold, but surely Ted can’t spend a whole new year as assistant to Coach Chilton? Sure, he might be a better father and finally make it to watch some of his son’s games, but admirable parenting hardly screams “satisfying TV.”

After all these years, what Ted really deserves is to finally get his hands on some silverware. His message of positivity was all well and good as we watched him get Richmond relegated (season one), promoted (season two) and eventually narrowly finish second in the Premier League (season three), but it feels like unfinished business if he doesn’t get to actually win something.

Admittedly, it was Manchester City that pipped him to the title that third year, but you’d be hard-pressed to ring much excitement out of watching lawyers argue to have the history books corrected in Ted’s favor over financial irregularities.

No, Ted has earned a real-life, soppy, punch-the-air victory, just like Messi in 2022 or Rocky in Rocky II. For the millions of us still tuning in, that’s the unfulfilled promise that’ll likely keep us coming back for another season (or two): the hope that, just for once, nice guys might finish first.

News.title: Thomas Tuchel hails ‘brilliant, brilliant’ Harry Kane after landmark double
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thomas Tuchel says Harry Kane deserves all of the accolades after marking his record-equalling England appearance with a decisive display in the Nations League defeat of Czechia.

The skipper continued his wondrous form on Tuesday at Wembley, where he scored a brace having forced Vladimir Coufal into an own goal as he joined Peter Shilton on 125 caps.

Kane was given a standing ovation as he was taken off towards the end of a 3-0 victory that all but assured England of a place in the Nations League quarter-finals.

“Brilliant, brilliant,” boss Tuchel said. “I think the team performance was very good, and Harry’s performance was very good.

open image in gallery Harry Kane starred against Czechia on his record-equalling night (Adam Davy/PA)

“He was again decisive for us and on this very special day for him, to equal the record of Peter Shilton, puts him on this kind of level.

“Amazing. He deserves the stage, he deserves the praise.”

Kane is set to move clear as England’s most-capped men’s player next month against Croatia, who Tuchel’s team thumped 7-0 in Rijeka on Saturday.

That swashbuckling win and 2-0 victory in Prague last week helped make amends for the helter-skelter 3-2 loss to Spain the Group A3 opener as they continue to move on from the World Cup.

Asked if he feels the side are a step further ahead than they were at the end of the summer, Tuchel said: “Yeah, of course, and that’s what we have to do.

“That is our goal, to constantly improve and develop. We have these experiences together, and we had a big tournament together.

open image in gallery England enjoyed another victory (John Walton/PA)

“It was very positive and still it’s necessary to move forward and to improve, especially in sports and this is what we’re trying to do.

“We adjusted some details in our structure, and we didn’t compromise on the effort and the intensity and on the togetherness of the team.

“The players who were with us in the World Cup took care of these standards and of the culture within the team, off the pitch and on the pitch.

“I think that’s what you could see and you just could see the positive on a long camp is that you have time for debriefs, that you have time for meetings, you have more time for training, you spend more time.

“And together you can develop something because the common language sinks in, the patterns sink in, and, again like after a big victory in Croatia, we put in the things that we don’t want to compromise on.

“The intensity, the effort and we created a good momentum throughout the match, created chances, scored beautiful goals, so it was a very good camp overall.”

News.title: Harry Kane scores best goal of the Tuchel era to show what England were missing at the World Cup
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Another Nations League night, another comprehensive England win. This 3-0 victory over Czech Republic made it 12 goals without reply in England’s last three games, after that knife-edge defeat by Spain here at Wembley back at the start of the international break. And while this wasn’t as comprehensive as the 7-0 thrashing over Croatia, it featured perhaps the best goal of the Thomas Tuchel era, scored by Kane after a glorious move involving Elliot Anderson and Morgan Rogers, the sort kids will try to recreate on playgrounds tomorrow.

In doing so, England tightened their grip on a place in the Nations League quarter-finals in March. They still have Croatia and Spain to play next month, and are on course to finish second in the group which may lead to a more difficult quarter-final opponent. But in this form, no one will much fancy taking on Tuchel’s free-scoring England.

There are, as ever, multiple ways to interpret the past few weeks. On the one hand: wow, England play thrilling football, they smother teams, they dominate, they are both great goalscorers and scorers of great goals. On the other hand: where was this three months ago? Why did the same team toil against DR Congo? Why did they struggle past Norway? Why did they relinquish the entire concept of scoring goals against Argentina?

open image in gallery Harry Kane scores his first goal against Czechia (John Walton/PA) ( PA Wire )

The overriding sensation watching England over the past four games has been like watching another team entirely from the one who stumbled through much of the World Cup. What’s changed? The personnel is mostly the same, although Lewis Hall and Trent Alexander-Arnold have added a dash of quality in the full-back roles.

Well, for one, the conditions are different now. England played like a team who don’t have a care in the world, perhaps because they really don’t. Does anyone actually remember that Portugal won the previous Nations League? Does anyone care? It is a competitive tournament in the loosest sense, and England’s players have thrived outside the usual pressure cooker they play in for club and country.

And, of course, this is a team who carry a scar. Kane and Anthony Gordon spoke clearly at the start of this break about the lessons learnt from Argentina, and how they could only accept future defeats if they went down swinging. It is hardly a new lesson – Kane also referenced the semi-final defeat by Croatia in 2018 and the final defeat by Italy in 2021 in his list of limp exits – but they have shown a concerted effort to recalibrate the dials.

Perhaps the favourable conditions extend to the weather, too. England played a lethal high press here that would have been impossible to implement over eight games in the sticky heat of a North American summer. They didn’t let Czech Republic up for air, with such relentless dedication that their first shot on target came from the sheer force of an Anderson tackle.

open image in gallery Vladimir Coufal scores past his own goalkeeper ( PA )

After half an hour, England finally broke through Czech resistance in bizarre circumstances, when one captain assisted the other. Kane drifted out to the right where he whipped in a dangerous cross intended for Eberechi Eze on the far side. Sensing danger, Vladimir Coufal raced back towards his own goal where he momentarily lost his mind, burying a ruthless finish past his own goalkeeper, Lukas Hornicek.

What followed was a magical second goal. Alexander-Arnold rolled the ball into Anderson standing in the middle of the Czech half and he whipped a first-time ball curling over left-back Jiri Slama’s head, not unlike the pass he played to set up Jude Bellingham’s goal against Croatia at the World Cup. This time he drew a perfect parabola into the path of Rogers who arrowed a first-time, half-volleyed cross into the centre where Kane swept home from six yards.

Every element was carried out with only one touch, a goal both economic and ruthless, efficient and deadly. Again, the prevailing thoughts were: that was magnificent; could they do this in tournament conditions?

It was not just the goal that lit up the night. Eze swayed through Czech players with the easy breeze of a man striding between sunbeds on the beach. Bellingham produced a series of trademark dragbacks that toyed with his opponents. Myles Lewis-Skelly slipped through tackles leaving behind a trail of tacklers on the floor. Kane added the third with a header at a corner on what was his record-equalling international appearance, drawing him level with Peter Shilton’s 125 caps. It almost went under the radar that his goal tally is now into the 90s, and the century is surely only a matter of time.

These games might not feel particularly seismic in the grand scheme of Tuchel’s reign. He will be judged on the fine margins of major tournaments, on the unravelling of a World Cup semi-final rather than a thrashing in Uefa Nations League Group A3. But he made clear during World Cup qualifying how important the preceding autumn internationals were to his thinking. The “brotherhood” England created during those months formed the basis of his World Cup squad eight months later, and most of the players who didn’t show up in October and November missed their chance.

open image in gallery Jude Bellingham was excellent again for England ( Getty )

The stakes may not be as high here, but the significance of these performances may be similarly impactful when the Nations League reaches the knockout stages. Hall, for example, started all four games here in Nico O’Reilly’s absence and has earnt himself more chances. “I am very happy with Lewis Hall, he made a big impression and opened up the competition for sure,” Tuchel said before kick-off here.

O’Reilly was reliable in North America this summer and Tuchel now faces the same challenge Gareth Southgate wrestled with, weighing form against the trust he has developed with players fighting for the cause at a tournament. Nothing builds bonds like shared experience. “The longer together, the language seeps in,” Tuchel said. “We use different language and a different style of play than the clubs. If you have more games and sessions you can see it sink it.”

It was not a perfect performance, and the nervy display of Jordan Pickford with the ball at his feet was enough to give encouragement to James Trafford in his quest to usurp the Everton goalkeeper as England’s No 1. But that was just about the only blot on a night when England showed the team they can be; perhaps, too, the team they could have been.

News.title: UK property market warned over 'gathering dark clouds' as house prices stall amid rising mortgage rates
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

House prices across the UK failed to grow in September, an index has found, with prices showing no movement either month on month or compared with a year earlier.

The typical home was valued at £298,441 in September, according to the Lloyds index.

Mortgage costs have been climbing at the same time, with the average five-year fixed homeowner mortgage rate reaching the 6% mark on Monday for the first time in three years, financial information website Moneyfacts said.

Lloyds recorded a 0.0% month-on-month change in property values in September, after a 0.3% fall in August.

The annual picture was similarly flat, with the index showing a 0.0% change against September last year, following a 0.4% annual dip in August.

Andrew Asaam, mortgages director at Lloyds, said: “While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of (the Bank of England) base rate.

open image in gallery Lloyds recorded a 0.0% change in property values ( AFP/Getty )

“That’s mirrored in wider economic data, with household spending holding up better than many expected despite energy and other cost pressures arising from the Middle East conflict.

“Whether that picture continues is likely to depend on how confident consumers feel that the latest cost‑of‑living pressures will prove temporary.

“Confidence has long been a key driver of housing market activity, and will play an important role in shaping demand over the remainder of this year and into 2027.

“For now, the housing market appears to be balancing buyer caution with continued underlying demand.”

Ian Futcher, a financial planner at wealth manager Quilter said: “Lloyds’ latest house price index shows UK property prices flatlined in September, leaving annual growth flat at 0.0% and the average home valued at £298,441.

“The market is facing gathering dark clouds on several fronts, with affordability, confidence and borrowing costs all coming under pressure, which is in turn causing house prices to stall.

“The forthcoming Budget is adding another layer of uncertainty, with some buyers choosing to sit on their hands until there is greater clarity on the Government’s tax and housing policy agenda.

“When purchasing a home is one of the biggest financial decisions a person will ever make, uncertainty alone can be enough to delay a move by weeks or even months.

“The ongoing conflict involving Iran continues to cast a long shadow over the economic outlook.

“Concerns that elevated energy prices and broader geopolitical uncertainty could keep inflation higher for longer have filtered through to financial markets, raising questions about the path of future interest rates and leaving households facing a more uncertain economic backdrop.

“These concerns are already feeding through to the mortgage market. Borrowers who only a few months ago were becoming more optimistic about the prospect of cheaper borrowing are now seeing that outlook shift significantly.”

open image in gallery It has been claimed that the upcoming Budget has added more uncertainty over the housing market ( Getty )

Nathan Emerson, chief executive at property professionals’ body Propertymark, said: “Against a backdrop of continued pressure across the global economy, it is perhaps unsurprising to see some fluctuation in domestic house prices.

“It is important to remember that, over a prolonged period, house price growth is rarely a straightforward upward trend.”

Mark Harris, chief executive of mortgage broker SPF Private Clients, said: “The high cost of fuel and rising energy bills, combined with uncertainty surrounding the upcoming Budget, as well as the prospect of higher mortgage payments, are all giving buyers reason to pause.”

Amy Reynolds, head of sales at London-based estate agency Antony Roberts, said: “Buyers are still out there, but they’re being careful.”

Here are average house prices and the annual change, according to Lloyds (the regional annual change figures are based on the most recent three months of approved mortgage transaction data):

News.title: Weight loss jabs are safe for obese teenagers, WHO announces
News.content:
Obese teenagers can safely be given weight-loss drugs and undergo bariatric surgery, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.

The recommendations form part of the first set of global guidelines released by the WHO for the treatment of obese children and adolescents.

Previously, the WHO only recommended weight-loss drugs like Mounjaro and Wegovy and bariatric surgery, which alters the stomach and reduces appetite, for the treatment of obese adults – defined as someone with a body mass index of 30 or above.

However, the new guidelines say children over the age of 10 can safely be given the drugs, as well as undergo weight-loss surgery, if all other options, like managed exercise and diet programmes, have been exhausted. Children under that age should not be given drugs or surgery.

Obese children in the UK are currently not eligible for weight-loss drugs or surgery on the NHS, although specialised clinics may offer them to children over 12 under very strict conditions.

The WHO recommends first and foremost that obese children and teenagers undertake a structured diet programme and physical activity, which for children over five should include an average of at least 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous activity across the week.

According to Unicef an estimated 188 million children and adolescents are obese, and last year, the number of overweight children exceeded the number of underweight children for the first time in history.

While obesity rates are beginning to plateau in many rich countries, childhood obesity is rising rapidly in the developing world, including in sub-Saharan Africa, which is home to nearly a quarter of the world’s overweight children.

The drivers of obesity are complex, but experts believe a switch from traditional, fibre-rich diets to cheap, high-fat, high-sugar food has played a significant role in growing global obesity rates.

Obesity at any age carries significant health risks – but the consequences are thought to be more acute if obesity begins in childhood, accelerating the development of severe and life-threatening conditions, including type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular dysfunction, and liver disease.

The WHO guidelines also emphasise the importance of addressing mental health issues that are often associated with obesity and contribute to unhealthy eating patterns – including anxiety and depression, low self-esteem, and bullying.

“Our priority must be to ensure that every child and adolescent can access quality care and supportive environments from an early age, helping them achieve and maintain a healthy weight and laying the foundation for lifelong health and well-being,” Dr Luz María De Regil, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, WHO.

News.title: Russia’s plague outbreak shouldn’t scare us – but its secretive bioweapons programme should
News.content:
The facts about the laboratory accident in Russia are scant.

A lab technician at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Siberia is dead, 200 people have been quarantined, and the state security services are saying “nothing to see here, folks”.

Denials from the country that has run a covert biological weapons programme since the Cold War have done nothing to quieten speculation about what is really going on in the vast Siberian tundra.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, demanded on Tuesday that Russia be “transparent” about the situation, which he said Washington was monitoring “very closely”.

“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Mr Rubio said during a trip to Iceland.

A death from plague is a tragedy, but should not be something we need to worry about. We have moved on from the Middle Ages, when the Black Death laid waste to much of Europe.

It’s treatable with antibiotics and does not spread as fast as diseases like Covid. Its replication or R number does not get above 1.5 – measles, for example, has an R number of 12 to 18.

News.title: Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first
News.content:
One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.
