He said the examination had been designed by experienced officers to provide a fair, objective and professionally demanding assessment based on the approved syllabus.

According to him, the exercise is being conducted in accordance with the Nigerian Army Charter for Promotion Examinations 2022 (Revised).

Mr Malla urged the candidates to approach the examination with discipline, focus and determination, stressing that there were no shortcuts to success.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said performance in the examination would contribute to the officers’ selection for Junior Command and Staff Colleges within Nigeria and abroad.

The examination is part of the army’s professional development programme for officers and is intended to prepare them for higher command and staff responsibilities.

The General Officer Commanding 3 Division of the Nigerian Army and Commander of Operation Enduring Peace, Maxwell Dangana, assured the examination team and candidates of a conducive environment for the exercise.

Mr Dangana said the division would provide the necessary support for the successful conduct of the examination in Jos.

He also reaffirmed the division’s commitment to supporting professional military education and the development of officers for greater responsibilities.

The Army’s emphasis on examination integrity comes as the institution continues to strengthen professional standards and competency among its officers through promotion examinations and military education.

World.title: 2027: Defections from APC to SDP intensify as Adamu builds Nasarawa campaign
World.content:
The Social Democratic Party (SDP) campaign of former Inspector-General of Police, Mohammed Adamu, says the wave of defections from the All Progressives Congress (APC) to the opposition party is creating concern within the ruling party in Nasarawa State ahead of the 2027 governorship election.

Douglas Otaru, Director of Digital Media and Strategic Communications of the Adamu Campaign Council, made the claim while reacting to recent political developments.

Mr Otaru said the movement of APC members to the SDP reflected growing dissatisfaction within the ruling party and claimed that the APC was increasingly concerned about Mr Adamu’s emergence as a major contender for the governorship.

“The APC is battling political hypertension while we in the SDP are calm and confident,” Mr Otaru said.

He said recent defections demonstrated that more residents were beginning to consider the SDP as an alternative ahead of the 2027 election.

The former police chief was among the prominent APC governorship aspirants in the party’s May primary, which produced Senator Ahmed Wadada as the gubernatorialdo candidate.

Mr Wadada secured 195,285 votes to win the primary, while Mr Adamu came second with 39,675 votes and Professor Mohammed Sani Haruna scored 5,844 votes, according to the results reported by PREMIUM TIMES.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Adamu subsequently resigned from the APC, rejecting the outcome of the primary and accusing the party of compromising its internal processes.

He later joined the SDP and emerged as the party’s governorship candidate after a replacement primary in September following the withdrawal of Musa Angbazo.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that Mr Adamu was the sole candidate in the replacement primary conducted across the state’s 13 local government areas.

His movement to the SDP has since altered the political calculations in the state, with the former IGP seeking to attract supporters from the ruling party ahead of the election.

Among prominent APC figures to have left the party is Mohammed Ari, a retired Deputy Inspector-General of Police and former APC senatorial aspirant for Nasarawa South.

Mr Ari announced his defection to the SDP in September, citing the need for greater inclusiveness, internal democracy and accountability in political parties.

Four members of the Nasarawa State House of Assembly, Mohammed Omadefu, Isimbabi Garba, Kudu Ajegana and Inarigu Kana have also been reported to have left the APC amid disagreements within the party.

The defections have added to concerns about whether the APC can maintain the unity of its political structure ahead of the governorship election.

Mr Adamu is also benefiting from the political network of former Nasarawa State Governor, Tanko Al-Makura, who backed his governorship ambition during the APC primary.

Mr Al-Makura, a former two-term governor and senator, publicly supported Mr Adamu’s bid for the APC ticket before the primary.

His involvement has attracted attention because of his political history in the state and his ability to mobilise political networks.

PREMIUM TIMES reported in September that Mr Al-Makura’s backing could complicate the APC’s attempt to retain the governorship, particularly if a significant part of his political network eventually works for Mr Adamu’s SDP campaign.

Mr Al-Makura’s political relevance is also rooted in his 2011 governorship victory, when he defeated the incumbent governor, Aliyu Akwe Doma, on the platform of the Congress for Progressive Change (CPC), the political bloc from which he later became part of the coalition that formed the APC.

His current role, however, does not automatically translate into electoral support for Mr Adamu.

Mr Al-Makura remains associated with the APC and the Tinubu administration, making the extent of his involvement in the SDP campaign a significant political question ahead of 2027.

The former governor’s support for Mr Adamu nevertheless means the SDP candidate is not entering the race solely with the structure of a former IGP who lost an APC primary. He is also attempting to inherit elements of an established political network built over years of electoral activity in the state.

In May, even before the APC primary, supporters of some governorship aspirants who withdrew from the race announced their support for Mr Adamu.

The supporters, said to have been drawn from the state’s 13 local government areas, included groups associated with former National Primary Health Care Development Agency chief executive, Faisal Shuaib, and former aspirant Ahmed Mohammed.

The development came after Mr Adamu’s campaign had opposed moves to produce a preferred APC candidate without what it considered a sufficiently competitive primary process.

Mr Otaru described the subsequent defections as evidence that the SDP was gaining ground in the state.

He expressed confidence that Mr Adamu would defeat the APC candidate in the 2027 election.

The APC, however, retains a significant organisational advantage as the ruling party in the state. Mr Wadada won the party’s governorship primary with a substantial statewide margin and has the backing of Governor Abdullahi Sule.

READ ALSO: Defections hit House of Reps as 26 lawmakers switch parties

The contest is therefore increasingly shaping up as a battle between Mr Wadada’s established APC structure and Mr Adamu’s attempt to assemble a coalition from disgruntled APC members, former political allies and elements of Mr Al-Makura’s political network.

The SDP campaign’s claim of growing popularity for Mr Adamu remains a political assertion, and there is no independent polling evidence establishing the size of his support across the state.

There is also an unresolved electoral dimension to Mr Adamu’s candidacy. PREMIUM TIMES reported in September that his campaign insisted he remained the SDP candidate despite questions arising from a Supreme Court judgment concerning provisions of the Electoral Act and the implications for party membership registers and candidate nominations.

The APC had not responded to Mr Otaru’s latest claims as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: ₦3.5bn Ogun LG Severance: When leadership meets compassion, By Kayode Akinmade
World.content:
For many of the former political office-holders who gathered at the Oba’s Complex, Oke-Mosan, Abeokuta, the cheques handed to them were worth much more than the figures written on them. They represented something that money alone cannot adequately measure: relief after years of waiting, recognition after service and, perhaps most importantly, the restoration of hope.

The Ogun State Government’s payment of ₦3.503 billion in outstanding severance allowances to former political office-holders across the state’s 20 local government councils and Local Council Development Areas is therefore more than another government expenditure. It is a revealing moment in the character of governance and the meaning of leadership.

The beneficiaries, comprising former chairmen, vice-chairmen, secretaries to local governments, supervisors, special advisers and councillors who served between 2016 and 2024, had waited for years for their legitimate entitlements. The liabilities covered 526 beneficiaries from the 2016–2019 tenure and 516 from the 2020–2024 tenure.

For some of them, the passage of time had steadily eroded the expectation that the money would ever come. Then came the intervention.

Rather than allowing the obligation to disappear into the maze of inherited liabilities, the administration of Governor Dapo Abiodun subjected the claims to verification and reconciliation and proceeded to settle the verified obligations. That decision is where the story moves beyond the numbers.

Government is often discussed in terms of roads, bridges, schools, hospitals, investment figures and budgetary allocations. Those things matter. But there is another, less visible dimension of governance: what government does for people whose immediate needs do not necessarily make headlines. The former local government office-holders fall into that category.

They served their communities, left office and waited for what was due to them. For years, their claims remained unresolved. By the time the cheques arrived, some had moved from expectation to resignation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The words of Emiola Ghazal, former Chairman of Ijebu Ode Local Government, captured the emotion of the moment.

“This is unprecedented in Ogun State. We never believed a government could take responsibility for entitlements owed by its predecessor despite what the predecessor put the governor through. The governor is truly a promise keeper.”

Another beneficiary, Okunade Adebayo, alongside Hon. Abosede Balogun, commended the government for demonstrating that the contributions of former political office-holders to grassroots development had not been forgotten. They also praised the Ministry of Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs for what they described as a seamless, transparent and orderly process.

Ghazal went further, describing Governor Abiodun as “a leader with the milk of human kindness.” That phrase may sound simple, but it goes to the heart of what happened at Oke-Mosan.

Leadership is not only about making difficult decisions when the spotlight is on. It is also about making responsible decisions when the beneficiaries may no longer possess the political influence they once had.

In this instance, the administration had an opportunity to allow an inherited liability to remain an inherited problem. Instead, it chose to resolve the verified claims.

That is the practical meaning of responsible governance. The payment also fits into a broader picture of an administration that has sought to combine social responsibility with long-term economic transformation.

Abiodun’s years in office have been marked by programmes and policies aimed at expanding Ogun’s economic base, improving infrastructure, attracting investment, strengthening agriculture and industrial production, creating opportunities for young people and positioning the state as a major destination for domestic and international capital.

The significance of that economic agenda goes beyond individual projects. A state cannot sustainably meet its obligations to its people without expanding the productive capacity of its economy.

The logic is straightforward: care for the people today, while building an economy capable of supporting generations tomorrow.

That is why the severance payment should not be viewed in isolation from the administration’s wider development strategy.

The same government that is pursuing investment, industrialisation, infrastructure and economic expansion is also confronting inherited obligations to people who served at the grassroots. One addresses the future; the other honours the past. Both are important dimensions of responsible leadership.

There is also an institutional lesson in the episode. Public administration should not operate on the principle that every change of government wipes the slate clean. Legitimate obligations do not cease to exist because the administration that incurred them has left office. Where such obligations are verified, government has a responsibility to deal with them within the law and available resources.

That principle was at the centre of the administration’s decision to undertake the verification and reconciliation exercise involving the Ministry of Local Government and Chieftaincy Affairs, the State Audit Department and the Local Government Service Commission.

The process mattered because compassion in government must be accompanied by accountability. It is not enough to say that people deserve to be paid; the claims must be established, verified and properly documented. The Ogun exercise sought to combine the two.

For the beneficiaries, however, the accounting procedures were secondary to the outcome. They received their money.

For some, it will settle debts. For others, it will support families, businesses or long-delayed personal commitments. For many, perhaps the greatest value is simply the knowledge that after years of uncertainty, government eventually honoured what they believed they were legitimately owed. That is why the emotional response to the payment has been so strong.

The ₦3.5 billion is significant, but the deeper significance lies in what the payment communicates about the relationship between government and citizens who have served it.

It says that service should have value. It says that legitimate obligations should not be forgotten. It says that inherited problems can be confronted rather than endlessly deferred.

And it says that governance, at its best, must retain a human face. The beneficiaries have urged serving political office-holders to remain committed to quality service and expressed hope that policies promoting the welfare of workers and other stakeholders will continue.

Their message is perhaps the most fitting conclusion to the episode. A government builds roads and infrastructure to connect people to opportunities. It builds schools and healthcare facilities to improve lives. It attracts investment to create jobs and expand prosperity.

But sometimes, leadership is simply about putting a smile on the face of someone who had stopped expecting one.

At Oke-Mosan, that is what the ₦3.503 billion severance settlement represented for more than a thousand former local government political office-holders. It was not just a payment. For many, it was a restoration of hope.

*Akinmade is the Special Adviser to Governor Dapo Abiodun on Information and Strategy.

World.title: 2027: Why Nigerians should replace Tinubu with Makinde – APM Campaign DG
World.content:
The Director-General of the Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation, Felix Hyat, has warned Nigerians, particularly young people in the North, against voting for President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 presidential election, describing the president as a “wrong product from the South-west” that should be replaced with the Allied Peoples Movement (APM) candidate, Seyi Makinde, also from the region.

Mr Hyat said this on Tuesday in Abuja at the inauguration of the Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation, where he also criticised northern youths for repeatedly supporting politicians seeking the presidency while younger aspirants remain sidelined.

He said although every Nigerian had the constitutional right to contest for political office, young people in the North should question whether repeatedly supporting older politicians seeking multiple presidential bids serves their interests.

“Everybody has the right to aspire to any of these positions, no doubt about it. But for goodness sake, the teeming young people in the North, talented, agile, active, would they now fold their arms and allow one person who wants to be president for three times, even if he doesn’t get it, for four times, even if he doesn’t get it, will you hold your arms until you are also old? That means you don’t have a future,” he said.

Mr Hyat argued that since Mr Tinubu, from the South-west, is already serving the first four years of his administration, the North should allow a southerner to complete what he described as an eight-year southern tenure.

“We all know Nigerians are saying, let the South complete its eight-year tenure. And if the South is going to complete its eight-year tenure, we know that the North now has the responsibility, even if not constitutionally, but morally, to support it and make sure it goes that way due to the interest of Nigeria as one indivisible country,” he said.

He also challenged the South-east, which he said was seeking four years in the presidency, to consider the aspirations of younger politicians from the region.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Hyat said the APC administration had failed Nigerians despite producing a president from the South-west, arguing that the solution was not to reject the region but to replace Mr Tinubu with another candidate from the same region.

“We are crying today; the president is from the South-west. Is the South-west not crying? Is the South not crying? So, we have a wrong product from there that will have to change. And we have to replace him with a good product, Seyi Makinde from the South-west,” he said.

He described Mr Makinde and the APM vice presidential candidate, Lawal Daura, as tested politicians capable of addressing Nigeria’s insecurity and other challenges.

Mr Hyat said the campaign was not merely a political exercise but a responsibility to future generations, urging young Nigerians not to allow religion, ethnicity or regional sentiments to determine their political choices.

“This is not the responsibility of only the campaign management committee; it is not the responsibility of only the APM, but the responsibility of Nigerians to serve themselves,” he said.

“Because nobody is going to protect it for you. If you follow it, either based on religion, or tribal sentiments, or regional things, it is you who is going to cry tomorrow.”

Daura targets 68.7 million votes

Speaking at the event, Mr Daura said the campaign would target at least two-thirds of the more than 103 million registered voters ahead of the 2027 election.

He described the target as a “herculean task” but said the campaign would rely on canvassing and presenting its candidates and programmes to voters rather than electoral malpractice.

According to him, the campaign would ensure that its activities complied with the Electoral Act while warning politicians planning to manipulate the election that “they have a surprise coming.”

Mr Daura said the campaign was seeking to “reset” Nigeria, arguing that the country’s existing political and governance structures needed to be reviewed, amended or replaced.

He said the campaign had therefore assembled a team of people with experience, focus and determination to deliver victory for the party.

“We are aiming to get nothing less than two-thirds of the 103 million,” he said.

“A lot of those that are thinking that there is a way to get votes other than canvassing for them, telling the people how qualified you are, your programmes and the rest of it, maybe there are those who may think there is a shortcut. Well, this time around, the struggle is for real.”

He added: “We must make sure that everything is done in accordance with the law and the Electoral Act. And for those who really want to rig, that they can pull a fast one, well, they have a surprise coming.”

Campaign team inaugurated

Mr Hyat was appointed director-general of the National Campaign Management Committee of the Makinde-Daura Campaign Organisation.

Inna Ciroma, a former minister of Women Affairs, was appointed deputy director-general, Administration, while Anthony Aziegbemi was appointed deputy director-general, Operations.

The campaign said its leadership would work with the party’s National Leader and Governor of Bauchi State, Bala Mohammed, National Chairman Yusuf Dantalle and other party leaders to coordinate its national campaign.

READ ALSO: Opposition can still unite behind single candidate for 2027 APM chieftain

Other members of the campaign management team are Hamza Koshe, director, Contact and Mobilisation; Mark Jacob, director, Legal and Compliance; Ade Adeagbo, director, Administration and Strategy; Richard Ihediwa, director, Strategic Communications; and Yusuf Alkali, director, Finance.

Others are Emmanuel Dennis, director, Volunteers, Special Interests and Support Groups; Suleiman Kankia, director, Security and Intelligence; Toyin Balogun, director, Women Coordination; Umar Ndabrama, director, Monitoring, Evaluation, Reporting and Documentation; Armstrong Adah, director, Youth Coordination; and Adeyemi Moyegun, director, Organisation and Coordination.

Babangida John, a retired commissioner of police, was appointed deputy director, Security and Intelligence.

World.title: Reps panel issues final summons to FCT councils over N100bn financial queries
World.content:
The House of Representatives Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has issued a fresh seven-day summons to officials of the six Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Area Councils over unresolved audit queries involving about N100 billion.

The committee, chaired by Bamidele Salam, issued the summons on Tuesday in Abuja.

This decision followed the failure of the six council chairpersons to honour the committee’s invitation to appear before it on 22 September, despite having requested the date themselves.

The committee has now directed the Directors of Personnel Management and Finance and Heads of Audit of the six councils to appear before it on 14 October or face sanctions under the relevant service rules.

The affected councils are Abaji, Abuja Municipal Area Council (AMAC), Bwari, Gwagwalada, Kuje and Kwali.

The latest action stems from financial queries contained in the Annual Audit Report of the Auditor-General for the Six FCT Area Councils for the year ended 31 December 2021.

The report identified about N7.65 billion in outstanding liabilities across the six councils, including unremitted pension deductions, Pay As You Earn (PAYE), Value Added Tax (VAT) and withholding tax, as well as unpaid obligations to contractors.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

AMAC had the highest outstanding liability at N2.19 billion, followed by Bwari with N1.49 billion and Kwali with N1.46 billion.

Gwagwalada recorded N1.01 billion, while Kuje and Abaji had outstanding liabilities of N892.2 million and N593.8 million respectively.

The auditor-general said the outstanding sums were owed to tax authorities, Pension Fund Administrators and contractors.

The report stated that the liabilities comprised “unremitted pension deduction, unremitted Pay as You Earn (PAYE), unpaid capital projects, unpaid value added tax and withholding tax.”

N24.87bn spending under scrutiny

Beyond the outstanding liabilities, the committee is seeking explanation and supporting documents on N24.87 billion spent by the six councils on personnel, overheads and capital expenditure in 2021.

AMAC accounted for N5.03 billion of the expenditure, while Gwagwalada spent N4.66 billion.

Kuje recorded N3.85 billion, Kwali N3.84 billion, Bwari N3.74 billion and Abaji N3.71 billion.

The auditor-general also raised concerns over the management of fixed assets by the councils, saying asset registers were not properly maintained or updated.

Gwagwalada was specifically queried over non-current assets valued at N336 million.

According to the audit report, “the Auditor General for the Six Area Council reported that the value of non-current assets of Gwagwalada Area Council stood at N336m.

“However, the Auditor General observed that the ledger records of the non-current assets were not properly maintained and updated as and when due, which could give room for loss of assets without being traced. This exception is common among other FCT Area Councils.”

PAC uncovers more irregularities

Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, Bamidele Salam, said on Tuesday that the repeated failure of the council chairpersons to appear before the committee had frustrated efforts to resolve the audit queries.

“The last date of appearance of the Abuja Area Councils was September 22, 2026, which was a date they requested and which was graciously granted by the committee. Yet, they failed to appear or send in any representation,” Mr Salam said.

He said the committee had consequently resolved to summon the Directors of Personnel Management and Finance and Heads of Audit of the councils.

“The committee has therefore decided to issue summons to the Directors of Personnel Management and Finance of these local governments, including their Heads of Audit, to appear without fail on Wednesday, October 14, failure of which they will be made to bear consequences according to service rules,” he said.

Mr Salam said the committee’s scrutiny had also revealed additional concerns in the councils’ 2022 and part of their 2023 audit reports.

These, he said, included alleged understatement of Internally Generated Revenue (IGR), unauthorised disposal of assets, non-disclosure of statutory revenue and failure to remit withholding tax to the appropriate authorities.

He added that the councils had also failed to audit and submit their financial accounts for 2023, 2024 and 2025 as required by law.

The lawmaker said the committee would insist on accountability in the management of public funds and warned that officials found culpable would face the consequences provided by law.

The Public Accounts Committee is empowered by the Nigerian Constitution to examine audited accounts of public institutions and investigate financial irregularities identified by the Auditor-General.

The latest summons is intended to compel the relevant officials of the six FCT Area Councils to provide explanations and documents needed to resolve the outstanding audit queries.

World.title: Tinubu congratulates India’s PM on 25 years in public leadership
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has congratulated Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the 25th anniversary of his assumption of office as head of government.

Mr Tinubu, in a statement issued on Wednesday, described the milestone as a “historic” achievement.

He also said it reflected the confidence the Indian people had continued to place in him as their leader.

“On behalf of the Government and people of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, and on my own behalf, I extend warm and fraternal congratulations to His Excellency Shri Narendra Modi, Prime Minister of the Republic of India, on a truly historic milestone,” Mr Tinubu said.

Mr Modi first became Chief Minister of Gujarat in 2001 and served in the position for more than 12 years before becoming Prime Minister of India in 2014.

According to Mr Tinubu, the uninterrupted years of public leadership are considered a rare achievement in a democracy, particularly in India, the world’s most populous country.

He praised Mr Modi’s leadership, citing developments in infrastructure, digital public goods, financial inclusion and innovation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Across these 25 years, Prime Minister Modi has led with vision and an unwavering commitment to development,” Mr Tinubu said.

He said Mr Modi’s leadership contributed to Gujarat’s transformation and India’s emergence as one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing economies.

“India’s emergence as one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing economies, his leadership in infrastructure, digital public goods, financial inclusion and innovation has lifted millions and inspired nations across the Global South,” he said.

Mr Tinubu also highlighted the bilateral relationship between Nigeria and India, describing both countries as “great nations” and leading voices of the Global South.

He recalled Mr Modi’s State Visit to Nigeria in November 2024, during which Nigeria conferred the Grand Commander of the Order of the Niger (GCON) on the Indian leader.

“That visit gave fresh impetus to our cooperation in trade and investment, energy, defence and security, health, education, and technology,” he also said.

READ ALSO: Nigeria has reduced reliance on oil revenue Tinubu

He noted that Nigeria valued its “strategic partnership” with India.

“As fellow democracies and leading voices of the Global South, Nigeria and India share a common commitment to a fairer, more inclusive and more representative International order.

“I remain confident that, under his continued leadership, the bonds of friendship between our peoples will grow ever stronger,” he said.

World.title: Police arrest suspected kidnappers who collected ₦10.3 million ransom
World.content:
The police in Rivers State have arrested two suspected members of a six-man kidnapping syndicate who allegedly collected a ransom of ₦10.3 million for the release of a kidnap victim.

Operatives of the Violent Crime Response Unit (VCRU-AKU) arrested the suspects following an intelligence-led operation, the police said.

The police identified the suspects as Victor Ifeanyi, 24, alias Big Boby, from Aguleri Community, Otuocha Local Government Area of Anambra State, and Aniekan Michael, 36, alias Duff Man, from Ikot Ukpor, Essien Udim Local Government Area of Akwa Ibom State.

The state police spokesperson, Blessing Agabe, disclosed this in a statement posted on Facebook on Monday.

According to the police, the victim, identified as Mr Hassan, a resident of Rivers State, was abducted on 6 September 2026 near Fidelity Bank, Garrison, Port Harcourt.

The kidnappers allegedly took him to Igbugulu Waterside, Borikiri, Port Harcourt, where he was held captive for three days.

The police said the victim was released after his relatives paid a ransom of ₦10.3 million.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Police launch investigation

The command said it received credible information about the abduction on 7 September and immediately deployed operatives of the VCRU-AKU to investigate the incident.

The intelligence-led operation subsequently led to the arrest of the two suspects.

“Preliminary investigation revealed that the suspects confessed to their alleged involvement in the operation,” the police said.

The suspects reportedly told investigators that the gang consisted of six members and that they used a white mini-bus, popularly known as a Keke bus, during the operation.

The police said efforts were ongoing to arrest the four other members of the syndicate.

READ ALSO: Police commissioner in Bayelsa orders crackdown on cult groups

Police intensify anti-kidnapping operations

The arrests come amid other recent police operations against suspected kidnappers in Rivers State.

In one recent case, police arrested four suspected kidnappers and rescued an abducted woman in the state. This newspaper reported that the operation was part of efforts by security agencies to dismantle kidnapping networks operating in the region.

In another operation, police rescued a kidnap victim and apprehended a suspect, PREMIUM TIMES reported.

The Police Commissioner in the state, Olugbenga Adepoju, urged residents to provide credible information that could help the command identify and arrest criminal elements.

Mr Adepoju assured the public that the command would treat such information in confidence.

He said the command would continue to deploy intelligence-led operations to disrupt kidnapping syndicates and other criminal networks across the state.

The commissioner also urged residents to remain calm and cooperate with security agencies.

World.title: World Bank: Fuel price to slow Nigeria’s poverty reduction
World.content:
•Says rising pre-election spending may derail reforms

•Raises Nigeria’s 2026 growth forecast to 4.3%

•Projects 15.7% inflation rate for 2026

•44% of firms in Nigeria, Kenya adopt AI, power constraints threaten gains

By Babajide Komolafe, Economy Editor

The World Bank has warned that elevated fuel prices could slow Nigeria’s poverty reduction efforts despite an expected improvement in economic growth and a sharp decline in inflation in 2026.

The warning was contained in its latest Africa Economic Update, which projected that Nigeria’s economic growth would accelerate from 4.0 per cent in 2025 to 4.3 per cent in 2026, before rising further to an average of 4.4 per cent in 2027 and 2028.

The World Bank attributed the projected improvement to strengthening macroeconomic stability, improved investor confidence and a gradual recovery in private investment.

It said: “Economic activity in Nigeria is projected to strengthen from 4.0 percent in 2025 to 4.3 percent in 2026, before edging up to 4.4 percent annually in 2027–28, supported by improving macroeconomic stability, strengthening investor confidence, and a gradual recovery in private investment.

“Growth continues to be driven primarily by the service sector, particularly financial services, ICT, and real estate, which have benefited from ongoing digitalization and resilient domestic demand.

Agricultural activity is expected to recover in 2026, while growth in the industrial sector is projected to moderate, reflecting softer momentum in oil production and manufacturing.”

On inflation, the World Bank projected a substantial decline from 23.0 per cent in 2025 to 15.7 per cent in 2026, with the rate expected to fall further to 12.2 per cent by 2028.

However, it cautioned that the improvement in living conditions could be constrained by elevated fuel prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East.

The report stated: “Inflation is projected to decline from 23.0 percent in 2025 to 15.7 percent in 2026, easing further to 12.2 percent by 2028 as the effects of monetary tightening, exchange rate stabilization, and improving supply conditions continue to feed through the economy.

“Lower inflation is expected to support household purchasing power and contribute to a gradual reduction in poverty. However, the pace of poverty reduction is likely to remain constrained by elevated fuel prices associated with the conflict in the Middle East, which continue to weigh disproportionately on low-income households.”

The World Bank also noted that higher international oil prices could provide some support to Nigeria’s fiscal and external accounts through stronger oil earnings.

It projected Nigeria’s current account surplus to widen from 4.8 per cent of GDP in 2025 to 6.0 per cent in 2026, before narrowing to 3.4 per cent by 2028 as oil prices normalise and import demand strengthens.

However, the World Bank warned that the economic outlook remained exposed to significant downside risks.

These include tighter global financial conditions, a prolonged Middle East conflict, insecurity, climate-related shocks and disruptions to oil production.

It also singled out rising government spending ahead of the 2027 general elections as a major domestic risk.

The report stated: “Nevertheless, the outlook remains subject to significant downside risks, including tighter global financial conditions, a prolonged conflict in the Middle East, insecurity, climate related shocks, disruptions to oil production, and rising pre-election spending ahead of the 2027 elections.

These factors could weaken reform momentum and erode the social consensus needed to sustain ongoing macroeconomic adjustment efforts.”

The report also highlighted Nigeria’s emerging position in Africa’s artificial intelligence ecosystem, but warned that inadequate infrastructure could limit the economic benefits.

According to the World Bank, 44 per cent of surveyed firms across Nigeria and Kenya with at least 20 employees reported using AI technologies, compared with 61 per cent of surveyed firms in the United States. However, the report said adoption in Africa remains relatively shallow, with only 36 per cent of AI-using firms in the developing-country sample using AI agents or AI for automation, compared with 56 per cent in the US.

The bank identified unreliable electricity, limited internet access, high data and device costs and inadequate computing infrastructure as major constraints.

World.title: Thoughts of Chief Ralph Obioha on Nigeria
World.content:
Chief Ralph Obioha

(Late elder statesman, Chief Ralph Obioha’s last interview with Vanguard, originally published on January 20, 2026 with the headline “There was never an ‘Igbo coup’ — Ralph Obioha”)

By Chioma Gabriel

Chief Ralph Obioha, an elder statesman and former chieftain of the National Democratic Coalition, NADECO, is a prominent figure in Nigeria’s democratic history. In this interview, he revisits the ‘Igbo Coup’ tag that has rubbished the reputation of the Igbo for years in Nigeria, saying that the January 15, 1966 coup was anything but an Igbo coup.

Read Also: 60 Years After: Remembering the bloody coup that changed Nigeria forever

It has been 60 years since the first coup, and a lot of people have lived with the belief that it was an Igbo coup for which the Igbo are suffering in Nigeria. Was the coup of January 15, 1966, plotted by the Igbo?

Definitely not. It is just a language that has been conceived by those who wish to put the Igbo down, to label that coup as an Igbo coup. It was not an Igbo coup.

I was an adult during the civil war, and a lot of people have given different accounts of it, but I’m emphatic that it was not an Igbo coup.

There was nowhere the Igbo gathered to give anybody a license or a warrant to cause a coup. There’s nowhere. The reality on the ground then was that the Igbo dominated the officers’ corps of the Nigerian Army. And because of that, participation in a coup in Nigeria will not be done by groups. It has to be done by officers of the Nigerian Army. As there were many prominent Igbo officers in the army, it was wrongly perceived that Igbo people organised the coup.

Having said that I am also emphatically clear that the coup then was just not necessary. There was nothing that was on the ground to warrant it, except, of course, what was sweeping through Africa at that moment. These were young officers who wanted things done faster than they were being done. I can use the word that my behaviour today is different from my behaviour 40 years ago when I was 40 years old.

So, it was just the restlessness of the young men, who wanted to change things in Nigeria their way. If you look at the people who were involved in that coup, they were Igbo, they were Yoruba, and even I was told there were Hausa participants in that coup. That the Igbo predominated only reflected the population of the Igbo officers then.

To label it as an Igbo coup was a confidence for those who want to put Igbo down. It’s a pity that it happened. It’s unfortunate that it happened. But that does not make it an Igbo coup.

But the Igbo are still suffering for it today

There has been a conspiracy of what other Nigerians call the Igbo question and Igbo solution. So, what is happening now is actually a play out of that Igbo question and Igbo solution. But like all conspiracies in life, it’s going to be for a while. You cannot diminish the spirit of the Igbo. These are people who are very energetic, very industrious, very enterprising. You can’t change them. You can’t cage them, just as you cannot change certain attributes of other tribes in Nigeria.

If you go to look at what happened to Great Britain, the combined population of the Irish that is in Northern Ireland and the Scots and the Welsh there, the English predominates in Great Britain, but they have certain provisions that don’t make that domination draw them back. It doesn’t impede their progress.

But in the case of Nigeria, the way they have been treating the Igbo in Nigeria has hindered the growth of Nigeria. Whether they want to accept it or not, It has hindered Nigeria. And one day, there will be a change of mind to incorporate all Nigerians and give them equal opportunity.

Is the maltreatment of the Igbo not traceable to their defeat during the civil war?

Well, don’t forget that the same people who said they defeated them declared there was no victor, no vanquished. And if you look at the forces that supported Nigeria in that war, Britain, Russia, the whole of the Arab world, it was predictable after a while that the war would go the way it went.

I admit that the treatment of the Igbo may be derived from having lost that war. If we had not lost the war, we would have been another nation. And let nobody deceive you, in the spirit and the core heart of the Igbo, they still want to have their Biafra. Never mind whatever anybody will tell you.

They still want that?

They still want it any day. 90% of the Igbo will tell you, give them Biafra. No matter whatever you tell them it may not be a very viable option they will say let them have it than to go through the indignities they suffer in Nigeria.

There are people spearheading the new Biafra, but the way they are doing it seems to be causing more problems for the Igbo in Nigeria than finding solutions to the Igbo question

I agree totally with that observation. I agree. It can be done differently. But maybe also on the other hand, if you want to balance it, maybe if they didn’t adopt the way they are doing it, maybe the world would not have begun now to change the opinion that these people have demonstrated that they want this.

Let me tell you the truth, it’s only a matter of time when there is a consensus in the world to say, let Biafra be. I believe that. And we may not be very far away from that time.

Do you believe it will be possible?

I believe that it will come.

During the first coup, the name Col Nzeogwu was prominent, but some people from Nzeogwu’s side in today’s Nigeria don’t see themselves as Igbo. Even then, they were called the Midwest. They are South-South now, and some Igbo people from the South-South will tell you they are not Igbo

I had tried to describe the unfortunate lot of the Igbo in the way that you have just put it. But not all people from the area where Nzeogwo hailed from refuse to identify as Igbo.

A majority of them know they are, but it’s laughable when some say they are not. Even the name, Chukwuma Nzeogwu, was Igbo at least. Many of them speak Igbo as their language and bear Igbo names, but will quickly jump to say they are not. It’s laughable.

But a man like Philip Effiong was not implicated in the coup. This is a fact, but he fought in the war on the Biafran side. He was the number two man in the Biafran war to the very end. As a matter of fact, history has it that he was the one who formally surrendered the Biafran sovereignty to the federal government. But these sides of the South-South are just innocent bystanders. They were not happy with the way Nigeria was going. But then, there’s always a tendency for people to play it safe. I would say that they were playing it safe. And if Biafra materialises tomorrow and there’s a plebiscite in all those regions, the majority of them will say they would rather go with Biafra than go with the present Nigeria.

Is the situation that was prevalent at the time the first coup happened still prevalent now?

This is talking about El Dorado and hell. That was like an El Dorado in Nigeria then. But today, you know, it’s hell. It’s a place where about 80% of the population is poor. There are no comparisons. I happen to have lived through the two times. I was a full adult then, and I’m very old now but I saw the condition of things then, and I’m also looking at the condition of things now. Now is hell.

Will Nigeria get out of this hell someday?

Yes. Let’s take China. China in about 1945 was a time of drug addicts. Heroin addiction was so prevalent in China. As a matter of fact, the British that was imposing it on them then, knew the danger, but they still did it. But today, nobody can compare with China’s progress. They were able to get out of poverty in a record cycle of less than 25 years.

Maybe there was no tribalism, nepotism, and all those things that are happening in Nigeria and China.

Those things were in China, too. China has over 50 tribes. And when you talk about cultism, that’s the word. Cultism is a perfect word for China, then, but look at China today.

You believe Nigeria can be better, will be better?

Definitely, that is why I have advocated for the president to call for a conference of all Nigerians to really sit down and say, let us have another start. And if there is a meeting of like minds, then things will be done the way it should be done, equal rights for everybody, irrespective of where they come from, and eliminate all this entitlement of a superior group or privileged group. Nigeria will kick off very quickly because we have resourceful people. And the truth of the matter in Nigeria is that everybody contributes to and has the ability to contribute to Nigerian greatness.

Look at the food basket of Nigeria. It’s not in Igbo land. Neither is it in Yoruba land. It is the middle belt of Nigeria. The Middle Belt is the place feeding Nigeria. There are more mineral resources in the north than in any other part of Nigeria, but those resources are not being put into the national basket for equal distribution of such resources. But the resources from the south are called national resources. Now, that is the language of marginalisation.

That’s what marginalisation really means, not what people are saying. Nobody marginalises you over what you wear or what you eat. The marginalisation is in some people keeping their own natural resources and taking those of another region to be exploited for the national cake. That’s what marginalisation means.

There have been many coups since the first coup. Many failed. Many succeeded, but can Nigeria say it can never happen again?

I can’t come to that conclusion. Never say never. What all of us should be asking is, let there be a meeting of minds where we eliminate the marginalisation syndrome, the enlightenment, the entitlement complex, and all those things will probably find a permanent solution one way or the other.

Well, to dismiss the idea that nothing can happen is not living in reality.

Vanguard News

World.title: Climate change threatens Nigeria’s food systems as farmers count losses
World.content:
….experts call for urgent, sustainable measures to mitigate impacts

By Gabriel Ewepu

ABUJA — Nigeria’s food system is facing growing threats from climate change as erratic rainfall, prolonged dry spells, flooding, rising temperatures, pests and diseases disrupt farming activities, slash yields and leave farmers counting losses running into billions of Naira.

The situation, according to farmers and agricultural experts who spoke with Vanguard Agrobiz, is also discouraging investment in food production, with farmers, agribusinesses and financial institutions becoming increasingly cautious about committing capital to a sector whose fortunes are heavily dependent on weather conditions.

Climate change is also aggravating desertification in northern Nigeria, while the spread of pests and crop diseases continue to threaten large hectares of farmland.

Meanwhile, the Nigerian Meteorological Agency, NiMet, in its 2026 Seasonal Climate Prediction, warned of significant variations in rainfall patterns across the country, with early onset expected in several southern and North-Central states and delayed onset in Borno State.

The agency also projected variations in the end of the rainy season, with some areas expected to experience earlier cessation and others a longer-than-normal season, which were to impact on farmers and their activities. While normal annual rainfall is expected across most parts of the country, above-normal rainfall is projected in parts of the North, South-East, South-South and the FCT, with below-normal rainfall expected in parts of Katsina, Zamfara, Kwara, Oyo and Ogun states.

NiMet further warned of dry spells in parts of 14 states, including Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kano, Kebbi, Niger, Plateau, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara, raising concerns over possible disruptions to planting and crop development.

For farmers who have suffered the consequences of climate variability in previous seasons, the forecasts have heightened concerns over the risks ahead.

‘Climate change impact demands urgent action’

The Chairman of the All Farmers Association of Nigeria, AFAN, Dr Nkechi Okafor, described climate change as a major threat to food production, warning that its worsening impact could push more farmers out of business and deepen food insecurity.

Okafor said farmers who traditionally relied on predictable rainfall patterns could no longer depend on established planting calendars, “Climate change is real. It has come to stay. The only thing now is how we can work around it to make headway.”

According to her, irregular rainfall has become a major challenge, with farmers sometimes planting after the first rains only to experience prolonged dry spells afterwards.

She said as a crop farmer who produces cereals, legumes and root and tuber crops, late commencement of rainfall and early cessation had affected the production of several crops.

She particularly identified rice production and root and tuber crops as being vulnerable where adequate water is unavailable, stressing the need to expand irrigation infrastructure to reduce farmers’ dependence on rainfall.

Farmers lose billions to climate shocks

The FCT AFAN boss also said Nigerian farmers were recording huge losses as a result of climate-related shocks, “Losses incurred cannot just be stated. It is not only about me; it is about Nigerian farmers. Nigeria farmers are running losses into billions of naira, and it is unfortunate.”

While noting that the government could not control climate change, Okafor called for greater investment in building farmers’ capacity to adopt climate-smart agricultural practices.

She also expressed concern that many rural farmers were not receiving timely weather information despite forecasts from NiMet.

“My fear is clear. Before this challenge of climate change, every farmer knew the period that rains start in each region, but today, no one can predict when rain will start,” she said.

She called for stronger collaboration between farmers’ groups and relevant government agencies to train farmers on climate-smart agriculture and help them cope with increasingly uncertain weather conditions.

Okafor also urged the government to address the rising cost of agricultural inputs, saying farmers were currently facing a situation where inputs were expensive while farm produce remained relatively cheap.

She called for greater investment in irrigation, capacity building and all-year-round farming systems that would reduce farmers’ dependence on rainfall.

Planting calendars disrupted, yields reduced

For the Chief Farmer and Lead of JetFarmsNG, Jerry Olanrenwaju, climate change has had a direct impact on crop production, with unpredictable rainfall, prolonged dry spells and excessive flooding disrupting planting calendars and reducing yields.

He said the effects were particularly noticeable in crops such as ginger, turmeric and garlic.

According to him, irregular rainfall affects germination and root development, while excessive moisture increases the risk of fungal diseases.

Olanrenwaju said some farmers within the company’s network had recorded losses of between 30 and 40 per cent of expected yields in some seasons.

He explained that a farmer investing between N500,000 and N800,000 per hectare could lose hundreds of thousands of naira due to adverse weather conditions alone.

“As we approach the wet season, my major concern is the uncertainty. Will the rains come early, late, or excessively? This unpredictability makes planning very difficult and increases the risk of crop failure,” he said.

To reduce the risks, he said JetFarmsNG was promoting climate-smart practices, including improved land preparation, organic soil enhancement, better drainage systems and adaptive planting schedules.

The company is also exploring irrigation and water-management solutions while working with partners to introduce improved seeds capable of withstanding changing weather conditions.

He, however, said government interventions were yet to reach farmers on the scale required, calling for increased access to extension services, finance, insurance and reliable climate information.

Climate change fuels fear among farmers

Similarly, the Co-Founder of DeBranch Farmers Limited, Sandra Victor-Gwafan, said climate change had created fear and hesitation among farmers in Kaduna and other parts of the country.

Victor-Gwafan, said farmers could no longer confidently determine the appropriate time to plant because early rains could suddenly stop, while heavy rains could arrive later than expected.

DeBranch Farmers, which works mainly with rice out-growers, is already taking precautionary measures, including farmer sensitisation, drainage planning, coordinated mechanisation and staggered planting.

Victor-Gwafan said some farmers had previously invested between N250,000 and N400,000 per hectare on inputs, labour and land preparation but lost between 30 and 50 per cent of their expected harvest due to flooding and prolonged dry spells.

She called for increased investment in climate-smart agriculture, irrigation, resilient seeds, extension services, timely climate information and affordable financing.

‘I now plan for irrigation before planting’

A vegetable farmer in Osun State, Oluokun Remi, said the impact of climate change on crops such as tomatoes, pepper, okra, cucumber, cabbage, onion and fruits had become increasingly significant.

“When the rain is excessively too much, it will wash away nutrients from the reach of the plant roots”, he said, adding that he had suffered losses when expected rainfall failed to materialise or stopped suddenly after planting.

To reduce the risk, Remi said he now plans for irrigation before planting, “If the rain comes, fine, and if it doesn’t come, there is a plan,” he said, adding that climate pressures are ‘varied and severe’.

An environmental expert, Prof Babatunde Bolaji Bernard, said climate change had moved from being a distant environmental concern to an immediate threat to Nigeria’s agricultural productivity and food security.

He said farmers across the country were facing erratic rainfall, delayed onset of rains, prolonged dry spells, rising temperatures and extreme flooding.

According to him, drought and desertification are particularly affecting the northern belt, while flooding in central and southern parts of the country is destroying crops, eroding soil nutrients and damaging agricultural infrastructure.

He also identified heat stress, pests and diseases as growing threats to crops and livestock.

“Crops most affected include maize, which is highly sensitive to water stress; rice, which suffers from both drought and flooding; sorghum and millet, which are relatively resilient but still impacted by extreme heat; and cassava, a staple that is increasingly threatened by shifting rainfall patterns and disease outbreaks”, Bernard said.

He warned that the cumulative impact was contributing to declining food production, higher production costs and rising food prices.

Experts seek shift to climate-smart agriculture

Bernard called for urgent adaptation measures, including the adoption of early-maturing and drought-resistant crop varieties, improved irrigation, mulching, conservation agriculture, crop diversification and agroforestry.

He also advocated stronger weather information and extension services to enable farmers to make informed planting and harvesting decisions.

At the policy level, he called for increased investment in irrigation, rural roads, storage, market infrastructure and agricultural insurance.

He also urged the government to strengthen environmental regulations aimed at addressing deforestation and land degradation while leveraging international climate financing to support agricultural adaptation.

Nigeria needs sustainable climate resilience strategy – ActionAid

The Country Director of ActionAid Nigeria, Dr Andrew Mamedu, said climate change was already a lived reality for millions of Nigerian smallholder farmers, particularly women who constitute a significant part of household food production.

Mamedu said farmers in northern Nigeria were experiencing prolonged droughts, desertification and shorter rainy seasons, while communities in the Middle Belt and southern riverine areas were increasingly exposed to flooding.

According to him, climate shocks were disrupting planting calendars, reducing yields and increasing production risks.

He noted that the effects extended beyond production to post-harvest losses, saying extreme weather conditions, poor storage, inadequate processing facilities and weak rural infrastructure were worsening losses.

Mamedu also highlighted the disproportionate impact on women farmers, who often face additional barriers to land, finance, irrigation, extension services and climate information.

‘Government response remains fragmented’

While acknowledging ongoing government and development-partner interventions in climate-resilient agriculture, agroecology and farmer support programmes, Mamedu said the overall response remained insufficient compared with the scale of the challenge.

He identified underinvestment in agriculture, limited irrigation infrastructure, weak extension services and inadequate access to finance as major constraints.

He called for a deliberate shift from reactive interventions to a coordinated and adequately financed transformation of Nigeria’s food system.

According to him, government and development partners must scale up investment in drought- and flood-tolerant crop varieties, soil restoration, regenerative agriculture, sustainable livestock systems, irrigation and water harvesting.

He also advocated investment in climate-resilient storage, cold chains, rural roads and local processing facilities to reduce post-harvest losses and improve farmers’ incomes.

Mamedu urged the government to expand access to affordable credit, insurance and targeted subsidies, with particular attention to women and young farmers.

“Ultimately, Nigeria cannot achieve food security without building climate resilience, and it cannot build climate resilience without prioritising the farmers who produce the country’s food”, he said.

Smallholder farmers must include insurance to survive floods, drought – Leadway Assurance

Meanwhile, the Global Head, Agricultural Risk at Leadway Assurance, Mr. Ayoola Fatona, counseled that farmers need to make provision on insuring the inputs and farms as a way to reduce the impact of flood and draught.

According to him, many farmers do not treat insurance as a critical farm input when budgeting for the planting season, focusing only on seeds and fertiliser.

“The smallholder farmer is at high risk. They are very much exposed, especially with this issue of climate and weather. Those are the little risk factors that smallholder farmers have to grapple with. And so that is where insurance goes in,” he said.

He added: “Also, at the beginning of the season, when farmers are drawing out their budget, insurance is really not their preference. If you take a look at it as a service, they may do without it. You think about procuring seeds, procuring fertilizer, they don’t really think at that particular point.”

World.title: Aiyedatiwa backs NAF crash recovery operation
World.content:
— NEMA deploys swamp buggies to recover wreckage

By Dayo Johnson, Akure

AKURE — Ondo State Governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, has pledged the full support of the state government to agencies involved in the search and recovery operation following the Nigerian Air Force aircraft crash in Igbokoda, Ilaje Local Government Area of the state.

Aiyedatiwa made the commitment when the Director of Search and Rescue, National Emergency Management Agency, NEMA, Air Commodore Bature, paid a briefing visit to him at the Government House, Akure.

The governor said he immediately directed relevant state authorities to mobilise after receiving news of the incident while on an official engagement in Abuja.

He described the crash as a national tragedy and a huge loss to the country, saying the young officers who died had paid the ultimate price in service to Nigeria and in defence of its territorial integrity.

Aiyedatiwa commiserated with the families of the victims and acknowledged President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for declaring three days of mourning in honour of the fallen personnel.

The governor said the recovery operation had continued despite the difficult terrain, noting that the crash site was located in a swampy area with narrow and shallow creeks.

He said local residents had been assisting the operation by using smaller boats to navigate the creeks and gain access to the crash site.

According to him, the residents worked with the Navy and other responders in efforts to rescue the victims and take them to hospital, but there were no survivors.

Aiyedatiwa said he would proceed to Igbokoda to meet with residents and ensure that the recovery operation continued.

He thanked NEMA, the military, local government authorities and residents for their efforts, assuring all agencies involved of the state government’s continued support.

Earlier, Air Commodore Bature said NEMA had deployed three swamp buggies to the crash site to strengthen the recovery operation.

He said the operation involved NEMA, the State Emergency Management Agency, SEMA, the Nigerian Air Force, Navy and local residents.

Bature explained that the swamp buggies were being deployed into the swamp to enable the recovery team to access the crash location and retrieve the wreckage.

He said he was in Ondo State on the directive of NEMA Director-General, Hajia Zubaida Umar, who is currently outside the country.

According to him, the NEMA DG directed him to meet with Governor Aiyedatiwa and appreciate him for his prompt response to the incident.

Bature also commended SEMA, the Navy, Army, Air Force, Police and local residents for their prompt response to the crash.

The NEMA director said the agency was collaborating with the state government and local residents to coordinate resources for effective disaster management.

He expressed confidence that the aircraft wreckage and other parts trapped at the crash site would be recovered soon.

World.title: ‘I would like to play for Argentina forever’ – Messi
World.content:
Photo by Luis ROBAYO / AFP.

Lionel Messi described his retirement from international football as the “saddest day of my career” on Tuesday after playing his final game for Argentina in a 3-0 defeat of Benin.

Messi, who scored a goal and provided two assists in the victory at the Monumental Stadium, took to the field after the win to express gratitude to fans and team-mates as he reflected on his 21-year career with Argentina.

“It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years,” Messi told the stadium.

“Even in the worst moments we went through and that I had, I never stopped fighting, never stopped being here.

“Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I’d like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you.”

Messi said that returning to the Monumental — where Argentina played their first game after winning the 2022 World Cup — was bittersweet.

“Now I’m here on the saddest day of my career, which is the day I have to say goodbye to the national team, goodbye to all of you.

“But now I’ll be on that side (with the fans), supporting all the boys, everyone who comes in. Always united,” he said.

Messi though said that despite the sadness, he had no regrets about the timing of his international exit, citing the exertions of Argentina’s campaign at this year’s World Cup, where the South Americans battled through to the final only to lose to Spain.

Messi said the emotional roller coaster of that tournament — which included a 2-1 defeat of bitter rivals England in the semi-final — had taken a toll.

“Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through,” said Messi.

“We had the dream of fulfilling my dream and the dream of the whole country, of becoming world champions again.

“In the last World Cup we were very close, and the reality is that nothing strange happened, as people say. The match against England took a huge toll on us physically, and emotionally it was very big.

“We arrived with just enough, we fought like we always did with this jersey, with all the teammates I got to be with and share things with, not only them but also those who were around in the time when we managed to win. We were very close.”

Vanguard News

World.title: 2027: APC doesn’t want opposition candidates to campaign anywhere  -  Galadima
World.content:
Buba Galadima

A chieftain of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Buba Galadima, has accused the All Progressives Congress (APC)-led Federal Government of creating obstacles for opposition politicians ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Galadima alleged that opposition candidates were being prevented from freely campaigning across the country, claiming that some were attacked whenever they visited certain areas.

He made the allegations during an appearance on Arise Television’s Prime Time on Tuesday, where he discussed the political environment ahead of the 2027 elections.

“There are blocks put in the path of the opposition. This APC and its government does not want any opposition person to campaign in any part of the country, as they are stoned wherever they go. They also want to make life impossible for those opposite them,” he said.

Galadima questioned whether such an environment could be described as democracy, arguing that democratic governance should guarantee political freedoms, including the right to campaign, speak and move freely.

“So, why should we call it democracy? We can just as well call it fascism, or dictatorship, or monarchy. They can’t claim to be democrats and not imbibe the tenets of democracy, which is free choice, free speech, free movement, and that is in the constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria,” he said.

The NDC chieftain, however, blamed citizens for allowing what he described as restrictions on political activities to continue.

“But all this they are doing is because we citizens have allowed them to do so,” Galadima said.

He also questioned the enforcement of campaign spending limits, citing the cost of political advertising and billboards across the country.

According to him, the Electoral Act limits campaign spending by political parties to N10 billion, but the cost of erecting billboards in some states could make compliance difficult.

“Do you know how much they are asking for one billboard in Abuja? In Imo, it is N1 billion. One billboard, not the whole state. Just to fix one billboard, you pay N1 billion,” he said.

Galadima argued that the cost of campaign billboards across the states could exceed the statutory spending limit.

“So, if you have to pay every state one billion, and you pay 37 states, which is 37 billion naira, including Abuja, did you run foul of the Act or not? So, why can’t somebody say anything?” he asked.

World.title: Messi retires with goal, assists as Argentina beat Benin 3-0
World.content:
Argentina’s forward Lionel Messi. Photo by Luis ROBAYO / AFP.

Lionel Messi brought the curtain down on his 21-year international career on Tuesday, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in an emotional final appearance for the former world champions in Buenos Aires.

In a perfectly scripted finale, the 39-year-old widely regarded as the greatest football player in history signed off with his 126th international goal in front of 85,000 supporters as Argentina cruised to a 3-0 victory over Benin.

Messi, playing in his record-extending 208th international, also provided the assist for the opening goal scored by veteran Nicolas Otamendi, with Nico Paz also scoring.

But the match was a footnote to the occasion itself, which saw Messi savoring the adulation of the Monumental Stadium crowd one last time for an event which had been billed as ‘The Last Tango’.

“It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years,” Messi told fans in a post-match address.

“Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I’d like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you.”

Messi though said he had no regrets about his decision to retire, citing Argentina’s grueling World Cup campaign, which took place as his late father was seriously ill, as a factor.

“Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through,” said Messi.

Beforehand, Messi wiped away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina team-mates made its way through crowds of wellwishers en route to the stadium.

Messi took the field alongside his three children and received affectionate waves from his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and his mother, Celia Cuccittini, who were watching from a VIP box.

Shortly before kick off, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word “Gracias” (Thank You) above the football superstar’s No.10 was laid out on the pitch as the crowd roared their approval.

Messi welled up again as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana sang the national anthem beside a banner which read — “The Malvinas are Argentine” – the same banner held aloft by players after their 2-1 World Cup semi-final win over England.

The match was halted in the 10th minute – in tribute to Messi’s famous shirt number – for a minute-long ovation to the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star.

He crowned the occasion with a goal from the penalty spot in the 71st minute.

‘Gave it my all’

At the final whistle a drone show lit up the night sky above the stadium, showing Messi’s image and thanking the eight-time Ballon D’Or-winner for his career.

Messi’s farewell came two and a half months after Argentina’s World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss.

“I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote at the time.

Before Tuesday’s game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters.

Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction.

“To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!,” he joked.

Outside the Argentina Football Association headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentine flag with his image inscribed “The joy of my life.”

Former Barcelona team-mate Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on X.

“It’s not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more,” he said.

Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.

Messi’s departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international football, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country’s 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona’s heir.

“I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn’t bother me at all that he’s leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest,” Cecilia Adriano, 52, told AFP.

During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina won one World Cup, were runners-up twice (Brazil 2014 and North America 2026) and were also crowned Copa America champions in 2021 and 2024.

Vanguard News

World.title: Why Nigeria’s digital economy lack strong female flavour
World.content:
…How cost of data, smartphones, lack of digital skills exclude women

…Just 35% used internet, compared with 52% of men – GSMA report

…Only 14.8% of rural females have Internet access – NBS

By Juliet Umeh

For many Nigerian women, owning a smartphone should be a gateway to opportunity -digital banking, online shopping, e-commerce, remote work, online learning and government services.

But for some, the smartphone in their hands remains little more than a device for making and receiving calls.

Nigeria’s digital economy is expanding rapidly, yet millions of women are still struggling to cross the gap between owning a phone and being able to use technology meaningfully.

The 2025 GSMA Mobile Gender Gap Report found that 91 percent of adult women in Nigeria owned a mobile phone, but only 47 percent owned an internet-enabled phone. Just 35 percent used mobile internet, compared with 52 percent of men.

The implication is stark: the challenge is no longer simply connecting women. It is ensuring that they can afford smartphones and data, acquire digital skills, obtain identity documents and confidently use online services.

‘I have a smartphone but don’t know what it can do’

At a business centre in Aba, Abia State, Mrs Abigail Maduka has witnessed the problem repeatedly.

She said women with expensive smartphones still come to her shop to perform simple transactions they could handle themselves if they had the skills.

“I have many women with big phones who do not even know what their phone is capable of doing aside from receiving calls,” she said.

Maduka said some women regularly visit her centre to recharge their electricity: “The truth is that they don’t even have the idea that it is what they can do on their phone to start with. They don’t know they can download the app and do it on their own,” she said.

The dependence, she added, is sometimes so severe that women call her at night asking her to recharge their electricity.

“Many people are with smartphones but the only thing they know is just to answer calls, that’s all,” Maduka said.

Her experience exposes an important distinction: phone ownership is not the same as digital inclusion.

‘Educated illiterate’

Sarah Nwokeoma, not her real name, a senior staff member of the Secondary Education Management Board, Aba Zonal office, said the problem is particularly noticeable among older women working in rural schools.

She described some as “educated illiterate” – women who have formal education but lack the digital skills required in today’s workplace.

Nwokeoma recalled a female principal of a rural secondary technical school who struggles with basic digital tasks.

“She does not even know her right from her left. She is still living in the past. They have been cheated all the time,” she said.

According to her, the woman sometimes depends on others to perform tasks she should handle herself.

“Even what they are supposed to do on their own, people will charge them to do it for them and junior staff will just be insulting them because they don’t know what they are expected to do,” she said.

Some women, she added, travel from rural communities to cities simply because they cannot access information sent digitally.

“There are some things they may be expected to do with their phone but because they are not internet savvy, they will even enter a bus from the village school where they are and come to the city to receive information already passed on a platform or in the mail,” she said.

The problem, therefore, is not always literacy. It can be digital confidence and practical skills.

The cost of staying connected

Mrs Bukola Olawale, secretary of women fellowship in a Methodist Church in Nigeria, said financial limitations prevent some women from even owning smartphones.

“A lot of our members don’t have an Android phone and when I send a message on the platform, I normally assume that everybody is on the same page,” she said.

She has had to send important information by SMS to women who cannot access the digital platform.

“However, it is not illiteracy that is the cause but lack of financial power,” Olawale explained.

Even women who own smartphones can struggle with data costs.

“Most times, some of them do say that they are always offline because they can’t afford data,” she added.

The experience mirrors findings from the World Bank and GSMA, which identify affordability and digital skills among major barriers to women’s internet use. GSMA’s 2025 report also found that women in low- and middle-income countries were 14 percent less likely than men to use mobile internet.

Rural women face a double disadvantage

NBS data further show how geography compounds the problem.

The National Bureau of Statistics’ General Household Survey Panel Wave 5, conducted in 2023/24, found mobile-phone access of 66.0 percent for males and 66.8 percent for females, showing virtually no national gender difference in phone access.

Internet access, however, was much lower: 21.6 percent for males and 21.1 percent for females.

The urban-rural gap was considerably wider. Internet access was 38.7 percent for urban males and 37.8 percent for urban females, compared with only 15.5 percent for rural males and 14.8 percent for rural females.

This means a rural woman can face several barriers simultaneously such as poor connectivity, inadequate electricity, expensive smartphones, data costs and limited access to digital training.

Nigeria’s data boom — but who is benefiting?

Nigeria’s growing appetite for mobile data shows how deeply the internet has become embedded in everyday life.

But national growth can conceal unequal participation.

While digitally connected Nigerians use the internet to trade, work remotely, learn, make payments and access services, women who cannot afford regular data may remain offline or depend on intermediaries.

That dependence has economic consequences.

For a trader, it can mean losing customers who shop online.

For a teacher, it can mean missing an official instruction sent through a digital platform.

For a small business owner, it can mean losing access to digital payments or online markets.

For an unemployed woman, it can mean missing a remote-work opportunity.

Financial inclusion is also at stake

The digital divide is closely linked to financial inclusion.

EFInA’s 2023 Access to Financial Services survey found that financial inclusion in Nigeria rose to 74 percent, from 68 percent in 2020, while formal financial inclusion reached 64 percent. Yet women continue to experience significant disparities.

EFInA’s Women’s Economic Empowerment analysis found persistent gender disparities in financial inclusion and highlighted women’s continued reliance on informal financial services.
