The matter is being investigated by Kirinyaga County Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) officers, local Sub-County police and Central Regional Police Command, led by the Regional Criminal Investigations Officer.

According to NPS, the Inspector General of the National Police Service has also been briefed on the incident and directed the Director of Criminal Investigations to expedite the probe and establish the facts surrounding the woman's death.

World.title: Ruto downplays rivalry over oil refinery in East Africa
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Former Nigeria President Olesugun Obasanjo, Ali Dangote, President William Ruto and Uganda President Yoweri Museveni during launch of the Lamu Refinery on September 30, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has played down suggestions of rivalry between Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania over competing refinery projects, saying East Africa’s growing demand for petroleum products can support several facilities across the region.

Speaking during a media interview at State House Mombasa, Ruto said Kenya had no objection to Uganda and Tanzania pursuing their own refinery projects, arguing that the different facilities could complement rather than compete with one another.

“There is no bad blood at all. There is no problem,” Ruto said.

His remarks came a day after he presided over the groundbreaking of the Lamu refinery project, which the government is positioning as a major component of a wider industrial complex on the Kenyan coast.

Ruto said he had discussed Uganda’s plans with President Yoweri Museveni and agreed that Kampala could proceed with a smaller refinery without threatening Kenya’s investment in Lamu.

He said Kenya would even be prepared to buy petroleum products from Uganda if they could reach the Kenyan market at competitive prices.

“If it is manufactured there in Uganda and the oil from that place is near Busia, and it can reach Busia at a lower price, we will buy oil from anywhere and bring it to Busia,” Ruto said.

The President argued that the size of the regional petroleum market meant there was room for more than one refinery.

“This one in Lamu cannot serve all of us; it will be necessary to expand,” he said, adding that East Africa had “enough opportunity” for multiple facilities.

Ruto also extended the same approach to Tanzania, saying Kenya could participate in a refinery project in Tanga if it is eventually developed.

“Even if the one in Tanga is built, we as Kenya will go and buy some shares there. There is no problem,” he said.

The comments point to a regional energy market in which petroleum products could move across borders depending on availability, transport costs and prices. Rather than treating refinery projects as competing national investments, Ruto said the facilities could strengthen economic cooperation within the East African Community.

The President said the Lamu refinery would also address some of the challenges Kenya faces from dependence on imported refined petroleum products.

“Lamu will give us an opportunity to have fuel without the fluctuations that we have now,” he said.

He linked the proposed refinery to the need to reduce Kenya’s exposure to international oil price shocks, disruptions caused by instability in oil-producing regions and costs associated with transporting petroleum products over long distances.

Ruto said local refining could reduce expenses related to insurance and transportation while providing Kenya with greater access to locally processed fuel.

However, he said the larger economic opportunity would extend beyond the refinery itself. The government plans to develop industries around the facility, including petrochemical, chemical and plastics manufacturing.

The refinery could also provide raw materials for industries producing fertiliser and bitumen, potentially reducing reliance on imports of some petroleum-based products.

The broader development is expected to create opportunities for employment, investment and trade while strengthening Lamu’s position as an industrial and logistics centre.

Ruto said Kenya’s policy would be guided by competitiveness, allowing businesses and consumers to obtain petroleum products from whichever regional facility can supply them efficiently and at favourable prices.

The President maintained that Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania therefore did not need to view their refinery plans through the lens of rivalry.

Instead, he said, multiple facilities could create a larger and more integrated petroleum market capable of serving the needs of East Africa.

World.title: Outrage as KDF officers detain human rights team along Malindi-Lamu highway
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Activists clashed with police at a Gamba roadblock after being stopped en route to Lamu. [Vocal Africa]

Six members of Muslims for Human Rights (MUHURI), including five staff and a board member, were detained by Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) officers along the Malindi-Lamu highway, prompting condemnation from human rights organisations.

The incident occurred on Monday as the team travelled from Lamu to Mombasa after a field mission. The officers reportedly intercepted them between Gamba and Minjila, detained them for about two hours, then released them.

The Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC) and MUHURI said the officers covered their faces and refused to identify themselves when the human rights team challenged them.

The five staff members were identified as Francis Auma, Abdulrahman Mwanga, Fredrick Okado, Lathan Yusuf and Mohamed Abdla, while the board member was identified as Khelef Khalifa.

In a joint statement, the two organisations said the officers' actions violated a High Court ruling by Justice Bahati Mwamuye requiring security personnel to wear clearly visible name tags or identifiable service numbers on their uniforms.

The ruling also prohibits security officers from wearing hoods, balaclavas or face masks to conceal their identities.

"We call on the KDF and other security agencies to comply with the court order. Officers who violate the directive should be held accountable and face legal consequences," the joint statement read in part.

The organisations also demanded immediate compliance with a recent court order lifting the dusk-to-dawn curfew that had been imposed for more than a decade along the Minjila-Lamu highway.

They argued that the curfew had created conditions for arbitrary stops, harassment and detention of travellers using the route, citing the detention of the MUHURI team as an example.

The organisations urged security agencies to respect court orders and protect the rights of travellers using the highway.

However, a senior Anti-Terror Police officer aware of the incident told The Standard that the officers from the Border Police Unit (BPU) manning such roadblocks and tactical borders conceal their faces to protect their identities.

"In high-risk areas prone to insurgent or terrorist retaliation, including Kanyoyo in Kitui heading to Garissa, Moyale and Lamu, anonymity is framed as a matter of personal and operational survival," she stated.

World.title: Kalonzo signals at working with Ruto if 2027 poll is free and fair
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka at St Michael and All Angels ACK Cathedral in Bondo, Siaya County on September 27, 2026. [Clinton Ambujo, Standard]

Wiper Patriotic Front leader Kalonzo Musyoka has signalled that the Opposition could accept the outcome of the 2027 General Election and consider working with President William Ruto if he wins through a free and fair contest.

Speaking at St Michael and All Angels ACK Cathedral in Bondo, Siaya County, Kalonzo said the political class must commit itself to democratic competition and be prepared to accept the verdict of voters.

“If you beat us, we will have to consider if you have behaved yourself, and if we beat you, we have to look at all these things,” he said.

The Wiper leader also called for stronger democratic institutions, warning against political confrontation that could deepen divisions in the country.

“We have a nation here. We have to make this country truly democratic. I do not think we have a shortcut,” he said.

Kalonzo used the church service to make a broader appeal for a united and effective Opposition, saying political leaders had a responsibility to work together in the national interest.

“Kenya needs a functional official opposition; one that is united and does not thrive on disunity. As leaders, we have a responsibility to work together and play our part in fixing this nation,” he said.

He said he had remained in the Opposition even when some political allies moved into government.

“I have stood in the opposition all these years. Even when others joined government, my brother Eugene Wamalwa and I remained steadfast, and we will continue to stand firm,” he said.

Kalonzo also turned his attention to Parliament, claiming that the National Assembly had been “captured” and challenging lawmakers in both Houses to exercise their constitutional responsibilities.

“The National Assembly has been captured. Let this message reach every leader in the National Assembly and the Senate: you have the power to change things, not just to complain later,” he said.

He urged legislators to defend the interests of the people who elected them and to put the country ahead of political considerations.

The former Vice President also defended retired President Uhuru Kenyatta against claims that he is financing the Opposition ahead of the 2027 contest.

Kalonzo argued that presidential campaigns have historically relied on networks of political allies and supporters rather than family resources alone.

“But here we are saying, please let Uhuru rest; he is a retired President. Stop saying he is our financier,” he said.

Kalonzo cited previous presidential campaigns involving Uhuru, former President Mwai Kibaki and Raila Odinga, arguing that major political campaigns require support from friends and associates.

“Even when Uhuru was running for President, or Kibaki and even Raila, no family has enough resources to support a presidential campaign. It is friends who support you,” he said.

He warned that Kenya was at a delicate political moment and urged leaders to avoid actions that could deepen instability.

“We should not allow the country to get to a worse situation than where it is. We are on the edge of a cliff; the country is at a crossroads,” he said.

World.title: Alleged Flydubai hijacker likely wanted to target Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport, sources say
World.content:
The alleged hijacker of the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv likely wanted to target Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport, the country’s main international gateway, according to an Israeli official and an Israeli source familiar with the matter.

Hamam al-Hammami, the suspect in the hijacking attempt and co-pilot on board the flight, was stopped by the actions of the captain and several passengers who restrained him and wrested control of the airplane.

The official and the source said Israel is receiving updates from the Emiratis and that the investigation was still in its early stages. There are still questions about the suspect’s intentions, they added.

Israel’s Channel 12 News first reported that Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport may have been the target of the hijacking.

It’s unclear why al-Hammami allegedly attacked the captain, Smit Machchhar, over Saudi airspace if his goal was to target an airport in Israel. When Israel detected an inbound commercial jet signaling a potential hijacking on September 30, authorities there scrambled Israeli fighter jets as a precaution – standard procedure for such an emergency scenario.

The United Arab Emirates is leading the investigation into the attempted hijacking on board Flydubai’s FZ1073 to learn the motives behind the attack and understand how the suspect was able to get through the safeguards of two countries known for their strict security protocols.

A plane, carrying passengers who were on the FlyDubai aircraft bound for Israel from the UAE, which was diverted to Saudi Arabia following an emergency signal, arrives at Ben Gurion Airport, in Lod, near Tel Aviv, Israel, September 30, 2026. Ammar Awad/Reuters

Israel’s Tax Authority confirmed the names of all passengers and crew were in the hands of Israeli authorities before the flight had taken off, but it said questions about the vetting of crew members should be referred to the Ministry of Transport. Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, also referred CNN to the Ministry of Transport, which it said is “responsible for all security matters concerning foreign airlines.”

The Ministry of Transport said that its procedures do not include checking the names of flight crew members, although those names are submitted to the Israel Tax Authority, which collects them in case of requests by security services.

The ministry added that all flight crew members are required to have a travel visa to enter the country, and an Omani passport should have been flagged at check-in. But the ministry also said its “procedures do not address the threat from a pilot.”

Suspect likely acted alone

CNN reported on Sunday that the suspect probably acted alone, and Israel is so far not aware of a link to any terrorist organization that trained, funded, or organized the attack.

The attorney general of the UAE, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the co-pilot on board the flight had attempted to seize control of the plane by attacking his colleague with a crash ax – a piece of equipment required on most aircraft. The attorney general called the attempted hijacking a “terrorist act.”

The suspect, al-Hammami, had been removed from his previous job at Oman’s national airline on the track to be a pilot following concerns about his extremist views, sources told CNN earlier. He was moved to a desk job at the company, one of the sources said.

Flydubai said it couldn’t comment on the matter while an investigation was underway. CNN has also reached out to Oman Air, the UAE Foreign Ministry and the Dubai government’s media office for comment.

Aviation experts have told CNN that when it comes to vetting pilots, the responsibility lies with local governments, airlines and security services. Experts said pilots’ licenses and security passes are handled at the national level, and the rules vary depending on the country.

World.title: This city is on track to run out of water by 2030. For many residents, that day is already here
World.content:
Shazia knows what life will be like in a major city that’s run out of water because she’s already living that reality — and it’s unbearable.

The 34-year-old lives in the Khair Khana neighborhood of Afghanistan’s capital Kabul with her three children and her husband, who ekes out a living as a street vendor. They have no running water and can’t afford to buy it from the water tankers that often outnumber cars on the city streets.

Every day she and her kids must walk to a local mosque and wait in hour-long lines to fill buckets from a hand pump, before heading back with their heavy loads. Her back aches and she hates having to drag her kids out after school, “but we have no choice,” she said.

Kabul is on track to be the first modern city to run out of water, and could do so as soon as 2030, according to a recent report from the nonprofit Prosper Global. But for Shazia, and many other residents across this fast-expanding city, that day is already here. They are on the frontlines of a spiraling urban water crisis that isn’t confined to Kabul.

Cities across the world — from Corpus Christi, Texas, to Iran’s capital Tehran — are teetering on the edge of water shortages so severe that residents are bracing for a “day zero,” the point at which taps run dry for large parts of the city.

Their crises tend to follow familiar beats: Booming populations colliding with insufficient, underfunded water infrastructure. Beneath it all hums the climate crisis, driving hotter, drier weather and pushing the water cycle off balance.

Of all the urban areas facing day zero, Kabul’s situation may be starkest. It’s one of the fastest-growing cities, located in one of the most climate-vulnerable countries. Afghanistan has also suffered from decades of conflict and global aid has all but dried up since the return of Taliban rule in 2021.

Kabul is staring down a “human catastrophe,” said Mohd Faizee, a professor at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health. “We have only a limited window of time.”

Those who want to understand what the future of water looks like in our changing world should look to Kabul.

Eight-year-old Sanaullah gives water to his younger brother while their mother is preparing lunch at their home, in Kabul, Afghanistan, August 28, 2025. Sayed Hassib/Reuters

The search for water beneath the ground

On the streets of Kabul, water is a huge topic of conversation, said Mirza Jan, who lives in the city’s Taimani neighborhood. Everyone is affected.

When Jan’s family bought their house in 1990, they could pull up water by hand in a bucket from a shallow well. Over the years, he has had to dig the well down farther and farther as it kept drying up. It’s now more than 700 feet deep, an expensive endeavor only possible because of money sent by his two sons who live in the US.

As groundwater shrinks, those like Jan who can afford the upfront cost keep digging deeper; those who can’t rely on expensive tanker water or hand pumps at mosques. None of these options are sustainable. “It is an invisible catastrophe in the making,” Jan said, “the city will soon run completely out of water.”

An Afghan boy collects water from a well on the outskirts of Kabul, Afghanistan, on May 12, 2020. Mohammad Ismail/Reuters

Kabul should not be water scarce. Sprawled across a wide valley, it is framed by the Hindu Kush Himalaya.

The rugged peaks of Afghanistan’s section of this vast mountain range act as water towers. Melting snow and glacial ice feed the Kabul River, which cuts through the city, and recharge aquifers, which form the backbone of the city’s water system, supplying 80% of residents. Just a fifth have access to piped water.

Over the past decade, however, groundwater levels have plummeted nearly 100 feet, according to Prosper Global. Water is now being pumped out far faster than it can be replenished, leaving an estimated shortfall of more than 1.55 billion cubic feet a year. Nearly half the city’s boreholes have dried up. “In many neighbourhoods, water has already run out,” Faizee said

It’s the result of soaring demand, from homes, greenhouses and businesses. But the human-caused climate crisis also plays a role. The country has endured six consecutive years of drought, with last year one of its most severe. Snowfall reached a 25-year low in Afghanistan at the end of last year, according to UN data, and it’s part of a long-term trend which has seen snow levels fall by nearly 20% between 2014 and 2020.

⛅ Get CNN Weather in your inbox The forecast is just the beginning. We’ll send you expert coverage and the stories behind the weather — so you always know more than just the number. 

When the rain does fall, Kabul’s hard, impermeable surfaces mean the water doesn’t replenish aquifers, but instead sweeps through the city as flash floods, destroying homes, killing people and rolling away.

Kabul’s vanishing groundwater isn’t a crisis, said Najibullah Sadid, a Germany-based water and environment researcher with the Afghanistan Water and Environment Professionals Network. That word implies a short-term shock to the system. He prefers the term “water bankruptcy” because “you’re running out of a resource which is not recoverable anymore.”

A boy stands on the dried-up Kabul river bed, amid a serious water crisis in Kabul, Afghanistan, August 29, 2025. Sayed Hassib/Reuters

Unchecked expansion

Said Agha and his family live in an apartment in the densely packed Kabul neighborhood of Karte Naw. He makes decent money working for a company, but the city’s water crisis spares few.

His building is home to 14 families but relies on one well that dries up every few months. Most of the time they only have running water for short bursts. Sometimes it’s off for days.

Agha is convinced the city’s aquifers will soon run dry and he doesn’t know what to do. His job is tied to Kabul and leaving would be a “calamity,” he said.

Kabul is expanding vertically, with multistory buildings stacked on top of existing structures. Instead of one family on a plot of land, there are now dozens and it’s dramatically increasing pressure on already strained water resources, Sadid said.

A man fills the water tank of his home in Kabul on July 13, 2021. Sajjad Hussain/AFP/Getty Images

Kabul is one of the fastest growing cities in the world. Experts estimate its population has ballooned from less than 1 million in 2001 to 6 million today.

People have gravitated there for different reasons. Many returned after the fall of the Taliban in 2001, in the hopes of better opportunities. More recently, there’s been a surge due to the large-scale expulsion of Afghans from neighboring Iran and Pakistan amid increasing regional tensions.

People are also migrating to the city from rural regions, in search of jobs and sometimes, ironically, a better water situation.

As water runs out, residents pay

For the last two years, Asadullah Ahmadi has been spending at least 150 Afghanis ($2.35) a day, a big chunk of his income, to get enough water for his family of seven. Even then, the water they get is dirty and must be boiled. “It is not sustainable, and I don’t know how long we can afford this,” he said.

Running out of water is expensive. Many in Kabul, like Ahmadi, are forced to rely on tanked in water from private companies. Some of these companies are motivated to help people, but others are simply looking for big profits, said Marianna von Zahn, the former Afghanistan director of programs at Prosper Global. They pump groundwater and sell it back to residents at inflated prices.

A water tanker on a hillside in Kabul. Residents have to lug water in heavy jugs from wells or buy it from tankers, which charge at least twice as much as the state-owned utility. Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty Images

The impacts are most acute for residents already facing high levels of poverty, said a UN official based in Afghanistan. That’s “the most dangerous part” of the situation, they said.

Poorer people are spending up to 30% of their total income on water, analysts estimate. The UN considers affordable water costs to be 3% or less of household income.

To add to the dire situation, up to 80% of large parts of the city’s groundwater is contaminated, both by sewage and by naturally occurring substances such as arsenic. It’s “another hidden crisis.” said Jalal Naser Faqiryar, a Netherlands-based water specialist and former director general of Kabul River Basin.

Kabul residents have few options. Ahmadi fears he’ll need to abandon his home but “even if I do leave, where can I go in search of water? The whole city is suffering from this problem.”

Some may leave Kabul altogether, but water scarcity is common in many parts of Afghanistan. And leaving the country is fraught with difficulty. Neighboring Iran and Pakistan are forcibly returning Afghans, and further afield in Europe, fervent anti-immigration rhetoric makes the situation very challenging.

“There’s not really anywhere to go,” the UN official said.

An Afghan man fills water in a can from a river in the Istalif village of northwest Kabul on November 22, 2023. Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty Images

Attempts to harness rivers and rain

There are plans to help alleviate Kabul’s impending catastrophe by harnessing surface water.

The Shahtoot Dam, which would be built on a tributary of the Kabul River, could provide water for more than 2 million people in the city. India agreed to fund it, but the project stalled after the Taliban’s return to power in 2021.

The Taliban insists it’s going ahead imminently but construction has yet to begin, and it faces steep opposition from Pakistan, which claims the dam will significantly reduce the water it receives from the Kabul River.

Another plan is a 124-mile pipeline that would transport water from the Panjshir River to Kabul, to supply 2 million city residents. But it’s still at the survey and design stage.

Even if these projects move ahead, they would take years to construct and would also require treatment plants and a proper network to bring the water into people’s homes. “The Taliban do not have the capacity to deal with a problem this big, and they know it,” Faizee said.

Kabul’s water situation is “heading toward a serious crisis,” said Matiullah Abid, the spokesman for the Afghanistan Ministry of Energy and Water. He said the ministry is acting, including by constructing dams and thousands of wells in the city to recharge groundwater, controlling commercial water use and completing the Shah wa Arous Dam in 2024, designed to supply 20,000 households.

There are many ongoing efforts to tackle the water problem but “these measures require time and resources,” Abid added.

People ‘continue to suffer silently’

The Taliban, itself, is an added complication in Kabul’s water story. It is not recognized as a legitimate government by most of the international community due to its human rights abuses, including stripping away the rights of women and girls.

As a result, international aid has plummeted, even as Kabul and other parts Afghanistan edge toward water disaster. The world is “watching the crisis unfold” instead of preventing it now, Faizee said. “Later, it will pay for the emergency response, such as water trucking, disease outbreaks and displacement.”

For now, people will “continue to suffer silently,” said Susanne Schmeier, professor of water cooperation, law, and diplomacy at IHE Delft Institute for Water Education in the Netherlands.

A woman collects water from a water tanker on a hillside in Kabul. Wakil Kohsar/AFP/Getty Images

Kabul shows what a day zero looks like. It’s not every single tap suddenly running dry, it’s a slow-moving catastrophe that sees residents forced into ever-harder decisions.

Do they sink money into expensive, deeper wells that will inevitably run dry, or rely on private water tankers that push them further into poverty? Do they make arduous, daily journeys to hand pumps, taking kids away from schoolwork and play, while also risking their physical health and safety? Or, do they move away from the city and their jobs, and risk finding themselves in an equally bad water situation?

What’s happening offers a snapshot of what may be coming for many other cities, as climate change meets urban water systems built for a very different world.

For Kabul residents, it’s trauma on top of trauma. “Years ago, we were running away from bombs and rockets in Kabul,” said city resident Said Agha. “Now we may have to flee because of a lack of water.”

World.title: US and China discussing reciprocal nuclear site visits amid concerns about a new arms race
World.content:
The Trump administration has discussed beginning reciprocal nuclear site visits with China and plans to continue pushing for that possibility during in-person meetings in the coming months, according to sources familiar with the matter.

The discussions, which have been informal and preliminary, come amid mounting US concerns about China’s rapidly growing nuclear weapons program and after the last remaining arms control agreement between the US and Russia expired last year. The effort to establish a trilateral agreement began in Trump’s first term, but no tangible progress has been made and formal talks on a new accord have not begun, with China and Russia largely ignoring substantive US outreach efforts.

The idea of reciprocal visits was initially raised by the Chinese while meeting US officials this year, one source said, giving some indication that the communist nation may be open to pursuing confidence building measures that could pave the way for a grander agreement. Visits to the US Department of Energy national labs and to China’s equivalent facilities were discussed, and the US would be open to discussing visits to nuclear testing sites, the source said.

The nuclear discussions between the US and Chinese officials at the working level so far this year have largely occurred on the sidelines of gatherings by the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, known as the P5, sources said.

The concept of allowing nuclear site visits could move the needle on the US efforts to engage China on issues related to strategic stability and potentially serve as a building block for a trilateral agreement, but China remains adamant that they will not engage on discussions that could limit their nuclear buildup. The US currently has a much bigger nuclear arsenal with about 5,000 total nuclear warheads while China has about 600, but it is expanding its nuclear weapons infrastructure and has been projected to produce hundreds more warheads over the next decade.

A State Department spokesperson referred questions to the White House, which did not provide a comment. CNN has requested comment from the Chinese embassy in Washington, DC. Last Thursday, China began its weeklong National Day holiday, during which all government offices are closed.

Paul Dean, who previously served as an acting assistant secretary of state overseeing US arms control efforts, told CNN that the administration needs to approach any Chinese nuclear negotiations with its “eyes wide open,” but said that reciprocal visits would be “an extremely valuable confidence-building measure” that could lay the informational and diplomatic foundation for additional work to reduce nuclear risk between the two countries.

“This is a very dangerous time, and there are very few guardrails in place on the US-China nuclear relationship,” Dean, now a vice president at the Nuclear Threat Initiative nonprofit, said.

Photo taken at a newsstand in Beijing on July 7, 2026, shows a local newspaper reporting on the Chinese military’s test-firing the previous day of a nuclear-capable ballistic missile from a submarine toward the Pacific. Kyodo/AP

President Donald Trump expressed support for trilateral arms control negotiations between the US, Russia and China when he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping last month, but they didn’t discuss the possibility of site visits during their talks, a US official said.

Xi did not leave the door open to discussing a trilateral agreement, pointing to the US and Russian nuclear arsenals being larger than China’s – a point that Chinese officials have routinely used to shield themselves from any discussions that could lead to limiting their nuclear stockpile before they are on par with the US, the official added.

Still, the topic of nuclear arms control has long been a focus for Trump, who is expected to meet with Xi twice later this year. By the time the two leaders meet again it is expected that further lower-level discussions on possible nuclear site visits will have taken place, the sources said.

Visiting nuclear sites for on-site inspections have historically been used as a vital verification tool by the International Atomic Energy Agency to be sure that nations are abiding by their commitments to using the facilities for peaceful purposes.

Skepticism about China’s motives

Experts and former US officials who spoke with CNN were encouraged by the talks but were not confident that they will immediately lead to concrete progress on a breakthrough agreement.

“It has to be taken seriously. It could be a great start,” said a former US official who has engaged China in track two discussions related to strategic stability in recent years.

Still, skeptics noted that the Chinese may have floated the idea in an effort to create a positive atmosphere or to appear serious on the topic of nuclear arsenals, said former US officials and experts who questioned the authenticity of such an offer.

“In advance of a big summit if the Chinese can put good feelers out there they will do that,” said another former US official who focused on nuclear issues. “It makes them seem more magnanimous as the two sides are engaging.”

The Chinese may have a “maligned motivation” they said.

About a year ago Trump said that the US would resume nuclear testing on an “equal basis” with China and Russia, but there has been no known US nuclear testing since that pronouncement. The administration earlier this year accused China of carrying out a secret nuclear test in 2020 using a technique known as “decoupling” designed to evade detection by firing the explosion in an empty cavern to minimize seismic shaking.

The National Nuclear Security Administration’s nonproliferation directorate conducted a 16-ton underground non-nuclear explosion last week at the Nevada National Security Site that was the second in a years-long series of experiments designed to mimic the alleged Chinese test, according to an agency spokesperson. The decoupled test explosion offered NNSA and other entities a chance to validate the effectiveness of new methods and equipment for detecting such stealthy tests.

“You cannot evade American innovation,” NNSA Administrator Brandon Williams said in a news release announcing the test.

The Trump administration is also working on a proposal that would enable assure verification that low-yield nuclear testing is not happening at nuclear sites and could share that with the P5 group later this year, a US official said. It is unclear what kind of technical equipment could be part of that proposal.

President Donald Trump is greeted by Chinese President Xi Jinping during a welcome ceremony at the Great Hall of the People on May 14 in Beijing. Alex Wong/Getty Images

Gerald Brown, who studies China’s military at the Council on Foreign Relations nonprofit, said he is “not particularly optimistic” but that the reciprocal visit scheme, if enacted, is “a potential glimmer of hope” for reducing nuclear risk between the US and China.

Brown, a former State Department intel analyst, said that China’s ongoing nuclear buildup “is deeply linked with political goals, namely its aggressive ambitions regarding Taiwan.” China historically has viewed nuclear talks as “tool to gain political concessions” on Taiwan, he argued, rather than as a genuine policy goal.

“You won’t know what’s on the table until you engage in a thoughtful, rigorous way to see if this is something in our interest — and it might be,” said Dean.

Dean, whose nonprofit has engaged with Chinese entities in nonofficial diplomatic discussions in recent months, said he sees mutual “interest and acknowledgement that the risks are real.”

He pointed at the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, which sparked some of the first US-Soviet risk reduction measures like a 24-hour phone hotline, as a historical warning.

“We don’t need to wait for a crisis to start reducing nuclear risks,” Dean argued. “And the risks are very real right now.”

Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.

World.title: Trump draws backlash after he suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
World.content:
Officials in California denounced comments made by President Donald Trump as “dangerous” on Monday after he appeared to suggest Iran could “take out” Los Angeles or San Diego – major cities in a state he has often criticized.

Speaking at a rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, ahead of the midterm elections, Trump once again called the consequences of the war with Iran a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe,” adding that Iran could potentially take out an American city.

“Let, let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego,” Trump said in comments that drew swift backlash from California’s leaders.

“This is a very small price to pay and it’s gonna be over with very soon,” he said of the war.

Trump has repeatedly made the argument that high gas prices are a small price to pay for the war in Iran and in his Nebraska comments, he appeared to contrast that with a dramatically higher price to pay – an attack on a US city.

CNN has reached out to the White House for more information on what Trump meant by his comments about the two cities.

Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom called the president “deranged and dangerous,” while Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the statements about the city “could potentially compromise our safety.”

“The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” said Bass, also a Democrat.

The Democratic mayor of San Diego, Todd Gloria, said the city “is not collateral damage. We are not expendable. And we are never a ‘small price to pay.’ Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.”

Trump’s comments also drew criticism from Republican congressional candidate Jim Desmond, who said he “vehemently” disagreed with the president.

“America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our Commander in Chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” said Desmond, who is running in California’s 48th Congressional district. He added, “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

Trump’s highlighting of cities in California that could be targeted by Iran comes as he has frequently criticized the state and its leaders over immigration, state elections and wildfires.

The president also repeated during his speech in Nebraska that the war is “going to end very soon.”

At the onset of the war, Trump had vowed that the conflict would only last a few weeks, but it has since gone on seven months.

The president made the new argument last week that his initial four- to six-week timeline had just been about the time it would take to eradicate the nuclear threat from Iran and not the time it would take to conclude the entire war.

This story has been updated with additional information.

CNN’s Kaanita Iyer contributed to this report.

World.title: Mona Zaki’s newest series to premiere October 10th on Shahid platform
World.content:
Actress Mona Zaki discussed her upcoming series, “Tale’ Nazel” (Going Up, Going Down), scheduled to premiere on October 10 on the Shahid platform.

In a teaser posted on Shahid’s Instagram page, Zaki said: “They say that behind every great man, there is a great woman—but no one ever mentioned what happens when that woman is deeply hurt. This isn’t a story about infidelity; it’s about what happens afterwards.”

“Tale’ Nazel” stars Mohamed Shahin, Mariam al–Khosht, Laila Ezz el–Arab, Mimi Gamal, and Hamza Diab. The series is written by Samah Ahmed Abdel–Khalek and Engy al–Kassem, and directed by Hany Khalifa.

The series revolves around a musician living what appears to be a stable married life with his wife—a powerful businesswoman who owns a major company.

Although the couple had agreed not to have children, the wife secretly harbors a genuine desire to start a family.

Her life is upended when she discovers her husband’s infidelity and the fact that he has secretly married another woman. Faced with this devastating revelation, she struggles internally—torn between the pain of betrayal and the need to reclaim her dignity—before events escalate toward a confrontation that could drive her to seek revenge.

Shahin discussed the character of “Ali”—whom he portrays in the series—alongside Zaki’s character, “Noura,” saying: “Noura and Ali are the kind of characters that make you envious—you wish you could live even a fraction of their lives. He achieved his dream and became Egypt’s most famous musician; they had everything, yet human nature is greedy.”

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: FM reiterates Egypt’s condemnation of attacks on Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty reaffirmed Egypt’s condemnation of all attacks against Saudi Arabia and its full support for the Kingdom’s security and stability during a phone call with Prince Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah Al Saud, Saudi Minister of Foreign Affairs.

The phone call came as part of the ongoing communication and coordination between the two brotherly countries to consult on various issues of mutual concern.

The call underscored the depth of the fraternal and strategic relations between Egypt and Saudi Arabia and the importance of strengthening various mechanisms of bilateral cooperation across all fields.

The two ministers also discussed regional developments, including the crisis with Iran, security in the Red Sea region, and the situation in Sudan. They agreed on the need to safeguard the security and freedom of maritime navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The two ministers renewed their affirmation of the two brotherly countries’ steadfast position in support of Sudan’s unity and sovereignty, stressing the importance of preserving its national institutions to safeguard its security and stability in a manner that meets the aspirations of the brotherly Sudanese people.

World.title: FM, Fatah official discuss developments in Gaza, West Bank
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, discussed with Fatah Central Committee Secretary-General Jibril Rajoub developments in the Palestinian territories, particularly the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, as well as efforts to support the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.

During the meeting, Abdelatty reviewed efforts aimed at supporting the completion of the implementation of US President Donald Trump’s comprehensive peace plan, Foreign Ministry spokesman Ambassador Nader Zaki said.

He stressed the importance of fully meeting the commitments of the first phase, including ensuring the unhindered flow of humanitarian aid into the Gaza Strip and advancing early recovery efforts.

Abdelatty condemned repeated attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their property in the West Bank, as well as the escalation in such attacks.

He further condemned repeated incursions into Al Aqsa Mosque compound and provocative practices there, warning of the dangers posed by the continuation of these violations and attempts to undermine the existing historical and legal status quo at the holy sites in Jerusalem.

The meeting also addressed the importance of continuing Palestinian national dialogue in a way that contributes to unifying ranks.

The meeting tackled Egypt’s efforts to support reform and empower the Palestinian Authority and strengthen its capabilities to assume its responsibilities in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, in a manner that supports the unity of Palestinian decision-making and institutions and paves the way for the establishment of an independent Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967 lines, with East Jerusalem (Al Quds city) as its capital.

World.title: Health Minister chairs 7th board meeting of Medical Professions Risk Compensation Fund
World.content:
Minister of Health and Population Khaled Abdel Ghaffar chaired on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, the seventh meeting of the Board of Directors of the Medical Professions Risk Compensation Fund, in the presence of Hussein Dahroug, the fund’s executive director, and representatives of the ministries and authorities serving as board members.

Health Ministry Spokesman Hossam Abdel Ghaffar said the meeting addressed a number of issues on the agenda, including a review of the fund’s financial position, follow-up on compensation payments, and plans for investing its funds, in addition to discussing proposed areas of cooperation aimed at supporting medical professionals.

The board reviewed the fund’s total revenues and balances through the end of August 2026, as well as compensation paid to eligible beneficiaries in cases of death and injuries resulting in total or partial disability.

It also discussed the fund’s investment plan through the end of August 2026 and its total balances held with commercial banks, along with ongoing monitoring of its investment and financial position to preserve its resources and strengthen its ability to meet its obligations toward beneficiaries.

The meeting also reviewed the latest developments regarding the fund’s new headquarters at the Ministry of Labor and the proposed date for relocating there in December.

The board further discussed a number of proposed cooperation protocols with the Ministry of Health and Population through its National Projects and Medical Professions Development sectors, as well as cooperation with the Egyptian Health Council and the Supreme Council of University Hospitals.

The minister stressed the importance of directing the fund’s cooperation and spending toward areas that provide direct and tangible benefits to medical professionals, contribute to reducing risks associated with practicing health professions, and enhance the support and protection provided to them.

He added that such efforts would positively contribute to improving the working environment and the quality of healthcare services provided to citizens.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-President Sirleaf Admits Her Government Failed to Defeat Corruption, Says Menace Persists
World.content:
MONROVIA — Former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf has made a candid admission that her administration failed to defeat corruption in Liberia, acknowledging that despite extensive institutional reforms during her 12-year presidency, the menace remains deeply entrenched and continues to confront the country today.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

“We did not succeed,” Sirleaf said Tuesday while delivering the keynote address at a Governance Commission symposium on good governance in Monrovia. The event marks the inaugural ceremony marking October as Liberia’s Month of Good Governance, an initiative declared by President Joseph Nyuma Boakai.



The former president said she wished her administration had won the fight against corruption but conceded that its efforts fell short.

“I wish that I could, with all these efforts, have won the corruption fight. We did not. And we are facing the same thing today,” she said.

Sirleaf’s admission comes nearly two decades after she famously declared corruption “public enemy number one” during her inauguration in January 2006, shortly after becoming Liberia’s first post-war president and Africa’s first democratically elected female president.

She served two constitutional terms, leaving office in January 2018 after peacefully transferring power to then-President-elect George Manneh Weah.

‘Audits Were Published and Then Forgotten’

Reflecting on the shortcomings of her administration’s anti-corruption campaign, Sirleaf pointed to weak enforcement, inadequate funding for integrity institutions and the failure to prosecute individuals accused of wrongdoing.

“I have said so before, and I will say it again. Audits were published and then forgotten. Too few cases reached the courtroom, and fewer ended in conviction,” she said.

She also acknowledged that some institutions were given broad mandates without the budgetary resources required to effectively perform their functions.

Sirleaf said the experience taught her that establishing institutions and passing laws, while important, were insufficient to defeat corruption.

“Institutions are necessary, but they are not enough. Accountability without consequence will only be a report on the shelf,” she said.

According to Sirleaf, laws provide the framework for accountability, but their effectiveness depends on leaders, citizens and institutions working together to enforce them.

Reforms, But Corruption Fight Fell Short

Sirleaf defended the governance reforms undertaken during her administration, recalling that her government inherited a country emerging from years of civil war, institutional collapse and widespread public distrust.

“We inherited a nation that had been looted by the people who had lost faith in government,” she said.

She said her administration understood that sustaining peace would require rebuilding public confidence in state institutions.

Among the measures undertaken, she cited strengthening the General Auditing Commission and establishing the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission.

Her administration also established the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission and reviewed concession agreements signed during the civil war, canceling some contracts it determined were not in the national interest.

Sirleaf also pointed to the National Forestry Reform Act of 2006 and the 2009 Community Rights Law, which she said strengthened legal benefits for communities.

Through the Liberia Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative, she said Liberia became the first African country to meet the global standard for publishing information on what companies paid and what government received from the extractive sector.

Her government also passed the Freedom of Information Act in 2010, which she described as the first such law in West Africa.

The administration also secured relief of approximately US$5 billion in Liberia’s public debt, which Sirleaf said enabled the country to meet requirements for national reconstruction.

Yet, despite those achievements and the creation or strengthening of accountability institutions, she acknowledged that corruption remained unresolved.

‘It Starts From the Very Top’

Sirleaf said the responsibility for fighting corruption ultimately begins with political leadership.

“Accountability begins at the top, the very top, or it does not begin at all,” she said.

She argued that citizens are more likely to follow what leaders do than what they say.

“It’s not enough to make laws; enforcement is cardinal,” she said.

The former president stressed that public officials must lead by example and demonstrate integrity in the exercise of their responsibilities.

“It starts from the very top,” she emphasized.

She also called for Liberia’s integrity institutions to receive the full budgetary allocations required under the law, while challenging those institutions themselves to uphold the standards they are mandated to enforce.

Judiciary Must Enforce Its Decisions

Sirleaf also called for greater respect for the judiciary and implementation of court decisions, while warning against treating the courts as the sole solution to Liberia’s governance problems.

“The judiciary and our courts, yes, must be respected, and decisions rendered must be fully implemented,” she said.

But she added that the judiciary itself must be properly staffed with competent and highly principled officials capable of making decisions in accordance with the law.

“Waiting for the courts, waiting for the Supreme Court to take the lead to resolve the problem is not going to help us on this matter,” she said.

‘Exclusion Breeds Resentment’

Beyond corruption, Sirleaf used the symposium to place Liberia’s governance crisis within the broader context of the country’s history.

She recounted Liberia’s establishment by the American Colonization Society for the resettlement of freed Black people from the United States and the declaration of independence in 1847.

She noted that Liberia and Ethiopia were the only African countries to maintain their sovereignty during the period of European colonial expansion and the Scramble for Africa.

But Sirleaf said Liberia’s history was also marked by the exclusion of the indigenous majority from political and economic power.

She argued that the prolonged exclusion created resentment that eventually contributed to the 1980 military coup and the civil wars that followed.

“For more than a century, our Republic was governed and taught the school of loyalty, affirming the axiom that a government that answers only to a few will sooner or later serve only a few,” she said.

“This is what happened. Exclusion breeds resentment. Resentment bred the problems of 1980. And then 14 years of civil war that reportedly took 250,000 lives.”

She said the country’s years of militarism and civil war also destroyed infrastructure, weakened institutions and damaged Liberia’s democratic culture.

Accountability Is Not a Foreign Concept

Sirleaf rejected the notion that accountability and good governance are foreign concepts imposed on Liberia.

“Let us also be clear that accountability is not a foreign idea brought to us from outside,” she said.

She invoked the traditional Palava Hut system, where chiefs who abuse their authority can be challenged by elders and members of the community.

“Leadership is trust and can be withdrawn,” she said, stressing that public authority must be accompanied by responsibility and accountability.

For Liberia, she said, good governance should be viewed as a restoration of balance between government and citizens.

‘Freedom of Information Law Belongs to You’

Sirleaf urged Liberians to take greater responsibility for demanding accountability from their leaders and institutions.

She called on citizens to understand and use the country’s laws, particularly the Freedom of Information Act, as a tool for demanding transparency.

“To the citizens of Liberia, our Freedom of Information Law belongs to you as a democracy,” she said.

She also had a direct message for journalists.

“To our journalists, keep asking the hard questions,” Sirleaf said.

Analysts say her remarks at the Governance Commission symposium offered one of the clearest assessments of the limitations of her administration’s anti-corruption campaign, while placing responsibility for confronting the problem on Liberia’s current and future leaders, institutions and citizens.

Recognizing Sirleaf’s ‘Enduring’ Legacy

The event was convened by the Governance Commission in Monrovia and brought together government officials, diplomats, development partners, civil society leaders, media executives and governance stakeholders.

Alaric K. Tokpa, Acting Chairman of the Governance Commission, described Sirleaf’s participation as particularly significant because she was the first chairperson of the Governance Reform Commission, the institution from which the current Governance Commission evolved.

Tokpa praised Sirleaf’s political career and her role as Africa’s first democratically elected woman president, saying her journey from imprisonment to the Executive Mansion had helped challenge longstanding assumptions about women’s capacity to lead.

He also credited the establishment of the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Presidential Center for Women and Development with extending her influence beyond her presidency.

“Your leadership example and great legacy” should continue to inspire women and young people across Africa, Tokpa said in welcoming the former president.

He said the Governance Commission considered Sirleaf’s presence at the inaugural Good Governance Month event especially meaningful because of her historical connection to the commission and Liberia’s governance reform process.

Tokpa urged Liberians and Liberia’s international partners to embrace good governance as a requirement for national renewal, peace, stability and socioeconomic development.

He identified transparency and accountability, effective government, public participation and inclusion, the rule of law, justice, equity and decentralization of power as essential pillars of good governance.

World.title: Liberia: LSEZA Joins Africa’s Economic Zones Network, Eyes Investment, Jobs and Exports
World.content:
MONROVIA — For decades, Liberia’s economy has leaned on the same narrow pillars: iron ore, rubber, timber and, more recently, gold. Raw materials leave the country, and finished goods come back in.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Policymakers have long argued that breaking this cycle requires places where investors can set up quickly, operate under predictable rules and export at scale.



That argument has now gained a continental platform. The Liberia Special Economic Zones Authority (LSEZA) has secured membership in the Africa Economic Zones Organization (AEZO), the continent’s main network for the institutions that build and run economic zones. Authority officials say the move is designed to make Liberia West Africa’s leading destination for special economic zone (SEZ) investment.

A club of zone builders

AEZO is not a lender or a regulator. It is a peer network. The body was founded in November 2015 by Tanger Med, the Moroccan port and logistics complex that is itself one of Africa’s best-known economic zone success stories. It brings together the agencies and operators responsible for developing, managing and promoting economic zones across Africa, and it now counts roughly 80 members from more than 40 countries.

What members get is practical: a one-stop shop for information on partners and regulations, capacity-building, regional workshops and training.

Authorities that regulate and manage zones join as active members, with access to the full range of services and voting rights at AEZO’s annual General Assembly.

The scale of the network matters. AEZO has reported that Africa has about 203 active SEZs, with 73 more in development, spread across 47 of the continent’s 54 countries. Morocco, Nigeria, Egypt, Ethiopia and Kenya host the most. Liberia, a latecomer, now sits in the same room as the operators of those zones.

A long road to the starting line

Liberia’s zone ambitions are not new. The Liberia Free Zone Authority was created by an Act approved in July 1975, but it never transformed the economy. The modern framework came with the Special Economic Zones Act, adopted on October 9, 2017, which created LSEZA to oversee and regulate SEZs nationwide.

The law offers investors a defined package: special tax incentives, clear rights and obligations for licensees, developers and operators, the free transfer of funds from zone activities, and a one-stop shop in each zone for registrations, licences, permits and tax collection.

Yet for years, the Authority existed mostly on paper. Executive Chairman Prince Wreh has said that although LSEZA was established in 2017, it only became operational under President Joseph Nyuma Boakai. Wreh was appointed its first Executive Chairman in April 2024, followed by a Board of Directors. Since then, the Governance Commission has led a reform of the Authority’s internal structure aimed at efficiency, fiscal accountability and investor confidence.

Where the zones will rise

LSEZA says it is developing five potential zones, supported by land secured in six counties: Montserrado, Margibi, Grand Bassa, Grand Cape Mount, Bong and Nimba.

The most advanced concept is in Grand Bassa, where about 500 acres near the Port of Buchanan have been designated for export-oriented manufacturing, logistics and value-added industry. In Margibi, the Authority is pitching an “airport city” beside Roberts International Airport, combining residential, commercial, industrial, hospitality and recreational facilities.

The government frames the programme as part of Pillar 1, Economic Transformation, of its ARREST Agenda. The administration recently renewed its push to position the zones as platforms for investment, industrial expansion and employment, following a high-level engagement between LSEZA and the Minister of State for Presidential Affairs.

What membership could change for LSEZA

For a young authority with a limited track record, AEZO offers three things it cannot easily build alone.

The first is know-how. Morocco, Ethiopia, Rwanda and Ghana have each learned costly lessons about zone design, incentive structures and infrastructure sequencing. Peer exchange can help Liberia avoid repeating them.

The second is visibility. Investors scanning the continent for manufacturing sites tend to look first at countries already on the circuit. Membership places Liberia on that map.

The third is positioning under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). AEZO’s leadership has argued that African zones must connect quickly to global value chains as the AfCFTA takes hold. A Liberian zone that can export across the continent on preferential terms is a far more attractive proposition than one serving a domestic market of just over five million people.

What it could mean for Liberia

The promise is jobs. Liberia’s young, fast-growing workforce faces chronic underemployment, and SEZs are designed to concentrate the infrastructure, services and incentives that labour-intensive industries need. Spreading zones across six counties, rather than clustering them around Monrovia, could carry that opportunity to rural communities and ease pressure on the capital.

There is also the prospect of adding value at home: processing agricultural produce, timber and minerals before export rather than shipping them raw.

The caveats

Membership of a network is a beginning, not an outcome. Across Africa, many zones have underperformed, hampered by unreliable power, poor roads, weak port links and slow land titling. Liberia faces all of these constraints. Its zones will be judged not by declarations or affiliations, but by signed tenants, functioning one-stop shops, reliable electricity and the number of Liberians on factory payrolls.

Land is a particular sensitivity. Securing large tracts in six counties will require transparent engagement with host communities and respect for customary land rights if the zones are to avoid the disputes that have dogged earlier concessions.

For now, LSEZA has secured its seat at the continental table. The harder task, turning designated land into working industry, still lies ahead.

World.title: Cllr. Charlyne Brumskine Among Five Judges Sworn in at ECOWAS Court As Regional Bloc Chief Demands Impartial Justice
World.content:
ABUJA, Nigeria — Liberian lawyer, law professor and former vice-presidential candidate, Cllr. Charlyne M. Brumskine, has been sworn in as a judge of the Community Court of Justice of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), giving Liberia a seat on the regional bench for the Court’s 2026-2030 term.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Brumskine was one of five judges inducted on Tuesday, October 6, at the ECOWAS Commission headquarters in Abuja. Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, Chairman of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government, administered the oath of office.



Four other judges join her

The other newly inducted judges are Désiré Henri Aihou of Benin, Awa Bah of The Gambia, Henrietta Uzoamaka Didigu of Nigeria and Yaouza Ouro-Sama of Togo.

They succeed judges whose four-year mandates have ended: Ricardo Cláudio Monteiro Gonçalves of Cape Verde, Sengu Mohamed Koroma of Sierra Leone, Dupe Atoki of Nigeria, Gberi-Bè Ouattara of Côte d’Ivoire and Edward Amoako Asante of Ghana.

The new judges are expected to choose a president and vice-president from among themselves. Each will serve a two-year leadership term.

Chairman’s charge: impartiality and credibility

In his charge to the judges, President Faye urged them to uphold impartiality, independence and credibility as they take on the responsibility of administering justice in the West African bloc.

He said the judges must work to strengthen public confidence in the Court at a time when the region continues to face significant political, economic, security and environmental challenges.

About the Court

The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice, headquartered in Abuja, is the judicial organ of the regional bloc. It is mandated to hear disputes over the interpretation and application of ECOWAS legal instruments and to provide judicial protection within the regional community.

Who is Charlyne Brumskine?

Brumskine was appointed to the Court in July 2026 for the 2026-2030 term. Her induction marks a shift from national legal practice and politics to regional judicial service.

Educational background

She is a graduate of Columbia University and the Howard University School of Law in Washington, D.C. That training laid the groundwork for a career built on constitutional law, gender rights and governance reform.

Career in law

Brumskine is the founder and managing attorney of CMB Law Group, LLC, a law firm based in Monrovia. She has practiced as an attorney and advocate on constitutional questions, the rights of women and girls, and reforms aimed at strengthening governance in Liberia.

She has also worked in legal education, teaching law at the University of Liberia’s Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law, the country’s leading institution for legal training.

In 2022, she finished first in Liberia’s Supreme Court Bar Examination, a feat that made her one of the country’s most notable young legal professionals.

Through her legal and philanthropic work, she has promoted education for girls, expanded access to justice and encouraged political participation among women and youth in Liberia.

Political background

Brumskine’s political profile rose in the 2023 Liberian general election, when she served as vice-presidential candidate of the Collaborating Political Parties (CPP), running alongside standard bearer Alexander B. Cummings.

Her political roots run through her family. She is the daughter of Charles Brumskine, founder of the Liberty Party and a former President pro tempore of the Liberian Senate. She later became involved in Liberty Party affairs, particularly during the party’s internal leadership dispute.

A new chapter

Her appointment places a Liberian jurist on a court that plays a central role in protecting rights and interpreting the legal framework of the West African community. It comes as Liberia continues to engage more closely with regional institutions on governance, human rights, rule of law and justice.

For Brumskine, the new assignment moves her from national legal practice and politics to a broader regional judicial role, alongside judges responsible for advancing the rule of law across West Africa.

World.title: Liberia: Expelled Montserrado District 10 Lawmaker Who Vowed Never to Beg Pres. Boakai Now Calls for Reconciliation
World.content:
Liberians who have watched him for years know better than to bet on the obvious. This is a man who has been an ally, a critic, an exile from his own seat and a mystery, sometimes within the same year. Whether Sunday brings a handshake, a new fight or a surprise nobody has predicted, the oath is the part the country will remember

MONROVIA — In Liberian public life, a man’s word is currency, and a man’s oath is something close to a mortgage on his name. Yekeh Kolubah took out a heavy one. Now, with a press conference set for October 11, the expelled lawmaker is being asked whether he is about to default.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

‘The Street General’



Long before he held a legislative seat, Kolubah was a man of the street. His brand was never polish. It was volume, defiance and the ability to put a crowd where he wanted it. Politicians courted him for that reason, and none more usefully than Joseph Boakai.

By Kolubah’s own telling, the call came from Boakai’s farm. Former President George Weah was about to announce a political movement, and Boakai wanted the street answered. “Yekeh, you need to get into the streets,” Kolubah recalls being told. He says he went, and in 2023 he helped carry Boakai and the Unity Party past Weah.

Then, he says, the favor was forgotten. “Today, they have turned around and made me their enemy,” he complained in remarks he made while still in the House. He claimed that people who had worked with him were told to “go and support Joseph Boakai,” and he asked a question that has hung over the feud ever since: “Does President Joseph Boakai even know my true value?”

A quick turn

The honeymoon was short. Within four months of the new government taking office, Kolubah had become one of its loudest critics, accusing it of failing to fight corruption and repeating the vices it had condemned under Weah. The ruling establishment came to see him as a nemesis. The opposition, especially members of Weah’s Congress for Democratic Change, embraced him.

He then did something few expected: he publicly apologized to Weah, saying he had not known Boakai was “more corrupt.” He promised to help ensure that Boakai and the Unity Party do not win in 2029. It was the language of a man not just leaving a political marriage but burning the house down behind him.

April 17

Almost three years into his second term, the House voted. On April 17, 2026, 49 lawmakers expelled Kolubah, following controversy over remarks attributed to him about the Liberia-Guinea border dispute. It remains one of the most debated decisions of the 55th Legislature.

For Kolubah, the explanation was never about a border. He blamed Boakai for using the Legislature to engineer his removal, and the opposition backed that reading, calling it punishment for criticizing the presidency. Government officials rejected it flatly, saying he was removed for wrongdoing. Kolubah took the fight to the Supreme Court, where the full bench has yet to rule and his District 10 seat remains vacant.

The word “delete”

Expulsion did not soften him. After appearing before the Supreme Court on April 29, he told reporters he would “delete” President Boakai. He never said what he meant or what he planned to do. He also called Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Koung “former leaders,” as though the offices had already changed hands.

Then he went on the road. He toured almost all of Liberia’s 15 counties, and along the way he was widely reported to have sworn the oath that now defines the story: that the day he reconciles with Boakai, it is he who killed his mother. The exact wording has circulated in different versions, but the weight of it is not in dispute. In Liberian culture, few vows go deeper.

The turn

Then, three weeks before his announced return, a Facebook post from his media consultant said the former lawmaker was set to reconcile with the President. It cited his frustration with the “disintegration and unseriousness” of the opposition. His PRO, Samson Moseray, reportedly confirmed that a meeting with Boakai was being planned, saying Kolubah had chosen to “mend fences and put Liberia first.”

Kolubah fed the speculation by promising to return to the country on October 10 and address the media. It was classic Kolubah: a date, a stage and a mystery.

Two interviews, two moods

His two interviews this week offered very different readings. On Sunday, the Spoon TV show asked him bluntly whether he was coming home to beg the President for forgiveness. Kolubah’s opening line was that he regrets his relationship with Boakai. Peacemakers rarely begin that way, and that there was little softening as the conversation went on. On the border dispute, Kolubah did not retreat, maintaining that the land Liberia occupies belongs to Guinea.

On Tuesday, before appearing on OK FM’s Morning Rush, he posted his message. “There is nothing wrong with reconciliation,” it began. It spoke of division as one of the reasons the country remains where it is, of healthcare, roads, infrastructure and education, and of choosing “peace, dialogue, and national development over division.” It did not name Boakai.

On the program, host Clarence Jackson asked whether he was ready to reconcile with the President. “Anything is possible in this world,” Kolubah said. Asked about the oath, he deflected: “Wait for the press conference on Sunday, October 11, and see the outcome.”

Nothing is settled. No agreement has been made public, and the President has not given his account of any talks. All that is known is that on October 11, Kolubah has promised to speak.

Liberians who have watched him for years know better than to bet on the obvious. This is a man who has been an ally, a critic, an exile from his own seat and a mystery, sometimes within the same year. Whether Sunday brings a handshake, a new fight or a surprise nobody has predicted, the oath is the part the country will remember.
