World.title: Liberia: Nimbaians Overwhelmingly Back War and Economic Crimes Court in a New Survey
World.content:
Nine in every 10 people surveyed in Nimba County said they wanted to see a war crimes court.

Summary:

A FrontPage Africa/New Narratives survey of 100 Nimba residents found that 90% support establishing a War and Economic Crimes Court, with respondents saying those responsible for atrocities during Liberia’s wars should face due process and that victims deserve justice and the truth about what happened to their families.

For many Nimbaians, support for the court is rooted in personal experiences of war. Residents including Yah Dumbar and Jackson Beh described killings, displacement and loss of family members, saying accountability is necessary to address Liberia’s painful history and prevent a repetition of the violence.

The survey also raises questions about lawmakers’ claims that they need to consult constituents. Only three of the 100 Nimba respondents said they had heard of consultations by their representatives or senators. Some respondents said they would not support lawmakers who oppose the court, while Representative Nyah Garmie Flomo said he supports the court and plans to engage his constituents.

By Jerome Saye with New Narratives

SANNIQUELLIE, Nimba County—They are the second biggest voting bloc in the country. They’re also the former constituents of long-time senator, Prince Johnson who was the loudest opponent to a war and economic crimes court. He even threatened to take up arms if he were indicted. So the views of citizens of Nimba, almost two years after Johnson died, have been closely watched as the Liberian Legislature decides whether and in what form to hold a court.



A new survey by FrontPage Africa/New Narratives suggests the people of Nimba County overwhelmingly want to see a court established and will punish lawmakers at the ballot box if they do not get it. (The survey can be viewed here .)

“Let them people that do bad, bad thing in this war here where some of them are still alive, let them come and face the court,” said Yah Dumber, a 45-year-old small business owner in Gbedin Town. She said Nelson Gweh of ULIMO-K, Alhaji Kromah’s wing of the rebel faction led the invasion of the Central Agricultural Research Institute in 1994 when it was serving as the headquarters for the rival National Patriotic Front of Liberia. They killed her family members who were sheltering there. She has been aching for justice for more than 32 years.

The survey interviewed 100 people in Nimba’s seven administrative districts – Sanniquellie Mah, Saclepea Mah, Gbehlay Geh, Zoe Geh, Bain Gar, Yarpea Mah and Tapitta. Ninety percent or nine in every ten interviewees said they wanted the establishment of the court. The survey was not done under scientific conditions, but the overwhelming margin among the 100 people interviewed provides a strong indication of the views of the county.

Nine in every 10 people surveyed in Ganta, Bain Gar District said they wanted to see a war crimes court.

Jackson Beh, 40, is a farmer and a resident of Peelar Old Town in Yarpea Mah District. He said his brother Emmanuel Yaye was killed by a group of soldiers of the Krahn ethnic group serving with the government’s Arm Forces of Liberia in 1990.

Beh said his brother was on his way to celebrate a major achievement when he was killed.

“Our brother, he graduated from high school and he was trying to go to America,” he said. “He came home and showed us his graduation card. That was the last time we saw him. We never imagined that the graduation card he brought home would become one of the last memories we had of him.”

The survey comes as President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s administration pushes legislation for the establishment of the court which would prosecute those bearing the greatest responsibility for war crimes, crimes against humanity, economic crimes and serious human rights violations committed during Liberia’s conflicts from January 1979 to August 2003.

Six bills have been submitted to Legislature which is in the process of considering them and deciding what version of the court, if any, they will pass. Stakeholders say there is still considerable opposition from some lawmakers.

Stakeholders and the international community are urging the Legislature to pass a bill by December when Liberia takes its rotating seat in the presidency of the United Nations Security Council and the world’s eyes will be on it. They said it will give Liberia a chance to present a new face to the world to replace images of child soldiers that dominated global news coverage during the war.

The survey was part of a national survey of 1,150 people in 11 of Liberia’s 15 counties. Across the country, the number mirrored that in Nimba. Nine in every 10 people interviewed said they wanted to see a court.

For many Nimbaians, the issue is not simply about punishing individuals. It is also about knowing what happened to victims, establishing responsibility and ensuring that the violence of Liberia’s past is not repeated.

Madam Yah Dumbar spoke about the ongoing trauma of Liberia’s wars. She described how she and other people were forced to flee; walking barefoot from Gbarnga to Nimba, while seeing atrocities committed by ULIMO-K forces.

“The people came there, they destroyed so many things from us,” said Madam Dumbar. “I left from in Gbarnga with night gown, with one under cloth to come in Nimba, without wearing slipper. Some of our children them left in water [drowned]. They started catching us on the road and killing your husband and children in front of you.”

Her account reflects a broader sentiment expressed by participants: they said their support for a court is not driven by revenge, but by a desire for accountability and historical truth.

Advocates in Nimba welcomed the survey findings.

“Once ninety persons agreed for the War and Economic Crimes Court to come, it means that the advocacy we being doing it means that we are making progress,” said Carlton Zayzay, 39. And he had a warning for opponents.

“Those remaining ones that say War and Economic Crimes Court should not come in Liberia; it means that those people were not affected during the war time. Or those people don’t know about war. It means those people parents were not here.”

An overwhelming number of respondents at the Saclepea Road said they would not vote for lawmaker who did not back the court.

Joseph G. Suah, an attorney-at-law at the Eighth Judicial Circuit Court in Sanniquellie said the court would set important precedents for accountability and help strengthen the country’s justice system. “

“Nobody will commit crime and just go free. If you commit crime, you need to be given a due process of law,” Suah said. “And those that all involved should be arrested and go to court let them explain themselves as they have been accused.”

The survey also carried a warning for Nimba’s lawmakers including Nyah Garmie Flomo, Ernest Manseah, Samuel N. Brown Sr., Nehker E. Gaye, Kortor Kwagrue, Dorwohn Twain Gleekia, Musa Hassan Bility, Saye S. Mianah, Taa Z. Wongbe and senators Nya D. Twayen Jr. who will be seeking reelection in 2029. The overwhelming number of survey participants said they would not vote for them again if they did not support a court. Just seven said they would.

“I will not vote for any representative who will say no to the establishment of the War and Economic Crimes court,” said Zayzay. “They are on their way already before 2029 if they don’t pass the bill.”

Nyah Garmie Flomo, Sr. Nimba representative

The survey also exposed potentially misleading statements on the part of lawmakers. They went on break in July without passing the war crimes court bill claiming they needed to consult their constituents before the house reopened in October. But of the 100 people interviewed, just three said they had heard of any consultation by their senators or representatives about the proposed legislation.

Nyah Garmie Flomo, Sr., Nimba County District Two representative, said he supports the establishment of the court but admitted that he has not consulted constituents. Flomo said that he and colleagues will consult constituents once they have a chance to understand it.

“I have a plan: before our break can be over, certainly I will be having engagement with my people and one of the things we will be discussing is the War and Economic Crimes Court,” said Flomo. “If, for example, a document is introduced, you need to fully understand the document because you have to explain to your people. So, a document that was introduced to us about two months ago, you don’t expect all of the lawmakers on their feet passing with the document.”

Nimba citizens are watching what happens next. But experts say the message from the survey is clear: pass the law, consult the people and move Liberia’s long-delayed search for justice forward or pay a price in the next election.

World.title: Liberia: Amid Kemayah’s Fiery Defense, Lawyer Accuses AREPT of Witness Tampering; Task Force Denies Allegation, Wants Claim Tested in Court
World.content:
Monrovia – A troubling confrontation outside the courtroom has opened a new front in the criminal trial, with defense lawyer Gbawou Kowou accusing the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Taskforce AREPT of intimidating or improperly engaging defense witnesses after they testified.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The drama unfolded as former Foreign Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah insisted on the witness stand that he “did not steal one grain” of the Saudi-donated rice.



AREPT has categorically denied the allegation, saying the witnesses were not summoned for questioning, were not interviewed, and were immediately asked to leave its premises after agency lawyers discovered that they had recently appeared in court as subpoenaed defense witnesses.

The dispute, coming as prosecutors prepare to present rebuttal witnesses in the Saudi rice case, has raised a question over the treatment of witnesses in an ongoing criminal proceeding, and whether witnesses who have already testified for the defense can be approached or brought to a prosecutorial agency without their lawyers being informed, and concern over where legitimate investigation ends and improper interference begins.

The answer, both sides now said, should come from the court.

AREPT, in a statement signed by its Public Relations Officer, Joseph F. Daniels, said the incident resulted from a misunderstanding rather than an attempt to interfere with testimony.

According to the task force, a potential witness who had previously provided a statement during the investigation was asked to appear at its office along with other persons familiar with the Saudi rice matter.

The agency said the potential witness arrived with two individuals whom he identified as persons knowledgeable about the matter.

AREPT said its lawyers did not initially know that the two individuals had recently appeared before Criminal Court “C” as defense witnesses.

“Upon recognizing them, AREPT lawyers immediately asked the two individuals to leave the premises,” the statement said.

The agency stressed that the witnesses “were not invited by AREPT, were not interviewed, and no statement was taken from them.”

AREPT therefore rejected the accusation that its lawyers threatened, intimidated or attempted to influence the witnesses.

The agency challenged the defense to take the allegation before the trial judge.

“If defense counsel has evidence of witness tampering or intimidation, that evidence should be presented to the court, where such allegations can be properly addressed,” AREPT said.

But Kowou is not backing away.

The defense lawyer has characterized the circumstances surrounding the witnesses’ presence at the AREPT compound as serious, particularly because the individuals had already testified on behalf of the accused.

Kowou said the witnesses included members of the Group of 77 and members of the community of persons living with disabilities who had appeared before Criminal Court “C” as defense witnesses.

According to the lawyer, the witnesses told him they had been pressured or threatened to report to AREPT following their appearance in court.

Kowou subsequently went to the taskforce’s headquarters in Paynesville, where he livestreamed the confrontation and demanded access to the compound.

“I’m live at AREPT. Witnesses who testified on our behalf yesterday were brought here and threatened,” Kowou said during the broadcast.

At another point, he accused officials of locking the facility’s gate.

“They have locked the gate. The witnesses are in there,” he said. “If the witnesses are not there, open the gate.”

The confrontation eventually drew the attention of Liberia National Police officers, with Kowou continuing to insist that the matter involved possible interference with witnesses in an ongoing criminal proceeding.

He was later allowed into the compound and subsequently taken to a police station following the confrontation.

Kowou later said AREPT officials characterized the incident as a misunderstanding.

But the defense lawyer maintained that the circumstances remained troubling.

Harassing Vulnerable Witnesses?

The controversy is particularly sensitive because of the identity of some of the witnesses at the center of the dispute.

Kowou said the witnesses were drawn from vulnerable and organized community groups and had appeared in court to give evidence for the accused.

For the defense, the central issue is not simply whether AREPT lawyers spoke to the witnesses.

It is whether any contact occurred in circumstances capable of influencing, intimidating or otherwise affecting witnesses who had already placed their testimony on the official record.

That distinction could become important as the matter moves before the trial court.

Under Liberia’s Penal Law, witness tampering is a serious offense where prohibited conduct is used with the purpose of influencing testimony or preventing or altering a person’s participation in an official proceeding.

Kowou did not speak further on the next course of action, but a defense lawyer who prefers anonymity told FrontPageAfrica that the defense team has already taken action against the alleged situation, in line with the laws of Liberia.

However, an accusation of witness tampering is not itself proof that tampering occurred.

AREPT’s position is that its lawyers did precisely the opposite of what Kowou alleged; once they realized that the individuals were defense witnesses, they asked them to leave.

The agency said no interview took place, no statement was taken, and no effort was made to influence their testimony.

The competing accounts now create a factual question that may have to be resolved through evidence.

A Trial Already Defined By Contested Evidence

The witness controversy comes against the backdrop of an increasingly combative Saudi rice trial, where the prosecution and defense have presented sharply different accounts of how a Saudi government-to-government donation was received, stored, transferred and ultimately distributed.

The case involves 13 former government officials accused of corruption-related offenses arising from the handling of the Saudi-donated rice.

The defense has consistently challenged the prosecution’s interpretation of the documentary record, the quantity of rice received, the role of the National Disaster Management Agency, the involvement of the General Services Agency and the authority exercised by officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

That battle intensified when Kemayah himself took the witness stand.

Kemayah: ‘I Did Not Steal One Grain’

Kemayah delivered a forceful and emotional defense of his role in securing and managing the humanitarian rice project.

His central message was blunt: “I did not steal one grain of rice.”

The former minister acknowledged that he personally negotiated with Saudi authorities to secure the donation.

But he rejected the prosecution’s characterization of his involvement as an abuse of authority.

Kemayah told the court, in substance, that his intervention was motivated by the need to secure food assistance for vulnerable Liberians.

He said the government could have routed the rice through institutions such as the Liberian National Red Cross Society or the World Food Programme but instead selected NDMA to handle the humanitarian component.

For Kemayah, that decision undermines any suggestion that he secretly seized control of the project.

“I negotiated this rice,” he emphasized, arguing that no one ordered him to seek the donation and that he took the initiative because Liberians needed assistance.

The Saudi Video

Kemayah also relied heavily on a video documentary showing what he described as the formal signing ceremony between the Government of Liberia and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

He presented the footage as evidence that the rice donation was the product of an official government-to-government arrangement.

According to his testimony, the documentary showed Liberian officials and Saudi representatives participating in the process surrounding the donation.

Kemayah said Saudi representatives were assured that the rice would reach vulnerable Liberians rather than government officials.

For the former minister, that assurance is important because it contradicts any theory that the project was created as a mechanism for personal enrichment.

“Where Is the Note of Exchange?”

Kemayah also seized on testimony from Acting Foreign Affairs Minister Etta Davies, who reportedly told the court that officials searching the Ministry of Foreign Affairs failed to locate the Note of Exchange connected to the Saudi donation.

The former minister questioned how the absence of a copy from Liberia’s current ministry records could invalidate the existence of the diplomatic transaction.

He argued that because Saudi Arabia remains a diplomatic partner of Liberia, missing government-to-government documentation could be sought through diplomatic channels.

The issue has now become another point of contention over the reliability and completeness of government records.

The 29,412-Bags Question

Perhaps one of the most key factual battles in Kemayah’s testimony centered on the quantity of rice.

Kemayah maintained that 29,412 bags of 25-kilogram rice were received from Saudi Arabia.

The defense has repeatedly challenged figures presented by the prosecution, arguing that the physical quantity of rice, its monetary value, and the logistics surrounding its transportation and storage must be reconciled with the documentary evidence.

Kemayah questioned figures he considered inconsistent with the actual shipment.

For the defense, the dispute over quantity is not merely mathematical.

It goes directly to the prosecution’s theory of what was allegedly diverted or unlawfully handled.

‘To Rescue the Rice’

Kemayah also rejected the allegation that he improperly interfered with NDMA’s statutory responsibilities.

He relied on testimony from former GSA Director-General Mary T. Broh and former NDMA Board Chairman Varney A. Sirleaf concerning the movement of rice from NDMA facilities to GSA warehouses.

Kemayah characterized the decision as an effort to protect the rice from deteriorating because of storage concerns.

He described his intervention as an attempt to “rescue the rice.”

He argued that the movement involved several government officials and institutions and was therefore not a unilateral decision taken secretly by him.

Kemayah further pointed to NDMA officials’ participation in meetings concerning the rice as evidence that the agency’s statutory responsibilities had not been taken over.

‘I Never Distributed A Grain’

The former minister was equally categorical in denying personal involvement in the distribution of the rice.

He told the court that he never recommended, authorized or personally distributed a single grain of the donated rice.

He challenged the prosecution to produce documentary evidence proving otherwise.

“If there is anything, I am prepared beyond this case to redeem my name,” he maintained.

‘Conspire With Who? Rice?’

Kemayah also attacked the conspiracy allegation.

With visible emotion, he questioned why he would conspire with others over humanitarian rice that he had personally worked to secure.

“Conspire with who? Rice? For what?” he asked rhetorically.

He maintained that the project involved multiple government institutions and officials and that the evidence should be viewed in the context of a government humanitarian operation rather than an individual scheme.

His Mother’s Death

The testimony also took a deeply personal turn when Kemayah recounted the circumstances surrounding his arrest and the subsequent death of his mother.

He said armed security personnel arrived at his residence to execute a search and arrest while his mother was staying with him.

According to Kemayah, his mother suffered from a pressure-related illness and was deeply distressed by the events surrounding his arrest.

She was later taken to a Catholic hospital but, he said, never fully recovered.

Kemayah carefully stopped short of directly accusing security personnel of causing her death.

Instead, he maintained that the emotional trauma surrounding his arrest contributed to the deterioration of her condition.

‘This Is Not My Area’

Kemayah ultimately returned to the central theme of his defense, that stealing was not his motive and that his involvement in the Saudi rice project was part of his responsibility as Foreign Minister to mobilize international support for Liberia.

He cited his administration’s efforts to pursue reforms at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, engage international partners, and improve services for ordinary Liberians.

He maintained that the Saudi rice project belonged within that record of public service.

“Stealing is not my area,” he declared.

But the prosecution continues to maintain that the defendants unlawfully handled and diverted a substantial portion of the Saudi donation.

The New Battle, Witnesses

Now, as the prosecution prepares to present rebuttal evidence, another battle has emerged, this time over the treatment of witnesses.

The defense said witnesses who had already testified were taken to or summoned to AREPT’s headquarters and subjected to pressure.

AREPT said that account is false.

The taskforce insists that the witnesses were not invited, questioned or interviewed and that its lawyers asked them to leave as soon as they recognized them as defense witnesses.

That leaves the court with a potentially consequential question of what actually happened inside and around the AREPT compound, and was any attempt made to influence witnesses who had already testified.

The answer could determine whether the episode remains a heated dispute outside the courtroom, or becomes a formal evidentiary and legal issue inside it.

For now, both sides are pointing toward the same place for resolution, the court.

And with Kemayah fighting to dismantle the prosecution’s case from the witness stand while his lawyer raised allegations of possible witness interference outside the courtroom, the Saudi rice trial has entered an increasingly volatile phase, one in which the credibility of witnesses, the integrity of government records and the conduct of the parties themselves may prove just as consequential as the rice at the center of the case.

The final determination remains with Criminal Court “C” and the jury after consideration of the evidence presented by both the prosecution and defense.

World.title: Liberia: As Talk of a Truce with President Boakai Swirls, Ex-Lawmaker Kolubah Says He Regrets His Relationship with the Liberian Leader
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberian politics has no shortage of dramatic turnarounds, but few would have raised eyebrows like this one. Yekeh Kolubah, the outspoken former Montserrado County District 10 representative, was said to be preparing to sit down with President Joseph Boakai, the leader he backed in 2023 and later turned on.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The rumor ran for days. Then Kolubah went on air and, intentionally or not, poured cold water on it.



A Rumor with Official Fingerprints

The talk did not come from nowhere. It began with a Facebook post by Kolubah’s own media consultant, which said the former lawmaker was ready to reconcile with the President. The post blamed his frustration on what the office called the “disintegration and unseriousness” of the opposition.

His PRO, Samson Moseray, reportedly backed it up. A meeting with the President was being arranged, he said, and Kolubah had chosen to “mend fences and put Liberia first.”

Kolubah himself added fuel. He has repeatedly said he will return to Liberia on October 10 to address the media on the matter. For a politician known for theatrical announcements, that was enough to convince many that something big was coming.

Sunday Night on Spoon TV

On Sunday, the Spoon Show gave him the chance to settle the question. The host asked bluntly whether he was coming home to “beg the president for forgiveness.” Kolubah’s opening line was that he regrets his relationship with President Boakai. Peacemakers rarely start that way. Expressing regret over a past association is the language of someone closing a chapter, not reopening it. And as the conversation went on, there was little sign of the softening one would expect from a man about to extend a hand.

The Statement That Started It All

To understand why reconciliation looks so hard, one has to go back to April 17, 2026, when 49 lawmakers voted to expel Kolubah from the House of Representatives. The move followed uproar over remarks attributed to him about the Liberia–Guinea border dispute. It remains one of the most debated decisions of the 55th Legislature.

On Spoon TV, the host pressed him on the subject. Kolubah held his ground and maintained that the land Liberia occupies belongs to Guinea.

In other words, the position that cost him his seat is one he has just repeated in public. It is hard to picture a reconciliation that leaves that issue untouched. If Kolubah has not changed his view, and his words suggest he has not, then the cause of the breakup has not gone away. It has simply been restated.

An Oath That Raises the Stakes

The most dramatic piece of the puzzle is a pledge Kolubah is reported to have made. According to those accounts, he has said that the day he reconciles with President Boakai, it will be him who killed his mother.

Whatever one makes of the rhetoric, the vow changes the calculation. Most political disputes can be patched up with a communiqué, a handshake, or a quiet word from respected elders. A promise that invokes a mother’s memory is different. Breaking it would hand his opponents a weapon they could use for years. For a figure who has built his brand on defiance, it could cost more than any seat in the Legislature.

Weariness With Allies, not a Change of Heart

Since his expulsion, Kolubah has toured the country alongside the opposition and spoken harshly of the government. His camp’s recent message about the opposition’s disintegration points to growing disillusionment with that coalition.

That could explain why the reconciliation story gained traction. A politician who feels let down by his allies might start looking for a way out. But there is a difference between being fed up with friends and warming to a former benefactor turned adversary. So far, nothing Kolubah has said publicly suggests he has made that leap.

The Empty Chair in District 10

The saga also unfolds against a constitutional backdrop that critics say is being ignored. Article 37 of the 1986 Constitution says that when a legislative seat falls vacant through death, resignation, expulsion or otherwise, the presiding officer must notify the National Elections Commission within 30 days. The Commission must then hold a by-election within 90 days, unless general elections fall within that window.

Nearly 170 days have passed since the expulsion. Commentators say no replacement has been chosen and that the presiding officer, Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon, has apparently not notified the Commission. For residents of District 10, that means months without a voice in the House. Some observers suspect the vacancy may be part of the political bargaining, a seat left open while the larger drama plays out.

There are reasons to take the reconciliation talk seriously. It came from Kolubah’s own office. It was framed around national interest. Kolubah has a history with the Unity Party, and the October 10 media address suggests an announcement of some kind is on the way.

But the case against is stronger. He opened his Spoon TV interview with regret over his relationship with the President. He has refused to retreat on the border claim. He has reportedly bound himself with a deeply personal vow. And every grievance that produced the split remains in place.

The most likely outcome, if anything happens at all, is something smaller than a true reconciliation: a conversation framed around peace and national unity, with neither side conceding much. A full return to the President’s camp would require Kolubah to unsay nearly everything he said on Sunday night.

On October 10, the country will find out which Kolubah steps off the plane: the peacemaker his office has described or the combatant who spoke on Spoon TV. For now, his own words are the best evidence available, and they point firmly toward no.

World.title: Liberia: A Government Assessment Shows Liberia Is 69 Percent Ready for Ebola. Frontline Health Workers Say the Missing 31 Percent Matters
World.content:
Dr. Sia Wata Camanor, National Public Health Institute of Liberia’s acting director general, spoke at the Ministry of Information press briefing this month, where she released the findings of the Institute’s Ebola preparedness assessment.

Summary:

• A nationwide Ebola preparedness assessment found Liberia 69 percent ready overall, while logistics scored only 47 percent, leaving major gaps in equipment, supplies, isolation facilities and training.

• Frontline health workers say those logistics gaps can mean the difference between safely isolating a suspected patient and exposing staff, other patients and communities.



• Health authorities say they are tightening procedures at major points of entry, but the next steps, funding and timetable for closing the gaps remain unclear.

By Augusta S. Lafalay, senior reporter with New Narratives

Liberia has stronger disease surveillance and laboratory systems than it did during the 2014 Ebola crisis, but the country is still only 69 percent prepared to respond to another outbreak, according to a nationwide Ebola preparedness assessment by the National Public Health Institute of Liberia. The weakest area was logistics, which scored just 47 percent.

At a September press conference to release the findings of the assessment, Dr. Sia Wata Camanor, acting Public Health Institute director general, said the country was in the “medium” preparedness range. “We don’t have the tools. We don’t have the materials,” she said. Though the risk remains low, she warned against complacency.

Health experts welcomed the government’s transparency, but they said that the number is more than a technical score. It points to shortages and weaknesses in the things health workers would need first if a suspected Ebola patient arrived at a clinic or hospital: personal protective equipment, functioning isolation space, transport, laboratory supplies, ambulances, trained staff, and a system able to move those resources quickly.

“When we say there is a lack of logistics, it can sound like we are simply talking about supplies. But for a health worker, it is much bigger than that,” said Lela Dolo, executive director of Help a Mother and Newborn in Liberia and a medical student training to become a doctor. “Do I have the personal protective equipment I need? Can a suspected patient be safely isolated and referred? Can a specimen be transported quickly? Is there an ambulance or vehicle available? Can the response team reach the community?”

The question is foremost in the minds of the country’s healthcare workers who bore the brunt of the disease in 2014. If an Ebola case reaches the country, gaps could put frontline workers at risk, slow the response and increase the chance that an infection spreads beyond a health facility and into communities.

The National Public Health Institute of Liberia’s assessment, conducted across all 15 counties, examined surveillance, points of entry, emergency operations centers, laboratories, isolation facilities, county health teams and rapid response structures. Health authorities have said surveillance officers and rapid response teams are operating nationwide, while laboratory testing and specimen transport have improved. But officials also identified the need to replenish protective equipment, maintain isolation facilities, run more simulation exercises and continue training newly deployed health workers.

For Liberia, the warning carries a painful history. During the 2014-2015 epidemic, 378 health care workers in Liberia had confirmed Ebola and 192 died, according to a U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention review . Weak infection-prevention systems left health facilities vulnerable, with many lacking triage and isolation protocols, protective gear, or running water early in the crisis.

The toll weakened a health system that was already short of skilled workers. The infected health workers represented about 12 percent of Liberia’s confirmed Ebola cases, even though health workers made up only a small share of the population. Early in the epidemic, many facilities closed after transmission occurred among staff. Health workers who did not feel protected, walked away.

Dolo said the Liberian health system has learned from the last epidemic and has stronger surveillance and response systems. Her concern is whether those systems are backed by the practical resources needed when an emergency begins.

“You can train health workers to recognize Ebola and follow the right protocols, but knowledge alone cannot protect them,” she said. “They also need the tools and systems to safely do what they have been trained to do.”

Joseph Somwarbi, a pharmacologist and former head of the Legislature’s health committee, said logistics failures can quickly become safety failures. He said all parts of the chain must work together.

A shortage in one part of that chain can put frontline staff in a dangerous position. If protective gear is insufficient health workers may have to delay care or risk exposure. If laboratory agents or specimen transport are unavailable, confirmation can take longer. If supplies are concentrated in Monrovia, rural facilities can lose valuable time waiting for materials to arrive.

“Delay in procurement, delay in transportation means no access,” Somwarbi said. “No access means not available. Not available means you’re not prepared.”

Those weaknesses become especially serious in an Ebola outbreak, he said, because the first response begins before laboratory confirmation. A patient with symptoms and a relevant exposure history must be identified, separated from other patients, reported to surveillance teams, safely assessed and tested, while health workers use infection-prevention measures. Contacts may then need to be identified and monitored.

“When the system is not prepared, even 24 hours is too much of a time for disease to spread,” Somwarbi said.

The threat of Ebola remains constant. The latest outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (the country’s 17th outbreak) has reached 7,890 confirmed cases and 3,799 deaths, according to the World Health Organization , making it the second largest outbreak after the 2014 outbreak in West Africa. Experts said cuts to international aid, especially by the United States, have dramatically reduced the capacity to contain the virus. That same outcome would likely play out in Liberia, which relied heavily on U.S. help to stamp out the 2014 outbreak, were the virus to reach the country.

Liberia has responded to the DRC’s outbreak by increasing screening and surveillance at airports, seaports and land crossings. Travelers are required to cooperate with screening and reporting procedures. Procedures, health experts said, are in place to make clear who screens travelers, what happens when someone meets a suspected-case definition, how referral and transport should work, and how information moves from border health staff to surveillance and response teams.

But the country has struggled with capacities at points of entry. A 2024 peer-reviewed evaluation of eight designated Liberian points of entry found gaps in areas including quarantine, communication, water, electricity, transport, and trained personnel.

Experts said the importance of clear procedures was underlined in May, when health authorities monitored 16 travelers arriving from countries of concern. None developed Ebola symptoms during the required 21-day follow-up, according to the Institute. But a WhatsApp voice message circulated claiming suspected Ebola patients had been taken to John F. Kennedy Medical Center, sparking fear and mistrust in the community.

Experts said the incident highlighted a basic communication challenge: officials needed to clearly communicate to the people what they were doing to increase trust. Dr. Camanor’s press conference and transparency about the assessment were a sign the government has learned from the May experience.

From here, Camanor said the assessment findings would be shared with the Ministry of Health, World Health Organization and other partners, and that the National Public Health Institute planned to take the findings to the Ministry of Finance, Cabinet and Legislature to seek support for closing the gaps.

In May, Dr. Louise Kpoto, the health minister, told lawmakers that the Ebola preparedness budget was $US4.2 million.

FrontPage Africa/New Narratives contacted Dr. Kpoto and National Public Health Institute leadership by telephone and email seeking answers on what the government will do next, whether any of the $US4.2 million has been approved or released, a timetable for addressing the gaps, and how progress will be measured. Neither responded by the publication deadline.

Somwarbi said a follow-up assessment would be one way to show whether new spending improves preparedness. That would allow the public and health workers to compare the current weaknesses with what has been fixed, rather than relying only on promises or budget figures.

For Dolo, the practical test is simpler. “If the first suspected Ebola patient walks into a health facility tomorrow, does the health worker who meets that patient have everything they need to recognize the risk, protect themselves, protect other patients and activate the response system immediately?” she asked. “If the answer is not yet a confident yes, then there is still work to do.”

World.title: WORLD BANK UPGRADES ZAMBIA’S GROWTH PROSPECTS
World.content:
Zambia is among the Sub-Saharan African countries whose economic growth prospects have been upgraded by the World Bank.

The World Bank says economic growth in the region is expected to rise from 4.1 percent in 2025 to 4.3 percent in 2026.

It says Zambia is among the countries recording an improved growth outlook.

The Bank says the outlook is being supported by stronger domestic demand, improved economic resilience and increased investment in digital technologies and the global energy transition.

However, the World Bank says economic growth across the region remains insufficient to create enough jobs for Africa’s rapidly growing labour force or significantly reduce extreme poverty.

World Bank Chief Economist for the Africa Region Andrew Dabalen says the next challenge is to turn economic growth into more jobs and better opportunities.

Mr. Dabalen says investment in the foundations of an Artificial Intelligence-ready economy could help African countries increase productivity, promote innovation and accelerate economic transformation.

The World Bank says countries such as Zambia will need to invest in reliable electricity, affordable internet connectivity, digital skills, quality data and other infrastructure to take advantage of Artificial Intelligence.

It says Zambia and other countries can also benefit from regional cooperation and stronger digital policies to expand AI-enabled solutions and create more employment opportunities.

The World Bank has, however, warned that rising global fuel, fertiliser and food prices, geopolitical tensions, climate-related shocks and tighter financial conditions remain risks to the region’s economic outlook.

World.title: KALABA BACKS REMOVAL OF LUSAKA STREET VENDORS
World.content:
Citizens First President Harry Kalaba has commended Lusaka Mayor Chitambala Mwewa for removing street vendors from undesignated areas in Lusaka’s Central Business District.

Mr. Kalaba says the move is necessary to restore cleanliness, order and dignity to the capital city.

He says good leadership should be acknowledged regardless of political differences when decisions are made in the interest of residents.

Mr. Kalaba, however, says the Lusaka City Council must ensure that traders affected by the exercise are provided with safe, accessible and affordable trading spaces.

He says keeping Lusaka clean should not be treated as a political issue, but as a matter of civic pride, public health and responsibility to future generations.

Meanwhile, Kafue West Member of Parliament and UPND Lusaka Provincial Chairperson Obvious Mwaliteta has backed efforts to restore cleanliness and order in Lusaka’s Central Business District.

Mr. Mwaliteta says maintaining cleanliness in the Lusaka CBD is among the core responsibilities of the Mayor’s office and should receive the support of all well-meaning Zambians.

He says the Mayor has the full support of the UPND Lusaka Provincial leadership in restoring cleanliness and order in the city.

Mr. Mwaliteta has called for the approach being implemented in Lusaka to be extended to other towns and cities across the country, including Kafue West.

World.title: Media advised on upcoming by – elections
World.content:
Ministry of Information and Media Permanent Secretary, Thabo Kawana, has urged the media to uphold accuracy and truthfulness, and to verify information before reporting, as they cover the upcoming by-elections scheduled for November 5th, 2026.

Mr Kawana says journalists have a responsibility to act as a mirror of society by providing the public with credible and factual information rather than just participating in the electoral process.

The Permanent Secretary was speaking at a press briefing organised by CIC Press in Lusaka today.

Mr Kawana stressed that the media has an important role to play in keeping the public informed, particularly at a time when social media platforms are awash with unverified information and propaganda.

“Your role is to give coverage so that the rest of the country remains informed with verified, critical and truthful information,” Mr Kawana said.

He also cautioned media organisations against giving prominence to sources whose information could promote disunity or harm other people.

Mr Kawana said the media should instead contribute to national unity by providing responsible reporting and information that contributes positively to national development.

He further noted that the media also has a role to play in advancing the government’s Grow Zambia Agenda by asking what individuals, groups and organisations can do to contribute to national development.

The Permanent Secretary said the growth of the country’s economy requires collaborative efforts between the public and private sectors.

Meanwhile, CIC Director, Edward Makayi, disclosed that his organisation has deployed 54 journalists and media professionals to cover by- elections in 11 selected districts of the country.

Mr Makayi said CIC will cover the Mandevu parliamentary by -elections in Lusaka, Lumezi North constituency in Eastern Province, alongside 10 other local government elections in selected parts of the country.

He further called for enhanced engagement between government and the media to strengthen collaboration and improve the working environment for journalists.

The Electoral Commission of Zambia set November 5th, 2026, as date for the holding of the Mbala Mayoral Election in Mbala District of Northern Province, the Lumezi Parliamentary Election in Lumezi Constituency of Lumezi District, Eastern Province, and the Mandevu Parliamentary Election in Mandevu Constituency, Lusaka District of Lusaka Province.

On the same day, the Commission will also conduct elections in 11 wards across the country.

World.title: MoH calls for heightened cancer awareness, screening
World.content:
The Ministry of Health has called for heightened cancer screening and awareness as Zambia continues to record numbers of cancer cases and deaths annually.

Cancer Diseases Hospital Health Promotions Officer, Chosha Mulungu, says Zambia records about 16,000 new cancer cases each year, with more than 9,000 people dying from the disease, underscoring the urgent need to strengthen early detection and community awareness.

Mr Mulungu says the Ministry of Health and Cancer Diseases Hospital cannot address the cancer burden alone, hence the need for partnerships with organisations such as House of Hope Africa, to take screening and health information closer to communities.

Mr Mulungu was speaking during a health expo organised by House of Hope Africa in Mtendere East, where members of the public were offered free cancer screening and health education.

He said the National Cancer Control Strategic Plan goes beyond treatment and focuses on awareness and early detection, which he said are critical to improving treatment outcomes.

Mr Mulungu stated that partnerships with organisations such as House of Hope Africa provide an important platform for reaching people who may not have adequate information about cancer and other non-communicable diseases.

He further attributed the rising cancer burden to lifestyle factors, including unhealthy diets, smoking and alcohol consumption.

“Let me mention that cervical cancer remains the leading type of cancer among women, followed by breast cancer, while prostate cancer is the leading type of cancer among men,” he said.

Meanwhile, House of Hope Africa Founder, Michael Mesiti, said the organisation has been working with Cancer Diseases Hospital for nine years, supporting patients and caregivers.

Mr Mesiti said the health expo, held as part of Cancer Awareness Month, is providing cervical, prostate and breast cancer screening, alongside other medical services.

He encouraged members of the public to take advantage of free screening opportunities being offered throughout October, saying early detection can help save lives.

“Avoid home traditional treatment once you notice pain in your breasts, cervix, or any sensitive organ, instead visit the clinic for screening,” said Mr Mesiti.

And community member, Esther Daka, encouraged residents to make regular cancer screening a priority and to go to health facilities to know more about their health status.

World.title: Govt. refuses false claims of ban of church meetings and public gatherings
World.content:
Government has noted information circulating on social media alleging that Secretary to the Cabinet, Patrick Kangwa, has directed the suspension of church meetings, overnight prayers, crusades and other public gatherings until 1st November, 2026.

Information and Media Permanent Secretary, Thabo Kawana has clarified that no such directive has been issued by the Secretary to the Cabinet or government.

In a statement issued to the media this evening, Mr Kawana said the information circulating on social media is therefore false and does not represent a government decision or directive.

The Permanent has stressed that government remains committed to upholding the constitution and the laws of Zambia, including the rights and freedoms relating to freedom of conscience, religion, or belief and peaceful assembly.

He said government has in this regard noted with concern the attribution of the alleged directive to the Secretary to the Cabinet and urges members of the public to verify information purporting to originate from government institutions or public officials before sharing or acting upon it.

Mr Kawana has further encouraged the media and other persons engaged in the dissemination of information to verify such information with the relevant authorities before publication or circulation.

He reiterated that official government decisions and directives are communicated through established government channels and authorised spokespersons.

Mr Kawana has therefore encouraged members of the public to rely on official government communication channels for accurate and verified information on government policies, decisions, and directives.

He has assured that the government will continue to provide timely and accurate information to the public on matters of national interest.

World.title: 28-year-old man dies mysteriously in Nakonde
World.content:
A 28-year-old man of Katozi Village in Chieftainess Waitwika’s Chiefdom in Nakonde District has died under unclear circumstances at a liquor store where he used to work from.

Muchinga Province Police Commissioner, Lubinda Mayamba confirmed the incident in a press statement made to the media.

Mr Mayamba identified the deceased as Cletus Bwalya.

He said brief facts are that, the now deceased was employed by his elder brother, Chrispine Mulenga, owner and operator of a liquor store at Katozi Village.

He added that the deceased had been working at the said liquor store since 10th June, 2026 and had been sleeping there.

“The deceased used to sleep at the liquor Shop due to the fact that he usually knocked off late and feared being attacked while returning home,” he said

The Police Commissioner alleged that on 4th October, 2026 at around 17:00 hours, liquor store owner Chrispine Mulenga checked on the deceased at the liquor store and found him selling beer and appearing to be in good health, saying the deceased did not complain of any illness or discomfort.

Mr Mayamba disclosed that the incident occurred between 4th October, 2026 at around 17:00 hours and 5th October, 2026 at around 06:00 hours, at Katozi Village in Nakonde district.

However, on 5th October, 2026 at around 06:00 hours, Chrispine Mulenga went to the liquor store to conduct a stock taking exercise with his younger brother, the now deceased, upon arrival, he found the door to the liquor store widely open, with music still playing inside.

Mr Mayamba said upon checking the premises, he found his younger brother lying motionless on the floor and subsequently discovered that he was dead.

The matter was then reported at Nakonde Police Station.

Acting on the report, Mr Mayamba said officers rushed to the scene, and it was established that the body of the deceased was found lying on the floor inside the liquor store, facing upwards, near the counter.

Mr Mayamba stated that after conducting a physical inspection of the body no visible physical injuries were observed.

He further said the body of the deceased is currently in Nakonde Urban Health Centre Mortuary awaiting a post-mortem examination to ascertain the actual cause of death.

An inquiry file has since been opened, and investigations are underway.

World.title: Eastern Province steps up world food day preparations
World.content:
Eastern Province has heightened preparations for the 2026 World Food Day commemoration slated for 16th October.

This year’s provincial commemoration will be held at Chipata Trades Training Institute, under the coordination of the Eastern Province Administration.

Provincial Food and Nutrition Coordinator, Norman Siame, confirmed the development in an interview with the media in Chipata.

Mr Siame said the province has partnered with the Provincial Nutrition Coordinating Committee (PNCC), Ministry of Health, German Corporation for International Cooperation (GIZ), Food and Agriculture (FAO), World Food Programme (WFP) and other stakeholders.

He said the commemoration aims to promote good nutrition, dietary diversity and sustainable food systems in the region where stunting still stands at 32 percent.

“The stakeholders are eager to promote nutrition in the province. We want to move from just food availability to nutritious food,” Mr Siame said.

He disclosed that a number of activities have been lined up to mark the day, including exhibition and cooking demonstrations of local nutritious foods such as orange maize, beans, groundnuts, soyabeans, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes, and traditional vegetables.

Mr Siame said agricultural field visits will also be conducted in Chipata District to showcase climate-smart farming and bio fortified crops supported by GIZ and the Ministry of Agriculture.

He added that school activities have been included, with learners from selected primary and secondary schools expected to present poems, songs and drama performances on nutrition and food security.

According to Mr Siame, the Ministry of Health will take centre stage during the commemoration to conduct educational sessions on healthy diets, infant and young child feeding, and prevention of non-communicable diseases.

This year’s commemoration will be held under the theme “Innovate today, Nourish Tomorrow” which emphasises science-based innovations and inclusive approaches to build resilient and sustainable food systems.

Mr Siame said as the day draws closer, more stakeholders and cooperating partners have come on board and pledged full mobilisation and logistical support to ensure the event is a success.

World.title: Mwanakampwe commends FSP for reducing poverty
World.content:
Central Province Permanent Secretary, Milner Mwanakampwe is impressed with the milestones the Food Security Pack (FSP) Programme is recording in poverty alleviation among vulnerable households in the region.

Dr Mwanakampwe says the FSP programme has continued transforming the lives through distribution of agricultural inputs to vulnerable but viable farmers across the province.

He was speaking when a delegation from the Ministry of Community Development and Social Service paid a courtesy call on him in Kabwe.

He said the programme, which is implemented by the Ministry of Community Development and Social Services, has done wonders in all the districts but particularly in Chitambo, Mkushi and Chisamba.

Dr Mwanakampwe says the department of community development in some districts has used part of the recoveries from the beneficiaries to build offices and skills development centres, which are impacting local communities.

He has urged the World Food Programme (WFP) and other cooperating partners to continue supporting the programme for the benefit of the vulnerable in society.

And Ministry of Community Development and Social Services, Chief Community Development Officer, Martin Mwansa, says the government remains committed to implementing social protection programmes to alleviate poverty at community level.

World.title: South Africa: Mandrax Lab Uncovered Near Hartbeespoort - South African News Briefs - October 7, 2026
World.content:
press review

Mandrax Lab Uncovered Near Hartbeespoort

Police are investigating an alleged drug-production laboratory uncovered near Hartbeespoort Dam in the North West, reports EWN. Four people, including a 39-year-old Zimbabwean national and three women aged between 23 and 29, were arrested. Police found firearms, marijuana, drug tablets and equipment allegedly used to manufacture mandrax at the property. The discovery comes amid a wider investigation into an alleged international drug route, following other recent mandrax-related arrests and laboratory seizures.

Sibiya Bail Hearing Continues

Suspended Deputy National Police Commissioner for Crime Detection, Lieutenant General Shadrack Sibiya, is set to return to the Randburg Magistrate's Court to continue his bail application, reports SABC News. Sibiya faces charges including rape, human trafficking, firearm law violations and the alleged sexual grooming of a minor. The court has heard graphic evidence from the investigating officer, including allegations that Sibiya raped an 18-year-old after giving her alcohol and later sought explicit images and videos from a 16-year-old girl.

Taxi Fares Remain Unchanged Amid Fuel Price Surge

South Africa’s rising fuel prices are pressuring the taxi industry, but SANTACO has not yet decided to increase fares, reports EWN. The organisation said it will first consult government, fuel suppliers and taxi operators on ways to manage the impact, urging commuters not to act on speculation. Diesel has reached R33 a litre, while petrol now costs R30. COSATU has warned that the increases will further strain workers and households, fuel inflation and deepen debt.
