World.title: Kenya: Young People Must Shape Their Own SRHR Future, Says Kenyan Activist
World.content:
Adolescent girls and young women (AGYW) in Eastern and Southern Africa continue to face a disproportionate burden of HIV, early and unintended pregnancy, and poor sexual and reproductive health outcomesâparticularly during key life transitions such as leaving school, early pregnancy, migration, or exposure to violence.

Across Africa, young people are being told that their sexual and reproductive health and rights matter. But for many, accessing those rights remains a daily struggle.

Progress on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) has been made by governments and health systems, but this progress is not equal. Many adolescents, particularly girls and young women, still face obstacles to accessing the information, services, and legal protection they need to make informed choices regarding their bodies and futures. Fear of being stigmatized and concerns about confidentiality and who to go to for help can also be reasons why young people are not able to access sexual and reproductive health information and services when they need them.

Millions are still being affected by preventable risks, such as new HIV infections, early pregnancies, child marriage, gender-based violence, and period poverty. The gap between the rights that are promised on paper and the rights that are experienced in everyday life is further exacerbated by the fact that access to contraception, HIV prevention, comprehensive sexuality education, and youth-friendly health services remains a challenge for many.

Young people are increasingly demanding that this gap be taken seriously. They are calling for better access to sexual and reproductive health services and for comprehensive sexual and reproductive education in schools and health centres, free of stigma and shame.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Kenyan HIV and SRHR activist Jerop Limo said that closing that gap means moving beyond simply talking about young people and giving them a meaningful role in designing, implementing and holding health systems accountable.

"The reality is that we have made progress, but that progress is not being experienced equally by young people," Limo said. "We have more knowledge, more HIV prevention options, more conversations around SRHR, and stronger recognition of young people's leadership. But for many adolescent girls and young women, especially those living in poverty or in underserved communities, the ability to actually benefit from these advances remains a dream."

She said the biggest gap lies between what exists on paper and what young people experience in their everyday lives. She said policies, guidelines and new technologies mean little if a young woman cannot get accurate information, afford transport to a facility, or find a service in stock, or if she encounters stigma from a provider or fears being judged.

Limo warned against treating young people as a single group.

Their realities, she said, are shaped by where they live, their economic circumstances, disability, gender, HIV status, relationships, and many other factors. She added that the response has to be much more community-centered and responsive to those different realities.

Limo's own experience with HIV shaped her path into adolescent health advocacy. She began working in the HIV response eight years ago as a facility peer educator. As a young person living with HIV, she quickly discovered that access to treatment was only one part of what young people needed. Young people were also grappling with adherence, disclosure, fear, grief, relationships and self-worth, and with the question of what life could look like beyond an HIV diagnosis.

Her work has since taken her beyond Kenya and onto the global stage.

In 2025, Limo was recognised by the Gates Foundation's Goalkeepers community for her leadership in HIV and youth reproductive health. But she said the recognition is not hers alone. It belongs to the young people who have shared their experiences with her and the peer educators working in health centres every day.

The platform, she said, allows her to carry their everyday priorities directly to global decision-makers.

One of the biggest lessons she has learnt is that young people do not need adults to constantly tell them what their problems are or what solutions they need. They need people and systems that are willing to listen, trust them and create space for them to shape those solutions.

Today, Limo is Executive Director of the Ambassador for Youth and Adolescent Reproductive Health Program (AYARHEP), a youth-led organisation working on adolescent HIV and SRHR in Kenya.

A central part of Limo's advocacy is changing how institutions understand youth participation.

"Youth leadership, for me, is not simply putting a young person on a panel or giving young people a speaking slot," she said. "It is about young people having actual influence over decisions, programmes and resources."

At AYARHEP, she said, young people are not only beneficiaries but also peer educators, advocates, community mobilisers, programme designers and accountability actors. Limo said that peer connection is one of the strongest tools youth-led groups have.

"There is something very powerful about a young person sitting with another young person and saying, 'I understand what you are going through,'" she said. That peer connection, she said, can open conversations that may not happen in a formal institution.

Youth-led organisations also tend to sit closer to the realities of communities, she added. They hear first when a service is failing, when a product is unavailable, when a young person is too afraid to visit a facility, or when a national policy is failing to translate into meaningful change at community level. However, Limo said that youth-led organisations cannot be expected to carry the responsibility alone. Governments, donors and larger institutions need to recognise young people's expertise and provide the resources needed for youth-led organisations to lead at scale.

Misinformation is a growing concern too.

The challenge is particularly acute in an environment where misinformation and opposition to SRHR continue to shape what young people hear and believe. Young people need information that is accurate, understandable, relevant to their realities and delivered through channels they actually use and trust.

AYARHEP uses peer engagement, community dialogues, social media and youth-friendly spaces to allow young people to ask questions without fear of judgement. The organisation also engages caregivers, teachers, health workers, community leaders and other gatekeepers because young people's SRHR needs cannot be separated from the communities around them. Creating an enabling environment is essential, said Limo.

Limo said misinformation must be countered without shaming those who believe it. "If we want young people to trust us, we have to create spaces where they can say, 'I heard this, is it true?' and receive a respectful answer," she said.

Digital platforms have become increasingly important in the HIV and SRHR response, but Limo believes that young people should not only consume information online. They should also have the skills to identify misinformation and make informed decisions.

Limo said that stigma remains one of the biggest barriers preventing young people from accessing care. It surrounds HIV, sexuality, contraception, pregnancy and abortion, and extends to young people simply wanting to make decisions about their own bodies.

She said practical challenges, including services that are not youth-friendly, inconvenient operating hours, stock-outs, transport costs, lack of confidentiality and judgmental providers, can further discourage young people from seeking care.

Limo also said another major challenge is the information gap.

Young people today can reach enormous amounts of information, she said, but not all of it is accurate."Access to information has to mean access to trusted, evidence-based and understandable information," she said.

For Limo, one of the most urgent issues is ensuring that the incredible progress we are seeing in HIV prevention science actually reaches the people who need it. She cited lenacapavir, an injection that protects against HIV for six months and is given twice a year. Kenya became the first country in East Africa to roll it out in February. Limo said clinical studies show it can be up to 96% effective.

For many young women, she said, taking a pill every single day is hard to keep up, so an option they need only twice a year gives them real choice and more control over their own protection.

The rollout has begun in 15 high-burden counties, with plans to expand to all 47.

"Making the injection free at public health facilities isn't enough," Limo said. The next hurdle is ensuring that adolescent girls and young women know about the injection, can obtain it locally, and feel safe asking for it without judgment.

Young people as decision-makers

Limo said meaningful participation means far more than consultation. Young people, she argued, should be involved at every stage: identifying the problem, designing the response, implementing it, monitoring it, and holding institutions accountable.

"Young people are experts in their own lived realities," she said.

Even a team of highly experienced technical experts can produce an excellent programme on paper, she said, but if young people are not part of designing it, they can still miss important realities about how it will work in someone's life.

At AYARHEP, she said, the value of this approach has been clear through community scorecards, peer-led programming, youth support groups and community dialogues. Young people can tell you not only whether a programme is reaching them, but whether it is actually working for them.

Limo believes the question should therefore change. "We need to move from asking, 'How can we involve young people?' to asking, 'What decisions should young people have power over?'" she said.

What frustrates Limo most is when young people's participation stops at the conversation.

She said conferences and policy dialogues matter, and that she values every opportunity to be in those rooms. They are where community realities reach decision-makers directly, and many of the partnership discussions most important to her work begin there.

"My frustration is when young people speak, our quotes go into a report, and we are not included in the discussions and decisions on the next steps," she said.

Young people are often described as the leaders of tomorrow, Limo said, but they are already leading today. They are implementing programmes, mobilising communities, collecting evidence, shaping policies and creating solutions.

Sustained youth leadership, she added, needs sustained investment. Partners and funders can work with advocates who keep showing up and delivering results when they invest in young leaders.

"The opportunity now is to move from youth visibility to youth investment by bringing young people in early and keeping them in the process, from design through to accountability," she said.

Funding under strain

The push for meaningful youth leadership comes at a difficult time for HIV and SRHR programmes, as funding pressures affect community-based organisations across Africa.

Funding pressure is being felt most directly at the community level, she said. When funding shrinks, it is not just an organisational budget that changes.

"We have seen fewer community activities, fewer peer educators, reduced outreach, fewer spaces for young people to access psychosocial support and less capacity for youth-led organisations to hold systems accountable," she said.

Limo said there is a contradiction in asking communities to take greater ownership of the HIV and SRHR response while the organisations rooted in those communities struggle to survive.

"We need to stop seeing youth-led and community-based organisations as temporary project implementers," she said. "They are part of the infrastructure of the response. Communities built the response."

Close 

Sustaining that infrastructure, she said, will require longer-term and more flexible funding, investment in organisational capacity, and genuine recognition that communities hold expertise that cannot simply be replaced.

"We also need to protect the gains we have made. We cannot keep rebuilding community systems every time a funding cycle changes," said Limo.

A call to policymakers and funders

For policymakers and funders, Limo said, is to listen differently.

She said that young people need more than programmes designed for them. They need the opportunities, resources and decision-making power to help design and lead those programmes themselves.

She urged decision-makers to recognise that young people's priorities do not always fit neatly into programme categories. HIV, mental health, education, economic empowerment, relationships, violence, SRHR and digital safety are interconnected in a young person's life, she explained, and responses need to reflect that.

She also urged decision-makers to invest in choice.

She pointed to the exciting scientific developments in HIV prevention, but said innovation only becomes meaningful when communities can access it, understand their options, and make informed choices about what works for them.

Limo asked funders not to stop at paying for activities.

"Invest in the people and organisations that make the activity possible, the young leaders, peer educators, community organisations and networks that remain in communities long after a particular project has ended," she said.

What gives Limo hope, she said, is young people themselves.

She has watched young people who were once afraid to speak in meetings grow into peer educators, advocates and leaders, she said. She has seen young people living with HIV move from simply trying to survive their diagnosis to becoming powerful voices in the response, and young women challenge systems, ask difficult questions and create solutions for their communities. "I am one of them," she said.

"That is the future I am working towards," Limo said, "one where young people are not spoken about only as vulnerable populations and beneficiaries, but recognized as people with agency, expertise and the ability to shape their own futures."

Through AYARHEP, she wants to keep building spaces where young people can access information, services, support and opportunities, and where they can also influence the systems around them. Ultimately, she said, she wants a future where a young person does not have to fight the system to access basic healthcare, accurate information, or dignity.

"And perhaps most importantly, I want young people to believe that their lives can be bigger than the challenges they were born into," said Limo.

World.title: Kenya: Nairobi Hospital Says Ebola Patient Was Isolated From Main Facility
World.content:
Travelers being screened for the Ebola virus at the Kenyan border (file photo)

Nairobi — The Nairobi Hospital has moved to reassure patients and staff that its operations remain normal after the death of a patient who tested positive for Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease.

The patient died at the hospital on Monday evening, two days after being admitted to its isolation facility, the hospital said in a statement issued Tuesday.

The facility said the patient was managed by a dedicated clinical team in coordination with the Ministry of Health, but declined to disclose further details about the deceased in keeping with patient privacy.

The hospital said its Ebola isolation unit is physically separated from the main hospital and has a dedicated entrance, access route and staff.



"There is no shared clinical space with the main hospital, which has remained fully operational throughout," the hospital said.

It added that emergency services, maternity, theatres, wards and outpatient services were continuing normally.

The hospital said infection prevention and control measures remained in place, with patients presenting an infectious disease risk identified through screening and managed under controlled isolation protocols.

Staff involved in the patient's care worked while wearing full protective equipment and under supervision, the hospital said.

It further said all identified contacts were being monitored in coordination with the Ministry of Health for the required 21-day period.

The hospital said it would continue working with the Ministry of Health and other public health authorities and would implement any additional measures recommended by the government.

The statement comes as health authorities intensify contact tracing following Kenya's confirmation of its first imported Bundibugyo Ebola case.

The patient had travelled into Kenya after spending time in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak was first reported, before travelling through Uganda and eventually arriving in Nairobi.

Health authorities are tracing people who may have come into contact with the patient, including healthcare workers and passengers who travelled on the same flight.

The Nairobi Hospital sought to reassure the public that the facility remains safe and operational.

"We want to reassure our patients, families, staff and the wider public that the hospital remains open, safe and fully operational, with appropriate measures in place to protect everyone who comes through our doors," the hospital said.

World.title: Zimbabwe: Mnangagwa Declares State of Disaster As 8,500 Homes Lose Roofs in Masvingo Hailstorm
World.content:
PRESIDENT Emmerson Mnangagwa has declared a State of Disaster following a severe hailstorm that hit Masvingo on Monday, leaving thousands of homes and infrastructure damaged.

The hailstorm caused extensive destruction across residential areas, public utilities, education and health institutions, as well as commercial establishments.

Preliminary assessments indicate that about 8,500 households had their roofs completely blown off, while 90% of the 17,000 households assessed had shattered windowpanes, leaving families exposed at the start of the rainy season.

Several major institutions were severely affected, including Great Zimbabwe University's Mucheke Campus, Masvingo Polytechnic, Masvingo Teachers College, Maud Muzenda Training Centre, the Passport Office, Grain Marketing Board, Chiefs Hall, Veterinary Office, District Development Coordinator's Office, ZIMRE Building, Masvingo Urban VTC, Runyararo Clinic Maternity Ward, Rujeko Hall, 4.1 Brigade, Masvingo Airport and the ZEC Provincial Office.



Business operations in Masvingo City were also disrupted, with major retail and hospitality outlets suffering roof damage, severe leaks and damage to assets.

The storm also extensively damaged electricity infrastructure, with ZESA power lines brought down.

The resulting power outages have affected water pumping systems, municipal drainage and sewer networks, creating an immediate public health risk.

Garwe said government had mobilised all available resources and called on government agencies to assist affected communities.

He also made an urgent appeal to the private sector and development partners to join government in relief efforts.

"The Government remains fully committed to ensuring that no person and no place is left behind as we rebuild and restore normalcy," he said.

Government said assessments were continuing, while relief interventions were being rolled out to affected communities.

World.title: Mali: Junta Forces Retake Strategic Town of Kidal
World.content:
A military pickup carrying armed fighters drives past the iconic painted boulder marking the entrance to Kidal, a remote desert town in northern Mali long at the heart of the country's decade-long conflict between government forces, Tuareg movements, and armed groups operating across the Sahara.

Mali's military regained control of the strategic town of Kidal after forcing Tuareg separatists and al-Qaeda-linked jihadists to withdraw following an offensive backed by Russia's Africa Corps.

Mali's army, supported by Russian paramilitary forces, has re-entered the northern town of Kidal, forcing the Tuareg separatists to withdraw from the strategic hold, in a symbolic boost for the country's military government and its Russian allies.

The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) said in a statement it had "decided to carry out a strategic and controlled withdrawal of its forces from the town of Kidal." It said the withdrawal took place without direct fighting.

This followed the "disproportionate use of aerial assets by Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps," according to an FLA spokesperson.



How did Kidal fall earlier this year?

The FLA and al-Qaeda-linked Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) seized Kidal during a series of attacks earlier this year in April that also killed Mali's defense minister.

Tuareg separatists from the Azawad Liberation Front have been fighting for years to create an independent state in northern Mali.

Mali's junta, which came to power in back-to-back coups in 2020 and 2021, has increasingly relied on Russian paramilitary support against fighters linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State.

What does Kidal's recapture mean for Mali's junta?

Analysts say the latest advance is largely a symbolic victory for Mali's junta.

"A successful recapture... affirms the military-led government's authority and boosts the army's morale, particularly after several high-profile setbacks both in the north and the central regions in recent weeks," Beverly Ochieng, associate director of Control Risks, told Reuters.

Ochieng, however, added the retaking of Kidal is largely "symbolic" and not "decisive" in Mali's campaign against jihadist and separatist groups.

Human rights organizations have often accused the Malian army and Russian paramilitaries of killing civilians during military operations, with all sides also accused of committing war crimes.

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: South Africa: Stick-Wielding Vigilantes Harass Asylum Seekers
World.content:
A member of the vigilante group stands outside the Home Affairs gate. Police moved the group from inside the gate after the harassment of several asylum seekers.

Immigrants queuing at Home Affairs in Durban targeted by xenophobic group

Immigrants queuing at Home Affairs offices in Durban to apply for asylum were harassed on Tuesday by a group of about 15 vigilantes.

Some wore masks and most carried sticks.

They pushed people in the queue in the parking area and shouted insults.

Police sent them away from the parking area.

Home Affairs announced on Monday that all asylum seekers would be able to apply for asylum, ending a six-year closure of the asylum system to new applicants.

Asylum seekers waiting in line at the Home Affairs Refugee Reception Centre in Durban were harassed on Tuesday by stick-wielding anti-immigrant vigilantes, some of them wearing masks.

A group of about 15 vigilantes appeared at the centre around 12:30pm. Some wore masks and most of them were carrying sticks or knobkerries.



They walked past the SAPS officers stationed outside the centre and into the fenced-off parking lot. Several of them began shoving the people waiting in the parking lot to apply for asylum documents, telling them to leave.

Only after a few minutes did the police officers intervene and tell the vigilantes to leave and stand outside the gate.

According to Wandile Mhlongo, the leader of the group, the intention of the protest was to block people from seeking asylum in South Africa.

After being moved across the road, the vigilantes shouted insults at the asylum seekers, including "kwerekwere" (a xenophobic term for immigrants from African countries) and "criminals". Some told the refugees they must leave South Africa and seek asylum in the closest country to their home country.

Police reinforcements arrived and SAPS officers allowed Mhlongo into the centre so he could see the application process and report back to the others. But when he came out, tensions remained high with police forming a barrier to stop the vigilantes from crossing the road.

The protest was not organised by March and March, said Mhlongo.

However, at around 3pm, Xolani Zuma, the husband of March and March leader Jacinta Ngobese-Zuma, arrived at the centre to speak to SAPS.

Zuma said he was shocked that the Home Affairs Department was able to assist so many refugees while there were so many South Africans who did not have identity documents. "We want Home Affairs to stop processing the refugees because we believe that its resources should be utilised by South Africans," said Zuma.

March and March had previously raided a makeshift refugee camp that formed outside the office in the wake of the organisation's 30 June deadline.

A long wait

The long line of asylum seekers outside the Refugee Reception Centre on Tuesday followed an announcement last Monday that all asylum seekers would be able to apply for asylum, ending a six-year closure of the asylum system to new applicants.

Close 

The announcement was made by Home Affairs following a Constitutional Court ruling in July this year.

Many of those queuing on Tuesday were people who had been locked out of the refugee system during the covid lockdown.

Bihh Mutombo, who fled the Democratic Republic of Congo 12 years ago, told GroundUp that he had been going through the asylum application process when he was locked out in 2020. He had been queuing on Tuesday since 6am.

Mutombo had to leave all his family behind after fleeing the DRC out of fear for his life, he said. "I don't know if there's anyone left there."

Hundreds of people had been waiting since the early hours of the morning, and some had slept on the street to secure their spot in the queue. By the end of the day, officials had only managed to process 20 of the asylum seekers, and the rest were told to return on Wednesday.

One of the women waiting in line said she ran a small salon and that coming to Home Affairs every day cut into her income. "I am a single mother and I am paying rent for my flat. I have been in the country for five years now," said the woman, who did not want to be named. "Not having proper documents has lots of challenges. Sometimes I even struggle to be assisted at the hospital when I am sick."

World.title: Nigeria: Anti-Graft Agency Opposes Diezani's Move to Present Evidence of UK Court Acquittal in Abuja Case
World.content:
EFCC maintained that the UK judgement was irrelevant to the case Diezani filed in court for the recovery of her auctioned assets.

The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) has opposed former Minister of Petroleum Resources Diezani Alison-Madueke's application to present evidence of her acquittal of bribery charges by the Southwark Crown Court, London in the United Kingdom.

The anti-graft agency urged Judge Inyang Ekwo to dismiss the application.

The commission, which filed a counter-affidavit against the application, maintained that the purported acquittal of Mrs Alison-Madueke by a foreign criminal court was not material or relevant to the specific issues for determination before the instant court.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

In an earlier filing, the EFCC stated that the assets Mrs Alison-Madueke was seeking to retrieve through the legal action, which has been ongoing since 2023, had been auctioned off based on court orders.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the judge, on 1 July, granted the application filed by the ex-minister to present evidence of the London court.

Mofesomo Oyetibo, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN) who appeared for the EFCC at the time, did not oppose the application.

EFCC's concession to the application, moved by the former minister's lawyer Godwin Iyinbor, prompted the judge to grant the application.

The UK acquittal

The UK court's judgement delivered on 17 June cleared Mrs Alison-Madueke of all bribery charges brought against her by British prosecutors.

Mrs Alison-Madueke, who served as Nigeria's petroleum minister between 2010 and 2015 under former President Goodluck Jonathan, was acquitted of five counts of accepting bribes and one count of conspiracy to commit bribery.

British prosecutors alleged in the case that Mrs Alison-Madueke received lavish benefits and enjoyed what they described as "a life of luxury" in London, funded by oil and gas industry figures seeking favourable treatment and lucrative contracts in Nigeria's petroleum sector.

They argued that the benefits were provided in exchange for the oil and gas contracts she awarded during her tenure as petroleum minister between 2010 and 2015.

However, the former minister had maintained throughout the trial that she neither accepted bribes nor exercised direct control over the award of government contracts.

The UK discharged and acquitted the embattled former minister of the bribery charges after a jury at the London court returned not-guilty verdicts.

Mrs Alison-Madueke faces pending corruption charges and a flurry of forfeiture orders on slews of assets traced to her back in Nigeria as she came under investigations and prosecutions in the UK.

Battle to recover forfeited assets

The former minister who left Nigeria in 2015 shortly after she left office commenced her suit, suing EFCC as the sole defendant in 2023, to stop the auctioning of her forfeited assets.

She filed an amended version of the suit in February 2025.

In the aftermath of her acquittal by the EFCC in June, filed an application to showcase the UK judgement as evidence of her innocence and legitimate acquisition of the assets.

EFCC has stated in a filing that the assets had been auctioned off based on court orders.

During the previous court sitting, Mrs Alison-Madueke's lawyer, Mr Iyinbor, moved a motion seeking the permission to file a further/supplementary affidavit for the purpose of bringing fresh and material development with respect to her acquittal by the UK court.

EFCC's lawyer, Ms Oyetibo, did not raise any objection to the filing the application, leaving the judge with no choice than to grant the request.

The former minister's lawyer then proceeded to file the further/supplementary affidavit, against which the EFCC filed a counter-affidavit.

In the agency's counter-affidavit sworn by Oyakhilome Ekienabor, a litigation officer in Ms Oyetibo's law firm, the EFCC opposed Mrs Alison-Madueke's request to present the evidence.

EFCC's opposition

At Tuesday's proceedings, Queen-Ubokutom Uwe, who appeared for Mrs Alison-Madueke, informed the court the EFCC had just served with EFCC's further counter-affidavit in response to her client's further/supplementary affidavit.

She equally reminded the court of their motion to regularise their processes.

Responding, Paul Mgbeoma, who appeared for the EFCC on Tuesday, expressed surprise at the frequency of Mrs Alison-Madueke's new filings as if it was an election petition case.

Mr Mgbeoma then told the court that he was ready to proceed with the hearing.

The judge consequently fixed 11 November for hearing of the motions.

NAN reports that EFCC's further counter-affidavit filed on 5 October, described several claims in Mrs Alison-Maduelke's further affidavit as misleading, immaterial and irrelevant to the substantive issues for determination in her present suit.

"The proceedings before the Southwark Crown Court, London, United Kingdom, and the purported acquittal of the applicant therein, are in respect of a proceeding that is not being prosecuted before any Nigerian court and have nothing to do with the substantive suit before this honourable court," wrote Oyakhilome Ekienabor who swore the anti-graft agency's counter-affidavit.

The agency maintained in the filing that there is nothing in the public sale notice indicating that any of the properties listed therein belong to the applicant.

It added that "the order for forfeiture relates exclusively to items of jewelry and does not extend to any other category of assets or properties."

It accused the applicant of trying to expand the scope of her case through the fresh filings.

"The applicant's further/supplementary affidavit introduces irrelevant facts into this suit, thereby diverting attention from the core issues before this honourable court," the counter-affidavit read.

He, therefore, urged the court to reject the further/supplementary affidavit seeking to present evidence of her acquittal in the UK court.

The suit

NAN recalls Mrs Alison-Madueke filed the suit through her lead counsel, Mike Ozekhome.

She argued, as part of the 10 grounds cited in support of the suit, that she commenced the suit challenging, among other things, the public notice issued by the EFCC for the public auction/sale of properties and/or personal effects affecting her proprietary rights.

"A major plank of the applicant's case before this honourable court is that the respondent had sought to visit the applicant with grave proprietary consequences without conviction, without fair hearing, and without strict compliance with the relevant statutory provisions regulating forfeiture, management and disposal of properties," her lawyer argued.

The filing added that the amended suit was filed on 19 February 2025 based on the leave of the court granted on 17 February 2025.

Close 

"After the filing of the applicant's processes and while this suit was still pending before this honourable court, a subsequent and material event occurred, to wit: the applicant was acquitted by the Southwark Crown Court, London, United Kingdom, on 17 June 2026, of criminal allegations of bribery brought against her, a proceeding of obvious material relevance to the allegations repeatedly referenced in relation to the applicant.

"The said subsequent development is material and relevant to the applicant's case, particularly as it relates to the issues of absence of conviction, fair hearing, due process, propriety of irreversible proprietary deprivation, and the need for strict compliance with statutory safeguards before disposal of properties affecting the applicant's proprietary rights," the court document read.

It added that the ex-minister did not seek by this application to invite the court to sit in appeal over the said foreign decision or to treat the decision as automatically conclusive of the Nigerian proceedings.

However, the document stated the application is to enable Mrs Alison-Madueke to place before the court subsequent material fact which would assist the court in doing substantial justice.

According to Mr Ozekhome who filed the application on behalf of the former minister, the said fact was not available at the time the applicant filed her earlier processes and could not have been pleaded or deposed to earlier.

He submitted that the court had the power and discretion to allow a party to file the application where such facts would assist the court in the just determination of the issues before it.

He said EFCC would not be prejudiced by the grant of the application.

He said it would be in the interest of justice to grant the application.

World.title: Namibia: President Nandi-Ndaitwah Addresses Foot-and-Mouth Disease Outbreak and Calls for National Cooperation
World.content:
High-level address by H.E. Dr Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, President of the Republic of Namibia, on the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak.

Fellow Namibians,

The outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in the Karasburg Veterinary District of the //Kharas Region has brought uncertainty and distress to farmers, workers and businesses across our livestock industry. Livelihoods are at stake. Government is acting to contain the disease, and I call on every Namibian to support this effort.

The livestock and meat industry is one of the cornerstones of our economy. From the farmer and farmworker to the transporter, processor and exporter, its value chain sustains families and communities far beyond the affected areas. Protecting that value chain is a national responsibility.



Our immediate task is clear. We must contain the outbreak, prevent its spread and protect unaffected herds, so that normal production and trade can resume as quickly and safely as possible.

The outbreak was confirmed on 23 September 2026 through laboratory testing of samples collected during veterinary surveillance. Namibia has experience in responding to foot-and-mouth disease in the zone north of the Veterinary Cordon Fence. We must now draw on that experience and ensure that our response meets the demands of this outbreak.

When the disease was detected, the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform and I were attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Our response mechanisms were activated immediately. I thank the Acting Minister, Dr. Charles Mubita, the Ministry's leadership, veterinary officials and all personnel who acted promptly and continue to work under difficult conditions.

As confirmed cases increased, I directed the Joint Cabinet Committee to convene urgently on 3 October 2026. Cabinet met the following day to assess the situation and determine the interventions required under the Animal Health Act.

As of 5 October 2026, surveillance teams have inspected 29,313 animals across 68 farms. There are 127 confirmed positive cases across 15 farms. Twenty surveillance teams have been constituted, and 10 roadblocks established across the //Kharas Region to support the response.

Cabinet has directed the immediate implementation of the relevant provisions of the Animal Health Act and the strengthening of disease-control and biosecurity measures. The responsible institutions must act with urgency and coordinate their work to contain the outbreak.

The Critical Containment Response Plan, approved by Cabinet on 4 October 2026, includes establishing a containment buffer zone in the Karasburg Veterinary District to prevent the disease from spreading to unaffected regions. It also provides for repairs to the Namibia-Botswana border fence and the erection of veterinary cordon fencing in high-risk areas along the border with South Africa to strengthen animal movement control.

Fellow Namibians,

I recognise the strain that movement restrictions and disruptions to trade are placing on farmers, workers and businesses. For many families, this uncertainty concerns their next income and their ability to sustain their livelihoods. These concerns must remain central to our response. The measures we take now are necessary to prevent wider losses and safeguard the industry's recovery.

We are also mindful of the financial pressures on farmers and businesses servicing loans with financial institutions. Government will continue to assess these effects and engage relevant stakeholders to ensure that this animal health crisis does not lead to prolonged financial distress for otherwise viable farmers and businesses.

Through the Directorate of Veterinary Services, teams are conducting surveillance, testing, farm inspections and livestock movement tracing. Their findings will guide our decisions. Where conditions permit, restrictions may be adjusted. Where risks remain, controls will be maintained or strengthened.

The Veterinary Public Notices issued by the Directorate of Veterinary Services remain the official and authoritative source of animal health guidance. I urge all stakeholders to comply fully with these notices and cooperate with the officials implementing them.

Government is also engaging the European Union on consignments of Namibian meat products produced before 23 September 2026. Under European Union legislation, consignments certified by Namibia's Veterinary Competent Authority before confirmation of the outbreak are likely to be permitted entry. Similar engagements are underway with other trading partners to limit disruptions to trade while we address the disease situation.

We will provide our partners with verified information and uphold international veterinary requirements. Maintaining confidence in our veterinary systems is essential to protecting Namibia's reputation as a reliable producer and exporter. We will also continue pursuing opportunities to diversify and strengthen our export markets.

Fellow Namibians,

This response requires all hands on deck. Government must lead and coordinate, but success depends on the cooperation of everyone across the livestock and meat value chain. Every livestock owner, trader, transporter, auctioneer and industry stakeholder has a role to play.

I call on livestock owners to remain vigilant, cooperate with surveillance teams and ensure that animal identification and movement records are accurate, complete and up to date. Traders, transporters and auctioneers must observe movement controls and comply with veterinary instructions. Our collective discipline will help protect unaffected herds and the livelihoods that depend on them.

The Namibia Livestock Identification and Traceability System is central to this effort. It enables officials to track livestock movements, identify potentially exposed animals and make timely disease-control decisions. Keeping reliable records is therefore a practical contribution to the protection of the entire industry.

Our veterinary services and laboratories must have the resources they need to respond effectively. Government will continue strengthening surveillance, laboratory capacity, traceability and long-term biosecurity to improve our preparedness for future outbreaks.

Close 

I thank the stakeholders and partners who have already offered support. I call on businesses supplying livestock products, critical materials and emergency supplies to act responsibly. This outbreak must not become an opportunity to exploit distress through inflated prices. Our efforts must support containment and recovery.

The Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform, supported by the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology, will continue providing regular updates. I ask the media, industry stakeholders and the public to rely on verified information and avoid circulating unconfirmed reports that cause confusion or undermine the response.

Fellow Namibians,

We must meet this difficult period with resolve and a shared sense of responsibility. Every measure we take, and every act of cooperation, must serve our common purpose of containing the disease and protecting livelihoods.

Government will continue to lead this effort. I call on all Namibians to do their part, support affected communities and work together to safeguard this industry on which so many of our people depend.

I thank you.

High-Level Address by Her Excellency Dr. Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, on the Foot-And-Mouth Disease Outbreak, 05 October 2026 WindhoekDownload

World.title: Federal judge blocks Trump administration fines of up to $1.8M for migrants
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration's attempts to fine migrants up to $1.8 million for failing to leave the country after receiving final deportation orders.

U.S. District Judge George O'Toole in Boston issued the ruling on Monday in response to a class-action lawsuit filed last year by two of the thousands of migrants who have received civil penalties from the Department of Homeland Security.

The judge granted preliminary relief to the plaintiffs, finding that the administration's process for imposing the fines violated federal law, and that migrants in the "economically precarious position" of addressing the fines could be pushed into "insolvency."

"The plaintiffs live in an economically precarious position even without the imposition of the government’s exorbitant fines," he wrote.

DHS ISSUES $84B IN FINES TO ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

"They face the possible garnishment of their already modest wages, loss of any vehicles and homes, federal collections lawsuits and other adverse collateral consequences," O’Toole added. "If they were ultimately successful in this suit, there is no indication that simply requiring the government to vacate their fine notices would –– or even could, at that point –– make the plaintiffs whole or return the circumstances to the status quo."

O’Toole, an appointee of former President Bill Clinton, described how the plaintiffs worked for low salaries and had come to the U.S. to escape political violence.

"Nancy M. was fined over $1.8 million," O’Toole wrote, referring to one of the plaintiffs. "She is a laborer working over 60 hours a week with two jobs, and she reports feeling serious anxiety affecting her ability to sleep, eat and live a normal life."

The judge also found that the administration's fine notices violated the Administrative Procedure Act by failing to provide specific allegations explaining why an individual's conduct warranted a penalty.

Fox News Digital reached out to DHS for comment.

As recently as July, DHS said it had issued more than 103,000 fines to migrants totaling about $84 billion since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

DHS has defended the penalties, saying people who refuse to leave the country after receiving a final order of removal could face fines of $998 per day.

Although Congress authorized civil penalties under the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, no administration had attempted to impose the fines until Trump's first term.

Last year, the Trump administration began imposing fines of $998 per day for migrants who did not leave the country following a final order of deportation. The fines have been imposed retroactively for up to five years, with a maximum penalty of $1.8 million.

20 STATES SUE TO BLOCK TRUMP ADMIN RULE THAT WOULD MAKE IT HARDER FOR IMMIGRANTS TO OBTAIN VISAS, GREEN CARDS

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In July 2025, DHS and the Department of Justice implemented changes aimed at streamlining the assessment of fines by scrapping a 30-day notice period and shortening the process for challenging penalties.

The plaintiffs successfully challenged that policy and what they described as an Immigration and Customs Enforcement policy of issuing fines using boilerplate forms without independently assessing whether a person's failure to leave was "willful" or "voluntary."

O’Toole also found that the administration had failed to comply with rulemaking processes in implementing its streamlined fine-imposition process because it did not offer the public a chance to first comment on the policy change.

Congressional lawmakers have attempted to challenge the administration’s fines against migrants through the Immigration and Nationality Act. Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., and Dick Durbin, D-Ill., urged DHS and DOJ to pause the "improper application of certain civil penalties" in the law to "law-abiding immigrants."

Reuters contributed to this report.

World.title: Padres hold off Brewers in must-win Game 3 to survive elimination and force Game 4 at Petco Park
World.content:
The first two games of the National League Division Series matchup between the San Diego Padres and Milwaukee Brewers have been playoff baseball at its best.

Drama, late-inning heroics, the American Family Field roof suddenly coming into play, and series-changing moments between two of the best players in Major League Baseball. Game one saw William Contreras launch a go-ahead homer in the 7th inning, while Ty France tried to hit a go-ahead one in the top of the ninth, only to be thwarted by the roof support system in Milwaukee.

The Brewers held on to win that game, 3-2, setting up a must-win for the Padres in game two. Michael King out-dueled Logan Henderson, and the Padres' talented bullpen mostly held Milwaukee's lineup at bay ... until the bottom of the ninth inning.

CLOSER MASON MILLER HITS PATERNITY LIST 45 MINUTES BEFORE THE PADRES' SEASON IS ON THE LINE

All-world closer Mason Miller, starting his second inning of work, suddenly couldn't find the plate. After three walks in the inning, star outfielder Jackson Chourio crushed a line-drive single to center field, walking off the Padres and giving the Brewers a commanding 2-0 series lead with the series shifting to Petco Park.

With Miller pushed to 40 pitches on Sunday, his availability for Tuesday's must-win matchup was already in question. But some stunning pregame news, that he'd be placed on the paternity list and unavailable, removed any doubt.

Fortunately for San Diego, they had Nick Pivetta starting against Dustin May, seemingly providing a clear matchup advantage. Through the early part of the game, that's exactly how it played out.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Pivetta used some spectacular defense from Jackson Merrill to work a scoreless first inning, with the young center fielder making a fantastic catch to rob Chourio of a double.

While Dustin May got through the first few innings unscathed, the third quickly unraveled. Samad Taylor singled and stole second, with Jake Cronenworth bunting him to third. Fernando Tatis Jr. hit a run-scoring grounder to make it 1-0, followed by Merrill lacing a single to center.

He too stole second, and Manny Machado, struggling through the first two games, finally came through and drove in the second run to send the San Diego crowd into a frenzy.



In the top of the fourth, Milwaukee struck back. William Contreras, coming off a down year by his standards, delivered again, launching a mammoth homer to left field off Pivetta. And he took his sweet time admiring it, adding some celebrations while rounding the bases.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

That made it 2-1, and when the Padres worked a lead off walk in the bottom of the fourth, Brewers manager Pat Murphy didn't hesitate, removing May from the game and going to the strong Milwaukee bullpen.

Milwaukee didn't stay down for long. In the top of the fifth, Cooper Pratt and Sal Frelick set the table with back-to-back singles, allowing Jackson Chourio to knot the game at 2-2 with a sacrifice fly to center.

But Jake Cronenworth wasn't having it. In the bottom of the fifth, Cronenworth launched a majestic solo shot to right field off Antonio Senzatela, restoring San Diego's lead at 3-2 and sending Petco Park into a frenzy.

The Padres tacked on a crucial insurance run in the sixth when Xander Bogaerts came home on a Cooper Pratt throwing error to push the lead to 4-2.

Milwaukee battled back in the eighth, scratching across another run off Bradgley Rodríguez to cut the deficit to 4-3. But Padres manager Craig Stammen turned to starter-turned-reliever Michael King to finish the job. King tossed two gritty innings out of the bullpen, stranding the tying run in the ninth to secure the 4-3 victory.

With the 4-3 win, San Diego fended off the sweep, cut Milwaukee’s NLDS lead to 2-1, and set up a massive Game 4 at Petco Park.

This entire series has been a showcase of top-tier baseball; elite pitching, powerful bullpens, and stars coming through in big moments. If this doesn't go five games, it'll be a missed opportunity for neutral fans who enjoy the drama of playoff baseball. Though Milwaukee is certainly hoping it doesn't.

World.title: French PM rejects police brutality claims after teens severely injured in protests: 'Accidents happen'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu defended the police response to student protests after one teenager lost a hand in an incident involving a police grenade and another lost sight in one eye after being struck by a projectile.

In parliament on Tuesday, Lecornu pushed back on accusations of police brutality or state repression, adding that the term "police brutality" implies that officers had been instructed to use force, according to Politico.

"What triggers police action is the occurrence of urban violence," Lecornu said.

"Can accidents happen? The answer is yes," he added.

FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION

Lecornu and Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez have both argued that the police response was sparked by urban violence, arson and vandalism, while maintaining that officers have acted within their authority. Nuñez also called the police response proportionate in "almost all cases."

The prime minister also accused opposition party France Unbowed of exploiting the student protests to sow chaos and score political points ahead of next year’s presidential election.

President Emmanuel Macron convened an emergency meeting with senior ministers to address the nationwide student protests and their potential political fallout.

The French government is facing mounting pressure after more than 6,500 people were arrested and hundreds were injured as students demand better funding and learning conditions in schools. Most of those arrested were minors, according to the Associated Press.

Lecornu said 215 students and 85 school staff members had been injured since the protests began, while his office said 715 police officers had also been injured.

"I hope we can provide a political response to a very real anxiety among high school students," Lecornu acknowledged.

As Lecornu delivered his remarks on Tuesday, demonstrators from several French unions and teachers’ groups gathered with high school and university students. Members of France’s left-wing parties were also at the protest, according to Politico.

The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations nationwide Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris.

The Paris demonstration was largely peaceful, although smaller groups later clashed with riot police, according to the Associated Press.

The protesters' movement began at high schools in the Paris region in mid-September before spreading nationwide.

TEEN'S HAND BLOWN OFF BY POLICE GRENADE DURING FRENCH STUDENT PROTESTS: REPORT

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

On Monday, a 15-year-old boy in northern France lost a hand after a police grenade exploded during the protests, Politico reported. A prosecutor said he could not "say for certain whether the student picked up the grenade or whether it was thrown at him."

In the city of Tours, a 16-year-old lost sight in one eye after being hit by a projectile, according to the outlet. The prosecutor said the projectile may have been fired from a sub-lethal riot-control weapon used by police.

Boris Vallaud, leader of the center-left Socialist group in parliament, said the group's lawmakers would introduce legislation restricting the use of sub-lethal riot-control weapons at student demonstrations, warning that they can cause irreversible injuries, the outlet reported.

World.title: Former German spy chief arrested on suspicion of espionage, attempted treason
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A former spy chief for Germany's foreign intelligence service was arrested Tuesday on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason over allegations that he obtained classified documents and used secret information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service, prosecutors said.

August Hanning, 80, led Germany's Federal Intelligence Service, known as the BND, from 1998 to 2005.

According to federal prosecutors, Hanning is "strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage."

A former aide, identified as Manfred D., was also arrested in western Germany and is accused of aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage in connection with the case.

RUNAWAY BRAZILIAN EX-SPY CHIEF CONVICTED IN COUP REPORTEDLY DETAINED BY ICE AT FLORIDA TRAFFIC STOP

Prosecutors said Manfred D. worked as Hanning’s chief of staff before going on to serve as chief of staff to several of Hanning's successors at the BND between March 2012 and March 2026, giving him access to confidential information.

Beginning in 2010, the men allegedly reached an agreement under which Manfred D. would routinely transmit intelligence to Hanning in exchange for payment.

The arrangement continued until June 2022, with Manfred D. allegedly providing Hanning with roughly 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information intended strictly for internal use, according to prosecutors.

Hanning allegedly used the information in his private consulting work.

US COUNTERINTELLIGENCE ‘WAY BEHIND,’ POST-9/11 RECORD ‘EXTRAORDINARILY NEGLIGENT’, FMR TRUMP WH OFFICIAL WARNS

A spokesperson for the federal prosecutor’s office told German broadcaster RTL that investigators believe Hanning used classified information to prepare an analysis for an employee of a foreign intelligence service.

Prosecutors also said Hanning passed along information following extensive exchanges with an employee of another intelligence service.

German authorities have not publicly identified the foreign intelligence services allegedly involved.

The investigation grew out of an apparently unrelated case involving the 2024 abduction of the children of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block during a custody dispute.

Prosecutors said Hanning's arrest stemmed from evidence gathered during that investigation.

CALIFORNIA REALTOR NABBED AT LAX IN ALLEGED CHINA SPY CASE TARGETING TAIWAN PRESIDENT’S RELATIVE

Hanning's arrest marks the first detention of a former head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, according to Reuters.

Hanning and Manfred D. were expected to appear before a judge at Germany's Federal Court of Justice following their arrests.

Fox News Digital has reached out to GLOBSEC, where Hanning previously held an affiliation, for comment on his arrest and the allegations against him.

World.title: Man pleads guilty to 2023 killing of Lauren Heike on Phoenix hiking trail
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Zion Teasley has pleaded guilty to the 2023 murder of Lauren Heike, who was found dead with multiple stab wounds along a trail in north Phoenix.

Teasley entered the plea last Friday to first-degree premeditated murder, as well as a separate sexual exploitation of a minor charge stemming from conduct dating to 2019, according to the Maricopa County Superior Court. Under the plea agreement, Teasley is expected to be sentenced to natural life in prison, and prosecutors will withdraw their pursuit of the death penalty. His sentencing is scheduled for Dec. 4.

He was also charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and first-degree burglary in 2020, but prosecutors voluntarily dismissed those charges last week as part of the plea agreement.

In the aftermath of Heike's killing, a police report revealed that Teasley had been struggling with his sexuality and gender identity, ABC 15 said. Police previously said they believed Heike's killing was a random attack, and investigators found no prior communication between Heike and Teasley, according to the outlet. He was also a former Marine recruit who was separated from recruit training just months after enlisting in 2019, the outlet said.

PHOENIX WOMAN, 29, FOUND DEAD ON HIKING TRAIL

"Our records indicate that Zion W. Teasley entered recruit training at Marine Corps Recruit Training Depot San Diego on March 25, 2019. He was separated June 17, 2019, prior to completing boot camp," the U.S. Marine Corps told the outlet.

When questioned by the police, Teasley said Heike appeared to be "what I would want to look like," according to the outlet.



Investigators also uncovered a screenshot that they believed shed light on Teasley's state of mind. It read, "When I see a beautiful woman and I'm a man," ABC 15 said.

The outlet added that Teasley was fired from one of his jobs for being "aggressive toward female employees" and was "suspected of stealing merchandise."

PHOENIX POLICE ARREST SUSPECT IN CONNECTION TO LAUREN HEIKE'S DEATH

Heike was killed in April 2023 when a resident found her body along a community trail, officials said. She was found with 15 stab wounds and injuries to her hands and forearms, police reported.

Investigators said DNA, surveillance video and cellphone location evidence linked Teasley to the crime.

Heike's family said they had supported prosecutors' initial decision to seek the death penalty but ultimately agreed with the plea agreement, which ensures Teasley will spend the rest of his life in prison without the possibility of release.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Based on the condition of Heike's clothes and officials finding her belongings scattered along the trail, investigators believe Heike was chased over a barbed wire fence during the attack.

"The suspect ran after Lauren and then sprinted away before returning to the location where Lauren's body was found and climbing over the barbed wire," Teasley's probable cause statement read.

Fox News Digital's Sarah Rumpf-Whitten contributed to this report.

World.title: Closer Mason Miller hits paternity list 45 minutes before the Padres' season is on the line
World.content:
San Diego Padres All-Star reliever Mason Miller will miss an elimination game against the Milwaukee Brewers after being placed on Major League Baseball’s paternity list ahead of Game 3 of the National League Division Series.

Miller couldn't have picked a worse time to step away, leaving San Diego without its top bullpen weapon right before a win-or-go-home Game 3. The team placed him on the paternity list 45 minutes before the start of the game.

Under MLB’s postseason paternity rules, Miller is allowed up to three days off.

The Pads plugged that hole by putting veteran lefty Wandy Peralta on the active roster. If San Diego somehow manages to keep its season alive, Miller gets his spot back whenever he returns.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Baseball fans couldn't help but draw comparisons to Yankees starter Max Fried, who finds himself in the exact same boat. Seeing Fried post up for his team while Miller sits out an elimination game brought the debate over playoff priorities right to the forefront.

Congratulations are in order for the new dad, but if San Diego gets eliminated, fans won't be in much of a mood to celebrate.

World.title: USMNT adds to sports wins over Canada this year with international friendly victory in Minnesota

The latest clash between the United States and Canada in sports has led to another victory for the Stars and Stripes.

World.title: Alleged killing by Marine prompts US military to restrict off-base liberty in Okinawa
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The U.S. military in Okinawa, Japan, is beginning an operational pause for 48 hours, prohibiting off-base liberty and ordering training after a Marine was arrested on suspicion of killing and robbing a woman.

Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, Okinawa Area Coordinator and commander of III Marine Expeditionary Force, said in a letter on Tuesday that incidents like this "demand we pause for reflection" and that serving on the island "comes with responsibility."

"We speak often about standards and discipline. Standards are what we expect, and my standards are clear: be accountable for your actions; do the right thing, especially when no one is looking; and always be guided by our core values that govern our conduct at every rank," he wrote.

"We live, work, and socialize alongside the people of Okinawa; their home is our home. Every interaction with our neighbors either builds or undermines the trust that is essential to our team. When that trust is damaged, it affects the strength of our alliance and the security of this region. Accordingly, we will take time to think hard about discipline, standards and our alliance responsibilities," Watson added.

THAI RESORT CITY CRACKS DOWN ON PROSTITUTION AHEAD OF USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN ARRIVAL

The arrest of the Marine has sparked protests against the heavy American military presence on the southern Japanese island and concerns over military-related crime.

Japanese officials have also lodged a formal protest with the U.S. government. Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned U.S. Ambassador George Glass and called for cooperation with the investigation, stricter discipline among U.S. personnel and measures to prevent similar incidents.

The killing could complicate Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s push to both strengthen the Japanese military on Okinawa and work more closely with the U.S. military to deter China.

The pause in operations will last from Wednesday through Friday, during which no "off-base liberty" or alcohol will be allowed. Restricting troops from leaving military bases and interacting with the local community is a common response by military leaders to major crime incidents.

Service members will receive training on standards, discipline and "our responsibilities as members of the Okinawan community," Watson said.

"This Period of Training will include discussions on liberty policy, enforcement mechanisms, alcohol awareness, Okinawan culture, and alliance responsibilities. Every member of this force must understand that individual conduct has consequences," he said.

After the training, which will begin on Friday, troops will transition into a 30-day "Period of Reflection."

NAVY SAILOR SENTENCED TO 44 YEARS FOR STRANGLING FELLOW SERVICEMEMBER IN VIRGINIA BARRACKS ROOM

During this period, Watson said there will be "restrictions on liberty" to remind all military personnel that "liberty is a privilege and a collective responsibility." These restrictions will include a curfew and enhanced supervision.

"Liberty is a mission, and like any other mission it requires discipline, trust and teamwork to complete it successfully," he said. "Take care of your teammates. Hold one another accountable. Live up to the high standards that come with the uniform you wear."

Okinawa prefectural police said they arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the island’s capital city of Naha early Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack.

Ballard has denied the allegations.

Security camera footage showed a man entering the hotel with the woman and later leaving alone.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Ballard was arrested after a patrolling officer spotted him walking later on Saturday in an entertainment district in Okinawa City, about 15 miles northeast of Naha. His shaved head and the tattoos on his arms matched those of the man seen in security footage, Kyodo News agency reported.

People in Okinawa have long opposed the heavy U.S. military presence on the island, although some have acknowledged its strategic benefit due to what is seen as a growing threat from China.

Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from World War II until 1972. Now, the U.S. population on the island is nearly 80,000, with nearly 30,000 being active duty troops from all four branches of the armed forces. The Marines make up most of the service members on the island.

A rise in crime linked to U.S. military-related personnel has led to renewed protests on the island. The number of criminal cases involving U.S. military-related personnel rose from about 40 in 2020 to 101 in 2025, according to Okinawa prefectural police.

After three U.S. service members raped a 12-year-old girl in 1995, huge crowds protested the U.S. military presence on Okinawa. There was also frustration over a U.S. service member's rape of a teenage girl in 2024 and the delayed disclosure of the case.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Susan Collins and Troy Jackson clash over Trump and seniority in Maine’s first Senate debate
World.content:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson debated for the first time Tuesday in Maine, trading attacks over President Donald Trump, the cost of living and abortion in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country.

Maine is central to Democrats’ path to the Senate majority as they try to capitalize on Trump’s unpopularity. Jackson tried to do just that Tuesday by tying Collins to Trump, name-checking him at least 20 times in one hour of debating on WGME-TV.

“It matters who you stand with,” Jackson said in his opening statement. “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does.”

Collins, meanwhile, emphasized multiple instances when she opposed the Trump administration.

She also sought to localize the race and pitch her seniority — and her perch as chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee — as a boost to Maine. She touted $1.5 billion in federal funds that she has brought home to the state for 672 projects in the last five years, “from Madawaksa to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford.”

“I’ve been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers,” Collins said.

Jackson set the tone for the debate early by connecting Collins to Trump and repeatedly saying she votes in alignment with him 96% of the time. Collins questioned the methodology of the study he cited.

In a moment that captured her tricky relationship with her party’s leader, Collins dodged two questions about whether she would stand with Trump if he visited Maine, with Trump having recently teased a visit to the Pine Tree State. Collins said only that she doesn’t expect him to come and that she’s “not exactly his favorite senator.”

Collins’ answer prompted a grin from Jackson. Trump has said Collins is “not my favorite person” but nevertheless endorsed her for re-election, and Vice President JD Vance has gone to Maine and backed her at events.

Polls show a neck-and-neck race between Collins and Jackson, often within the margin of error, as Collins seeks to defy gravity yet again and win a sixth term in the blue-leaning state. She is the only GOP senator representing a state Trump lost in 2024.

Both parties are spending tens of millions of dollars on a seat that carries major implications for control of the chamber, and a victory for Collins would constrict Democrats’ path to the Senate majority.

Jackson also highlighted Collins’ pivotal vote in 2018 to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was part of the majority that overturned Roe v. Wade, doing away with the federal right to abortion. Tuesday’s debate fell on the anniversary of Kavanaugh’s confirmation vote in the Senate.

Collins said she judges all nominees by their qualifications, and she noted that she also supported justices who voted to uphold Roe v. Wade.

“In fact, I am the only Republican senator to have voted for Justice [Sonia] Sotomayor, [Elena] Kagan and [Ketanji Brown] Jackson, who were nominated by a Democratic senator,” Collins said.

Collins also hit back against attempts to tie her to the end of Roe v. Wade, referring to Jackson’s more conservative stance on abortion earlier in his career and quipping, “There’s only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that’s me.”

Jackson did not engage with the barb in the moment, but he noted in his closing statement that he pushed for progressive abortion policies in the Legislature.

Jackson’s spokesperson, Dan Gottlieb, told NBC News earlier Tuesday that he would oppose any Trump Supreme Court nominee in his final two years should a vacancy open up — a view shared by some other Democrats.

Jackson also said Collins voted to advance Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which included about $1 trillion in unpopular Medicaid cuts.

That sparked a brushback from Collins, who noted that she voted against the legislation when it came to final passage. She said she has “never voted” to cut Medicaid.

“He knows I voted against President Trump’s signature legislative accomplishment,” Collins said, adding that she used the process to support a $50 billion rural healthcare fund.

Jackson doubled down.

“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said. “She could have stopped it.”

Collins went after Jackson’s “failed” policies as a state lawmaker, connecting them to higher housing costs and property taxes. She also questioned his talents as a legislator and whether he could be effective as a junior senator in a divided Senate.

When the topic turned to immigration, Jackson cited an ICE officer’s killing of a Mainer this year, saying it happened because “Sen. Collins would not push back against ICE.”

Collins said the shooting was “horrific” and “demonstrates that ICE needs further reform.” She said that she supported increased funding for body-worn cameras, as well as training of officers, and that she teamed up with the Maine delegation to demand answers from the Trump administration.

In her closing statement, Collins said: “To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation.”

Jackson questioned whether she has used her power well.

“Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is,” he said in his closing statement. “But power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people may need it.”

World.title: Sally Yates, former acting attorney general who defied Trump, to lead Cornell investigation
World.content:
Sally Yates, whose career in the Justice Department spanned about three decades, will lead an independent review on how Cornell University responds to sexual harassment, assault and misconduct on campus, the university announced Tuesday.

The decision comes in the wake of national outrage over a former Cornell student’s allegation last month that she was gang-raped and plied with drugs at a fraternity in 2024.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is also investigating the allegation. A spokesperson said staff members from the attorney general’s office have “spoken with the Tompkins County District Attorney, Jane Doe’s attorney, and several candidates for outside counsel to support the investigation.”

The independent probe headed by Yates will look into how the university responded to those allegations and whether the school followed its policies and procedures, according to the university.

More broadly, the review will examine Cornell’s policies and practices spanning from prevention to response. It will include how reports are investigated, how disciplinary decisions are handled and how students are supported, the university said. The investigation will also look into the role and response of campus police, and its coordination with other law enforcement agencies and prosecutors. Yates did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“Sally Yates brings extraordinary experience, independence and judgment to this work,” Anne Meinig Smalling, the chair of the university’s Special Committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees, said in a statement.

An attorney for one of the Chi Phi members who was accused of sexual assault, Gillio Lopes, said they welcome the independent investigation.

“Sally Yates has tremendous experience as a prosecutor and investigator, and she and her team should have access to the full record and the freedom to follow the facts wherever they lead,” attorney Andrew Miltenberg said.

Lopes denies sexually assaulting the former student and disagreed with the Title IX finding, he said. Attorneys for several of the other men have denied wrongdoing or disputed Doe’s account.

Yates is a longtime federal prosecutor who became known in 2017 for refusing to enforce President Donald Trump’s ban on travelers to the U.S. from predominantly Muslim countries. Currently a partner at the law firm King & Spalding, she also previously investigated allegations of abuse and misconduct at U.S. Soccer.

Yates was named the deputy U.S. attorney general, the second-highest-ranking in the Justice Department, with bipartisan support in 2015. During that tenure under former President Barack Obama, Yates wrote a memo directing prosecutors to focus on individual wrongdoers in corporate cases. The memo followed the fallout of the 2008 financial crisis, in which corporations were forced to pay fines but many individual executives were not prosecuted.

Yates was also the acting U.S. attorney general for 10 days in 2017 before she was fired for refusing to defend Trump’s travel ban. Trump’s order created an early flashpoint of protest against his aggressive immigration policies.

The White House said at the time that Yates had “betrayed the Department of Justice by refusing to enforce a legal order designed to protect the citizens of the United States.” The statement added that “Ms. Yates is an Obama Administration appointee who is weak on borders and very weak on illegal immigration.”

Yates wrote an op-ed in The New York Times in July 2017, after her firing, writing that Trump was “attempting to dismantle the rule of law, destroy the time-honored independence of the Justice Department, and undermine the career men and women who are devoted to seeking justice day in and day out, regardless of which political party is in power.”

“If we are not careful, when we wake up from the Trump presidency, our justice system may be broken beyond recognition,” she wrote.

Yates began her career in the DOJ in 1989 at the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia, where she was an assistant U.S. attorney. That office covers 46 counties and includes Atlanta. In 2010, Obama appointed her to lead the office, making her the first woman to do so.

She has also previously led investigations into sexual misconduct.

In 2022, Yates led an independent probe into U.S. Soccer that resulted in a damning report.

“Our investigation over the past year has revealed a league in which abuse was systematic. Verbal and emotional abuse and sexual misconduct occurred at multiple teams, was perpetrated by several coaches and affected many players,” she said at the time.

U.S. Soccer said that the findings were “heartbreaking and deeply troubling” and that it would work to thoroughly address the recommendations.

“The abuse described is inexcusable and has no place on any playing field, in any training facility or workplace,” U.S. Soccer President and former U.S. Women’s National Team member Cindy Parlow Cone said at the time.

In Cornell’s announcement on Monday, it said that Yates and her team have been asked to “examine Cornell’s overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer.”

The university said it would share the results of the review, along with any recommendations, with the Cornell community.
