World.title: Record Pacific temps fuel a ‘super’ El Niño with grave global consequences
World.content:
“Godzilla.” “Super.” “Very strong.”

There’s no shortage of superlatives to describe the El Niño pattern brewing in the tropical Pacific Ocean, with grave consequences expected in many corners of the world.

So far, data continues to back up the hype.

Sea surface temperatures have spiked to record levels in the tropical Pacific this fall, a sign that the pattern continues to strengthen. In the region where the El Niño trend is typically measured, temperatures are 6.1 degrees Fahrenheit higher than normal.

In its latest update, the National Oceanographic and Atmospheric Agency said the pattern was strengthening and that there was a 90% chance of a “very strong event” this fall and winter, with a 75% chance of becoming a historic event larger than any El Niño since 1950.

The index data NOAA uses to characterize El Niño suggests this season’s event is the second-biggest anomaly on record for the months of July through September, even when the influence of global warming on temperatures is not factored into the equation.

“It feels like super El Niño is appropriate,” said Abby Frazier, a climatologist and professor of geography at Clark University.

The children’s aid organization UNICEF said Tuesday its analysis suggests hundreds of millions of children could be exposed to dangerous conditions as a result of the climate pattern, which raises the risk of intense precipitation in some areas and drought in others.

“With over 347 million children living in areas expected to experience drier or wetter conditions because of El Niño, we must act now to protect communities and children,” UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell said, adding that El Niño was expected to increase water shortages, malnutrition and disease outbreaks.

00:46 Southern California faces coastal erosion concerns 00:00 00:00

The University of Chicago’s Climate Impacts Lab estimates that El Niño will raise global average temperatures enough to cause 451,000 excess-heat deaths worldwide.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that happens when winds near the equator slacken and the upwelling of cold water to the surface of the eastern Pacific Ocean stalls. The pattern typically drives up global average temperatures, causes marine heat waves off the U.S. West Coast and dampens the Atlantic hurricane season. El Niño is associated with intense rainfall and storms in the Southeast and warm conditions in the Pacific Northwest that can rob the region of its snowpack and water supply.

Scientists expect El Niño to batter the U.S. West Coast and cause unusual beach erosion, because storms are sending strong waves toward the shore, where sea levels are already rising because coastal waters are warmer than usual and therefore taking up more space.

El Niño’s influence is most obvious in the winter, because it often shifts the normal flow of the jet stream, the high-altitude air current that encircles the Northern Hemisphere and drives weather patterns. El Niño usually pushes the jet stream southward, scrambling weather patterns.

Some regions will likely suffer drought; others will be deluged with extreme rainfall and flooding. Now is the time to prepare for water restrictions in some locations and to watch rainfall forecasts in others, Frazier said. Expect those effects to ripple through agricultural economies — goods like rice, coffee and chocolate could be affected as growing conditions are affected.

“This could have cascading impacts through supply chains and other things, so it could impact the prices that we pay in the grocery store for some of our food,” Frazier said.

The signs of El Niño’s presence are growing more plain. The U.S. had a historically mellow Atlantic hurricane season, while powerful hurricanes raced across the Pacific, fueled by warm seas.

“The number of storms that have formed and have impacted, especially Hawaii, has been really incredible this year,” Frazier said.

Meanwhile, unusual marine species — including whale sharks, sea snakes and nesting turtles — have been spotted off the California coast, farther north than what water temperatures typically allow.

And earlier this summer, NASA satellites could tell that the height of seas had actually grown taller near the equator, a sign that the ocean water was growing warmer and expanding in volume.

World.title: Live updates: The absolute best October Prime Day deals, hand-picked by a shopping reporter
World.content:
October Prime Day (technically called Prime Big Deal Days) is happening now through October 7, offering discounts across categories, exclusive to Prime members. Some of the top newly added deals are Blink’s video doorbell and Tide Pods — they also happen to be at their lowest price ever.

I frequently cover shopping events like Amazon Prime Day, Black Friday and Cyber Monday as a reporter for NBC Selected, so I know how to find deals that are actually worth buying. I spent weeks combing through thousands of discounts to find the best October Prime Day deals — each one I recommend below is highly rated and 20 percent off or more, as well as at its lowest price in at least three months. I’ll frequently update this list throughout Prime Big Deal Days with my editor-approved picks.

Want more from NBC Selected? 

Top overall October Prime Day deals

This robot vacuum suctions up dirt and debris, and it has a built-in mop that scrubs floors to leave them shiny. It’s designed with sensors that map your home to detect and avoid obstacles, and it connects to the Roomba Home app so you can select cleaning modes, create cleaning schedules, adjust suction level and more. You can also set keep-out and no-mop zones where needed, like on area rugs. The appliance comes with a charging dock, reusable microfiber mopping pad and edge sweeping brush.

We named the Paperwhite Amazon’s best Kindle because of its extra-long battery life that lasts up to 12 weeks. It also has a front light that automatically adjusts depending on your environment, helping you see the glare-free screen clearly. The Kindle Paperwhite is water-resistant, and you can charge it via the USB-C port or wirelessly with a charging dock that’s sold separately.

Once you connect devices like lamps, fans and small kitchen appliances to the Amazon Smart Plug, you can control them through an app or via voice commands. The app also lets you set timers, schedules and routines — for example, I connect my Christmas lights to this smart plug and create a schedule for them so they turn on at 10 a.m. and turn off at 10 p.m. The plug is compact to keep your second outlet free.

I rely on this corded vacuum to get rid of dirt, dust and hair on hard floors and carpets in my three-pet home. It has powerful suction, a multi-stage washable HEPA filter to trap allergens and a swivel steering system that makes it easy to navigate. My favorite part of the vacuum is the detachable pod, which I carry around my home and use the extended reach tool to clean above door frames, under furniture and on stairs. Interchangeable wide upholstery and crevice attachments for the extended reach tool are included.

These were one of my best purchases during last year’s Prime Big Deal Days. Their ribbed silicone exterior helps me grip hot pots and pans, and they’re heat-resistant up to 500 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the brand. The material is also water-resistant, so I don’t worry about spills or splashes. The inside of the mitts are lined with cotton, making them soft against my skin.

Prepare for the cozy season ahead by adding Ugg’s faux fur blanket to your couch or bed. It’s double-sided, so it feels soft against your skin no matter how you use it, and it’s roomy enough for two people to share. While Ugg recommends dry cleaning the blanket, you can also machine wash it on cold, according to the brand.

Colgate’s toothpaste is made with 5 percent hydrogen peroxide, a bleaching ingredient that helps remove stains from teeth and make your smile less yellow. There’s also cavity-fighting fluoride in its formula. The minty whitening toothpaste is safe for daily use and doesn’t cause tooth sensitivity, according to the brand.

Apple’s AirPods Pro 3 made our list of the best earbuds, and I use mine every day while listening to music on runs, taking calls and blocking out noisy city streets. They’re comfortable and secure in my ears even when I get sweaty — they come with five interchangeable ear tips so you can find the right fit. The AirPods have three listening modes, including active noise cancellation, hours of battery life with the included charging case and advanced features like heart rate sensing during workouts, hearing aid mode and live language translation.

The most boring essentials on your shopping list are often the best deals to take advantage of during Prime Big Deal Days — you’ll need to restock eventually, so you might as well do it when items are discounted. Cascade’s dishwasher pods are a perfect example. They come in a pack of 62, and with the discount applied, you’re only paying about 0.28 per pod. Each one has soap inside that gets rid of grease and food residue, and it cleans your dishwasher’s filter, too.

I’ve beat up my Samsonite luggage while traveling over the years, but it still works perfectly, looks great and, perhaps most importantly, fits all my stuff. You get a matching expandable carry-on and checked bag with this set, both of which are lightweight and made with hard, protective exteriors. The suitcases have spacious interiors with elastic straps, a divider and a pouch for organization, plus they’re designed with smoothly gliding wheels, a built-in ID tag, a height-adjustable handle and a TSA-approved lock.

Urevo makes some of our favorite walking pads, and this model has features experts told us to look for while shopping, like multiple speed and incline levels, as well as a quiet motor. You can connect it to an app that lets you pick programs, control the settings and enroll in challenges to stay engaged. The brand says the walking pad is slim and compact enough to fit under most standard office desks.

Take LifeStraw’s Personal Water Filter on hikes and camping trips, or put it in your emergency kit. You use it like a straw, and its built-in filter removes over 99 percent of bacteria, parasites and microplastics from water, according to the brand. You can use it to filter up to 1,000 gallons of water before needing a new one.

I’ve never met a kid who doesn’t love Magna-Tiles, and if I’m being honest, I enjoy using them, too. This set comes with 70 magnetic blocks in a rainbow of colors and different shapes like rectangles, triangles and squares. In addition to letting kids be creative while building, the brand says the blocks help with hand-eye coordination and fine motor skills.

The internet-famous Shark DePuffi is currently on sale for the first time ever, so don’t wait any longer to get your hands on it. The skin care device has six customizable temperatures that go from cold to hot, and it’s made with a gua sha-inspired edge — as you massage it along your face and neck to encourage lymphatic flow, it depuffs, sculpts and temporarily relieves muscle tension, according to the brand. You get a travel case and charger with your purchase.

Top October Prime Day deals on household essentials and groceries

I’m very picky about dish soap because I don’t have a dishwasher, and out of all the options I’ve tested, Dawn Powerwash Spray is hands-down the best one. It easily removes dirt and grime from my dishes without pre-soaking, and it leaves them literally sparkling. Also, since the soap works without water, I don’t turn my faucet on until I’m ready to rinse. Beyond washing dishes, you can use Dawn’s spray on laundry stains, kitchen surfaces, appliances and grills, according to the brand. This starter kit comes with four bottles of liquid and one reusable sprayer head.

Premier Protein’s shakes are ideal for snacking on the go. Each one has 30 grams of protein, no added sugar and 160 calories, according to the brand, plus they’re gluten-free. They come in over a dozen creamy flavors, like chocolate, vanilla, cookies and cream, cafe latte and pumpkin spice, almost all of which are currently on sale.

These trash bags are multi-layered and slightly stretchy to prevent leaks and rips while you fill them to the brim, and they have a drawstring closure to keep everything inside once full. They’re also made with baking soda and added fragrance to neutralize odors. You get 80 13-gallon bags in this pack.

These Tide Pods don’t just clean clothes. The detergent inside each one also fights odors, pre-treats and removes stains, protects colors and boosts scents, according to the brand. I use them for all my laundry, including sweaty workout clothes and my pets’ beds, and I’ve never had an issue with them not dissolving, even in cold water. You get 63 Tide Pods in this pack, which come in a resealable container.

The dual-sided Scrub Mommy is the only sponge I buy. Its scrubber side is soft in warm water yet firm in cold water to get rid of stuck-on grime, while its sponge side is always soft and highly absorbent to create suds. The circular sponges are easy to hold, and the smiley face in the center is purposeful: You can put your fingers in the eyes for a secure grip and put utensils through the mouth to wipe them down. The Scrub Mommy is odor-resistant, scratch-free and dishwasher-safe.

I always buy batteries when they’re on sale so I never run out at home. This pack comes with 24 AAs and 24 AAAs, and they last for up to 10 years in storage, according to the brand.

Top October Prime Day tech deals

You can monitor visitors and deliveries at all times with Blink’s video doorbell. It connects to the brand’s app, letting you livestream head-to-toe video (including in night vision) and audio, as well as speak to people. The doorbell runs on two AA batteries, comes with a mounting kit and you can install it wire-free. There’s also a Blink subscription available for an additional fee, which gives you access to features like in-app person detection and motion-activated notifications.

Never worry about a dead phone or earbuds again with Anker’s Nano Power Bank, which has a built-in folding USB-C connector, eliminating the need for a cable. It fits in the palm of your hand and weighs 3.5 ounces, so you can put it in any bag or even your pocket. The Nano comes with a charging cable when you need to refill its battery, or you can connect it directly to a block.

Turn any TV into a smart TV with Amazon’s Fire Stick, which you simply plug into an HDMI port to use. It lets you stream entertainment from your favorite platforms and watch live TV in HD. The Fire Stick comes with a remote that lets you control the TV via buttons or voice commands. It’s also compact so it won’t block other ports.

Top October Prime Day beauty deals

When you leave this sheet mask on for three to four hours, or overnight, it turns transparent as your skin absorbs the serum it’s soaked in. It’s made with ingredients like hyaluronic acid and niacinamide to hydrate, refine enlarged pores, improve skin elasticity, brighten tone and smooth fine lines and wrinkles, according to the brand. You get four masks in this pack, and they’re each individually wrapped.

World.title: In Maine Senate debate, Collins and Jackson both criticize Trump — but spar over how
World.content:
In an often-testy Tuesday night debate, Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine touted her three-decade-long record in Congress and took aim at some Trump policies — while Democrat Troy Jackson argued Collins has failed to push back against the Trump administration.

The Maine Senate race is one of November's most closely watched contests, and could prove crucial to determining which party controls the upper chamber next year. While the state leans left, and hasn't voted for a Republican presidential candidate statewide since the 1980s, Collins' history of surviving tough reelection challenges has vexed Democrats for more than a decade. Most polls show a razor-thin race.

Collins highlighted her "knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships," including her ability to score funding for projects in Maine as chair of the influential Senate Appropriations Committee.

"I've been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers," said Collins, who is running for a sixth term in the Senate.

Collins also has a history of breaking with President Trump, criticizing his trade war with Canada and strategy in Iran, and voting against the Trump-backed One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year — themes that frequently emerged in Tuesday's debate.

Asked about Mr. Trump's suggestion that he may travel to Maine as part of a pre-election campaign swing, Collins said she doesn't expect the president to visit.

"I've heard nothing from his office, and I'm not exactly his favorite senator," she said.

But Jackson — a former state Senate president who hails from the same largely rural northern Maine county as Collins — argued that Collins has not used her power effectively to push back against Trump administration policies, and accused her of siding with the president too often.

He criticized Collins for voting to confirm Trump-nominated Justice Brett Kavanaugh to the Supreme Court, setting the stage for the high court to overturn Roe v. Wade and allow states to ban abortion for the first time in more than 50 years.

"Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?" asked Jackson.

Collins responded that when evaluating nominees to the Supreme Court, she "always look[s] at their qualifications." She said she disagreed with the decision to overturn Roe, but added that "there's only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice" — a reference to Jackson's previous opposition to abortion.

While Collins voted against the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut Medicaid and food stamp spending and extended a set of tax cuts from the first Trump term, Jackson repeatedly criticized the senator for voting yes on an earlier procedural measure to advance the bill, arguing she should've tried to block the legislative package.

Collins said Jackson "misrepresent[ed] the facts." She noted that she opposed the bill due to its Medicaid cuts, but argued that her decision to let the bill move forward on the Senate floor allowed her to secure a $50 billion fund for rural hospitals.

Jackson responded: "Senator Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out."

Collins also pointed to her votes to restrict Mr. Trump's power to wage war against Iran, saying the war is "not well-thought out" and noting its impact on global energy markets. Jackson criticized Collins for voting against prior Iran measures.

Both candidates were critical of Mr. Trump's tariffs on Canada, which have sparked a tit-for-tat trade war with Maine's neighbor. Collins said she is opposed to the trade war but has been "working behind the scenes" to get exemptions for goods that are key to Maine's economy or to the operations of municipal governments, like road salt.

"Canada is our friend. It should be treated as such," she said.

Jackson mocked Collins' approach as writing a "strongly worded letter."

"What about everything else?" he asked. "I mean, we can't eat road salt."

The two candidates were also deeply critical of Immigration and Customs Enforcement's conduct, after a man in Maine was fatally shot by an ICE officer during a traffic stop over the summer. Collins called it "horrific," and Jackson said he was "murdered." But they clashed over the policy response. Jackson said ICE should be "disbanded" and should not have received a surge of funding, while Collins said the agency needs "serious reforms" but needs to continue to exist.

"It needs reform, not to be abolished," Collins said.

A longtime state lawmaker, Jackson initially ran for governor. But after losing in the Democratic gubernatorial primary, Jackson was swapped in as the party's Senate candidate at the last minute after the winner of the Democratic primary, Graham Platner, dropped out amid sexual misconduct allegations. Platner has denied the allegations.

Collins took aim at Jackson's record in state politics. She argued many of the affordability challenges that have animated voters — including on energy prices and Medicaid reimbursement rates — are the result of failings by politicians in the state capital of Augusta.

She also questioned Jackson's effectiveness as a legislator, pointing to bills he introduced that were rejected in committee without Democratic support.

"If you can't find one person in your own party to vote for your bills when you were the Senate president in Maine … how do you think you're going to get things done in a closely divided Senate as the most junior senator?" Collins asked her opponent.

Jackson said Collins "doesn't understand the legislative process," saying it "gums the system up" to have "one or two people vote for a bill that's not going to make it."

World.title: GOP Super PAC pours $5 million into South Carolina Senate race, sources say
World.content:
A key Republican Super PAC is putting $5 million to support Sen. Darline Graham in the South Carolina Senate race, sources familiar with the investment confirmed on Tuesday, as President Trump is escalating his attacks against her opponent, Democrat Annie Andrews.

The investment from the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Super PAC, is a sign the party is concerned about the race, even though South Carolina is a solidly red state. President Trump won the state by 18 points in 2024 and Graham's late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham, won by 10 points in 2020, despite having a well-funded opponent in Democrat Jamie Harrison. Winning South Carolina has been at best a distant dream for Democrats since the end of the 20th century.

The $5 million investment was first reported by Axios.

South Carolina GOP Senate nominee Darline Graham was appointed to the seat in July after the death of her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, a close ally of Mr. Trump who had been in the Senate since 2003. Lindsey Graham had won a primary for the seat just weeks before his sudden death, and Darline Graham then won a subsequent special primary to be on the ballot in November.

Mr. Trump has campaigned heavily for Darline Graham, and posted an attack on social media against Andrews using an anti-transgender slur.

"Annie 'Trannie' Andrews is running against our wonderful Darline Graham for the Senate in South Carolina," Mr. Trump wrote on social media on Monday.

Andrews, a pediatrician, has said she does not support gender transition surgery for minors, but she had in the past voiced opposition to a bill that would ban transgender athletes in sports. She told The New York Times last week that she does not "support biological men playing in women's sports."

The most resonant campaign ad in 2024 seized on transgender issues as an emblem of the cultural divide in America: "Kamala is for they/them President Trump is for you." This year, some Republicans are trying to replicate that effort and tie their Democratic opponents to transgender issues, although it's unclear if it's been as successful.

Andrews responded late Monday without mentioning Mr. Trump's comments directly, but noted "if you care more about your bills than the politics in Washington, this campaign is for you."

Republican former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley told CBS News that Mr. Trump's comments on Andrews were "such a disgrace."

Beasley, who previously served as executive director of the World Food Programme, also called the post "abhorrent" on social media.

"Elections don't have to be about cruelty and lies," he wrote. "South Carolina deserves better. I urge voters to look at the merits of each candidate and cast their vote accordingly. We must reject politics based on division and hate"

World.title: Storm brewing off Mexico could impact Gulf Coast as hurricane this weekend
World.content:
With less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season, the potential for a ninth named tropical storm in the Atlantic basin is brewing in the southern Gulf.

Since the Atlantic's season began on June 1, it has only seen eight named storms this year, while El Niño continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The season ends Nov. 30.

What we know about the possible path

Tropical Depression Nine formed in the Gulf on Tuesday. As the storm brews over the warmer waters off Mexico, it's expected to become a tropical storm by early Wednesday and a hurricane on Thursday, according to the National Hurricane Center.

If it does become a tropical storm, it would receive the name Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs."

Forecast models are beginning to come to agreement that the northward motion of this tropical system brings it to the Gulf Coast this weekend.

A map shows the projected path of Tropical Depression Nine. CBS News

Regardless of its name or if it develops into a tropical storm, we do know that it will bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week. The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 6 inches of rain for the central Gulf Coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle.

Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.

A map shows the rainfall potential from the tropical system. CBS News

What we do not know

Timing, storm intensity and severity of impacts to land with this tropical system are what remain unknown.

While some models have impacts starting Friday evening, others show it beginning later in the weekend.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday signed an executive order declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of the storm's arrival. DeSantis said in a statement that the order "ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida."

A map shows possible paths for the tropical system. CBS News

Beware the "I"-named storm

While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.

The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017), and Irene (2011).

When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

World.title: Hundreds of Israeli flags vandalized outside church in McKinney, Texas, ahead of Oct. 7 observance
World.content:
It was designed to be a striking display of support for Israel during a week of remembrance of the deadly Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023. But the symbolic gesture outside a church in McKinney, Texas, has instead made it a target of threats and vandalism.

Len McLaughlin, senior pastor of Heritage Church, had 1,200 small Israeli flags placed around the property in memory of the approximately 1,200 victims of the deadly attack on Israel by the militant group Hamas that took place three years ago Wednesday.

"We feel it is biblical and deeply spiritual to be a church that supports Israel," McLaughlin said. "... We feel it is important to take a moment to remember those folks, and in their memory, we put the flags up."

CBS News Texas

But when the pastor arrived at his church Tuesday morning, he found hundreds of flags pulled up and tossed into piles.

"They pulled all of them up and stomped all them all of them into the ground, really just showed total disrespect," McLaughlin said. "... They came in the darkness of night. They're cowards who did this. They're not patriots."

The pastor filed a police report, but said he was moved by the sight of people he didn't know who came to the church and were working to restore the display.

"And to my surprise, there were five strangers from our community, a couple of ladies from the veterinary clinic across the street," McLaughlin said.

The church is also receiving support from residents in the neighborhood.

"It's beyond belief," resident Russ Mortenson said of the vandalism. "It's hard for me to understand that. I found them to be very impressive and hopefully meaningful."

McLaughlin says the church has also been receiving threats over the exhibit.

The flag display has been restored, and the church plans to expand its security while the display is up.

"I wouldn't want anybody to go to jail over it, but I certainly would like for them to be fined and treated as criminals because what they did was criminal," McLaughlin said.

World.title: Details emerge in case of former Cornell student alleging rape by frat members
World.content:
New details are emerging in the case of a former Cornell University student who claims she was drugged and gang-raped for multiple hours inside a fraternity house in October 2024.

The woman — identified only as Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged incident — recently filed a civil lawsuit against seven then-Chi Phi fraternity members and the university, claiming they failed to protect her and prevent the alleged assault. While Cornell conducted an internal investigation, and expelled or suspended several of the men, no criminal charges were brought against the accused at the time.

The Tompkins County District Attorney's Office confirmed on Monday, Sept. 28, that it was reopening the criminal investigation amid pressure from the community. The DA said the woman's sworn statement from November 2024 was different from what she alleges in the civil lawsuit, while her attorney claims investigators never followed up on her allegations.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Oct. 1 signed an executive order appointing New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor in the case. Hochul said James will "investigate the incident and, if warranted, prosecute any offenses arising from the investigation and present evidence to a grand jury."

Here is what we know about the case so far:

Claims against Cornell

In the lawsuit against the university and the then-fraternity members, the woman alleges she visited a friend at Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity house while she was already intoxicated, and alleges that two fraternity members pressured her into taking what they said was ketamine. She alleges they then sexually assaulted her.

According to the suit, on the night in question at around 1:42 a.m., one fraternity member sent a crude message to a Chi Phi Snapchat group chat suggesting that a woman upstairs was available for sex. The woman alleges more men entered the room and the assaults continued until 5:45 a.m.

The complaint says the woman filed a report with the university's police department three weeks after the alleged rapes.

"Once she was emotionally ready, she went to the University police and bravely shared what had occurred to her. She went to the police because she believed that she was the victim of a crime," her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, said in a statement to CBS News.

"Other than her initial contact with Cornell Police, she was not contacted by investigators from the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors," Giuffra said.

Cornell conducted an internal review of the allegations after she filed the report with campus police. Giuffra told CBS News New York that two of the fraternity members were expelled, while five others received lesser sanctions including suspensions, workshops and writing essays.

"Not one of these guys was arrested. Not one. That I can tell you for a fact," Giuffra told CBS News New York, adding that the woman dropped out of the school after the alleged assault.

Cornell disputed the idea that some of the accused only had to write essays for punishment.

"None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement," the university said.

Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff specified in a Sept. 29 meeting with the student government that two of the accused were expelled, two suspended for at least two semesters, one had already graduated before any punishment could be handed down, and two were found not to be responsible for sexual misconduct.

People walk on the campus of Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, in February 2024. AP Photo/Seth Wenig

The lawsuit accuses Cornell and the other defendants of breach of contract, negligence and violations of state law. She is seeking monetary damages, including compensatory and punitive damages. The lawsuit does not specify how much she is seeking.

Exclusive report on Jane Doe campus police interview transcript

According to a transcript of the alleged victim's interview with campus police, obtained by CBS News New York's Mahsa Saeidi from a source, Jane Doe distinguished the initial sexual activity from what she says happened later in the night.

She described drinking and using drugs the night of the alleged rape, and said she had gaps in her memory, according to the transcript.

When asked whether she was OK with the initial encounter, she said, "Yeah, as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there ... But I was pretty OK with all of this."

When describing what happened later in the night, the transcript says Jane Doe said, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

The interview began on Nov. 14, 2024 — more than three weeks after the alleged gang rape — and continued the next day.

The transcript was used as the basis for the alleged victim's written statement, and it shows the investigator read her account back to her word by word and gave her a chance to clarify or correct the record.

On the second day of the interview, Jane Doe reviewed the revised six-page statement. The transcript shows her adviser asked if she wanted her and another adviser to review the statement.

In the statement, obtained by CBS News, she detailed what she said happened the night of the alleged rape. She described being "pretty incapacitated" and things becoming a blur.

She recalled "multiple men" coming into the room at some point when she was naked.

"I had become extremely uncomfortable with how this night was turning out, so my thought was, if I do ketamine again, maybe I will pass out. My thought was that if I passed out and these men have sex with me, then they could have been charged with rape at this point," she said in the statement.

Later, she described two people walking in and saying they were "shutting it down," which caused "the group of men" to scatter.

She then described sexual encounters. "I remember being totally disgusted at the situation, and I felt very tired and intoxicated," she said, adding, "I would say that it was the most intoxicated I've ever been in my life. I felt like I was unable to make any decisions because of how intoxicated I was."

Before signing, the transcript shows Jane Doe said, "I'm very confident about this."

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told CBS News on Sept. 29 that he was never provided the full transcripts of those initial interviews Jane Doe conducted with Cornell police.

He said the sworn statement submitted to his office in November 2024 made no mention of the statements that were made in the transcript obtained by CBS News New York — specifically Doe telling school investigators, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."

"I never saw it, never heard it until tonight," Van Houten said in the interview. "If it exists, I will get it. You can be sure of that."

He added, "If that kind of thing was omitted from a statement, if it is true, it needs to be fully investigated by someone outside of Cornell."

Cornell University initially said its police department provided the results of the school's investigation to the DA. However, in an FAQ published on its website regarding the allegations, the university said in an Oct. 1 update that it "shared the victim's sworn statement and the Snapchat screenshot with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."

Jane Doe's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, remarked to CBS News, "What more did (Van Houten) need to do a thorough investigation and prosecute? He had a woman who told an officer she was raped and a group chat inviting sexual assaults. The failure to do anything is shocking.

"Neither I nor Ms. Doe have any confidence in DA Houten's ability to handle this investigation and prosecution. He seems more interested in protecting his reputation as opposed to seeking justice as is his duty as the District Attorney."

Title IX investigation transcripts

CBS News New York obtained transcripts of Cornell's Title IX investigation, distributed to the parties in January 2025, from a source. The documents are part of the record but do not include the Title IX panel's hearing minutes, reasoning or final findings.

The records offer a closer look at how Jane Doe described what she says happened to her that night and in the days that followed, as well as how people around her remembered it. They include interviews with Doe, six of the seven men named in Doe's bombshell civil lawsuit, and 20 witnesses.

One roommate recalls Doe saying "Oh my goodness, isn't that crazy?" the morning after the alleged incident at Cornell's Chi Phi house in October 2024. The roommate said Doe was laughing as she recounted it, but seemed to be in shock. The roommate said Doe did not call it rape or assault that next morning.

A second roommate said Jane Doe did tell her "I wasn't comfortable."

About a week later, that second roommate said she heard Doe tell one of the men, "You had penetrative sex with me. I had so much ketamine, my eyes were crossed, and you still had sex with me."

In her Title IX interview in November, Doe said she didn't show "excitement and enthusiasm, which is kinda the basis of consent." She said she told the men she was tired and didn't want to continue, and that she was sometimes encouraged to take more substances.

The men, now accused of rape and assault, also gave their accounts.

One said he asked Jane Doe if he could take ketamine from her body. He said she agreed.

Another, Scott Kretzschmar, said he was in the room for "tops, five minutes," did not see her naked, and did not do drugs. Kretzschmar told a Title IX investigator he asked Doe if she was OK. He said her response was "I'm good" and that "she didn't seem inebriated at all."

The allegation against Kretzschmar is that he snorted ketamine from Doe's body, something his attorney Jeremy Saland denies.

Cornell said its Title IX process lasted months, included a hearing before a panel of trained faculty and staff, and resulted in sanctions, including expulsions and suspensions.

"After investigation, and pursuant to federal law, the matter was sent to a hearing where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days," Cornell's statement said. "The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence."

Cornell's response and internal investigation

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said on Sept. 30 that Cornell has agreed to bring in outside counsel for an independent investigation. "I want answers. And I want accountability," she wrote on X.

Cornell said on Oct. 6 that former Deputy U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates will oversee a broad review of the university's handling of sexual misconduct claims, including Jane Doe's allegations.

The fraternity chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus.

"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," Cornell said. "A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."

The Ithaca Police Department told CBS News New York that the alleged incident was never reported to them.

Cornell said in a statement that Ithaca police were not involved initially because the "established protocol" when the school's police department believes a crime may have been committed is to share the investigation with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office.

"The Cornell University Police Department is a sworn law enforcement agency and performs the same functions as municipal police, but on Cornell property. This incident occurred in Cornell's jurisdiction," the school said.

Former Cornell University police chief Anthony Bellamy, who is now deputy chief at the Ithaca Police Department, told CBS News he has no comment.

Van Houten told CBS News that the DA's office didn't have access to Cornell's Title IX records on the alleged incident, and that he's asking Jane Doe's attorney to provide those documents.

He also said "we don't have any indication" campus police at the time interviewed the seven then-fraternity brothers accused in the lawsuit.

Snapchat and text messages

CBS News New York exclusively obtained additional video of the fraternity's group Snapchat conversation from the night the woman alleges the incident occurred.

A message sent to the group at 1:42 a.m. suggested in crude language that a woman was available for sex.

"Shop still open?" one fraternity brother wrote later.

The response was "Yea."

Screenshots of a separate text exchange, also reported exclusively by CBS News New York, show what a source describes as messages sent two days later between Jane Doe and one of the defendants now accused in the lawsuit.

The man started by apologizing for "how things went down." He said his memory is "kinda fuzzy," and that he and another man feel bad for being too intoxicated to "shut it down and kick people out before it got way out of hand."

The woman in the text chain replied that her memory is "super clouded too," and said they had all been heavily intoxicated.

She also wrote, "non(e) of the sexual stuff was illegal." She said she liked being with him and another man. Later, she suggested they smoke together again, "but like leave out the extra 5 billion men and ketamine."

The woman's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, confirmed she exchanged texts with this defendant shortly after the alleged assault, but he could not confirm whether these were the specific texts.

Giuffra said she was in denial and traumatized shortly after the alleged assaults. He said she was intoxicated to the point of incapacity that night and was trying to find out what happened.

He said she felt like she should not take an aggressive tone with this defendant if she wanted answers.

N.Y. Attorney General Letitia James appointed as special prosecutor

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order naming New York Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case.

"Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly, that they will be seen and heard," James said at a news conference Friday, Oct. 2. "That is the promise of our justice system. I stand ready to lead a process guided by the facts and the law."

Hocul said in a statement that she asked James to take over the case because "[n]ewly released information continues to raise serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute," saying it had "undercut my faith, and the public's faith, in the District Attorney's ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time."

A Cornell spokesperson said the university supports the decision to assign the case to James' office.

The appointment comes less than a week after the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office said it would reopen the criminal investigation — a decision Cornell also said it supported.

Before James' appointment, the DA, Matthew Van Houten, had told CBS News correspondent Lilia Luciano that he hoped they'd be able to bring the case to a grand jury "in the next 45 days," adding, "I want to move fast." He had said the grand jury could "consider the charges that were set out in the civil complaint, and they can consider other charges."

In a statement earlier, Van Houten said the allegations made in the civil lawsuit were different from the sworn statement made by Jane Doe in November 2024. He said her 2024 statement "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped" by multiple men.

"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," Van Houten's statement said. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later."

He told CBS News, "I don't see how more could have been done at the time, given that foundation of the case being her statement."

Van Houten called the Snapchat message chain "disgusting, vulgar," but said it "had nothing to do with the issue of consent, which is the legal issue."

Cornell said the Cornell University Police Department provided a screenshot from Snapchat to the DA back in 2024, along with Jane Doe's sworn statement.

Van Houten told CBS News the officer who took Jane Doe's original statement was "an experienced investigator" who was "trained in trauma informed sexual assault cases," and "not just somebody who was manning the desk."

He had told CBS News: "We want to treat her with respect and with humanity and compassion and hear from her what's changed since November of 2024. We want to sit down with her and talk through what she knows now and what she has processed over that time so that we can put all of the evidence before the grand jury and let the grand jury decide."

Giuffra, the woman's attorney, said she was not contacted by investigators from the DA's office after she made her report to Cornell's university police.

"Interviewing a survivor is a challenging process that takes a lot of time and experience. It is never easy for a survivor to share details of an assault with a stranger. Trust must be developed and a lot of time spent learning the facts and engaging with the survivor," he said. "It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint."

Giuffra told CBS News they welcomed the reopening of the criminal investigation, saying it was "a step in the right direction, albeit a late one."

Defendants deny accusations

The lawsuit identifies one of the accused then-fraternity members as Scott Kretzchmar, who allegedly sent two responses in the Snapchat group.

His defense attorney, Jeremy Saland, acknowledged to CBS News that the messages were inappropriate but said they are not evidence of sexual assault.

"This is a situation where there was an ugly Snapchat — ugly, period. … But that doesn't make my client a rapist, and it certainly doesn't make anyone a sex offender," Saland said.

Saland said Kretzchmar briefly entered the room where the woman was, in response to the message "that many people have seen," and said he did not touch her "in any way, shape or form" and left in a matter of minutes.

"She was not incoherent but in fact was coherent and again left that room without touching her or having any physical interaction with her whatsoever," Saland said.

The attorney said the university found Kretzchmar was not responsible for anything that the woman alleges in her complaint.

As for the accusation of ketamine use, Saland said Kretzchmar took a hair follicle test that determined he had no ketamine in his system.

"We certainly would present evidence of the hair follicle test which demonstrably and scientifically shows that he did not ingest ketamine as alleged by the complainant," he said.

Saland said that while no one has contacted him about a renewed investigation, "we welcome the opportunity."

"We are available to present exonerating evidence. I just hope the right thing is eventually done, this case is closed, and my client can live his life and not be subject to this selfish, repugnant, vile claim by this woman about him," he added.

Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney representing Gillio Lopes, another then-fraternity member accused in the civil lawsuit, told CBS News New York that his client "unequivocally denies the allegations against him."

"Cornell previously investigated these allegations. The allegations now being made publicly differ from what was reported and investigated during that process," Miltenberg said. "These are serious accusations, but accusations are not proof. Mr. Lopes should be judged on the evidence, not prejudged based on allegations made in a lawsuit or repeated in the media. We will address these issues through the appropriate legal process."

CBS News has reached out to the other defendants named in the civil lawsuit.

Mahsa Saeidi, Lilia Luciano and Kinjal Patel contributed to this report.

World.title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan to be executed Dec. 3, email states
World.content:
An execution date for former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, has been set for Dec. 3, 2026, and will take place at the same post where he carried out his attack, according to an email sent to the families of victims.

Hasan is set to die by firing squad in what will be the first military execution since 1961.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday that the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Trump.

CBS News

"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote.

CBS Texas has reached out to Fort Hood for comment and was directed to Army headquarters.

In addition to the 13 people Hasan killed on Nov. 5, 2009, 32 others were injured. Those targeted were unarmed soldiers who were at the readiness center as they were preparing to deploy. Hasan fired 146 times.

The last military execution took place 65 years ago, when the Army executed Pvt. John Bennett by hanging after he was convicted of rape and the attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl.

The last execution by firing squad happened during World War II, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was put to death in France for desertion.

Hasan, now 56, was an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shootings. He had served two decades in the Army. Witnesses described hearing Hasan shout "Allahu Akbar" before opening fire. Hasan was paralyzed from the chest down when police returned fire.

Since his conviction, Hasan has been on death row at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas.

Why a firing squad?

According to Army regulation 190-55, military executions can only be approved by the president. A 2019 revision removed the term "lethal injection" from this regulation and left the method up to the secretary of the Army's designation. According to the guidelines, the method is recommended to the secretary by the provost marshal general.

According to this order, the prisoner is informed of the president's decision in person by the commandant, who is accompanied by a chaplain and, if available, a defense attorney. After the notification, the prisoner becomes a "condemned prisoner."

The victims

Family members of those who died were notified of the planned execution before the announcement was made. They, along with survivors, were asked if they wanted to attend. The group, bonded in tragedy, has been intertwined over the last 17 years. This is what many hope will be the final chapter in the tragedy.

Below are the names of those who died.

Lt. Col. Juanita Warman, 55

Maj. Libardo Eduardo Caraveo, 52

Capt. John P. Gaffaney, 56

Capt. Russell Seager, 51

Staff Sgt. Justin DeCrow, 32

Sgt. Amy Krueger, 29

Spc. Jason Dean Hunt, 22

Spc. Frederick Z. Greene, 29

Pfc. Aaron T Nemelka, 19

Pfc. Michael S. Pearson, 22

Pfc. Kham S. Xiong, 23

Pvt. Francheska Velez, 21 (and her unborn child)

Michael Grant Cahill, 62

This is a developing story. Additional details will be provided once they become available.

World.title: California couple at center of surrogacy scandal arrested
World.content:
A California couple at the center of a surrogacy scandal was arrested on Tuesday. A law enforcement source confirmed the arrests to CBS News shortly before officials held a news conference to announce the latest developments.

Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang are being charged with multiple counts, including conspiracy to commit child abuse and dissuading a witness, Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman said.

The couple drew national headlines last year after authorities raided their Arcadia mansion in July 2025 and took 21 kids, mostly surrogate-born, into state custody.

Tuesday morning, detectives from the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department arrested the couple at their residence. They were then transferred to the Pasadena courthouse to be arraigned, Sheriff Robert Luna said. They both pleaded not guilty and are each being held on a $20 million bond.

A neighbor said Tuesday that helicopters and police could be seen at the couple's mansion and the entire block is taped off.

"What has been publicly filed in the complaint today is incredibly disturbing. It involves horrific punishment and beatings and child abuse," Hochman said at the news conference.

Officials said the investigation began in May 2025 when Zhang brought a 2-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury.

"She appeared to be untruthful with hospital staff about how the injury was sustained and the hospital staff notified law enforcement authorities," Luna said, adding that when Arcadia police went to the home, "what they discovered raised even more serious concerns."

The district attorney said Tuesday that the children were seated for hours a day in three different rooms called "Learning Centers" under the supervision of various nannies at the couple's home, which he called a "house of horrors." The couple kept a system of 32 motion-activated cameras in the various rooms in the Arcadia mansion, he said. Footage from these cameras went to a television near their desk that the couple used to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.

Hochman said the nannies were caught on video spanking, slapping or hitting the children. One nanny, Chunmei Li, allegedly struck the 2-month-old baby in the head, the district attorney said. A $105,000 warrant for her arrest was previously issued, but she remains on the run, he said.

Xuan's attorney, Mitchell Krems, said: "My client is innocent. It is the nanny's wrongdoing who went on the run. He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family."

Police photos of Guoiun Xuan and Silvia Zhang and a picture of their home in Arcadia, California. Background: I RYU/VCG via Getty Images; Inset photos: Arcadia Police Department

Melissa Brisman, an attorney for two of the surrogates involved in the case, told CBS News, "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system."

Brisman added that it's important surrogacy remains an option for those who need the help to become parents, but said there must "be adequate protections for those who enter the surrogacy system."

"We need to make sure bad actors don't ruin it for everyone else," she said.

On Tuesday, officials said the Arcadia Police Department requested assistance from the LA County Sheriff's Department in early September. A Los Angeles FBI spokesperson confirmed the FBI served a search warrant at the home, separate from a search conducted by the sheriff's department.

"We will continue to work together to pursue justice for all 21 children involved in this case," Luna said.

Maria Castellanos, a surrogate who carried two children for Zhang and Xuan, said after learning of their arrest, "I'm mad that everyone involved couldn't stop this so the kids wouldn't go through everything they went through. I'm just mad with the whole process, the whole thing. It's not just them."

"I trusted Silvia," she said.

World.title: Former CIA official accused of stealing $40M in gold bars pleads guilty
World.content:
Former CIA official accused of stealing $40M in gold bars pleads guilty

toggle caption i U.S. Dept. of Justice via AP

WASHINGTON — A former senior CIA official pleaded guilty Tuesday in Virginia to a charge that he abused his position and government funds to enrich himself by acquiring Florida real estate and hundreds of gold bars worth over $40 million, according to court records.

David J. Rush fabricated a "highly classified" government program to justify the acquisition of luxury property in south Florida that he intended to resell for personal profit, according to a court filing. Rush separately concocted a bogus "sensitive government activity" to obtain the gold bars, the filing says.

Rush's fraudulent conduct cost the federal government approximately $194 million in total losses, according to the Justice Department. The losses included over $1.8 million in privately chartered flights that Rush authorized for personal use at the government's expense.

Sponsor Message

Under questioning from investigators, Rush admitted that he provided a foreign government official with information about the identity of a secret source for the U.S. government, a new court filing says. The filing doesn't specify which country the foreign official represented.

Prosecutors also accuse Rush of lying to colleagues and government contractors about his military and academic credentials and the fake program that he invented, falsely claiming it was authorized by high-ranking U.S. officials.

"Rush used his legitimate government authority and manufactured personal bona fides to create confidence in his directions," the court filing says.

Rush, 49, of Ashburn, Virginia, pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years, court records show. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff is scheduled to sentence Rush on Jan. 28 in Alexandria, Virginia.

Several months ago, Rush tried to fraudulently authorize the release of $100 million from a government contract, according to Tuesday's filing. He directed somebody else to transfer approximately $145 million to a holding company formed at his direction, then used those funds to acquire four "luxury" properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida, the filing says.

In previous court filings, prosecutors said Rush stashed roughly $46 million worth of gold bars from the federal government at his Virginia home. They also accused him of fraudulently claiming tens of thousands of dollars in compensation for military leave after he was honorably discharged from the U.S. Navy in 2015.

Sponsor Message

"Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement.

CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency immediately referred the matter to the FBI after an internal investigation turned up evidence of Rush's crimes.

"David Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions," Ratcliffe said in a statement.

Rush was arrested after investigators searched his home and seized approximately 300 gold bars, roughly $2 million in U.S. currency and about 35 luxury watches, according to an FBI agent's affidavit. A judge ordered Rush to be held without bond after his initial court appearance earlier this year.

During a hearing in June, defense attorney Jessica Carmichael said Rush wasn't charged initially with any crimes related to the discovery of the gold bars, which she referred to as "basically a nonissue" and "nothing more than a sensational tidbit." She said her client properly obtained the gold bars and kept them locked in a safe in his basement.

"Mr. Rush never claimed they were his," Carmichael said.

Carmichael declined to comment on Rush's guilty plea after Tuesday's hearing.

Authorities say Rush lied about his education and military background on job applications, falsely claiming to be a former Navy pilot who graduated with a bachelor's degree from Clemson University in South Carolina and a master's degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in New York.

Investigators determined that he didn't serve as a Navy pilot and didn't attend either school. Rush enlisted in the Navy in 1997 and was honorably discharged from the U.S. Navy Reserve as a lieutenant in 2015, according to the FBI affidavit.

World.title: Israelis mourn on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 as Palestinians grapple with war it sparked
World.content:
Israelis mourn on the anniversary of the Oct. 7 as Palestinians grapple with war it sparked

toggle caption i Ohad Zwigenberg/AP

NETANYA, Israel — Israelis are gathering Wednesday to commemorate the Oct. 7, 2023, attack that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage, and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that Palestinians still grapple with.

In southern Israel, families will mourn at intersections, bomb shelters, and the site of a music festival that Hamas-led militants overran three years ago in the deadliest attack against Israel. This will be the first anniversary that all the hostages are home, marking a new stage of grief.

For Palestinians, the anniversary brings another day living with the results of Israel's retaliatory campaign in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of people. Most of the population of about 2 million people live in vast, squalid tent camps, with large parts of the strip's cities reduced to rubble. More than half the territory remains in the hands of the Israeli military, and despite a ceasefire deal reached nearly a year ago, Israeli strikes continue almost daily.

Sponsor Message

For the region, the day highlights a startling transformation over the past three years. Israeli troops occupy a large chunk of southern Lebanon in their conflict with Hezbollah, which began firing on Israel in 2023 in support of Hamas. Iran and the United States are locked in a confrontation that has seen attacks across Arab Gulf countries and has shaken the global economy — a conflict that Israel helped launch and that the Gaza war paved the way for even if they weren't directly connected.

A released hostage marks his first Oct. 7

Elkana Bohbot, 37, is marking the anniversary in Israel for the first time, after being released from 738 days of captivity last year. For most of that time, he said, he was held 50 meters (165 feet) underground in a dark, damp tunnel.

Bohbot, who was abducted from the Nova music festival, was kept in a small cell with other hostages, given very little food, and allowed to bathe only every few weeks, he said. His captors forced him to take part in several propaganda videos, including one where he acts out a fake call to his family.

In the 11 months since his release, Bohbot has undergone physical and emotional rehabilitation, written a book, begun a speaking career, traveled with his family, and celebrated all the holidays and birthdays he missed.

Sponsor Message

In August, his wife, Rivka, gave birth to a daughter, fulfilling a fierce promise that Bohbot made to himself in the tunnels to give his 5-year-old son, Reem, a sibling.

The newborn Michele is "not a symbol for my people, she is more of a symbol for the enemy," Bohbot told The Associated Press. "So this child is the message for you that we were here, and we will always be here forever."

toggle caption i Jehad Alshrafi/AP

In Gaza, Palestinians struggle to recover

No events are expected on Wednesday in Gaza, where Israel's offensive has devastated the narrow strip and displaced around 90% of its population, often multiple times. Restrictions on the entry of goods and aid have contributed to a severe hunger crisis.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Health Ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its figures but says around half were women and children. The numbers from the ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts.

While a ceasefire that took effect on Oct. 10 has halted the heaviest fighting, Israeli strikes have continued, targeting what Israel says are Hamas militants. Since the ceasefire, 1,145 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the ministry. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in that period.

Hamas portrayed the Oct. 7 attack as a response to decades of Israeli military occupation, land seizures and settlement construction. But the Palestinians' dream of an independent state appears even more distant.

The anniversary comes to a radically altered Middle East

A contentious election in Israel at the end of the month hangs over this year's anniversary. The government's official memorial services took place on Oct. 5, closer to the Hebrew-calendar anniversary of the attack. The separate commemorations are indicative of the deep divisions over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's handling of the war and his reluctance to launch an official inquiry into failings of the day.

Sponsor Message

The attack set in motion a cascade of events that led to wars across the Middle East as Israel confronted Hamas, Hezbollah and their backer Iran. Israel has seized swaths of territory in Syria and Lebanon, where more than 300,000 Lebanese remain displaced. The United States joined Israel in attacking Iran's military and nuclear program in two rounds, battering Iran and upending global markets far from the battlefield.

Violence has also risen across the Israeli-occupied West Bank, where Israel's far-right government has emboldened extremist settlers who have attacked Palestinians and destroyed their property.

World.title: Actress Eva Marie Saint, who won an Oscar for 'On the Waterfront,' dies at 102
World.content:
Actress Eva Marie Saint, who won an Oscar for 'On the Waterfront,' dies at 102

Enlarge this image toggle caption i Columbia TriStar/Getty Images Columbia TriStar/Getty Images

Eva Marie Saint, who starred in Elia Kazan's 1954 On the Waterfront and Alfred Hitchcock's 1959 North by Northwest, died Tuesday at 102 years old.

Saint grew up in Albany and Delmar, New York. She was a delicate, porcelain beauty. She attended the Actors Studio in New York, performed on Broadway and did live television in the late 1940s. But Saint didn't do a film until she was almost 30, after director Elia Kazan suggested she screen test with a guy named Marlon Brando. They did a scene from On the Waterfront in which Saint is supposed to keep Brando out of her house.

Sponsor Message

Enlarge this image toggle caption i Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images Silver Screen Collection/Getty Images

In 2000, Saint told WHYY's Fresh Air, "I don't know what happened, but ... [Brando] came in the living room. We were dancing, we were laughing, I was crying. He was taking my skirt and ... whipping it around, and the sparks flew. And Kazan saw that. And suddenly I was in On the Waterfront."

In that film, Saint plays Edie, a Catholic schoolgirl who finds herself in the middle of union corruption in Hoboken, N.J. When her longshoreman brother is murdered, Edie wants justice. Saint won an Oscar for performance.

Five years after playing the chaste heroine Edie, Saint played a femme fatale opposite Cary Grant in Alfred Hitchcock's North by Northwest. But Saint was no femme fatale off the screen. After marrying director Jeffrey Hayden in 1951, she limited her roles to devote more time to her children. She went back to TV in the '70s, and won an Emmy in 1990 for the miniseries People Like Us.

World.title: Cornell names former acting U.S. attorney general to review rape case
World.content:
Cornell names former acting U.S. attorney general to review rape case

toggle caption i Steven Senne/AP

Cornell University named Sally Yates, a former acting U.S. attorney general and career federal prosecutor, as head of an independent internal review into how the school handled a former student's rape allegations.

The announcement comes as the school continues to face outrage on campus and nationally after a former student filed a civil lawsuit alleging she was drugged and gang raped in 2024. The woman, identified in the suit as Jane Doe, also alleged failings by the school in how it handled her complaint and the aftermath.

Yates, a partner at King & Spalding who served as the U.S. deputy attorney general under President Barack Obama, was picked by the newly formed Special Committee of the Cornell University Board of Trustees. She will also examine the school's policies related to how it "prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus," the school announced Tuesday.

Sponsor Message

"Sally Yates brings extraordinary experience, independence and judgment to this work," said Anne Meinig Smalling, chair of the special committee, in the school's announcement. "The questions raised by the Jane Doe matter warrant a rigorous examination of Cornell's response to that case, but our responsibility is broader. We have asked Ms. Yates and her team to examine Cornell's overall approach to preventing and responding to sexual misconduct, identify where we are doing things well and where we can do better, and recommend changes that will help make our community safer."

Doe filed her lawsuit in mid-September. In it, Doe alleges that seven men drugged and assaulted her for several hours in October 2024 at their Chi Phi fraternity house on campus. No criminal charges were ever filed against the men. Those named in the lawsuit have denied all wrongdoing. Cornell University is also named as a defendant in Doe's suit.

The university has maintained that Cornell University Police investigated the case thoroughly and that the school held its own Title IX investigation, which resulted in suspensions and expulsions.

But in the weeks that have followed the lawsuit's filing, students have protested the university's response to the case. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to lead a criminal investigation into the rape case, after sharp criticism of its handling by campus police and the local prosecutor, Matthew Van Houten. The case also has renewed national conversations over consent and sexual assault on college campuses.

On Wednesday, students are planning to hold a 7-hour sit-in as part of a campus-wide "zero day" action. Students say they won't attend class or spend money for those seven hours.

Sponsor Message

"We have shared our collective demands. Now, we are asking our community to physically show up and stand—or, for seven hours, sit—with survivors," the university group, Cornell NAACP, said on Instagram.

World.title: France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country
World.content:
France's police fire tear gas and water cannons as school protests sweep the country

toggle caption i Jeremias Gonzalez/AP

PARIS — Police fired tear gas to control crowds in Paris and elsewhere in France on Tuesday as more than a quarter of a million people rallied nationwide to support high school students demanding more education funding, according to government figures. The protests increased pressure on the administration of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron.

As pupils blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron's nearly decade-long tenure.

"We need to listen to them," said Léa Monimart, an adult demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. "They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It's important to show that there are adults who support them."

Sponsor Message

The Interior Ministry estimated that 266,000 people took part in demonstrations across the country on Tuesday, including 56,000 in Paris, where small groups of protesters clashed with riot officers at a city square at the end of a largely peaceful march.

Nearly 500 people were detained Tuesday, the ministry said. The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Some student groups called for new protests Thursday.

toggle caption i Jeremias Gonzalez/AP

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the police response had been proportionate in "almost all cases" and that the protests had at times turned into riots, requiring police intervention.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the government and school leaders must listen to students' concerns and find solutions.

Questioned in parliament on Tuesday about the protest movement, Lecornu denounced "ultra violence" threatening schools. Responding to criticism of police tactics, he pledged that any "accidents" would be investigated and described allegations that the police are racist as a "lie."

Class boycotts with police making thousands of arrests

More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,500 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign.

Sponsor Message

Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make "any sense to hit minors."

"Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas," said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests.

toggle caption i Teresa Suarez/AP

The violence is "absolutely unbearable," Le Coq said.

Nuñez defended police tactics despite a growing number of severe injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons. In the latest case, a 15-year-old boy lost a hand Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. He said 715 officers had been injured.

The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties, such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war, to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term.

Against that backdrop, pupils' complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience.

"You say 'young people are the future,' so listen to them," read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school.

Ministry offers online portal for complaints

At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade.

Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry.

Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see.

Sponsor Message

Student protests have drawn attention to rundown classrooms

At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch.

"They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children's rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands," said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents.

Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France's national motto: "Liberty, Equality, Fraternity."

Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students' compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.

Suzanne Nijdam, president of the federation of student associations, vowed that demonstrations would continue until authorities address the complaints.

"So, we really need to act now, and it's in the government's hands, to see these demands through to the end," she said. "It's a matter of political priority, a matter of prioritizing the youth and the future of our country."

Neighboring Belgium is also seeing student protests. More than 30 were arrested Tuesday and several police injured in the eastern city of Liege, and smaller protests were held in Brussels and other cities.

World.title: Here are the finalists for the 2026 National Book Awards
World.content:
Here are the finalists for the 2026 National Book Awards

NPR

Does "the third time's the charm" apply to prestigious literary awards? Edwidge Danticat will have the opportunity to find out. She's now a three-time finalist for a National Book Award, which were announced Tuesday morning. Danticat's novel, Dèy, is about a woman who witnesses a violent gun attack in a Miami mall. Danticat's short story collection Krik? Krak! was a finalist for the prize in 1995, and her book Brother, I'm Dying, was a non-fiction finalist in 2007.

The other writers up for the 2026 fiction prize include Hannah Lillith Assadi, Julián Delgado Lopera, Valeria Luiselli, and debut novelist Morgan Thomas, whose book Mad Eden is a form-bending story following a patient navigator at a center providing gender-affirming care.

Sponsor Message

Similarly blending forms in the nonfiction category is Camonghne Felix. Her book Let the Poets Govern: A Declaration of Freedom is both a memoir and a call-to-action, drawing on Felix's background as a communications strategist. Felix is up against Colin Asher, Sara Nović, Joseph Osmundson, and Abdelrahman ElGendy, whose memoir, Huna, explores his time in an Egyptian prison.

The winners of the National Book Awards will be announced Nov. 18, 2026.

Find the full list below.

Fiction

Hannah Lillith Assadi, Paradiso 17

Edwidge Danticat, Dèy

Julián Delgado Lopera, Pretend You're Dead and I Carry You

Valeria Luiselli, Beginning Middle End

Morgan Thomas, Mad Eden

Nonfiction

Poetry

Young People's Literature
