World.title: What to know about nationwide protests in India over voter list changes
World.content:
What to know about nationwide protests in India over voter list changes

toggle caption i Rafiq Maqbool/AP

NEW DELHI — Protests have spread across India in the past week as opposition parties and civil society groups demand the resignation of the country's election chief over alleged manipulation of voter lists.

The campaign has been led in part by India's "Cockroach" youth movement, which previously organized street protests that forced the education minister to resign in July.

Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the poll body's ongoing revision of voter lists. They accuse the revision could disenfranchise millions of voters and benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP. The commission and government deny any wrongdoing.

Sponsor Message

Here's what to know:

Voter list changes fueling the protests

India is the world's largest democracy with hundreds of millions of people voting in national and state elections. The Election Commission plays a central role in determining voter eligibility and administering elections, making changes to electoral lists politically significant.

The dispute centers on a nationwide voter list revision known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR. It began last year in the eastern state of Bihar ahead of local elections and has since expanded to most of India's states and federally administered territories.

Under the process, voters are required to provide documents showing they are eligible to remain on the lists.

The Election Commission says the exercise is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible entries and ensure legitimate voters remain registered. Critics say it could instead exclude legitimate voters, particularly poorer and other vulnerable communities.

They also say the requirements are confusing and difficult for many people to provide, particularly those who lack older government records or other documents.

Critics say the changes could benefit Modi's party

India's Election Commission is an independent constitutional body overseeing elections and maintaining voter lists, but opposition parties accuse the commission of favoring Modi's party. They allege the changes could remove people more likely to support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters who favor the BJP.

Sponsor Message

The BJP and the Election Commission reject the allegations and say the revision has no political motive. Modi's party says the list is being updated to weed out what they call "infiltrators."

The issue was prominent in West Bengal's crucial state elections earlier this year after a voter list revision removed about 9 million names, or roughly 12% of the electorate. The deletions left millions of eligible voters unable to cast ballots. Modi's party won the state for the first time.

toggle caption i Rafiq Maqbool/AP

Politics can impact commission rulings

Indian law requires a majority vote of commission members to enact changes making disagreements among its members potentially significant.

The Indian Express newspaper reported in September that two of the three election commissioners had formally objected to several decisions involving voter list revisions, registration procedures and the commission's digital systems.

The newspaper reported Kumar, the election chief, rejected those objections.

The Election Commission said the report reflected "differing views and deliberations" rather than formal written objections.

Protesters seek end to changes that could reshape elections

The "Cockroach" movement, opposition parties and civil society groups have called for Kumar to resign or be removed and for an inquiry into his conduct, including possible criminal proceedings. They want the current revision halted and the previous electoral lists used for future elections.

They also demand a more independent and transparent process for appointing election commissioners.

Election Commission data indicates voter lists in some regions could shrink by as much as 30%, fueling concerns among opposition parties and protest groups over potential exclusions.

The dispute is likely to intensify as the changes resulting from the revision expand throughout India, which is facing a series of state elections early next year.

World.title: Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of prowling city streets at night, snatching cats for meat
World.content:
Vietnamese police arrest 12 suspected of prowling city streets at night, snatching cats for meat

toggle caption i Humane World for Animals/AP

HANOI, Vietnam — Police in Vietnam's Ho Chi Minh City arrested 12 men suspected of operating a citywide ring that stole and resold about 2,700 cats for meat, Vietnamese state media said.

Police identified 39-year-old Luu Thanh Binh as the alleged leader of the network. He and 11 others were being investigated for theft, state media said Monday.

Investigators said Binh bought stolen cats, kept them at a facility in the city's north and resold them for meat. He worked with suppliers who recruited others to ride motorcycles through residential neighborhoods between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m., hunting for cats and trapping four to 10 cats each night.

Sponsor Message

Eating dog and cat meat is not unique to Vietnam and has been practiced in parts of Asia, though it is not common practice. In Vietnam, cat meat traditionally is more commonly consumed in the north, among older generations.

The practice has declined with growing pet ownership and urbanization, and younger Vietnamese are more likely to regard dogs and cats as companion animals.

In 2024, more than 250,000 people signed a petition calling for an end to Vietnam's dog and cat meat trade. The city of Hoi An also pledged in 2021 to end the sale and consumption of dog and cat meat.

Some believe eating cat meat brings good luck, though there is no scientific evidence for such claims.

Police raided the network on July 8 and found about 50 cats and dozens of traps, state media reported.

The suspects told investigators they had stolen and sold about 2,700 cats, the reports said. Police did not say how long the operation had been running.

Police returned 13 of the cats confiscated in the raid to their owners. A nonprofit animal rights group was caring for the others while authorities sought to identify their owners.

Under Vietnamese law, dogs and cats are considered private property, and stealing them is considered theft. Criminal prosecution generally applies when the value of the stolen property exceeds 2 million dong ($77).

Sponsor Message

In a separate raid in June, police reported they had rescued more than 400 cats. At least 40 were reunited with their owners, but dozens of dead cats were found packed in ice.

World.title: U.S. resident charged with encouraging, aiding Tumbler Ridge shooter
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains disturbing details.

Court documents filed in Washington state are revealing new details about the months leading up to a mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., in February that left eight people, as well as the shooter, dead.

On Tuesday, the U.S. Department of Justice announced 30-year-old James Cody Bryant had been arrested and charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, a charge that is punishable by up to life in prison.

Officials allege Bryant had been in contact with the shooter, 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, on the social media platform Discord leading up to the attack.

The criminal complaint, which was published online, says Bryant "knowingly and wilfully" conspired with Van Rootselaar beginning in or before August 2025.

Search warrant for Discord account

The complaint says Discord voluntarily shared information with the RCMP, which then shared it with the FBI. Homeland Security investigators interviewed Bryant two days after the shooting at Bryant's home in Bellingham, Wash., the document says.

In early March, the FBI interviewed Bryant, and learned Bryant and Van Rootselaar met online about three years ago and had contact on and off through the years, court documents say.

A search warrant for Bryant's Discord account was issued in Washington state after Bryant did not give consent for the social media company to send the FBI social media communications with Van Rootselaar, according to the document.

Those records contained multiple conversations between the two, it adds.

On Aug. 8, about six months before the attack, Van Rootselaar detailed the most deadly shootings in Canadian history, and talked about how she could "steal that title," court documents show.

The documents show Bryant responded with advice on how to kill more people.

James Cody Bryant, centre, is seen in a court sketch drawn during an appearance in U.S. District Court in Seattle on Oct. 6, 2026. Bryant, 30, is charged with conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country in connection with the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C. (Lois Silver/CBC)

Van Rootselaar asked Bryant to record and broadcast a livestream of the attack, Bryant told investigators.

Bryant said they agreed to do it to "placate" Van Rootselaar, and admitted to testing the livestream equipment, the court document says.

Around Aug. 11, Bryant told Van Rootselaar they should "find a way to delete" their messages, the documents say.

WATCH | Bellingham, Wash. resident arrested, charged in relation to Tumbler Ridge shooting: U.S. resident allegedly gave advice, money to Tumbler Ridge shooter | Duration closed caption 8:26

The complaint says that on Aug. 30, 2025, Bryant helped Van Rootselaar test the quality of a livestream, and that Bryant said it "looks solid." They ran a test run of the livestream on Jan. 4, 2026.

Over the course of several months, the pair discussed weapons, stickers to decorate the weapons, shoes to wear on the day of the attack and money Bryant was providing for those items.

"Need to figure out smoe way to get you money\ I wanna make sure you get your stuff. Literally giving you access to my card," Bryant said in a message on Jan. 25.

Bryant sent Van Rootselaar about $125 on Nov. 21 for a pair of shoes she wanted to wear during the attack, according to the documents.

Another $14 was sent on Jan. 25, two weeks before the attack, for a lighter intended for an explosive device.

Van Rootselaar sent Bryant a photo of what the fully assembled explosive device would look like, according to the documents. A statement from the FBI in the documents said that device was deployed during the attack on Feb. 10, 2026.

A temporary memorial for victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting is seen on April 27, 2026. (Tom Summer/CBC)

In the interview with FBI investigators, Bryant said Van Rootselaar talked about a target for a mass shooting, and suggested a school — but said they told her it was a bad idea, "because there would be too many young victims."

Instead, Bryant said they suggested a church or grocery store, according to the court documents.

One message from August 2025 shows Van Rootselaar was considering an attack in another northern B.C. municipality — Dawson Creek, Fort St. John or Prince George — at either a mall or school.

'You don't have to die'

In November, Van Rootselaar told Bryant she would not hurt children, according to the documents.

"Murder is bad enough. I don't hurt animals, kids. Y'know. I'm not that bad but murder is one of the worst things," she said.

"Yeah if you said you'd go to a school then I'd take issue more staunchly but luckily you're an angel~you wouldn't do that," Bryant responded.

A police officer is seen on the grounds of Tumbler Ridge Secondary School the day after the shooting on Feb. 11. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

A couple of weeks later, Van Rootselaar said she wanted to hurt other people but remain unharmed herself, according to the criminal complaint.

"You don't have to die," Bryant responded.

WATCH | FBI says Bryant and Van Rootselaar met on Omegle: U.S. resident met Tumbler Ridge shooter on Omegle: FBI | Duration 1:27

In early January, Van Rootselaar said she was going to carry out the attack imminently, according to the document, and Bryant tried to get her to reconsider.

"I wish there were any other path for you, you shouldn't have to do something like this," Bryant said. "I wish I knew what I could say or do to change your mind."

That same month, they discussed the livestream and how important it was to Van Rootselaar.

"If I don't livestream it people can be detached from the gravity of how I feel. It's just another headline," she said in a message to Bryant that appears in the criminal complaint. "I need people to see it and personally witness the lives be impacted."

Bryant again agreed to facilitate the livestream, the court documents show, and the day before the attack, claimed to have adjusted to a different sleep schedule to be able to help run the livestream.

The court documents show that a few days before the attack, Bryant again tried to get Van Rootselaar to reconsider.

On Feb. 10, 2026, Van Rootselaar told Bryant she was dressed for the attack, and sent photos and video of herself and weapons she planned to use.

Bryant said they were ready to run the livestream, the criminal complaint says, and a few moments later, Van Rootselaar said she had killed her family.

When she couldn't figure out how to start the car to head to the school, she asked Bryant for help, the documents show. When Van Rootselaar finally got the car to start, she drove to the school, where she killed five students and an educator, and injured many more.

Throughout the pair's communications, the court documents show, Bryant repeatedly promised not to contact police.

"You believe me when I promise I won't snitch on you, right?" Bryant said in one message.

"I know I can like, save lives I guess but idk," Bryant said in another.

Bryant appears in court

Bryant appeared before a judge in Seattle, Wash., on Tuesday afternoon.

A preliminary hearing is set for Oct. 20 at 1 p.m. PT. If the grand jury indicts, there will be a separate hearing, the judge says.

Magistrate Judge Brian Tsuchida says the U.S. has requested Bryant be denied bail and detained. A detention hearing will be held next Tuesday to determine if Bryant will get bail or remain in custody.

World.title: FAA investigating after Delta plane 'clipped' Air Canada aircraft at LAX
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says it is investigating after a Delta Air Lines plane "clipped" an Air Canada aircraft at Los Angeles International Airport on Tuesday.

The aviation agency says the incident occurred around 10:30 a.m. local time as the Delta plane was taxiing for departure, and the Air Canada plane was being towed toward the gate.

An Air Canada spokesperson says there are no reported injuries.

Sean Davidson says in a statement that Air Canada Flight 785 had arrived from Toronto before "an aircraft operated by another airline made contact with its tail."

He says the plane will be taken out of service for inspection and repairs.

The U.S. agency says the Delta plane's left wingtip clipped the Air Canada aircraft's horizontal stabilizer, a wing-likestructure at the tail of a plane.

World.title: Niagara, Ont., nurse among 4 Canadians on lost medical air transport out of Hamilton
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The U.S. Coast Guard has released the names of the four Canadians who were on the medical air transport jet out of Hamilton that was lost in the Atlantic Ocean en route to Boston from Bermuda early Saturday morning.

Monday night, the Coast Guard said that the Canadian crew included Philip Gregory Childerhose of Oakville, Ont., Thomas Henry Farquhar of Brantford, Ont., Niagara nurse Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir.

The crew flew out of Bermuda with two Bermudians heading to the United States on a Gulfstream G100 jet operated by Hamilton's Latitude Air Ambulance.

The Bermuda government earlier in the day identified the Bermudians on board as 66-year-old Marilyn Lavonne Bean and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore. The Coast Guard confirmed they were the passengers.

The Bermuda government identified the Bermudians on board the medical air transport jet as as 66-year-old Marilyn Lavonne Bean, left, and her 41-year-old son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore. (Bermuda Broadcasting Company)

“During this incredibly difficult time, our heartfelt condolences go out to the families and friends impacted by this tragic incident,” said Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, commander of the Coast Guard Northeast District, in a news release Monday night. “We are grateful to the crews and partner agencies who quickly responded to this incident, and we will continue to support our Canadian partners as they conduct their investigation.”

Monday night, Latitude president Peter Byl said in a statement that while the Coast Guard has released the names of his company's crew, the crew members were more than names.

"They were colleagues, friends and members of our family. Each brought something special to our company, to the people they worked beside, and to the patients and families entrusted to their care," he said.

In an email Tuesday, Byl told CBC News the company's "immediate focus remains on supporting the families and our team and co-operating fully with the appropriate authorities as recovery efforts and the investigation proceed. We will not speculate about the circumstances or cause of the accident while that work is underway."

Childerhose was 'a person of great integrity'

He described Philip Childerhose, who was the captain, as "a person of great integrity, incredibly kind-hearted and extremely passionate about aviation. He was dedicated to his family, friends, and colleagues. He touched the hearts of everyone he talked to and helped anyone who was in need."

A LinkedIn profile for Childerhose now classified as "in remembrance" says he lived in Oakville.

Byl described first officer Thomas Farquhar as a "gentle giant" who reflected Jesus' love: a safe place and a helping hand to all.

"Tommy was loved by everyone who ever met him."

A LinkedIn profile lists Farquhar as being from Brantford.

Paton remembered 'always put others first'

Flight nurse Sarah Paton "was a bright, joyful presence whose kindness, humour and generosity touched everyone around her," Byl said. "A dedicated nurse, she devoted her life to caring for others and was known by her family as selfless, hardworking, determined and full of life. She was a larger-than-life daughter, family member and friend, and her loved ones take some comfort in knowing she was doing what mattered most to her: helping others.

"Sarah will be deeply missed and forever remembered for the love and joy she brought to those around her."

Hospital network Niagara Health sent a memorial to employees about Paton, who worked in the intensive care unit at Marotta Family Hospital in St. Catharines, Ont.

The memorial said she also worked in the Welland Hospital emergency department.

In addition to being a skilled and enthusiastic nurse, Paton "earned a reputation as a strong advocate for her patients, a trusted teammate and someone who could always be counted on," Niagara Health said.

"Colleagues remember Sarah as someone who always put others first," it said. "Many also remember her locker, always stocked with candy for teammates who needed a pick-me-up during a long shift."

Latitude president asks for space for families

Respiratory therapist Jolene Weir "was a presence unlike any other who loved her family and friends and had a passion for helping others," said Byl.

"With years of experience caring for others as a respiratory therapist in a hospital, combined with her love of travel and seeing the world, Latitude truly was her dream job. Her incredible ability to care for and love others extended not only to her patients but showed even more in her most favourite roles as a wife, mother, daughter, sister and friend."

In an Oct. 5 Facebook post, trade association the Respiratory Therapy Society of Ontario said it was "holding the entire Latitude Air Ambulance family especially close. We know that respiratory therapists are an important part of the Latitude team, making this tragedy one that feels especially close to home for Ontario's RT community."

Byl said he understands there is considerable public interest in the people who were on the jet. "We respectfully ask that the privacy of all six families be protected and that they be given the space and time they need to grieve."

On Tuesday, the government of Bermuda said, in a post on Facebook, "we extend our deepest condolences to the families, friends, colleagues and loved ones of Captain Philip Childerhose, First Officer Thomas Farquhar, Flight Nurse Sarah Paton and Respiratory Therapist Jolene Weir, who tragically lost their lives in the aircraft incident near Nantucket Island, Massachusetts."

The work of the Canadians was "an important service that has supported individuals and families during some of life's most difficult moments. We are deeply grateful for their service and the care they provided to our community," the statement said.

TSB to lead investigation

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada (TSB) announced on Monday that it will lead the investigation because the jet was registered in Canada. The agency said early indications are that something might have gone wrong with the jet's electrical system.

Latitude said in a statement Sunday night that any hope of finding survivors from the downed jet, which is named Heartbeat 104, appeared to be gone.

"Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search and rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104 are presumed to have died."

The Coast Guard and National Guard had used fixed wing aircraft, helicopters and sea vessels to search a huge area of 11,500 square kilometres off Nantucket from 2 a.m. Saturday until ultimately calling off the search Sunday night. The Coast Guard had been contacted by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration that contact had been lost with the Gulfstream aircraft.

Black box not yet been recovered, Coast Guard says

Sunday morning, the Coast Guard said in a news conference that a considerable amount of debris had been found from the jet in the water but Lake said as of then, the so-called black box likely containing valuable data had not yet been recovered.

Sunday morning, Lake said the Coast Guard was in the process of working with Massachusetts authorities to get some craft out in the area that are equipped with sonar to be able to do some detection on the seabed floor. He said the water was about 80 to 90 feet deep in the area.

This image of the interior a Gulfstream G100 jet operated by Latitude Air Ambulance out of Hamilton is shown on Latitude's website. (Latitude Air Ambulance)

Latitude said it will continue to cooperate fully with the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, the Transportation Safety Board of Canada and all other relevant authorities as recovery efforts and the investigation proceed.

"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

Hamilton Mayor Andrea Horwath said Monday she was "heartbroken by the tragic loss of life."

"My heart goes out to the families and loved ones of those who were aboard, and to the entire Latitude team as they mourn the loss of their colleagues and friends," she said in a statement. "Latitude is part of our Hamilton community, operating out of Hamilton International Airport. On behalf of the city of Hamilton, I extend my deepest condolences to everyone affected by this tragedy."

The Coast Guard said it will continue to coordinate with Canadian authorities. It said if people find debris from the jet in the water, they should contact the TSBC.

World.title: Eva Marie Saint, Oscar-winning On the Waterfront actor, dead at 102
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Eva Marie Saint, the pale, willowy actor who won an Academy Award for her first movie, On the Waterfront, and starred opposite Cary Grant in the Alfred Hitchcock thriller North by Northwest, has died. She was 102.

Saint, whose acting work lasted well into her 90s, died at her home in Los Angeles on Tuesday, confirmed family representative Jeff Sanderson.

Saint had one of the most spectacular debuts in Hollywood history as the love interest of Marlon Brando's tormented Terry Malloy in On the Waterfront, and her first trip to the Academy Awards was memorable, too. Pregnant with her first child, Saint accepted her Oscar from Frank Sinatra and smilingly murmured a unique winner's speech: "I think I may have the baby right here." (Her son, Darrell, was born two days later.)

The award for the 1954 classic made her an instant star, but she soon astonished Hollywood with a firm independence that would mark her career. She refused offers of studio contracts and declined chances to follow up on her great success, explaining that she was taking time off to become acquainted with her new son. (A daughter, Laurette, was born in 1958.)

In her first decade in Hollywood, Saint appeared in a mere seven films. She declined such top-level productions as The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit with Gregory Peck, Summer and Smoke with Laurence Harvey and The Rainmaker with Burt Lancaster. She credited her husband, TV and stage director Jeffrey Hayden, with persuading her to star in Hitchcock's North by Northwest, the classic 1959 thriller in which Saint plays a spy who seduces Grant's character, but ends up falling for him.

In her first decade in Hollywood, Saint appeared in a mere seven films. (Keystone Features/Getty Images)

"I vividly remember him saying, 'Honey, I think you should find a quiet spot. I'll take care of the children and I want you to really think about this and reread this script,"' she told Vanity Fair in 2014. "He was so right. And that's what husbands are for."

Instead of being put off by her selectivity, studios continued offering her starring roles in such films as Exodus (with Newman), Raintree County (with Elizabeth Taylor and Montgomery Clift) and All Fall Down, with Warren Beatty.

She turned more to television in the 1970s and enjoyed renewed popularity in the 1980s as the mother of Cybill Shepherd in the hit sitcom Moonlighting and as Tom Hanks's mother in the comedy film Nothing in Common. She won an Emmy for the 1990 miniseries People Like Us, and had roles in such 21st-century movies as Because of Winn-Dixie, Superman Returns and Winter's Tale, the latter of which was adapted from Mark Helprin's novel of the same name. In 2021, she played Marisa Tomei's aunt in the brief audio play The Bus Ride, part of The Pack Podcast.

Saint was married to Hayden for 65 years, until his death in 2016.

Saint, left, and husband, Jeffrey Hayden, attend an event in Los Angeles in October 1957. Saint was married to Hayden for 65 years, until his death in 2016. (Harold P. Matosian/The Associated Press)

When Saint emerged in the public consciousness, many believed her theatrical-sounding name must have been invented. She was born with it on July 4, 1924, in Newark, N.J. The family moved to Delmar, a small town near Albany, N.Y., where her father was a Goodrich Rubber Co. manager. Saint's goal was to become a third-grade teacher like her mother, but at Bowling Green State University in Ohio she tried out for a play and won the leading role.

After graduation she lived with her parents in Flushing, Long Island, and began hunting for acting jobs in Manhattan. After a fruitless year, she landed a two-line role as a telephone operator on a radio drama and soon was working steadily on soap operas and nighttime dramas, appearing for two years as Claudia on One Man's Family. Network television was booming in the early 1950s, and her looks and dramatic sense made her a favourite with casting people and producers.

A critical turn in Saint's career came when she auditioned before Elia Kazan and was accepted into the Actors Studio, which shaped a generation of method-actor stars. She credited acting coach Lee Strasberg with helping her overcome her shyness.

PHOTOS | Eva Marie Saint and some of her roles:

"Lee Strasberg, when he got to know me a little bit, gave me a scene to do where I had to cry in front of my peers," she told the Santa Barbara Independent in 2009. "I worried about it, I worked on it, I tried to use what I was learning at the studio. I finally did the scene, and I cried, and my peers were crying with me. It was just an incredible moment for me."

Saint was rejected for the single female role in the play Mister Roberts, but was hired to understudy the actor chosen, Jocelyn Brando, Marlon's sister. In six frustrating months, Saint never got to substitute for Brando. She finally made it to Broadway in A Trip to Bountiful, which she had played on television.

Kazan invited her to try out for the female lead in On the Waterfront by improvising a scene with Marlon Brando. She was told to try to stop a young man from entering her apartment. She told the Los Angeles Times in 2001: "All I know is that Marlon got in the door and turned on the music. We started dancing. He flicked my skirt. Kazan saw the sparks fly, and that's how I got the part."

World.title: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is awake and speaking at a hospital, her lawyers said Tuesday, six days after the state's failed attempt to execute her by lethal injection left her unconscious and on a ventilator.

Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as executioners attempted to put her to death last Wednesday for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The lethal injection drug didn't kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered.

Her survival raises further questions about her medical and legal future. Her attorneys said her prognosis remains unclear and that she faces a long recovery.

"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," attorneys for Pike said in a statement. "Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented."

Her lawyers said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital "who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her."

Recovery path unclear

As recently as Sunday, her attorneys said Pike had remained unconscious and on a ventilator since the failed execution attempt.

Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike's legal team, said the development "bodes well for a good recovery." But he added that it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like or whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try to execute her again.

"She's still in the ICU," he said. "She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well."

A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalized Tuesday.

Pike's attorneys are set to go to court Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection.

The attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the Sept. 30 attempted execution. Chancery Court Judge I'Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case.

Pike's attorneys said in their Tuesday statement that they continue to ask Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike's sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Lee halted further executions following Pike's hospitalization and ordered a "comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred." U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate to replace him, called on the state to explore other methods of execution to ensure it can continue carrying out capital punishment.

Questions about double jeopardy

In addition to questions about competency — whether Pike can understand why she would be put to death — Pike has strong arguments that it would be cruel and unusual for the state to try to execute her again, said Deborah Denno, a Fordham Law professor who has studied execution methods for 36 years.

It could also violate the prohibition on double jeopardy, trying or punishing someone twice for the same offence, Denno said.

In other recent cases, states have been allowed to try again after failing to establish a suitable intravenous line, she said, but Pike is the first person to survive after the lethal drug was actually administered.

"They carried out every aspect of the execution," Denno said. "She didn't die, but every process they intended, they did it."

Seattle University law Prof. Michael Russo, who handled capital cases as a public defender in Los Angeles, called the failed execution horrible, but said he doubted whether the U.S. Supreme Court would stop the state from trying again on double-jeopardy grounds, should it decide to do so.

"There's nobody else in the history of the death penalty in this country who has gone through what she's been through," Russo said. But, he added, "I think what this Supreme Court would say is, her sentence was to die — to be executed — not to suffer an attempt at execution."

World.title: Fitness influencer apologizes after hitching a bike ride in the Berlin Marathon
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There's so much to love about marathon season.

The gripping accounts of elite athletes pushing themselves to the very limit. The tales of runners uplifting and supporting each other to cross the finish line. The heartache when dreams are dashed.

And then there are the people who might think, "Well, maybe no one will notice..." at a global event.

In that vein, a Chinese fitness influencer has apologized and been dropped by her sponsor after being photographed hitching a ride on a bike during the 42.2-kilometre Berlin Marathon last week.

Images of the influencer from the Sept. 27 race were first posted by the O fficial Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) Instagram account, which calls out questionable race performances. In posts from Oct. 1, the account noted that her fastest time was recorded between the 35- and 40-kilometre marks, around the time "she was spotted on the back of a bike."

A composite image of three Instagram stories posted Oct. 1 by The Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) that allege to show a Chinese influencer hitching a ride in the Berlin Marathon, her times, and a finish line photo from the Sept. 27 race. (@officialunofficialtime/Instagram)

CBC News has reached out to OMTIU to ask how it obtained the photo and to the Berlin Marathon for confirmation, but has not yet received a response.

The influencer, who goes by Abeeeer on the popular Chinese social media platform Rednote, or Xiaohongshu, posted a "sincere apology" to her 520,000 followers Saturday for violating the rules. She explained that she had been feeling physically unwell during the race but acknowledged that was not an excuse.

"My behaviour to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the spirit of the marathon," she wrote in Chinese.

"I intentionally concealed this fact during my public sharing after the race. That was a truly dishonest behaviour."

The bib number shown in the images is registered to Yuanyuan Sun of China, who recorded a finishing time of 4:53:46.

Multiple media outlets report that she had previously posted about earning a PB, or personal best, on her social media, but has since deleted her Berlin Marathon posts other than the apology.

One of her sponsors, Brooks, confirmed with CBC News that it dropped a runner after becoming " aware of the situation involving a Brooks China collaborator and the 2026 Berlin Marathon."

"After verifying the facts, Brooks China terminated its relationship with the individual," Brooks told CBC in a statement Tuesday.

"Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition."

A general view as runners compete during the 2026 BMW Berlin-Marathon on September 27, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. Over 56,000 participant from 162 nations took part in the 52nd edition of Berlin Marathon. (Maja Hitij/Getty Images)

A short history of marathon cheaters

More than 56,000 runners from 162 countries entered the 2026 Berlin Marathon. It's known for being the flattest course of the official Abbott World Marathon Majors — and therefore the fastest. About 50,000 people crossed the finish line.

And while it's not known whether anyone else attempted a shortcut this year, marathon cheating is nothing new, and what's know as course-cutting is one of the more common tactics.

One of the more infamous course-cutting examples is Rosie Ruiz, who was the first woman to cross the finish line of the 1980 Boston Marathon. She was crowned with a laurel wreath and didn't even seem tired.

Officials later determined that she had emerged from the crowd near the end of the race and run only about the final mile. She had qualified for Boston after taking the subway for most of the 1979 New York City marathon.

In 2011, Rob Sloan placed third in the U.K.'s gruelling Kielder Marathon. It was later revealed that he had ridden a bus for part of the course.

In 2023, Scottish ultramarathoner Joasia Zakrzewski finished third in a 50-mile race but was later disqualified for riding part of the course in a car.

The same year, the Mexico City Marathon disqualified some 11,000 runners for cutting sections of the course, including by using cars, bikes and public transit.

World.title: Trump says call scheduled with Putin to discuss possible plague death in Russia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he has a call scheduled with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss a possible case of plague at a Siberian research institute.

Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said he would be talking with Putin about the case "very soon." Health authorities are investigating after the death of an employee at an anti-plague institute, which authorities attributed to pneumonia with an unknown cause.

Asked what the U.S. intelligence community was saying about the case, Trump said the U.S. is in "very deep discussions" on the topic. "We'll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow," Trump said.

The World Health Organization on Tuesday said the case presents a "very low" risk outside Russia. The United Nations agency said it was in contact with Russian authorities following reports of the death last week of a woman who worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.

On Monday, Trump said the U.S. would be willing to help Russia with the situation.

WATCH | What we know about the suspected plague death: What we know about the suspected plague death in Russia | Duration closed caption 2:01 Two-hundred people have been placed under medical observation in Siberia, Russia, after a laboratory worker died after a reported accident at a plague research facility. The World Health Organization says the public health risk remains low.

The call also comes as the Trump administration faces an Oct. 18 deadline to decide which Russian entities, if any, it will sanction under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which Trump signed into law on Sept. 18.

Ukraine has given the administration and Congress a wish list of Russian companies, vessels and individuals it would like to see hit with U.S. sanctions under that law.
