World.title: Dollar Holds as Central Bank Warns US Rates Could Push It Higher
World.content:
The U.S. dollar has given back part of its early-October rebound against the Costa Rican colón, but the head of the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) has warned that a widening gap between Costa Rican and U.S. interest rates could push the exchange rate higher again. The rate for today was ₡454.50 to buy and ₡460.35 to sell, down from ₡455.71 and ₡462.08 yesterday.

On the Foreign Currency Market (Monex), the dollar eached ₡460.45 on Oct. 1, up ₡13.65, or 3.1%, from the record low of ₡446.80 set on Sept. 17. It then eased to ₡458.67 on Friday, Oct. 2, ending a run of five consecutive daily gains, and averaged ₡457.03 on Monday, Oct. 5, in a session with about $68.7 million traded.

In real terms, $1,000 exchanged at yesterday’s Monex average was worth about ₡457,030, roughly ₡10,230 more than at the September low. The gains extended a dollar rebound from its record low that began in the second half of September. BCCR President Róger Madrigal has identified the interest rate differential with the United States as the main risk.

The Central Bank lowered its monetary policy rate from 3.25% to 3% in July and has held it there since July 24, while the U.S. Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate in September to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Madrigal said the gap between the two had widened to between 75 and 100 basis points.

Madrigal explained that when the financial return favors one currency, demand for it rises while demand for others falls. If dollar-denominated assets continue to offer better returns, savers and investors could move money out of colones, adding to dollar demand and putting upward pressure on the exchange rate.

He said such a shift had not yet occurred on a significant scale but described the widening differential as a genuine risk. The BCCR’s next scheduled monetary policy review is on Nov. 26.

Economists do not all read the situation the same way. Fernando Rodríguez, an economist at the National University (UNA), said after Friday’s session that keeping the policy rate at 3% would continue to make Costa Rica attractive to investors seeking yield, sustaining the flow of dollars into the country.

Seasonal factors could also pull in the other direction. Federico Quesada Chaves, director of the School of Administrative Sciences at the State Distance University (UNED), has said the extra foreign currency that typically enters the market with aguinaldo payments, bonuses and holiday spending from late October could renew downward pressure on the dollar.

Even after the rebound, the dollar remains well below where it began the year. Monex averaged ₡497.07 on Jan. 2, meaning the dollar has lost about 8% of its value against the colón in 2026. It also sits roughly 34% below its June 2022 peak of ₡696.76.

The colón’s strength has squeezed exporters and tourism businesses that earn in dollars but pay salaries and other costs in colones, and it has coincided with a wave of job cuts at major employers. For households, the rate determines what dollar-denominated rents, loans and imported goods cost in local currency.

Whether the October rebound resumes may depend less on local dollar supply than on the direction of U.S. rates in the weeks before the Central Bank’s November meeting.

World.title: Bukele and Colombia’s President Expected at Costa Rica Prison Opening
World.content:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella are expected to attend the Oct. 14 inauguration of Costa Rica’s new maximum-security prison, according to reports in Costa Rican media late Monday. The presidency had not publicly confirmed the foreign guest list as of Tuesday morning.

The High Containment Center Against Organized Crime (CACCO) is scheduled to open at 12:30 p.m. on Oct. 14, the presidency announced Sunday night. The facility sits on the grounds of the La Reforma penitentiary complex in San Rafael de Alajuela and was built from plans donated by the government of El Salvador, as detailed when the Oct. 14 opening date was announced.

The presence of both leaders would turn the ceremony into a regional showcase for the hard-line prison model Bukele built in El Salvador. Governments in Honduras and Panama have announced El Salvador-style prison measures this year.

President Laura Fernández invited De la Espriella to the opening during a visit to Colombia in September. She said at the time that she had asked him and his security teams to join the October ceremony, and that sharing intelligence with Colombia would strengthen Costa Rica’s fight against drug trafficking networks.

De la Espriella took office Aug. 7 after a campaign that drew on Bukele’s security message. Salvadoran Vice President Félix Ulloa said around the inauguration that his government was ready to advise Colombia on building large prisons.

Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar declined last week to say whether either leader would attend, saying the question should be answered by the presidency. If Bukele attends, it would be at least his third visit to Costa Rica tied to the prison system. In November 2024 he toured La Reforma and warned that Costa Rica showed symptoms of criminality similar to those El Salvador faced with its gangs.

In January, he returned for a ceremony marking the start of CACCO construction alongside then-President Rodrigo Chaves.That January visit came less than three weeks before Costa Rica’s presidential election and drew criticism from opposition parties, which described it as foreign interference. The Supreme Elections Tribunal allowed the visit to proceed but warned that foreign delegations must not intervene in domestic politics. Fernández won the Feb. 1 election and took office May 8.

The Justice Ministry has said the prison will hold about 5,100 inmates in five modules. It is intended for leaders of criminal organizations, inmates considered violent, people facing extradition and prisoners who require special protection. Inmates will wear orange uniforms and will not be allowed clothing from outside.

The opening also faces a legal challenge. Ricardo Zeledón, a University of Costa Rica professor, filed an amparo appeal on Oct. 1 seeking to block the inauguration and any transfer of inmates to the facility. He argues the center copies El Salvador’s model and would violate human rights. The appeal names Fernández, Chaves and Aguilar.

The government presents the CACCO as the centerpiece of its response to organized crime, which authorities blame for most of the homicides. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) recorded 873 homicides in 2025. Whether the new prison will change that trend remains an open question.

The Oct. 14 ceremony will be broadcast live on YouTube, according to the presidency.

World.title: Costa Rica Opens Probe Into Political Ties of Man Wanted by US DEA
World.content:
Costa Rica’s attorney general will investigate whether a naturalized Costa Rican detained for extradition to the United States had political ties or helped finance last February’s presidential campaign, after he was photographed at President Laura Fernández’s election-night celebration.

Guobin Tam Zhang, 54, who also uses the name Juan Carlos Tam Cheong, was detained Oct. 2 in Granadilla de Curridabat at the request of the U.S. government. He is sought by the United States in connection with alleged international drug trafficking, and Costa Rican prosecutors say he also faces a local investigation for alleged money laundering.

The Ministry of Public Security described Tam as one of the main launderers of drug-trafficking proceeds here. According to the ministry, he allegedly coordinated cocaine shipments bound for the United States and then handled payments for those shipments on behalf of the cartels involved.

The arrest was carried out jointly by the Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Drug Control Police, the Fuerza Pública, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the U.S. Treasury Department.

On Monday, the San José Criminal Court ordered two months of provisional detention while the extradition request proceeds, according to Tam’s lawyer, Moisés Chinchilla. Chinchilla said the court informed his client of the DEA file during the hearing, and that the United States must still submit formal documentation and the evidence supporting its request.

The same day, the Ministry of Justice and Peace ordered Tam into the prison system’s high-containment circuit. The ministry said he met the criteria because of his alleged links to criminal structures, and that he will be held in an individual cell with controls on his visits, calls, contacts and personal belongings.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said Monday that prosecutors will open an investigation on their own initiative into any political relationships Tam may have had, with a focus on money laundering and possible illegal campaign financing. Díaz said prosecutors will first await a report from the Supreme Elections Tribunal’s department that oversees political party financing.

Díaz said Costa Rica will prioritize sending Tam to the United States, applying a prosecutorial discretion rule that suspends local cases against an extraditable defendant. He said, however, that anyone found to have assisted Tam, including front men, corrupt officials or party representatives who knowingly accepted illegal money, would face investigation.

The attorney general also said a judge has authorized prosecutors to open five electronic devices seized from Tam, four of them cellphones, and that any evidence of crimes by other people would lead to new cases. Díaz linked the arrest to the second phase of a joint strategy with the DEA aimed at what he calls invisible narcos, people who would not be identified as possible traffickers without an investigation.

The case turned political after a photograph circulated showing Tam beside Pilar Cisneros, a former lawmaker who now advises the presidency on communications, at the Feb. 1 event at the Aurola hotel in San José where Fernández received the election results. Local reports say Tam was inside rooms reserved for campaign staff, party leaders and invited guests. The mother of two of Tam’s children also attended and was photographed with Fernández, according to those reports.

Fernández said Monday that she does not know Tam, has never met with him and does not know what he does for a living. Cisneros said she does not know him either and that many people approached her for photographs that night.

The two have given differing accounts of the photograph itself. Speaking yesterday in Mora, Fernández said she did not know whether the image circulating of Tam with Cisneros was authentic, adding that about 2,000 people attended the celebration and she did not know all of them. Cisneros, however, has confirmed that the photograph is genuine and was taken that night at the Aurola, while maintaining that she has never spoken with Tam.

The ruling Pueblo Soberano party issued a certification from its treasurer, Raúl Zamora, stating that party records show no donations, contracts, transfers or other transactions involving Tam under any of the names he uses. Party president Mayuli Ortega said neither she nor the party has any relationship with him, and secretary general Freddy González said Tam was not on the party’s guest list for the celebration.

Opposition lawmakers have demanded further explanations. Liberación Nacional legislator Marco Badilla said the Legislative Assembly’s Security and Drug Trafficking Commission will examine the case, and fellow party legislator Víctor Hidalgo formally asked the presidency whether Tam was invited to the May 8 transfer of power or has visited executive branch offices.

Frente Amplio leader José María Villalta called on the government and the party to explain Tam’s presence at official events, while Claudia Dobles, head of the Coalición Agenda Ciudadana caucus, asked the Supreme Elections Tribunal to examine campaign financing. Pueblo Soberano caucus leader Nogui Acosta questioned whether the Legislative Assembly should investigate, saying the faction has no relationship with Tam.

In a sworn statement dated Aug. 4, 2025, Tam declared that all his income came from lawful activities, mainly the rental of commercial premises and homes on properties he represents or manages. Public records reviewed by local media show no properties registered in his name or in companies where he sits on the board.

Tam has not been convicted of any crime. His case is one of a series of U.S. extradition requests Costa Rica has handled this year in connection with drug investigations, including the 24 requests under review as of August and the prosecution of former magistrate Celso Gamboa in Texas.

World.title: Michel Chebat named Minister of National Security
World.content:
Michel Chebat named Minister of National Security

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Cayo North Area Representative Michel Chebat is now in charge of Belize’s security forces.

Following a Cabinet meeting in Belmopan, the former Ministry of Home Affairs has been renamed the Ministry of National Security and placed under Chebat.

In his new role, Chebat will oversee both the Belize Police Department and the Belize Defence Force, bringing the country’s two main security arms under one ministry.

He will also keep his existing responsibilities for Energy and Ports.

The appointment comes at a critical time. Belize is dealing with heightened tensions with Guatemala, including the recent airspace incursion confirmed by radar data, as well as ongoing efforts to tackle crime.

Chebat now holds one of the most demanding portfolios in Government.

World.title: Julius Espat out of Home Affairs, future unclear
World.content:
Julius Espat out of Home Affairs, future unclear

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Julius Espat no longer heads the ministry responsible for the police, and there is still no official word on what comes next for him.

Following Tuesday’s Cabinet meeting, the Ministry of Home Affairs was renamed the Ministry of National Security and handed to Cayo North Area Representative Michel Chebat.

Espat had taken over responsibility for Home Affairs after Oscar Mira was sidelined in the wake of the so called “Mira Millions” scandal.

Just last week, Prime Minister John Briceño told the media that his decision on the substantive police portfolio would go to Cabinet first. That decision has now been made, and it did not go to Espat.

Government has not yet said whether Espat will receive a new portfolio or what his role in Cabinet will be going forward.

World.title: Monchi Cervantes gets Public Utilities and Solid Waste
World.content:
Monchi Cervantes gets Public Utilities and Solid Waste

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Orange Walk North Area Representative Ramon “Monchi” Cervantes has a new assignment.

Cervantes has been given the Ministry of Public Utilities and Solid Waste Management as part of the Cabinet shakeup announced after a lengthy meeting in Belmopan.

The portfolio puts him in charge of key public services that affect households and communities across the country.

The move is one of several changes as Prime Minister John Briceño reshapes his Cabinet.

World.title: Dr. Osmond Martinez promoted to full minister
World.content:
Dr. Osmond Martinez promoted to full minister

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Toledo East Area Representative Dr. Osmond Martinez is moving up.

Martinez has been elevated from Minister of State to full Cabinet minister and will now lead the Ministry of Economic Transformation.

The promotion was among the changes announced following a marathon Cabinet meeting in Belmopan.

The appointment gives Toledo a stronger voice at the Cabinet table at a time when the district is facing challenges, including the upcoming closure of Tropic Air’s Punta Gorda station.

World.title: The reshuffle is here, and it’s a big one
World.content:
The reshuffle is here, and it’s a big one

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A long Cabinet meeting in Belmopan has produced one of the biggest shakeups of the Briceño administration.

Here is what changed:

Michel Chebat, Cayo North, now heads the newly named Ministry of National Security, overseeing the Belize Police Department and the Belize Defence Force. He keeps Energy and Ports.

Ramon “Monchi” Cervantes, Orange Walk North, takes the Ministry of Public Utilities and Solid Waste Management.

Dr. Osmond Martinez, Toledo East, moves from Minister of State to full minister of Economic Transformation.

The biggest question mark hangs over Julius Espat, who had been responsible for Home Affairs since Oscar Mira was sidelined over the “Mira Millions” scandal. There has been no official word on his future.

The reshuffle comes days after Prime Minister John Briceño confirmed he plans to lead the PUP into the 2030 general election, and amid reports of tension within the party’s top ranks.

World.title: It’s official: PM announces Cabinet adjustments
World.content:
It’s official: PM announces Cabinet adjustments

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Prime Minister John Briceño has officially confirmed changes to his Cabinet.

In a release from Belmopan on Tuesday, October 6, the Office of the Prime Minister outlined the new portfolios:

Hon. Michel Chebat is now Minister of National Security, Energy and Ports.

Hon. Ramon Cervantes is Minister of Public Utilities, Logistics and Solid Waste Management. Hon. Ramiro Ramirez will remain Minister of State.

Dr. Hon. Osmond Martinez has been appointed Minister of Economic Transformation.

Hon. Henry Charles Usher will take up the substantive post of Minister with responsibility for Enterprise.

The changes follow a lengthy Cabinet meeting in Belmopan, and include the renaming of the former Ministry of Home Affairs to the Ministry of National Security.

World.title: Briceño thanks Espat for “stellar work” at Home Affairs
World.content:
Briceño thanks Espat for “stellar work” at Home Affairs

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Julius Espat’s time at the helm of Home Affairs has come to an end.

In announcing his Cabinet adjustments on Tuesday, Prime Minister John Briceño singled out Espat for special thanks, praising his “stellar work” as interim Minister of Home Affairs.

Espat stepped into the role after Oscar Mira was sidelined following the “Mira Millions” scandal. The ministry, now renamed the Ministry of National Security, has been assigned to Michel Chebat, who will also keep Energy and Ports.

The official release did not list a new portfolio for Espat.

Other changes include Ramon Cervantes taking on Public Utilities, Logistics and Solid Waste Management, Dr. Osmond Martinez becoming Minister of Economic Transformation, and Henry Charles Usher being confirmed in the substantive post of Minister responsible for Enterprise.

Ramiro Ramirez remains a Minister of State.

The reshuffle comes as the Prime Minister prepares to lead the PUP toward the 2030 general election, amid reports of tension within the party.

World.title: Money tight? Stretch your dolla the Belize way!
World.content:
Money tight? Stretch your dolla the Belize way!

By Zoila Palma: With the cost of food, fuel, utilities and other necessities continuing to put pressure on household budgets, finding ways to cut back on non-essential spending can make a significant difference.

While it may not be possible to reduce every bill, small changes in everyday habits can help Belizean families keep more money in their pockets each month.

Eat out less and cook more at home.

Buying lunch, ordering dinner or grabbing food on the go can quickly add up, especially for families. Planning meals for the week, cooking larger portions and taking lunch to work or school can significantly reduce food expenses. Home cooking can also make it easier to shop strategically when grocery shopping and avoid unnecessary purchases.

Cut back on drinks, casino trips and other leisure spending

Small purchases such as soft drinks, alcoholic beverages or casino visits may seem harmless individually, but they can become a considerable monthly expense.

Setting a specific entertainment budget—or taking a break from these expenses altogether—can free up money for groceries, bills, debt payments or savings.

Reduce unnecessary fuel runs

Fuel is another area where planning can save money. Instead of making several separate trips during the day, combine errands whenever possible. Families can also organize school and work transportation more efficiently, rather than making multiple unnecessary runs.

Be more energy- and water-efficient

Electricity and water bills can become much heavier when consumption is not monitored. Turn off lights, fans and appliances when they are not being used, limit unnecessary use of air conditioning and unplug equipment that does not need to remain on. At the same time, conserve water by fixing leaks, turning off taps when water is not needed and avoiding excessive water use.

Make a budget and track where your money goes

One of the simplest ways to reduce expenses is to know exactly where your money is going. Write down your monthly income and every expense, including the small purchases that are easy to overlook. Separate necessities from wants, set spending limits and decide how much you want to put toward debt and savings before spending on non-essentials.

For many households, reducing expenses does not mean giving up everything enjoyable. It means identifying where money is leaking out and making deliberate choices about what is truly necessary.

World.title: ‘OBJECTIVES MET’
World.content:
AFTER Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz booked their spot in the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals against Mexico, interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid believes a solid foundation has been laid for future success.

The national senior men’s team drew 1-1 away to Honduras at the Chelato Uclés National Stadium, which was enough to secure second place in Group B with seven points and a spot in the next round of the competition.

With Guatemala beating Suriname (seven points each) and Martinique and El Salvador (four points each) drawing minutes before the game, Jamaica only needed a point to advance as they would have a better goal difference than Suriname.

They looked set to top the group after Tyreece Campbell’s 27th-minute strike but Luis Palma’s stunning long-range effort earned the Hondurans a point.

Speid was pleased to move on the knockout stages and gave Honduras credit for their performance.

“We did what we set out to do, which was qualify for the next round. I think both Jamaica and Honduras are very happy tonight,” he said.

“Honduras were very brave tonight. They had players who were making their debut in such an important game. They had to get a positive result not to be relegated, and they made a lot of changes and brought on some young players, and I think that is the way going forward. That’s really a good move by them.”

Throughout the four group games which began at the end of September, Speid dealt with a number of injuries and withdrawals, but this also afforded him the opportunity to see several players making their competitive debuts, including teenagers Jahmarie Nolan and Jamone Lyle.

He believes this window has given him optimism that Jamaica can compete with the best, going forward.

“Jamaica is in a rebuilding phase. We carried some really young players here — a lot of them played their first game for Jamaica in this series — so I think one of our objectives has been met,” he said.

“We were able to look at about 25 players over the four matches, and it will form the basis of our squad going forward. We have been able to see all the players play in top-level competition games and, based on that, we are better prepared to pick players going forward.”

Honduras Head Coach Jose Molina believes his team has a bright future, despite not qualifying for the next round, after going unbeaten against Jamaica over two matches, having last done so in 2013.

“If you want to achieve something you have to follow a path, and that path is the process; and what we want to achieve is qualifying for the 2030 World Cup, which is the main objective. We remain convinced that at some point the criticism will turn into something else,” he said.

The Reggae Boyz will now meet Concacaf’s number oneranked team and last summer’s FIFA World Cup hosts, Mexico, in the two-legged quarter-finals next month.

Jamaica will host the first leg at the National Stadium, on either November 13 or November 14, before travelling to Mexico on November 17 for the second leg.

The other quarter-final matchups will see USA take on Haiti, Canada battling Guatemala, and Curacao taking on Panama.

The winners will not only book their spot in the Nations League Finals in March but the Concacaf Gold Cup next summer.

World.title: Messi retires from Argentina national team with goal and assist
World.content:
Argentina's forward #10 Lionel Messi celebrates scoring his team's third goal during the international friendly football match between Argentina and Benin at the Mas Monumental stadium in Buenos Aires on October 6, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina (AFP) — Lionel Messi brought the curtain down on his 21-year international career on Tuesday, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in an emotional final appearance for the former world champions in Buenos Aires.

In a perfectly scripted finale, the 39-year-old widely regarded as the greatest football player in history signed off with his 126th international goal in front of 85,000 supporters as Argentina cruised to a 3-0 victory over Benin.

Messi, playing in his record-extending 208th international, also provided the assist for the opening goal scored by veteran Nicolas Otamendi, with Nico Paz also scoring.

But the match was a footnote to the occasion itself, which saw Messi savoring the adulation of the Monumental Stadium crowd one last time for an event which had been billed as ‘The Last Tango’.

Beforehand, Messi wiped away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina team-mates made its way through crowds of wellwishers en route to the stadium.

Messi took the field alongside his three children and received affectionate waves from his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and his mother, Celia Cuccittini, who were watching from a VIP box.

Shortly before kick off, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word “Gracias” (Thank You) above the football superstar’s No.10 was laid out on the pitch as the crowd roared their approval.

Messi welled up again as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana sang the national anthem beside a banner which read — “The Malvinas are Argentine” — the same banner held aloft by players after their 2-1 World Cup semi-final win over England.

The match was halted in the 10th minute — in tribute to Messi’s famous shirt number — for a minute-long ovation to the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star.

He crowned the occasion with a goal from the penalty spot in the 71st minute.

– ‘Gave it my all’ –

At the final whistle a drone show lit up the night sky above the stadium, showing Messi’s image and thanking the eight-time Ballon D’Or-winner for his career.

Messi’s farewell came two and a half months after Argentina’s World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss.

“I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance,” Messi wrote at the time.

Before Tuesday’s game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters.

Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction.

“To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!,” he joked.

Outside the Argentina Football Association headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentine flag with his image inscribed “The joy of my life.”

Former Barcelona team-mate Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on X.

“It’s not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more,” he said.

Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.

Messi’s departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international football, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country’s 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona’s heir.

“I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn’t bother me at all that he’s leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest,” Cecilia Adriano, 52, told AFP.

During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina won one World Cup, were runners-up twice (Brazil 2014 and North America 2026) and were also crowned Copa America champions in 2021 and 2024.

World.title: MPs get $19 million each for Constituency Mitigation Programme
World.content:
Minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan has boasted that he is the first person holding the portfolio to be undertaking the repair/construction of 55 bridges (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

A minimum of $19 million has been allocated to each constituency under the Government’s Constituency Mitigation Programme.

Previously referred to as the Christmas Work Programme, the funds are being made available early this year.

Minister with responsibility for Works, Robert Morgan, made the announcement during Tuesday’s sitting of the House of Representatives. He said the money will be spent for road repairs, de-bushing, drain cleaning, beautification and sanitation. A minimum of $10 million must be spent on road repairs, which includes patching. A minimum of 50 per cent of that amount must be spent on main roads.

“Up to $5 million may be transferred into road rehabilitation from other eligible components, subject to their respective limits. The maximum available under the road component is therefore $15 million per constituency,” said Morgan.

The works minister said $4 million is set aside for the de-bushing component of the programme. This covers cutting and pruning trees, foliage, bush and undergrowth along roadways, pathways, sidewalks, medians, gully banks and other thoroughfares where overgrowth impedes movement or creates a safety or security risk.

Morgan said a maximum of $2 million may be transferred from de-bushing to road repairs or drain cleaning. At least $2 million must remain allocated for de-bushing.

Drain cleaning has been allocated $2 million per constituency. This includes cleaning, unclogging and desilting earth or paved drains. It also permits minor repairs to drain inverts, walls, culverts, grilles and covers so that storm water can flow freely.

The programme permits a maximum of $1 million to be reallocated from this component to other components. That leaves a minimum of $1 million committed to drain cleaning.

“Members should consider any proposed transfer carefully, taking account of the drainage needs that will remain. Flexibility must be exercised with a clear understanding of the consequences for the communities concerned,” Morgan told his fellow Members of Parliament.

Meanwhile, $3 million per constituency is allocated to beautification and sanitation, to be implemented by the National Solid Waste Management Authority (NSWMA). The work includes collecting and trucking municipal and bulky waste to approved disposal sites, and washing down or otherwise sanitising areas that may pose a health or safety risk.

Morgan said the $3 million allocation is fixed.

“No funds may be transferred out of this component, and no funds may be transferred into it. The full allocation must be used for its stated purpose,” he said.

Implementation will be undertaken by the National Works Agency (NWA) and the NSWMA. The NWA will implement road repairs, de-bushing and drain cleaning, while the NSWMA will implement beautification and sanitation.

-Lynford Simpson

World.title: Jamaica records 24 per cent reduction in murders – Chang
World.content:
Dr Horace Chang (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Jamaica has recorded a 24 per cent reduction in murders this year when compared to the corresponding period in 2025.

As at Tuesday, October 6, there were 407 homicides recorded across the country, according to the Minister of National Security and Peace, Dr Horace Chang, who provided the update during a ministerial statement in the House of Representatives.

Chang noted that this compares with 534 murders during the similar period last year. He also shared that between July and September, Jamaica recorded 123 murders.

“This is the lowest quarterly figure recorded in more than three decades,” he said while pointing out that September recorded 36 murders, the lowest monthly total in more than 30 years. It was also the fourth month this year in which Jamaica recorded 40 or fewer murders.

Chang highlighted that five of the first nine months of 2026 are among the lowest monthly murder totals recorded in more than three decades. Additionally, the first three quarters of 2026 are the lowest quarterly murder totals recorded over that period.

“Just a few years ago, 123 murders was a figure Jamaica could record in a single month. In May 2024, Jamaica recorded 134 murders. In 2017, the monthly average was 137 murders. Today, 123 murders represent an entire quarter,” said Chang.

He expressed that, “for decades, high levels of murder and violence became tragically normalised in our society. We are now seeing a sustained reversal of that trend”.

Chang told the Parliament that the Government remained committed to its policies even when they were questioned and criticised.

“We increased the strength of the Jamaica Constabulary Force. We invested in its people, infrastructure, technology, equipment and mobility. We provided our police officers with the resources they needed and the operational space to do their jobs effectively,” he said.

The security minister commended the leadership of the Jamaica Constabulary Force and all members for their execution of the Government’s policies and programmes.

“I especially commend the brave men and women on the front line. Their courage, professionalism and sacrifice continue to drive these gains. Every day, they place themselves in harm’s way to protect the Jamaican people. Their service must be recognised and appreciated,” he said.

-Lynford Simpson

World.title: 11-y-o among two killed in Denham Town house fire
World.content:
File photo

KINGSTON, Jamaica — An 11-year-old boy was among two people killed in a house fire along North Street in Kingston early Tuesday morning.

The deceased have been identified as 11-year-old Jaydon Whyte and 60-year-old Junior Barrett.

According to the Denham Town police, lawmen were alerted to a fire in the area about midnight.

Members of the Jamaica Fire Brigade extinguished the blaze and conducted cooling-down operations. The charred remains of Whyte and Barrett were subsequently discovered inside the home.

Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the fire and the deaths.

World.title: Reggae Boyz book ticket to quarterfinals of Nations League
World.content:
Jamaica's forward #11 Tyreece Campbell celebrates scoring his team's first goal during the Concacaf Nations League Cup football match between Honduras and Jamaica at the Nacional Chelato Ucles stadium in Tegucigalpa on October 5, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz have advanced to the quarterfinals of the Concacaf Nations League after a 1-1 draw with Honduras at Estadio Nacional Chelato Ucles in Tegucigalpa on Monday.

The draw saw Jamaica finish second in Group B of League A on seven points, the same as group winners Guatemala and third-placed Suriname, with goal-difference separating the teams.

The point was also good enough for Honduras to avoid relegation to League B.

Tyreece Campbell scored his first goal in Jamaica’s colours when he fired home in the 27th minute, curling a ball from the left side of the Honduran 18-yard box and off the inside of the far right upright.

Luis Palma equalised for the hosts with a goal of supreme quality, beating goalkeeper Andre Blake with a looping, curling shot from at least 30 yards out, the ball nestling in the far right corner.

Jamaica missed a number of other good scoring chances.

Javon East, the two-goal hero against El Salvador on Friday, had arguably the best opportunity to score with just the goalkeeper to beat on a breakaway late in the first half, but shot wide of the goal.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Doctors pleased
World.content:
TRADE unionist Senator Lambert Brown says doctors have welcomed the Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) ruling on emergency duty payments, urging the Government to comply with the award and work out a disbursement plan with the Jamaica Medical Doctors’ Association (JMDA).

“We are pleased, the doctors are pleased, and we know that the panel was unanimous in respect to the overtime rate,” Brown told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

Brown, who represents the JMDA in the dispute, was responding to the IDT’s October 5 ruling which ordered a new framework for emergency duty payments and rejected the Government’s proposal to place doctors under a standardised Extra Hours Worked (EHW) system.

The tribunal ordered that the new Emergency Duty Allowance (EDA) rates be based on the JMDA’s March 15, 2024 cost-reduction proposal, with some adjustments, and that the payments be applied retroactively from April 1, 2023.

The ruling also ordered the reinstatement of the incentive allowance for eligible medical officers from

April 1, 2023. Tribunal member Berita Locke, JP, dissented on that aspect of the award, while Chairman Dr Noel Cowell and member Beatrice Rhoden formed the majority.

Brown said the focus must now shift to implementing the award.

“I hope the Government will comply with the ruling of the IDT and will sit down with the doctors and work out a payment schedule, a payment plan to effect their award… the doctors have been suffering for too long, it’s time to put an end to this dispute. Forty-two months is too long,” he said.

Minister of Labour and Social Security Pearnel Charles Jr, in his response to the ruling, said the ministry has acknowledged the tribunal’s decision and would continue to focus on maintaining stable industrial relations.

The dispute centred on whether junior doctors should be placed under the Government’s standardised EHW policy or continue under a system that recognises the different types of emergency duties they perform.

The Government’s EHW policy was designed to establish a standard overtime system across the public service. Under the policy, overtime was generally paid at 1.5 times the normal rate for the first day and twice the rate for the second day and public holidays.

The policy also included a 15-hour weekly limit on extra hours worked, with an exception where an employee was unavoidably required to work beyond that limit to achieve a clearly defined objective and permission was obtained from the appropriate senior official.

The JMDA argued that the arrangement was unsuitable for doctors because of the nature of hospital services and the need for continuous medical care.

The tribunal agreed, finding that emergency duty payments were different from generic public sector overtime because they reflected the specific demands placed on medical officers.

It noted that junior doctors may be required to work 16-hour overnight emergency shifts during weekdays, from 4:00 pm to 8:00 am, as well as 24-hour weekend shifts. Doctors may also be required to cover multiple hospitals and deal with emergencies that cannot be treated as ordinary scheduled overtime.

The tribunal described EDA as a specialised form of overtime pay that takes account of the intensity of doctors’ duties, continuous 16-to-24-hour rotas, cross-coverage and location-based differences.

The JMDA had proposed retaining a multi-tiered emergency duty payment system while reducing the number of existing categories.

The association’s March 15, 2024 cost-reduction proposal grouped the payments into four main areas: rostered duty, covering multiple hospitals, Type C hospitals, and premium rates.

The tribunal accepted that proposal as the basis for its award, with minor adjustments.

Under the new arrangement, the EDA hourly rate is to be calculated using the midpoint of the relevant medical officer salary scale.

For rostered emergency duty, doctors are to receive 1.5 times the applicable hourly rate for a normal weekday, 1.75 times the rate for the first day off, and twice the rate for the second day off.

For doctors covering multiple hospitals, the rate is 1.75 times the applicable rate for a normal weekday, twice the rate for the first day off, and 2.25 times the rate for the second day off.

Ward sessional duty is to attract a rate of 25 per cent above the rostered duty rate, while premium duties — including casualty, Type C hospitals, health centres, and cross-coverage — are to attract a rate 50 per cent above the applicable rostered duty rate.

The tribunal ordered that the EDA payments under the new framework be made retroactively from April 1, 2023.

The Government had argued that revised sessional compensation rates should instead take effect from August 1, 2024, when the standardised EHW policy was issued.

The tribunal rejected that date, saying there was “no legal, contractual, or equitable justification” for using August 1, 2024 as the implementation date. It pointed to the March 16, 2023 Memorandum of Understanding between the Government and the JMDA, which required discussions on revised allowance policies by March 31, 2023.

The tribunal also found that the Government had not established that applying the April 1, 2023 date would create the level of financial or administrative disruption claimed.

It noted that other public sector groups, including the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) and the Jamaica Urban Transit Company (JUTC), had received overtime retroactivity dating back to April 2022 without causing a “knockon” effect.

The tribunal also ruled on the incentive allowance, which had been a separate point of disagreement between the parties.

The Government argued that the allowance had been discontinued and absorbed into the restructured basic salaries of medical officers, while the JMDA argued that it had not agreed to the removal of the allowance and that it remained protected by the March 2023 agreement.

The tribunal found that the JMDA’s position was supported by the evidence and concluded that the incentive allowance had survived the signing of the March 16, 2023 agreement. The majority therefore ordered its reinstatement from April 1, 2023.

Eligible non-rostered medical officers, including interns, senior house officers, and medical officers levels 1 to 3 working in emergency and clinical specialties at the Ministry of Health and Wellness’s head office, are to receive an allowance equal to 40 per cent of the midpoint of their respective salary scales.

An allowance of 55 per cent of the midpoint is provided for medical officers levels 2 and 3 serving as medical officers (health), as well as medical officers otherwise eligible under the 2017-2021 heads of agreement.

However, a medical officer who performs rostered emergency duty during a particular calendar month is disqualified from receiving the incentive allowance for that month.

Locke agreed with the EDA decision but issued a minority award arguing that the incentive allowance fell outside the tribunal’s terms of reference and that the tribunal therefore did not have the authority to reinstate it.

The dispute dates back to the March 2023 agreement between the Government and the JMDA, under which the parties settled the restructuring of doctors’ basic salaries, but negotiations on the EDA remained unresolved.

After months of unsuccessful negotiations, the JMDA took industrial action in December 2024. The matter was subsequently referred to the IDT on January 15, 2025.

The tribunal said the parties made written submissions and oral presentations over 53 sittings between April 24, 2025 and April 1, 2026, with evidence from 10 witnesses and 162 exhibits.

The JMDA represents approximately 2,500 public sector medical officers, including locum interns, medical interns, senior house officers and medical officers levels 1 to 3.

World.title: Insurance assurance
World.content:
HENRY… we have heard the concerns raised by the tourism sector and we take them seriously

THE Insurance Association of Jamaica (IAJ) has promised players in the tourism sector that its members are working to resolve some claims and questions surrounding settlement calculations, deductibles, property valuations, and the application of the average clause.

Last week the Jamaica Hotel & Tourist Association (JHTA) reported that a new survey of its members found that six in 10 tourism claims made after Hurricane Melissa last October remain unresolved, and that most operators expect to recover well short of what they lost.

According to JHTA President O’Brian Herron, major players in the insurance sector committed to accelerate the resolution of outstanding Melissa claims, with the objective of settling the vast majority, excluding complex and litigated matters, by the end of September 2026.

“We welcomed that commitment. The evidence from our members shows how far there still is to go,” said Herron.

In a media release over the weekend, the IAJ said it has taken careful note of concerns raised publicly by the JHTA.

“We have heard the concerns raised by the tourism sector and we take them seriously. Questions surrounding the time taken to resolve claims, settlement calculations, deductibles, valuations and the application of policy provisions deserve clear and constructive engagement. Our objective is to work with our members and stakeholders to address these concerns while ensuring that claims are assessed fairly and in accordance with the terms of each policy,” said IAJ President Rosemarie Henry.

She added that the IAJ believes policyholders should understand how their settlements are calculated, how relevant policy provisions are applied and have an appropriate channel through which questions or concerns regarding their individual claims can be addressed.

“The association remains committed to constructive engagement with the tourism sector and other affected policyholder groups as Jamaica continues its recovery from Hurricane Melissa,” said Henry.

The IAJ head pointed out that the Category 5 storm posed an exceptional test for policyholders, insurers, brokers, loss adjusters, reinsurers and the wider Jamaican economy, highlighting important lessons on catastrophe preparedness, claims communication, loss-adjusting capacity, and the timely provision of financial support to affected policyholders.

“Hurricane Melissa tested Jamaica at every level, including our insurance ecosystem. We must carry forward lessons, and the industry has a responsibility to learn from them. Our commitment is to support the completion of outstanding claims, strengthen the experience of policyholders and continue working with our partners to build an insurance sector in which Jamaicans can have confidence, particularly when they need it most,” Henry added.

The IAJ said it will continue working with its member companies, the Financial Services Commission, the Jamaica Insurance Brokers’ Association, the Loss Adjusters’ Association of Jamaica, the JHTA, other policyholder groups and relevant stakeholders to support the completion of outstanding claims and Jamaica’s continuing recovery.

In the meantime, the IAJ reported that its member companies are intensifying efforts to bring remaining claims to resolution, with industry data showing that 90 per cent of motor claims and 77 per cent of Jamaican dollar-denominated claims have been fully settled and paid, while progress has been slower among non-motor and US dollar-denominated claims.

The IAJ said it recognises that outstanding claims continue to place financial and operational pressure on families and businesses working to recover and rebuild. Additionally, greater attention is now being directed towards progressing these matters and strengthening communication with affected policyholders.

“Our responsibility is to ensure that the remaining claims receive the attention they require and that policyholders are kept informed throughout the process. Insurance is fundamentally about being there when people and businesses experience loss, and we understand the importance of delivering on that promise.

“Our members are focused on bringing outstanding matters to resolution and helping policyholders move forward with greater certainty,” said Henry.

The release noted that, as at the end of September 2026, 49 per cent of US dollar-denominated claims and 54 per cent of non-motor claims had been fully settled and paid.

“Transparency is essential as the industry works to complete the remaining Hurricane Melissa claims.

When we report a claim as closed, we mean that all outstanding obligations related to the claim have been paid.

These figures show where progress has been made, but equally important, they identify the areas where greater attention is required.

Our immediate focus is on working with our members to accelerate outstanding claims and move as many as possible through to final settlement and payment,” said IAJ Executive Director Everton McFarlane. The IAJ said it will continue to monitor claims progression with its member companies and will provide further industry updates as claims move towards completion.

“For insurers, the priority now is to work through the remaining claims with the level of attention each case requires and to keep policyholders informed as matters progress. Where additional information is required, an assessment remains outstanding, or there are questions about a settlement, there needs to be clear communication so those issues can be addressed and the claim can move forward.

As an industry, we recognise how important it is for policyholders to have clarity about where they are in the process and what comes next,” said Tammara Glaves-Hucey, chair of the IAJ’s General Insurance Committee.

The IAJ said its member companies have been asked to provide policyholders with up-to-date information on the status of their claims and any information still required; identify a clear point of contact through whom the claim can be progressed; explain the basis of settlement offers, including applicable deductibles, the average clause or other material policy provisions; and provide clear next steps and, where reasonably possible, an expected timeline for completion.

World.title: Behind closed doors, Europe braces for a deadly attack
World.content:
Russia’s hybrid attacks across Europe — cyberattacks, sabotage, drone incursions — have been ramping up in recent months. But European governments are quietly preparing for something much worse.

On today’s show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Ian Wishart discuss how EU ambassadors have been meeting in recent weeks to discuss what to do if a potential Russian hybrid attack were to result in mass casualties.

Next, Britain’s minister in charge of relations with Europe, Hamish Falconer, is making his first official visit to the European Parliament. Zoya was able to catch him on the phone to ask him more about EU-U.K. relations under PM Andy Burnham and a potential deal on farming, among other things, currently in the works.

Finally, what may sound like the plot of a spy novel is in fact real news coming out of Berlin where Germany’s former spy chief has been arrested on suspicion of espionage.

World.title: ‘Nobody wants a new Greece’: Calls grow for crisis election in Romania
World.content:
“Everybody says, ‘OK, if this won’t pass, we will go to snap elections,’ but they do not know Nicușor Dan as I do,” Simion said. The president is “very stubborn” and could defy calls for elections even if all parties want them, he said. “In that case we will have the numbers of signatures and votes to suspend him at least, if not sack him.”

Dan has refused to contemplate handing AUR a role in government. He defeated Simion for the presidency last year and regards his rival’s politics as a threat to Romania’s pro-Western, pro-European direction. The president says he opposes a snap election because the campaign period would delay budget reforms and healthcare funding.

‘A new Greece’

The Romanian leu has weakened against the euro in the months since the crisis blew up. Simion urged international investors to remain patient and sought to reassure them that AUR would be fiscally responsible if it won power. “Nobody wants a new Greece,” he said. “We will do everything it takes to respect our commitments to our international partners and for them to recover the debts.”

The call for an early election is gaining traction in Bucharest.

So far, the leader of Dan’s former party, the Save Romania Union, has joined politicians from the National Liberal Party, and the leader of the Social Democratic Party and AUR, in suggesting an unprecedented emergency election could be required.

George Simion has been building support in parliament to censure the president. | Robert Ghement/EPA

Dan’s latest plan still has time to work, but political feuding between parties remains a problem. The Liberals say they could support Niculescu as prime minister if the Social Democrats do not get too much influence, while the Social Democrats say they want the PM-designate to take the country in a new direction — away from the austerity policies of the outgoing Liberal premier, Ilie Bolojan.

World.title: Can ‘Berlin’s Mamdani’ convince Jewish Berliners to trust the Left?
World.content:
The Tel Aviv-born former businessman does not come across as a timid man: a firm handshake, a shirt straining at every seam and a deep and penetrating voice. Yet the mood at his conference table, where the community’s secretary general and its spokesperson also sit, is one of great concern.

The subject of that concern: The result of the recent Berlin election, in which the Left Party — a successor to the communist party that ruled East Germany until 1989 — came in first with 26% of the vote. It’s a record for the party in the capital, and more than double its previous result. Germany has been arguing about the consequences ever since.

Among the trio sitting at the table, the Left Party’s Berlin branch is seen as not just radically left-wing but also a hotbed of antisemitism. The party made opposition to Israel’s war in Gaza a central plank of its election campaign. While some Jews have declared their support for the Left, leading Jewish institutions have criticized it.

Elif Eralp, lead candidate of the far-left Die Linke, taking a selfie with a fan while campaigning in Marzahn district ahead of Berlin state elections on September 15, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

At the center of the debate is Elif Eralp, the Left’s lead candidate in the Berlin election who has become the face of the party’s transformation. Under Eralp and a younger generation of activists, many with immigrant backgrounds in the Muslim world, the party has expanded well beyond its East German roots and built a new urban coalition around housing, inequality and opposition to the war in Gaza.

Eralp and other prominent Left officials concede there have been troubling incidents among their supporters, and have condemned them. At a party conference shortly after the election, Eralp pledged to “strengthen the diverse Jewish life in Berlin and combat antisemitism.”

It was an acknowledgment of an issue that has been central to her effort to become mayor. In Germany, a single party is rarely strong enough to rule alone; forming a government means weeks of haggling among parties that dislike each other to varying degrees. If Eralp is to govern, she will need to form a coalition with the center-left Social Democrats and the Greens. Among their demands: “combating antisemitism and protecting Jewish life,” according to a joint statement by the two parties.

World.title: EU quietly braces for nightmare scenario of multiple-casualty hybrid attack
World.content:
EU capitals are quietly preparing for how the bloc should respond to a major hybrid attack that leaves several citizens dead — an outcome that looks increasingly likely, according to five EU diplomats and officials.

But the efforts to prepare are exposing splits on how much of a role the EU should play on security matters, and whether the bloc’s efforts are redundant with NATO.

The talks about a nightmare attack scenario have taken place in recent weeks among EU ambassadors from all 27 countries gathering in “restricted format,” meaning without phones or assistants. Discussions have ramped up since the discovery of an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig airport in August, said the diplomats and officials, who were granted anonymity to discuss the confidential exchanges.





While the EU has discussed such scenarios for years — unveiling a “hybrid toolbox” geared at coordinating responses to cyberattacks, election interference, and sabotage — the latest talks zeroed in on the risk of more serious attacks that cause large-scale casualties. Two diplomats said a meeting among EU ambassadors last Wednesday focused specifically on such examples.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU says Moscow has intensified a campaign of cyberattacks, sabotage and other covert operations across the bloc.

“Europe’s democracies are facing a growing number of threats,” European justice Commissioner Michael McGrath told POLITICO. “We are strengthening our capacity to anticipate and detect threats, improve early warning and ensure that Europe can respond quickly and collectively when our democratic resilience is tested.”

A pilot remotely steers a military drone at the Cognac air base in southwestern France on June 12, 2026. | Christophe Archambault/AFP via Getty Images

The talks among EU diplomats and ministers have focused on deploying emergency response teams, freeing up pockets of EU money to help the affected state, and how EU institution leaders should communicate, one EU official said.

“We have to be prepared for something serious,” a senior EU diplomat said. “Unfortunately, Leipzig showed us that a very serious incident, something that causes multiple casualties, is not out of the question.”

A second EU official added: “Given the scope and scale of Russia’s action there are bound to be casualties sooner than later. It’s sheer luck there haven’t been any yet.”

‘Very confusing’

The bloc is reeling from near-daily reports of so-called hybrid attacks — a label used by the EU and NATO to describe subversive activity that falls below the threshold of a direct act of war. On Tuesday, several sailors were declared missing after their ship was sunk by drones in the Black Sea, according to Bulgarian officials.

This followed the Leipzig airport incident, a suspicious fire at a Polish ground-link station handling Starlink communications, and a plot to plant incendiary devices in commercial transport hubs around the EU and U.K., alongside regular airspace violations.

“It is quite obvious that when Russia is using more and more lethal tools to test our preparedness and willingness to take counter measures, at some point there will be casualties,” said Teija Tiilikainen, director of the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats. “At some point, intentionally or unintentionally, this is what happens.”





If several EU or NATO-member citizens are killed in what appears to be an attack, the pressure to act will be overwhelming on both institutions. “We’re very afraid that at some point an allied life” will be taken, said one NATO diplomat, which will make the “pressure very high” to act.

Yet EU-level discussions are prompting criticism from some capitals that the EU is overstepping its security role and potentially duplicating NATO’s core functions, the transatlantic alliance that has underpinned European security for 80 years.

“It risks being very confusing for decision-makers at all levels,” said Oana Lungescu, a distinguished fellow at RUSI and former spokesperson for NATO. “If there is confusion or duplication, that risks slowing down the decision-making, which has implications because time is always of the essence.”

A helicopter of the German Federal Police lowers an emergency response team during a rescue exercise in Hamburg on October 15, 2021. | Axel Heimken/AFP via Getty Images

Another problem is the EU’s lack of secure communications and suspicion that sensitive information shared during ambassador gatherings can be leaked, several diplomats said. Reports that Hungary’s ex-foreign minister shared the contents of leader-level talks with his Russian counterpart only deepened these concerns, leading capitals to restrict truly sensitive information to NATO formats.

“My government is very suspicious of sharing sensitive intelligence in Coreper or even in the leaders’ room,” said a diplomat from an eastern flank state. “It either shows up in the media or goes straight to Moscow.”

Overlapping protocols

The pushback coincides with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s efforts to bolster the bloc’s security credentials.

In her latest State of the European Union speech in Strasbourg, the former German defense minister pitched an “emergency security protocol” to help EU states coordinate in exactly the kind of scenario being discussed. The protocol, along with von der Leyen’s pitch to create a “European Security Council,” is expected to feature in a landmark “European Security Strategy” due out in early November, according to two diplomats.

But several diplomats pushed back, arguing these efforts would take months to set up and potentially duplicate functions that already exist inside the EU.





Instead of creating new formats that add complexity, one senior national diplomat said the EU should double down on the crisis-response tools it already has.

“We’re very uncomfortable about [the] emergency security protocol,” the diplomat said. “We already have mechanisms in place. If there is a crisis, we have the Integrated Political Response (IPCR) that worked very well during the pandemic and other crises.”

Putin doesn’t care

Established under the scope of the Lisbon Treaty, the IPCR allows the holder of the EU’s rotating presidency, at the request of an affected country, to call emergency meetings involving experts from NATO, the U.N., or other international bodies.

In the event of a major hybrid attack, the onus remains on the affected country to decide on the best way forward. France triggered the EU’s Article 42.7 following the 2015 Bataclan attacks, marking the only time the mutual assistance clause has been invoked. However, Lungescu noted this was a “political decision” by Paris that did not lead to major displays of mutual assistance beyond coordinating terror investigations between France and Belgium.

To avoid confusion over who does what during a mass-casualty event, Lungescu said both parties should divide labor: NATO handling intelligence-sharing and military deterrence, and the EU focusing on civilian response.

NATO conducts a Cold Response military exercise in Norway on March 12, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images

For Tiilikainen, EU efforts to coordinate responses to hybrid attacks are useful — within limits. However, she noted they are “not comparable with resilience measures at a national level,” such as Finland’s “comprehensive security” approach.

Lungescu also stressed that Moscow makes no distinction between the two organizations. “Frankly, [Russian President Vladimir] Putin doesn’t care whether decisions are taken by Coreper 2 or the NAC,” she added, referring to the meetings of EU ambassadors or NATO’s decision-making body. “This is not how Moscow thinks.”

Victor Jack contributed reporting.

World.title: Latvia moves to expel Russian journalist who used to work for BBC
World.content:
In recent days, Ragozin said Russia is compelled to respond to assumed Western provocation with “brute force” on a podcast hosted by Aaron Maté of the Grayzone, a U.S.-based news outlet that is skeptical of Western support for Ukraine.

“They always consider themselves as the underdogs and as the side that is being under constant pressure from the West, encroaching on its sphere of influence, on its strategic interests. It compels them to respond to hybrid actions, to clandestine actions, to sort of invisible actions that change the landscape in the former Soviet Union,” added Ragozin, in remarks that stirred fury in Latvia.

As Russian forces maintain their assault on Ukraine, the Baltic nations — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — are looking at Moscow uneasily, as the Kremlin’s belligerence looms over eastern Europe.

Writing on X, Latvian Minister of the Interior Jānis Dombrava accused Ragozin of serving “Russian interests,” and said a situation where he remains living freely in Latvia is untenable. “Persona non grata is precisely the instrument intended for that purpose. The process has been initiated. Let’s await a swift result!”

The Baltic countries have repeatedly pressed Europe to take a tougher stance against Russia, and Latvia last month was the lone EU holdout against lifting sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov.

Ragozin did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

World.title: Read the charter for the White House’s ‘Super Intelligence Force’
World.content:
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who will lead the new force, during his confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington on July 15, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images

The new group has broad authority to determine how the government should protect against artificial intelligence threats.

The Trump administration has given its newly created “Super Intelligence Force” broad authority to determine how the tech industry and the federal government should address threats to national security and civil liberties posed by fast-evolving artificial intelligence technology, according to a charter obtained by POLITICO.

Three people familiar with discussions about the task force confirmed the document’s authenticity. The people were granted anonymity to share details that are not yet public.

The task force will identify “measures to improve the preparedness and response capability of both the government and the private sector to threats to the homeland and the American people,” the charter states. It will also produce a report on the risks of AI, focusing on “potential threats to civil liberties,” cybersecurity, standards for advanced models, and the impacts of possible overregulation.

World.title: Greens promise ‘campaign mode’ and continuity under new leaders
World.content:
But she also made clear that renewal would not mean a fundamental change of political course.

“Obviously it’s a renewed leadership,” Reintke said. “But we are also going to continue the line on engaging and fighting in this house for everything that we can achieve in the next two and a half years.”

Ștefănuță, meanwhile, presented the new leadership as an attempt to broaden the Greens’ appeal beyond their traditional environmental agenda, pointing to younger voters and bread-and-butter economic concerns.

He said the group had chosen to “invest in dynamism” and a leadership that takes seriously concerns such as “the fact that the cost of living is very high” and problems with energy prices and economic stability.

The pitch is a delicate balancing act: present a sense of renewal ahead of the 2029 European election without abandoning a long-held strategy.

Reintke has led the Greens/EFA group since 2022. Ștefănuță has risen rapidly through its ranks since moving from Renew Europe in March 2023. Nine months later, the group elected him as one of its vice-presidents. He went on to become a vice-president of the European Parliament in July 2024.

World.title: The EU shelved AI liability rules. Sam Altman has revived the debate.
World.content:
The proposal by the European Commission for an AI liability law was killed amid a deep effort in Brussels to deregulate and reduce the legislative burden on companies — with the Commission arguing at the time that the proposal had little chance of securing sufficient political support.

German conservative lawmaker Axel Voss, who led on the proposal for the European Parliament, wants Brussels to put liability back on the agenda in light of Altman’s comments.

“I welcome this overdue moment of honesty. For years, the tech industry has argued that liability would stifle innovation,” he said. "Now even the CEO of OpenAI admits: Without liability, there is no trust.”

The law, first proposed in 2022, “would have closed exactly the gap Altman is now describing: responsibility before deployment, during training and testing,” Voss said.

One way governments could reduce AI risks is to apply product liability law, assigning responsibility (and penalties) to the makers of the most advanced AI models to nudge their development toward a safety-first approach.

As concerns over the pace of frontier AI development and the harm caused make the question of liability impossible to ignore — and as proposals for AI liability rules gain support around the world — proponents say the EU’s decision to scrap the proposal hasn't aged well.
