World.title: Spat over Israeli flag removal engulfs the European Parliament on October 7 anniversary
World.content:
As an aside, be wary of the germs floating around Brussels. Although it’s not pestilence per se, my doctor said it is nasty, and has even struck down at least one senior European Commission spokesperson.

 

Tensions high: On the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks on Israel – in which Hamas killed around 1200 people and took 251 hostage, triggering an Israeli offensive in Gaza which has killed over 70,000 Palestinians – the European Parliament has become the scene of a fresh political clash.

Israeli flag removed: On Monday evening, Rima Hassan, a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) from the far-left France Unbowed party, reportedly knocked over an Israeli flag displayed at an exhibition dedicated to victims of the attack. Photos on social media show both the Israeli and EU flags lying on the floor.

‘Intimidation’: The Parliament’s President, Roberta Metsola, told the chamber yesterday that she took the incident “extremely seriously” and that all appropriate measures were being taken against Hassan, without naming her. “We cannot have actions that could make people fearful of speaking. We cannot have damage to property. And we cannot have attempts to intimidate rather than to debate,” Metsola said.

Hassan has acknowledged removing the Israeli flag but denied intentionally toppling the EU flag, with her office noting in a statement that neither flag was “stepped on or damaged”.

She has also framed her actions as a response to the Israeli state’s support for the exhibition, and claimed that speeches made during the event denied the existence of Palestine.

Outrage: The incident has sparked widespread outrage, with centre-right MEP François-Xavier Bellamy describing the act as a “form of complicity with those who want to reintroduce antisemitic hatred” in Europe. Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has also described the scenes as “shameful, outrageous, but sadly not surprising”.

‘Disrespectful’: “I cannot understand how a person that aims to be a politician, that aims to represent the public, can be so violent and disrespectful of the death of thousands of people that has been caused by the same cause that she's trying to help,” the Israeli ambassador to France, Joshua Zarka, told our chief editor Maria Tadeo in an interview.

He also claimed that the French people were “tired of her (Hassan’s) behaviour, of what she represents, of her attempt to import the Israeli conflict into France”. Hassan is currently awaiting trial over allegations she promoted terrorism in a post on X referring to a Japanese man responsible for a terror attack in Israel in the 1970s.

Antisemitism in France in the spotlight: Historical allegations of antisemitism within the far-right National Rally have also resurfaced in recent days ahead of a highly anticipated presidential election next year, after media outlet Mediapart published antisemitic messages reportedly attributed to the party’s Jordan Bardella. Bardella denies making the statements.

‘Only one anti-Semitic party in France’: Ambassador Zarka told Maria that Israel is following the allegations against Bardella closely and “will react (...) once it is clear that these allegations are true”. But he added that there is “one party that is openly antisemitic in France, and that’s LFI (France Unbowed)”. Watch.

D-Day: Meanwhile, Europe’s eastern flank continues to be rattled by hybrid warfare. But a fatal drone incursion off Romania’s coast on Monday, which killed two and injured scores more, begs the question whether these incidents continue to be “hybrid” – and who is to blame, Angela Skujins writes.

Another incident occurred on Tuesday 130 kilometres off Bulgaria’s coast, with drones sinking one commercial ship and the other catching fire. Crews were evacuated from the scene.

‘Absolutely unacceptable’: The country’s prime minister, Ruman Radev, didn’t mince words when decrying the incident, blasting it as an “absolutely unacceptable attack” and a “flagrant violation of international law and maritime norms”. He stopped short, however, of attributing blame.

Blame hasn’t been attributed to the Romanian incursion, either. But Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Monday’s “horrific strike” was carried out by the Kremlin on a civilian vessel in neutral waters.

Trifecta: A Turkish-owned vessel was damaged in the Romanian incursion, meaning a trio of North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) members were impacted by the spate of recent incidents. A press officer from the Alliance referred Angela to the Bulgarian authorities when pressed for a response.

Health alert: Meanwhile, Jorge Liboreiro reports that representatives from the European Commission and member states will today discuss the suspected outbreak of pneumonic plague in Siberia, Russia, as national authorities scramble to get a clear picture of the situation.

A meeting of the Health Security Committee, which evaluates serious cross-border health threats, was already scheduled for this morning. But the latest developments have brought a new item to the agenda.

Russia has denied that the lab worker in Siberia died from the plague, but circumstances remain murky. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said the suspicion of a plague outbreak was “not yet confirmed”.

“There is little travel between Irkutsk and the EU, particularly at present due to Russia's war against Ukraine,” the agency said in a statement. “Based on the limited information currently available, there are no reports of secondary cases or sustained human-to-human transmission.”

For those feeling anxious, our colleague Marta Iraola answers all your burning questions about pneumonic plague.

Almost there: EU ambassadors will today seek to finalise a list of over 1,600 people and companies accused of supporting Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The political talks have proceeded well, and the legal work is completed. The goal is to have a formal agreement next Monday when foreign ministers meet.

If approved, it will be the largest single expansion of the sanctions list, which currently covers almost 3,000 names. Brussels is keen to portray resolve and unity after the bruising saga last month that resulted in two high-profile oligarchs being removed from the sanctions list.

EU-China trade tensions: Five things to know as Brussels and Beijing face crunch talks

After months of tensions, relations between Brussels and Beijing are entering a crucial phase, with the European Commission having set October as a deadline to secure "tangible” results with Beijing to rebalance their trading relationship.

Talks will take place in Beijing at the end of this week between EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao. They will be followed by a meeting of EU leaders next week, with China set to top the agenda.

For European policymakers, the diagnosis is increasingly clear: the situation is unsustainable, with a new wave of Chinese competition putting pressure on the EU’s industrial base two decades after China’s rapid economic expansion began — and putting thousands of jobs at risk.

Euronews’ Peggy Corlin breaks down the five things you need to know ahead of the talks.

More from our newsrooms

Ex-German intelligence chief arrested over suspected espionage. Former German intelligence chief August Hanning is accused of obtaining classified information from a former employee of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) and using it in connection with his private consultancy work, with investigators reportedly examining whether information was passed to foreign powers. Patrick Drews and Sonja Issel have the details.

France's sovereign debt crisis explained: How dangerous could it be? French borrowing costs have hit their highest level since 2002, and the gap with Germany is the widest since 2011. Piero Cingari breaks down what’s driving France's debt crisis and how dangerous it could be.

Von der Leyen turns to Europe’s refineries as shrinking capacity raises energy security concerns. Europe wants to reduce its dependence on fossil fuels, but while it still relies heavily on oil — particularly diesel — reducing the infrastructure that processes that oil has increased vulnerability during the green transition. Marta Pacheco explores Europe’s energy crunch.

We're also keeping an eye on

The European Parliament’s plenary session continues in Strasbourg. MEPs debate the EU’s multi-annual budget in the morning and the influence of the Muslim Brotherhood network in the EU in the afternoon.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen attends the Summit of Southern European Union countries (MED-9) in Split, Croatia.

European Commissioner for Trade Maroš Šefčovič travels to Beijing to hold two days of trade talks with his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao.

The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas visits Lebanon.

European Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen meets French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu in Paris, France.

That’s it for today. Angela Skujins, Vincenzo Genovese, Jorge Liboreiro and Peggy Corlin contributed to this newsletter.

World.title: The EU agrees on new Return Order, longer detention and return hubs
World.content:
EU interior ministers met in Luxembourg on October 1, and agreed on stricter rules for returning migrants, shifting the bloc’s migration policy focus from paperwork to enforcement.

 

During the Home Affairs Council, ministers decided that people without the right to stay must leave and cooperate with authorities. If they do not, they could face sanctions such as reduced benefits, fines, or criminal charges.

A new European Return Order would let countries choose to recognise each other’s return decisions, with a review planned after three years. For security risks, countries could impose indefinite entry bans and detention longer than 24 months. Return hubs outside the EU are also allowed. These rules exclude unaccompanied minors and will take effect in the coming weeks.

The push follows a Munich meeting on 26 September where Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner said irregular arrivals dropped by 55% over two years. However, the number of people actually returned remains low. In 2025, the EU ordered nearly 492,000 people to leave, but only 135,000 did.

Greece’s migration minister, Thanos Plevris, said the first return hub could open in the second half of 2027 in an unspecified African country. The UN human rights office warned that the law lacks clear rules for monitoring, appeals, or conditions in host countries.

World.title: Christa Pike awake a week after lethal injection as her lawyers seek answers
World.content:
A US death row inmate who survived an attempt to execute her by lethal injection is conscious and speaking, her lawyers have said, as they go to court to find out what went wrong.

 

Christa Pike, 50, was given two doses of the drug pentobarbital at a Tennessee prison on 30 September. She is believed to be the only person to survive after lethal injection drugs were administered.

"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," her attorneys said on Tuesday.

"Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed," they said. "Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery."

Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, committed when she was 18. She would have been the first woman executed by Tennessee in more than 200 years.

Her lawyers are due in court in Nashville on Wednesday, seeking an order requiring the prison system to preserve evidence including drug lot numbers, needles and execution logs.

The Tennessee attorney general's office said the order was unnecessary because the prison system is "obliged to maintain this evidence in other cases and must assure it is preserved".

Experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream. A court filing said both Pike's arms were "swollen, burned, and blistered" when she arrived at hospital.

Governor Bill Lee called what happened "deeply disturbing" and ordered a "comprehensive, third-party review". He has suspended executions in the state pending the investigation, and the prison chief has resigned.

Pike's lawyers have again called on Lee to commute her sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

World.title: Invasive plant spreads across Portugal and lengthens allergy season
World.content:
For decades, pampas grass, also known as Cortaderia selloana, was seen mainly as an ornamental plant. Its large feathery plumes made it a familiar sight in gardens and, more recently, in decorative arrangements indoors. But what many still regard as a showy plant is, in Portugal, an invasive alien species that can spread rapidly and has potential consequences for health.

 

This invasive plant has already been identified in at least 208 municipalities in mainland Portugal, according to a study published in 2025 (source in Portuguese). The real number may, however, be higher, as existing maps depend on records submitted by people on the ground.

The species’ spread is particularly visible along the coast. Areas where there used to be isolated specimens have been turning into zones densely occupied by the species, according to biologist Hélia Marchante, a lecturer at the School of Agriculture of the Polytechnic University of Coimbra and a specialist in invasive plants.

"It is a very, very fast-spreading species", she told Euronews. Unlike other invasive plants that can benefit from specific triggers such as wildfires, the plant also known as cortaderia has an especially effective advantage for spreading: "It only needs the wind."

A plant that has learnt to escape the garden

The history of the invasion helps explain how serious the problem has now become. Native to South America, cortaderia was introduced in different parts of the world as an ornamental plant. For decades, the fact that only female plants were present in gardens is thought to have limited its ability to reproduce.

According to Marchante, that changed at the end of the last century, when hermaphrodite plants were introduced, 'almost certainly by accident', as "pollen donors". Fertilisation of the female plants then allowed the production of large quantities of seed.

"From then on it only needs the wind," the researcher said.

The process repeats itself every year. During flowering, the plants that produce pollen release it into the atmosphere. In female plants, once fertilisation has taken place, each flower can give rise to a seed. The plumes end up acting as a kind of transport system: thousands of tiny seeds can be carried by the wind and colonise new sites.

Spread does not depend solely on natural phenomena, however. People who move the plumes to use them as decoration, as well as vehicles, clothing or equipment, can also inadvertently help to carry seeds to other places.

"It is the movement of the plant itself that has the potential to spread it", warns Marchante, also pointing to cases where plumes are taken indoors.

Biologist Hélia Marchante during a training session with teams from different municipal departments in Condeixa Espécies Invasoras em Portugal/Facebook

Pampas grass is no longer just an ornamental feature of the landscape. It is also an invasive species capable of altering the ecosystems where it becomes established. Once the species moves from isolated specimens to large stands, it becomes dense enough to exclude other plants, which can no longer survive in those areas.

The impact extends to fauna as well, since the plant’s sharp leaves and the high density of the stands can make it harder for animals to move through.

There are also less visible effects. According to Marchante, some studies show that the species can also alter nutrient cycles and modify the soil and the microorganisms that live in it.

The problem goes beyond the environment

The environmental dimension of the invasion is only part of the story. Cortaderia also has consequences for human health.

Mário Morais de Almeida, an immunoallergology specialist and president of the World Allergy Organisation, explains that pampas grass belongs to the grass family and therefore releases pollen that can trigger symptoms in sensitised people.

"As this is a grass species, it will indeed release its pollen into the atmosphere, again carried by the wind, and it can cause significant allergic symptoms."

The problem is particularly serious because of the time of year when cortaderia flowers. The grasses most familiar to Portuguese people are prominent in spring and early summer. Cortaderia can extend that exposure into late summer and autumn.

For people with allergic rhinitis or conjunctivitis, exposure can lead to sneezing, itching, runny nose, congestion, red and watery eyes. In those with asthma, exposure can contribute to respiratory symptoms and more severe attacks.

"This grass, which can indeed release very, very large amounts of pollen, manages to do so throughout the summer, and even into autumn," says Morais de Almeida.

However, the doctor stresses that there is currently no specific epidemiological evidence that would allow a given number of allergy cases in Portugal to be attributed to pampas grass. What exists is knowledge about grass allergies, clinical experience and evidence of the allergenic capacity of this species’ pollen.

"At the moment we do not have evidence that is directly linked to pampas grass," he notes, adding that there is nonetheless a perception that allergic complaints are lasting longer. According to the specialist, the combination of climate change, different types of pollen and other agents present in the atmosphere makes the picture more complex.

Because the seeds are carried by the wind, the impact is not necessarily confined to the immediate vicinity of the plant. Marchante explains that the seeds can travel several kilometres, especially in conditions of strong wind, while the pollen can also be transported over long distances.

There is another issue: people can unwittingly help to move the pollen around.

"People pick the plumes because they are very beautiful, they paint them, they take them home," the biologist explains. In addition to contributing to the spread of seeds, that behaviour can bring potentially allergenic material into homes.

Morais de Almeida therefore offers an important piece of advice: do not take the plumes home and avoid handling the plant. On top of its allergenic potential, the leaves themselves are sharp enough to cause injuries.

"The pleasant appearance the plant may have" should not make people forget the risks associated with exposure to it, the doctor warns.

The danger of letting another year pass

For Marchante, one of the main challenges is precisely time. The more a plant grows and produces seed, the greater the likelihood that new individuals will emerge nearby and that the invaded area will expand.

"Each one that is left on its own in a more isolated area is another that will produce thousands of seeds, which will germinate and give rise to new plants next year," she explains, stressing that "if we fail to act now, next year it will be much, much more difficult, much more expensive and much worse to intervene".

The strategy does not necessarily have to focus on trying to eliminate all the large stands that are already established in one go. The biologist argues for the identification and priority removal of isolated specimens and small clusters on the edges of the areas currently occupied. The aim is to prevent these hotspots from acting as new starting points for invasion of fresh territory.

In some of the areas where the species has been established for longer, complete eradication will be much more difficult, if not practically impossible, the specialist believes. The alternative is control and ongoing intervention.

"What I think is that we still have a huge amount of work we can do, because there are so many places with small nuclei of individual plants," she says.

The timing of intervention is equally important. Removing only the plumes after the seeds have already been shed can mean working without preventing the spread that has already occurred.

"To be sure of eliminating this plant, there has to be a window of time before May; it is during that period that it should be pulled out," she explains.

And she has a clear message: "In fact, I say pull it up, pull it up by the roots, pull everything up, always pull it up; that is what we want."

However, during the period when the seeds are being released, any intervention must be carried out in such a way as to avoid the control measures themselves contributing to their dispersal.

Prohibited species still widespread

Cortaderia has been on the Portuguese national list of invasive species (source in Portuguese) since 2019. The legislation bans, among other actions, its possession, planting, sale and introduction into the wild.

In practice, however, it can still be found in private gardens, municipal spaces, industrial areas, roadsides and other locations.

Marchante points to a lack of awareness of the law and a lack of enforcement as some of the obstacles to controlling the species.

There is also a coordination problem. A municipality may remove plants from a garden under its management, only to find specimens in private plots or in infrastructure managed by other bodies.

The invasion also has a socioeconomic dimension, as the presence of large cortaderia plants makes vegetation management more difficult and more expensive, particularly in areas where vegetation has to be cleared for wildfire prevention.

There are already projects such as LIFE COOP Cortaderia (source in Portuguese), which brings together institutions in Portugal, Spain and France to fight this invasive species, and municipalities involved in control measures, but the researcher calls for a coordinated strategy.

The Institute for Nature Conservation and Forests (ICNF) has drawn up a proposal for a National Action Plan for the Control of Cortaderia under Decree-Law No. 92/2019 (source in Portuguese), although its official publication and implementation have been delayed.

The biologist hopes that the forthcoming National Action Plan against invasive alien species will set out priorities, responsibilities and ways of intervening.

To make those measures effective, she argues that the plan should be accompanied by funding mechanisms enabling municipalities, non-governmental organisations, parish councils, road management bodies and even private citizens to cover the costs of removal.

"To remove one of the big cortaderia plants, you often need a mini excavator," she notes, stressing that the size of some specimens makes control operations costly, and not everyone can afford them.

What can you do if you come across cortaderia?

For citizens, the first recommendation is not to plant or move the species. Anyone who has cortaderia in their garden should seek to remove it, ideally with technical support if it is a large specimen.

People who spot specimens in public spaces can also help to build knowledge about the species’ distribution. Hélia Marchante recommends using the iNaturalist (source in Portuguese) platform, where it is possible to photograph a plant and record its location. These data help build maps that can then be used to set priorities for action.

"That is very important when strategies are being drawn up to eliminate it," she stresses.

While the plant has not yet been removed, cutting the plumes before the seeds are released can help to curb dispersal. But that is only a temporary measure. "Removing the plumes does not solve the problem," the biologist stresses. "The aim must always be to remove the whole plant."

For people with respiratory allergies, Morais de Almeida also advises reducing exposure during periods of higher pollen concentration. In certain circumstances, wearing a mask and eye protection may be useful, along with sticking to medication prescribed for diagnosed allergic disease.

"We know that early in the morning and later in the afternoon are the times when pollen levels are highest, so at those times we should avoid airing or ventilating our homes; otherwise we may be contaminating the indoor environment. If we are travelling by car, we should probably keep the windows closed; if we are on a motorbike, we should opt for a full-face helmet and wear goggles," the immunoallergology specialist recommends.

The doctor also draws attention to specific weather conditions. During storms, humidity can contribute to the fragmentation of pollen grains, making them easier to inhale, which can worsen respiratory symptoms in sensitised individuals.

World.title: How Verifactu will affect Spanish SMEs and self-employed after its delay
World.content:
The Spanish government has postponed until 2027 (source in Spanish), and later to 2028, the entry into force of Verifactu, the electronic invoicing system designed to strengthen tax control over companies and self-employed workers. The move pushes back by one year the original timetable, which had set its implementation for 2026 (source in Spanish).

 

Under the new calendar, companies subject to Corporation Tax will have to adapt from 2028, while the self-employed and SMEs will have until 1 July of that same year.

The system requires invoices to be issued using certified software that guarantees the authenticity, integrity and traceability of records, as part of the fight against tax fraud.

More time, but also uncertainty

The postponement gives more time to adapt IT programmes and internal processes, reducing the immediate pressure on millions of small businesses.

However, different voices in the sector point out that the delay has also created confusion because of the lack of clarity about technical requirements and the final implementation deadlines.

These doubts are compounded by warnings from organisations representing the self-employed and from the business community itself. The National Federation of Associations of Self-Employed Workers (ATA) had for weeks been calling for an extension (source in Spanish), citing adaptation difficulties and a lack of clear information.

Even so, the union representing technicians at the Ministry of Finance, Gestha (source in Spanish), believes the extension is a "key tool" that could be "useful" for millions of taxpayers.

A structural change still to come

Despite the extension, Verifactu remains a structural change in Spain's tax system that will affect most of the business sector. The rules, promoted by the Tax Agency, form part of measures to digitise the economy and strengthen fiscal transparency, with possible sanctions for non-compliance once they come into force.

According to Eurostat data, only 58% of small and medium-sized enterprises in the EU have reached a basic level of digital services, well below the 90% target set for 2030. The gap is even wider compared with large companies, where the level of digitalisation reaches 91%, highlighting the specific difficulties SMEs face in adapting to technological and regulatory change.

In the case of Spain, the figures show progress but also limits to business digitalisation. According to a survey (source in Spanish) by the National Statistics Institute (INE), 44.3% of companies use cloud computing services and 21.1% use artificial intelligence, while 84.5% have a website.

However, the level of adoption of more advanced technologies remains uneven, especially among small companies.

Moreover, various official indicators place Spanish SMEs in an intermediate position within the EU: around 60% reach a basic level of digitalisation, in line with the European average, but still far from the goals set by Brussels for this decade.

World.title: Israel marks third anniversary of October 7 Hamas terror attacks with memorials
World.content:
Families gathered at the Nova music festival site and other attack locations in memory of those killed by Hamas on October 7, 2023.

Israel is marking the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas terrorist attack on Wednesday with memorials across the country.

At the site of the Nova music festival, where more than 300 people were killed, families gathered at dawn for a moment of silence and paid tribute in front of portraits both of festival-goers and security forces who died on October 7.

At the Kfar Aza kibbutz, another attack site, mourners watched in silence the raising of an Israeli flag.

Others are expected to gather at intersections and bomb shelters to mark one of the deadliest attacks against Israel, which killed more than 1,200 people in Israel and saw 251 others taken hostage.

The last living hostages were released a year ago under a US-brokered ceasefire deal.

On October 7, 2023, Hamas fighters breached the border, storming southern Israel with gunfire, rockets and grenades Image: Ronen Zvulun/REUTERS

The anniversary of the attacks also comes just ahead of the October 27 elections in Israel.

Germany stands firmly by Israel's side, says Merz

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday reaffirmed Germany's support for Israel on the anniversary, saying the country stood firmly by Israel's side and was committed to preventing a repeat of the October 7 attack.

"We stand for the security and existence of Israel," the German chancellor said.

The Israeli government’s official memorial services took place on October 5, closer to the Hebrew-calendar anniversary of the attack Image: Amir Cohen/REUTERS

Merz also called for a political settlement saying for peace and security in the region "can best be achieved through the establishment of a Palestinian state alongside Israel."

Warning of rising antisemitism in Germany, Merz said his government would "do everything in its power to consistently combat anti-Semitism in all its new and old forms."

Two dead in Gaza in Israeli strikes

New Israeli strikes in Gaza on Wednesday killed two people, Palestinian officials reported.

One of those killed was identified as a volunteer with the emergency rescue agency under Hamas. The European Union, as well as the United States, Germany, and other countries, classify Hamas as a terrorist organization.

Israel's war in Gaza following the October 7 attacks has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the territory's Health Ministry, around half of them women and children, and displaced most of the population.

World.title: Yemen’s Houthis claim strikes on Aden, Riyadh airports
World.content:
Yemen's Houthi rebels attacked Aden International Airport on Wednesday morning. According to the Yemeni Ministry of Transport, they used ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones.

Aden International Airport is Yemen's main international gateway outside Houthi control.

The missile reportedly landed near the airport runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, forcing it to divert to Jeddah. Two planes on the runway were moved away from the area for fear of further attacks, the Transport Ministry said.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had also attacked King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones. There was no immediate confirmation of an attack on the Saudi airport.

Another Houthi ballistic missile was intercepted and destroyed north of Riyadh by the Saudi-led coalition, which said it had tracked the launch to a site in Houthi-controlled Sanaa.

The attacks came as fighting intensified on several fronts in Yemen. Saudi-backed government forces have launched a counteroffensive against the Houthi as the Yemeni insurgent group has made territorial gains along the Red Sea coast in recent weeks.

Bid for the Red Sea

Government forces, backed by air support from the Saudi-led coalition, launched a lightning offensive to retake territory along the Red Sea coast. The operation succeeded in driving the Houthis out of areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the city of Mocha, which they had seized last month.

In a separate statement, Saree said the Houthis had targeted Abha International Airport and an air base in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones. It was not immediately clear whether this was related to the missile the coalition said it intercepted near Khamis Mushait. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha International Airport.

Houthis launch airport attacks Image: Saleh Al-Obeidi/AFP

Edited by: Elizabeth Schumacher

World.title: Germany news: Government presents plan for railroad revamp
World.content:
A new plan sets out a roadmap for development of Germany's railroad system Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

The German Transport Ministry has presented a five-year "Infraplan" setting out goals for the improvement of the derelict railroad system.

Transport undersecretary Ulrich Lange said the plan was to be the central compass for the goverment.

"We specify the direction, set priorities and monitor the progress of the implementation," he said as he handed the plan to Philipp Nagl, the chairman of railway operator Deutsche Bahn's infrastructure division, DB InfraGO.

The 160-page plan, which is to be revised each year, covers the period from 2026 to 2030.

The planned renovation measures include repairs, digitization and electrification of routes, reconstruction of stations, noise control and the extension or new construction of lines.

The plan sets out a performance indicator system to make possible a transparent evaluation of the developments in the railroad infrastructure.

There are eight indicators with mandatory targets, such as how many kilometers (miles) of new tracks are laid per year, how many kilometers have been electrified and how many minutes delay are caused by infrastructure defects.

One of the targets set out in the plan is to build 155 kilometers (96 miles) of new track by 2030.

The plan does not, however, contain provisions for financing the railroad renovations, which currently depend on the government budget.

The Transport Ministry is working on a law on a railroad fund that secures financing for several years.

As an example of the problems currently facing train passengers, in September, nearly every second long-distance train was delayed.

World.title: India news: Opposition protest clouds Modi's 25-year milestone
World.content:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) raised the the key benchmark policy rate, for the first time in over three years, as it looked to control rising inflation amid the US-led war on Iran.

The repo rate, which guides the short-term lending rate for commercial banks, was raised by 25 basis points to 5.5%. The rate hike will make home loans, vehicle loans and corporate loans more expensive for borrowers. Even equated monthly installments would go up for existing borrowers.

With this, the RBI has shifted gears to join several central banks around the world looking to curb rising prices or boost their currencies. It has changed its stance to a "calibrated tightening," the report said.

Prices of basic food items in India have risen sharply over the Middle East crisis Image: Diptendu Dutta/NurPhoto/picture alliance

"Driven by escalating energy costs and rising food prices, global inflation is projected to increase sharply prompting monetary policy tightening by major central Banks," RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra said in his opening remarks while announcing the rake hike.

He attributed the inflationary pressures to the "reescalation of the West Asia conflict in September and consequent hardening and volatility in global crude prices."

"Further tightening of global financial conditions, uncertainty about fair valuation of AI stocks, and an elusive resolution of the West Asia conflict pose significant downside risks to the global economic outlook," Malhotra said.

Nonetheless, the RBI governor said he expects India's "strong" economy to "remain resilient."

Apart from rising prices, the RBI's calculations likely involve the state of the Indian rupee which has been near record lows over the past week.

The central bank has rolled out a number of measures to attract dollar inflows to counter the rupee's fall but pressures from global investment outflows and crude prices persist.

World.title: Where is Spain headed after the snap election announcement?
World.content:
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is taking a gamble by calling an early election in Spain. The housing crisis, migration and the rise of the right-wing populist Vox party are all likely to dominate the campaign.

Spain's economic data has been positive recently, but politically, the country has been mired in a prolonged crisis for months.

On Monday, the social democratic Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez responded with a surprise move to break the deadlock: He is calling an early election for November 29.

Why is Sanchez calling an election now?

The sudden announcement followed a dramatic political defeat for the government. On Friday, October 2, Sanchez's emergency measures to tackle the housing crisis failed in parliament. Seven lawmakers from the conservative Catalan separatist party Junts, whose support the government has relied on since 2023, brought the measures down. Sanchez says he is now calling for a "much broader progressive majority."

Set to profit from the snap election: Vox leader Santiago Abascal Image: Gabriela Sardá Núñez/Europa Press/IMAGO

The defeat came after months of growing instability in the government's parliamentary base. Spain's parliament has not passed a regular budget since 2023.

The recent crisis over mass migration to Ceuta and several corruption scandals involving allegations against the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) and people close to Sanchez have piled pressure onto the government.

And then came Maricarmen. The forced eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal last month suddenly turned the housing shortage into the headline political issue.

The fact that his emergency measures were rejected in parliament allows Sanchez to position himself as a defender of tenants. However, it remains to be seen whether that strategy will pay off.

What role is pressure from the street protests playing?

The housing shortage has been at the top of Spaniards' list of concerns for around three years. According to estimates by the Bank of Spain, the country is currently short of around 750,000 homes, and the figure could exceed one million by 2028.

More than half of 18- to 34-year-olds live with their parents or depend on them financially. Property prices have recently been rising three times as fast as wages. In Spain, social housing accounts for just around 1.7 percent of the country's housing stock, putting it at the lower end of the EU scale in comparison with other member states.

Housing crisis triggers snap election in Spain To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

It is hardly surprising, then, that protest camps sprang up in Madrid and elsewhere in response to the plight of Maricarmen Abascal, and tens of thousands took to the streets across the country. After the government's measures were rejected, the trade unions CCOO and UGT even announced a 24-hour general strike.

These dividing lines, however, do not simply split the government and the opposition. The tenants' movement also views Sanchez's plans as insufficient. The conservative opposition People's Party (PP) and parts of the business community, meanwhile, warn that tighter rent controls could make the problem worse.

Is Sanchez's model of governance coming to an end?

Since the 2023 election, Pedro Sanchez has governed without a majority in parliament. His social democratic PSOE formed a coalition with the left-wing Sumar alliance, but also depended on the support of smaller parties. These included Basque and Catalan regional parties, but above all the Catalan separatists of Junts.

That meant its seven lawmakers were repeatedly able to determine whether government legislation secured a majority or not. Over the course of the parliamentary term, this arrangement became increasingly unstable. In the first half of 2026 alone, the government lost almost one in four votes.

For three years, the government has failed to get a budget through parliament Image: Elisabetta Trevisan/Vatican Media/Handout/REUTERS

Evidence of the extent of this political deadlock is the state budget: Spain continues to work with the 2023 budget because the prime minister has been unable to get a new budget through parliament in his entire term. Junts ultimately refused to support Sanchez on housing policy, leaving him without backing on an issue that has been at the top of the political agenda following nationwide protests.

What was the political fallout of the Ceuta crisis?

At the end of July, more than 70,000 people crossed the border from Morocco into Ceuta within a short period of time. Although the government declared the crisis over soon afterward, at least 10,000 migrants were still in the exclave two months later, which has a population of only around 80,000. It was not until last Sunday that police cleared an improvised camp where around 3,000 people had been living.

Spain: Tensions in aftermath of Ceuta mass migrant crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The crisis altered Sanchez's previously relatively liberal migration policy. A new draft seen by Reuters proposes accelerated asylum procedures and deportations, as well as tighter rules. Human rights organizations have voiced sharp criticism.

How strong is the opposition?

At first glance, Spain's conservative PP is entering the snap parliamentary election at the end of November as the frontrunner to become the largest parliamentary group.

The real winner of recent months, however, is the right-wing populist Vox party. It is now polling at just over 18%, around six percentage points more than in the 2023 election. A strong Vox turnout could increase PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo's chances of gathering enough seats for a governing majority from parties right of center.

The man hoping to become Spain's next prime minister: PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo Image: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/picture alliance

Vox leader Santiago Abascal is now confidently setting conditions for cooperation. Priority for Spanish citizens, economic deregulation and a significantly tougher migration policy, including the far-right concept of deporting foreign nationals to their countries of origin.

For his part, Feijoo faces a difficult balancing act. To replace Sanchez, he also needs to win voters from the political center. At the same time, he may need a partner for a governing majority who is steering the campaign significantly further to the right.

Will Spain also be voting on Trump and Europe's political direction?

In international media coverage, Sanchez is repeatedly portrayed as Europe's most prominent critic of Donald Trump. The prime minister rejected the US president's demand for defense spending to rise to 5% of GDP, refused to allow US bases in Spain to be used for the war against Iran and criticized US-Israeli attacks.

As a result, Trump even threatened at one point to cut off trade relations. At the same time, Sanchez explicitly contrasts his more liberal migration policy with Trump's deportation policies and attacks what he calls the "tech oligarchs" from the United States.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez (left) has positioned himself as a strong European voice against Donald Trump Image: Pablo Martinez Monsivais/AP Photo/picture alliance

Sanchez is also one of the most prominent social democratic leaders of a major EU country. If the left were to lose the upcoming Spanish election, the European Council would lose one of its most outspoken voices against Donald Trump . It would also lose a prime minister who has opposed climbing defense spending, defended a more liberal approach to migration and criticized Israel more sharply over the war in Gaza than most of his European counterparts.

This article originally appeared in German.

World.title: Mali: Junta forces retake strategic town of Kidal from separatists
World.content:
Mali's military regained control of the strategic town of Kidal after forcing Tuareg separatists and al Queda-linked jihadists to withdraw following an offensive backed by Russia's Africa Corps.

Mali's army, supported by Russian paramilitary forces, has re-entered the northern town of Kidal, forcing the Tuareg separatists to withdraw from the strategic hold, in a symbolic boost for the country's military government and its Russian allies.

The Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) said in a statement it had "decided to carry out a strategic and controlled withdrawal of its forces from the town of Kidal." It said the withdrawal took place without direct fighting.

This followed the "disproportionate use of aerial assets by Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps," according to an FLA spokesperson.

How did Kidal fall earlier this year?

The FLA and al-Qaeda-linked Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) seized Kidal during a series of attacks earlier this year in April that also killed Mali's defense minister.

Tuareg separatists from the Azawad Liberation Front have been fighting for years to create an independent state in northern Mali.

Mali's junta, which came to power in back-to-back coups in 2020 and 2021, has increasingly relied on Russian paramilitary support against fighters linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State.

Mali's junta in recent years distanced itself from former colonial power France and deepened military and political ties with Russia [FILE: May 9, 2026] Image: AFP

What does Kidal's recapture mean for Mali's junta?

Analysts say the latest advance is largely a symbolic victory for Mali's junta.

"A successful recapture... affirms the military-led government's authority and boosts the army's morale, particularly after several high-profile setbacks both in the north and the central regions in recent weeks," Beverly Ochieng, associate director of Control Risks, told Reuters.

Ochieng, however, added the retaking of Kidal is largely "symbolic" and not "decisive" in Mali's campaign against jihadist and separatist groups.

Human rights organizations have often accused the Malian army and Russian paramilitaries of killing civilians during military operations, with all sides also accused of committing war crimes.

World.title: Football: Lionel Messi plays final game for Argentina
World.content:
Argentinian superstar Lionel Messi bowed out of international football with one last goal for his country. For football in Argentina, and indeed across the world, it's the end of an era.

Lionel Messi made his 208th and final appearance for Argentina on Tuesday night, scoring his 126th and final international goal as the Albiceleste beat Benin 3-0 in a friendly in Buenos Aires.

In emotional scenes at a packed El Monumental stadium, Messi stepped up to convert a penalty in the 71st minute, prompting wild celebrations from teammates and fans alike.

Earlier, the 39-year-old superstar had already set up goals for teammates Nicolas Otamendi – who was also making his final appearance for the national team – and Nico Paz – the youngster who is widely tipped to inherit Messi's iconic number 10 jersey.

"It was a source of great pride for me to wear this jersey," Messi told fans in an address after the final whistle. "I can only express my gratitude... not coming back anymore will be deeply painful."

"Gracias, Leo!" read an intricate drone show in the sky above the stadium at full-time, which concluded with the drones forming a profile of Messi's face.

Messi (left) also set up a goal for Nicolas Otamendi (19), who was also making his final appearance for Argentina Image: Matias Baglietto/REUTERS

Messi: 'Proud to be Argentinian'

Widely considered the best player of all time, Messi announced his retirement from international football on August 31 – barely a month after Argentina lost 1-0 to Spain in the World Cup final.

"It was a decision which hurts and still hurts but I know it's the right time," he wrote in a statement composed just two days after the defeat in East Rutherford, USA.

"I swear that I have always given everything and that I have always fought for this shirt to make you happy and make you proud to be Argentinian through football," he said.

"Thank you, God for making me Argentinian."

Messi: following in the footsteps of Maradona

Argentina may have lost the 2026 World Cup final, but Messi's crowning moment came four years earlier when he led his nation to glory in Qatar, beating France on penalties after a spectacular final had ended 3-3.

The triumph crowned an international career which hadn't always been easy as Messi, so prolific in club football for Barcelona, struggled to live up to expectations in his home country, where fans worshipped him as the successor to the great Diego Maradona.

He announced his international retirement once before in 2016 after losing three consecutive finals with Argentina – the 2014 World Cup final vs. Germany in Brazil and the 2015 and 2016 Copa America finals, both to Chile.

But he reversed his decision and led his country to the Copa America title in 2021, ending Argentina's 28-year wait for a trophy, before finally winning the World Cup in 2022.

Messi may have retired from international football, but he still has a contract with his current club, Major League Soccer (MLS) side Inter Miami, until 2028.

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: Christa Pike awake after failed Tennessee execution: lawyers
World.content:
A death row inmate who survived a botched execution last week is conscious and talking in hospital, according to her lawyers, who want to commute her death sentence to life imprisonment without parole.

A prisoner who survived an attempt to carry out the death penalty in Tennessee, the United States, last week is conscious and speaking as she continues to receive treatment in hospital.

"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," the inmate's attorneys said in a statement on Tuesday.

"Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented."

Pike, who was sentenced to death for the beating, stabbing and murder of a classmate in 1995, survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital – which her lawyers said left her arms burned and blistered.

Christa Pike not 'free of further serious risk'

"She's still in the ICU," said Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta in neighboring Georgia, who consulted as an expert for Pike's legal team.

"She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well."

Tuesday's updates were the first indication that Pike's condition has improved since the failed execution attempt at a Nashville prison last Wednesday.

Her attorneys thanked first responders and medical staff who they said have "treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her" – as they prepare to go to court on Wednesday seeking to learn more about what went wrong with the lethal injection.

Christa Pike was sentenced to death on March 30, 1996 for her role as a teenager in the torture-murder of her 19-year-old schoolmate Image: WBIR-TV/AP Photo/picture alliance

Pike's attorneys seeking to commute sentence

The lawyers are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the attempted execution.

Ultimately, they are looking to have Pike's sentence commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

While Dr. Zivot said Pike's current state "bodes well for a good recovery," her attorneys warned that her prognosis is still "unclear" and said she faces "a long recovery."

"Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time," they said.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, which publishes data and analysis on capital punishment in the United States, Pike is the first prisoner ever to survive "after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs."
