World.title: Land sales offer only temporary relief for West Kowloon arts hub, experts warn
World.content:
Hong Kong’s West Kowloon Cultural District is betting on property development to ease its financial pressures amid a widening operating deficit, but experts have warned that land sales will only provide temporary relief and cannot replace a sustainable long-term funding model for the arts hub.

The warning comes as the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority prepares to tender a prime residential site in the first half of next year, a potentially lucrative project that property experts expect to attract interest from major developers.

Norry Lee, a senior director at property consultancy JLL, said the site’s location and potential harbour views made it attractive, particularly for larger flats targeted at wealthier buyers.

“If you are talking about larger flats, especially those with sea views, there will definitely be demand,” he said, adding that the development was likely to appeal to major developers given its scale and prime location.

World.title: Hong Kong’s first-store appeal grows as more Japanese, South Korean and Thai brands arrive
World.content:
Japanese, South Korean and Thai brands have increased their share of new entrants in Hong Kong’s retail property market by 7 percentage points to more than one-third in the first nine months of 2026, while the demand for shops from mainland Chinese brands has slipped, according to Cushman & Wakefield.

A slew of new brands helped lift the combined share of Japanese, South Korean and Thai brands to a three-year high, according to Cushman, which said it expected the trend to continue.

This year, Japanese fashion brand Cullni opened an outlet in Wan Chai, while second-hand goods retailer Ragtag took space in Hysan Place in Causeway Bay.

South Korean footwear brand Khiho entered Hong Kong through a store at K11 Musea in Tsim Sha Tsui.

World.title: Empowering a sustainable future: International Gas Union summit to be held in Hong Kong this October
World.content:
Hosted by The Hong Kong and China Gas Company Limited (Towngas), the IGU Council 2026 and the “Empowering a Sustainable Future” Summit will run in the city from 26 to 29 October. The Council meeting will bring together around 70 international delegates, whilst the flagship summit will convene approximately 500 government officials, energy business executives, academics and industry experts from around the world for a series of in-depth panel discussions.

Against a backdrop of persistent geopolitical uncertainties, global energy price trends and energy security have returned firmly to the spotlight. Taking place in Hong Kong late this month, the International Gas Union (IGU) Council 2026 and the “Empowering a Sustainable Future” Summit will offer an essential platform for cross-sector leaders to exchange perspectives on these pressing challenges.

[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]

Held on 29 October at Hopewell Hotel, the “Empowering a Sustainable Future” Summit will centre on four pivotal themes: Asia Pacific: The Engine of Global Natural Gas Market Development, China Natural Gas Market Development, Strategic Roadmaps for Asia’s Energy Evolution, and Finance as a Driver: Strengthening Support for Energy Development. The agenda covers low-carbon energy, artificial intelligence (AI) and green finance.

Distinguished keynote speakers will include Mr Tse Chin-wan, Secretary for Environment and Ecology; Ir Arthur Li Hok-yin, Deputy Director of Electrical and Mechanical Services; and Ms Li Yalan, Vice President of the IGU. Representatives from prominent energy, financial and academic institutions across various countries and regions have also been invited to take part.

The summit has secured widespread cross-sector support and sponsorship. On the day of the event, an on-site exhibition showcase will feature leading energy enterprises presenting their latest breakthrough technologies and services to attendees.

Towngas has launched Hong Kong’s first pilot modular hydrogen power generation project at a recreational venue in Sai Kung. Transporting gas through the existing network and extracting hydrogen on-site to generate electricity for EV charging, the facility will host visiting delegates for a technical tour demonstrating the practical deployment of hydrogen energy in Hong Kong. Global energy flagship event arrives in Hong Kong this October

The IGU is the world’s most influential and authoritative non-profit, member-based international organisation in the gas sector, with its membership representing more than 90% of global gas market share. As the corporate member representing Hong Kong, Towngas has long played an active role in supporting IGU initiatives, including the 29th World Gas Conference in Beijing and the Council Meeting in London last year.

Mr Peter Wong Wai-yee, Managing Director of Towngas, noted that bringing this edition of the IGU meetings to Hong Kong coincides with a pivotal moment when artificial intelligence presents both fresh opportunities and complex challenges for energy demand and applications. In response, the Hong Kong summit has specifically invited financial experts and scholars to share forward-looking perspectives on green financing and related topics.

Beyond the conference programme, Towngas will host delegates on a Victoria Harbour evening cruise to take in Hong Kong’s illuminated skyline. (Photo courtesy of Hong Kong Water Taxi) Hydrogen decarbonisation highlights Hong Kong's infrastructure strengths

During the event, host Towngas will organise technical site visits to give international delegates a firsthand look at Hong Kong’s diverse, real-world energy applications. Participants will inspect a pilot facility in Sai Kung that extracts hydrogen from the existing gas pipeline network for power generation. In addition to charging electric vehicles, the system supplies supplementary electricity and hot water through a combined heat and power (CHP) unit. Delegates will also tour a waste-to-energy project in Tseung Kwan O that converts landfill biogas into town gas. Furthermore, attendees will be treated to an evening cruise across Victoria Harbour, offering them a taste of Hong Kong’s vibrant cosmopolitan appeal whilst showcasing the city’s strengths on the global stage.

This year marks the start of the country’s 15th Five-Year Plan, which sets out a clear pathway for accelerating the green transition and advancing peak carbon and carbon neutrality targets. In tandem, the HKSAR Government has released the city’s first Five-Year Plan to align proactively with national development strategies. Convening the IGU Council meeting and Summit in Hong Kong at this juncture carries profound significance.

As host, Towngas looks forward to welcoming global industry leaders to Hong Kong to empower a sustainable future together. Through this premier international stage, Towngas seeks to showcase Hong Kong’s energy transition journey and contribute local expertise towards global energy security and high-quality, sustainable growth.

For event details and registration, please visit the official summit website: https://2026gassummit.com/en

World.title: Hong Kong approves average fee hikes of up to 4.75 per cent for non-public schools
World.content:
Hong Kong’s private, semi-private and international schools have been given the green light to raise tuition fees by an average of 4.75 per cent, 4.07 per cent and 4 per cent, respectively.

The Education Bureau said on Tuesday it had received applications from 185 schools as of August 31 to adjust tuition fees for the 2026-27 academic year.

They comprised 49 semi-private schools under the government’s Direct Subsidy Scheme (DSS), 74 private schools and 62 international ones.

World.title: Registration on both sides of border needed for Huanggang ‘joint clearance’
World.content:
Hong Kong and mainland Chinese residents will have to register with immigration authorities on both sides of the border to use automated “joint clearance” channels at the revamped Huanggang Port crossing, with around 100,000 travellers a day expected to use the control point when operations begin.

Hong Kong’s Immigration Department would deploy sufficient manpower to help passengers register at the checkpoint, assistant director Jacky Wong Ki said on Tuesday.

“The whole registration process at the automated channel is very quick, it takes a few seconds to complete,” Wong said.

The “joint clearance” model will enable passengers to complete both departure and entry clearance procedures by presenting one identity document required by their destination and passing through a three-gated automated channel.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.title: The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.content:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Your book explores how Transsion grew from the informal global phone market that emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when African and Arab traders began traveling to southern China to buy cheap knock-off — or shanzhai — handsets. What is the company’s connection to that era?

Lu Miao: Shanzhai phones were extremely common in the early 2000s. The Huaqiangbei electronics market in Shenzhen was a major hub, while Chungking Mansions in Hong Kong was an important gateway for knock-off phones going overseas.

The main buyers were small traders from Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Some scholars call them “suitcase entrepreneurs” because they would arrive with a few suitcases, buy phones, take them home, and distribute them to smaller towns.

By the time Transsion was founded in 2006, shanzhai phones had already swept through many African countries. On the one hand, they met the basic communication needs of many low-income users; on the other, they damaged the reputation of Chinese phones, which African consumers came to associate with cheapness and poor quality.

When I went to Ghana in 2019, I found that many of Transsion’s national distributors had started out-selling secondhand and shanzhai phones bought from traders in Chungking Mansions. After partnering with Transsion, they gradually became formal agents for a multinational company.

These local African distributors linked the shanzhai era to the Transsion era. The personal connections and distribution networks they had built up played a major role in helping Transsion establish itself.

There is also continuity in design. Features such as dual-SIM support and large batteries originated in the shanzhai phone ecosystem and were later adapted for African markets. Dual SIMs, for example, help users avoid costly cross-network calls in countries with patchy network coverage.

But Transsion also represented a break from that era. First, the phone business became more formalized and institutionalized. These distributors set up trading companies of their own, and their relationships with Transsion became governed by more formal contracts.

Second, Transsion did not want to make quick money and leave, as sellers had done in the shanzhai era; it wanted to build a brand and stay for the long term. That is why it invested heavily in its after-sales service network.

Shanzhai wasn’t simply about one manufacturer producing copycat phones. It was an ecosystem: factories, supply chains, designers, distributors ... Transsion grew out of that ecosystem, but also moved beyond the shanzhai model of the time.

Sixth Tone: Looking at the bigger picture, how has Africa’s digital communications sector evolved over time, and how has that affected Chinese companies like Transsion?

Lu: Take Ghana as an example. The country’s telecommunications companies were originally state-owned. But in the 1980s and 1990s, the country had to turn to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for loans to deal with ongoing economic and debt crises. One condition of these loans was structural adjustment, which meant privatizing the telecom sector.

After the reforms, one common outcome was a widening urban-rural gap. Commercial operators were reluctant to serve low-margin rural areas, where costs were high and consumer spending was low, so infrastructure such as base stations remained concentrated in cities.

The needs of rural and low-income communities were overlooked during the reforms, and after the state retreated, it did not step back in to meet those needs. That meant many people could only afford cheap Chinese shanzhai phones.

Transsion stepped into this market, offering affordable feature — or “dumb” — phones that were tailored to African users’ needs. It optimized its models for areas with sparse base-station coverage, making them better at picking up weak signals than many other phones. Electricity supply could also be unreliable in rural areas, so the long battery life of both shanzhai and Transsion phones was another important advantage.

Zhang Lin: Against this backdrop, you argue that we should understand global technology flows in terms of “technology translation” rather than “technology transfer.” What does this framework help us understand about how technology moves between countries?

Lu: I don’t really like the concept of “technology transfer” because it frames the process as one-way: advanced Western societies export technology to less-developed non-Western societies in order to help them develop. But the endpoint of development in this model is always Western modernity.

It also assumes that technology is neutral and fixed, as if transferring technology alone will solve social problems and generate economic growth. Yet many aid projects failed precisely because they transferred equipment without transferring the knowledge, skills, and institutional environment around it.

That is why I used the concept of “technology translation.” When a technology enters a new context, it is often reinterpreted, adjusted, and transformed. Examining the context and process of how technology is translated allows us to see how knowledge moves, and the politics embedded in the process.

Transsion did not simply take phones made in China and move them unchanged to Africa; its products were continually redesigned through their encounter with local markets. Chinese engineers and product managers, Ghanaian promoters, distributors, and repair workers all became “translators” in this process.

For example, Transsion’s dual- and multi-SIM functions were not simply extra hardware features; they responded to high communications costs, uneven network coverage, and users’ need to switch between operators. Cameras optimized for darker skin tones respond to the fact that imaging technologies have historically treated white skin as the default.

These features were not simply invented by an individual designer. They emerged through interactions among the company, users, distribution channels, and repair networks.

Zhang: You describe Transsion’s business strategy as “deep plowing” and contrast it with Silicon Valley’s “blitzscaling” model. How are they different?

Lu: “Blitzscaling” was a widely celebrated model in Silicon Valley from the mid-2010s onward. Popularized by (American internet entrepreneur) Reid Hoffman, it relies on large amounts of capital to expand rapidly, prioritizing speed over efficiency.

The idea is to capture the market first and then achieve winner-takes-all dominance. Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb are typical examples, as are Chinese companies such as ride-hailing firm Didi.

At its core, blitzscaling involves a deliberately inefficient use of capital. Companies sustain themselves through venture capital, and much of that money is wasted. It is a game only a small number of players can afford. Most fail; the few that survive can end up monopolizing the market.

“Deep plowing” is more commonly seen in the Global South. It is slower and depends much more on local knowledge and relationship networks. The term originally comes from agriculture, referring to a labor-intensive mode of production that requires long-term investment and continual care.

In business and technology, I use it to describe a market-driven, labor-intensive approach in which a company continuously interacts with local markets and adjusts its products and business strategies in response to feedback.

In many cases, this model is adopted out of necessity. Transsion chose to work deeply in rural markets overlooked by Western capital largely because it lacked large pools of capital and core technologies. It often had to create room for itself by understanding markets in much finer detail.

(Header image: An entrance to the Circle Market in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Courtesy of Lu Miao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.title: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.content:
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.

China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.

Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.

Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.

China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.

Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.

According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.

“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.

South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.

Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.

China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.title: When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.content:
SHANGHAI — “Great-grandma, your head seems to be a little loose,” Yu Mingrui jokes as he examines an ancestral portrait depicting nine members of a family across three generations.

The 28-year-old Shanghai restorer was commissioned to repair the Qing dynasty (1644–1911) portrait by a descendant of the family in Ningbo, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, which had been passed down through generations. Yu filmed the process and posted it on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

Amid the portrait’s cracks and damage, Yu found clean, deliberate cuts around one woman’s painted head, suggesting the section was once removed and replaced.

Yu commented that the painter might have added the faces after painting the bodies. But viewers offered their own explanations. Some hypothesized the painter had covered up a mistake and repainted the face. Others suggested that descendants of a male ancestor’s concubine had altered the portrait to replace his wife’s image.

The answer may never be known. But the mystery drew widespread attention online, with videos about the painting receiving more than 100 million views and likes across Chinese social media platforms.

On Chinese social media, independent restorers like Yu are demonstrating how damaged paintings, old books, and family records are taken apart, repaired, and preserved.

“A lot of people told me that they simply didn’t know that something damaged could actually be restored before watching my videos,” Yu told Sixth Tone.

The objects brought to independent restorers include ancestral portraits, genealogies, old books, and calligraphy passed down through families and kept in homes rather than institutions.

Often made from paper or silk, these objects are vulnerable to moisture, insects, light, and age. Even when damaged, they can retain names, images, and other details about the families that preserved them.

For restorers like Yu, the videos can also connect that work with owners who might otherwise have left such objects damaged at home. Those commissions provide restorers with work and, in some cases, allow families to recover information from records that had become too fragile or damaged to read.

Face value

When the Qing-era ancestral portrait arrived at Yu’s studio, its ink had faded, its paper had become brittle, and its edges were torn. A patchwork of old advertising flyers held it together, promoting everything from cakes to real estate.

At 3.4 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, the portrait barely fits into the worktable at the center of Yu’s roughly 40-square-meter studio in Shanghai’s rural Songjiang District.

Yu turned the makeshift repairs into another joke for his viewers. Families in China traditionally honor deceased relatives with food and other offerings. The flyers, Yu joked, had given the painted ancestors a modern assortment of their own.

“Whatever the ancestors are missing, they can just take it from behind the painting,” he said.

Repairing the portrait, however, was a more exacting process. Yu said the restoration is divided into four broad stages: washing away dust and stains, removing the backing paper and remnants of earlier repairs, patching tears and holes with paper matching the original, and retouching missing colors and lines.

Each stage depends on the painting’s condition. Even washing it requires the restorer to decide whether to use hot or cold water, whether mold and stains require chemical treatment, and how much the paper can withstand. Chemicals can remove stains quickly, but excessive treatment can damage the paper or alter the painting itself.

“The real difficulty lies in the uncertainty,” Yu said. “A restorer’s experience gives you certainty at the beginning, serving as a safety net to deal with the uncertainty that appears in the process.”

The portrait took around three months to restore. Before treatment, Yu said, face-detection software picked up only three of the nine painted faces. Afterward, when he photographed the restored portrait, the software marked all nine faces on screen. Yu charges around 10,000 yuan ($1,493) for a painting of this size and complexity.

Yu began posting restoration videos while studying Chinese antique restoration in college. After graduating in 2021, he opened his own studio. His videos often begin with an unusual detail, a question about an object’s history, or a joke designed to catch attention.

“History isn’t only made up of famous paintings or nationally protected cultural relics,” he said. “It is also made up of these seemingly insignificant objects. As I restore them, I’m also helping to pass that culture on.”

Genealogies, ancestral portraits, and other family documents offer a view of the past that differs from official histories and local gazetteers, Zhang Yi, a historian at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, told Sixth Tone. Genealogies, for example, can record more than 1,000 people, while larger volumes can include tens of thousands, sometimes with birth and death dates.

“These materials greatly enrich our understanding of the lives and personal histories of ordinary people in Chinese history,” Zhang said.

The videos have also helped Yu turn restoration into a livelihood. His online following attracts commercial sponsorships, which now account for roughly half his income, he said. Many clients bring him just one family object in need of repair, but together, those individual commissions have allowed him to build his own customer base.

Paper trail

Beijing restorer Lian Chengchun also works mainly for private owners, from collectors to families preserving books passed down through generations.

Her videos offer them a first lesson in how to handle and preserve those objects at home, and can prompt people to take a second look at old records before the stories they carry disappear.

“I see little distinction between collections held by organizations and individuals,” Lian said. “Whether a book is restored by a public institution, an independent restorer or a private collector, the goal is the same: to preserve it for future generations.”

Books kept in private hands can arrive in almost any condition. Some have been patched with tape, glue, calendars, or whatever paper was available, repairs that may hold them together temporarily but can cause further and sometimes irreversible damage.

“Others were stored in plastic bags, where trapped moisture can encourage mold and decay,” said Lian, 38, who’s spent 18 years restoring old books by hand.

Before starting such work, Lian studies a book’s age and history, along with its paper, printing style, and other materials, which can vary across periods.

“Only then can I decide how best to repair it,” she said.

Cai Yadong came across Lian’s videos just when members of his clan in Jiaozhu Village, in southern China’s Guangdong province, needed help repairing a badly damaged genealogy.

In 2023, two elderly clan members handed Cai a 111-page genealogy dating to 1920. The wider Huazhou Cai clan today numbers about 20,000 descendants across roughly 110 villages, but Jiaozhu’s own records had almost completely disappeared, leaving residents unsure how their branch fit into the family or even who its founding ancestor was.

“When I first saw it, it was barely recognizable,” Cai, secretary of the Huazhou Cai clan association, said. “The pages were mixed together. Some had been burned, and years of damage had left the book extremely fragile.”

After contacting Lian, Cai flew to Beijing to deliver it himself rather than risk shipping it. “It was simply too valuable to risk any accidents,” he said.

Restoring the genealogy took Lian nearly a year and a half. Because of the genealogy’s age and poor condition, the restoration required careful, piece-by-piece work, Lian said.

“We try to repair it in a way that preserves its original appearance, while retaining as much of the surviving text as possible,” she said.

Lian compared numerous samples before selecting restoration paper that matched the original pages in color and texture. She repaired torn fragments and holes one by one, reinforcing sections where the original characters remained legible.

“Saving each character felt like picking up the brush where the Cai ancestors had left off,” Lian said. “Each page I uncovered felt like a dialogue with people from hundreds of years ago.”

When the work was completed, the volume showed that more than 30 pages were devoted to Jiaozhu, detailing family members and major events.

One entry showed how Jiaozhu’s branch fit into the wider Huazhou Cai clan and identified its founding ancestor as Cai Wende. The restored volume also helped three other villages establish their own connections to the clan.

“If our generation does not do this, the family memory may be gone after another one or two generations,” Cai said. “Once it is lost, it will be very difficult to recover.”

Just weeks before the genealogy surfaced, Jiaozhu had held a ceremony to renovate an ancestral tomb. Villagers knew it as the tomb of their founding ancestor but no longer knew his identity. Once the book was restored, they added Cai Wende’s name to the tomb’s inscription.

Cai described the timing as uncanny. “Whenever we talk about it, we all get goosebumps,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Yu Mingrui at his studio in Shanghai, August 2026. Lü Xiao/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.title: Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.content:
Beijing Wildlife Park has turned its fight against a surge of invasive caterpillars into a public contest, offering up to 10 park tickets to visitors who collect the heaviest haul each day. From Sept. 28 to 30, participants caught an estimated 120,000 larvae weighing a combined 18.5 kilograms.

The safari-style zoo on the capital’s southern outskirts announced the event with a call for “warriors” to battle a leaf-eating pest it dubbed the “forest food monster.” Initially scheduled for two days, the contest was extended through Oct. 7 after drawing strong interest and now runs throughout the weeklong National Day holiday.

Participants first register and receive a brief lesson on identifying the pest before staff hand out disposable gloves, food containers, and chopsticks. They search the park for larvae and submit their catches by 2:50 p.m., when staff weigh them and determine the day’s rankings. The captured caterpillars are destroyed rather than fed to the park’s animals.

Prizes are awarded each day based on the total weight collected. The first-place entry receives 10 park tickets, with five for second place and two for third. Everyone who participates receives a commemorative pin, while those finishing fourth through 10th also receive a themed headband.

Competition was stiff from the opening day. A visitor surnamed Liang collected about 4,000 caterpillars weighing 596.3 grams, filling six containers but finishing second. The winning entry came from a five-person team that brought in 1,069.5 grams, while third place went to a catch weighing 391.4 grams.

“The winners were a team of five and caught nearly twice as many as I did,” Liang, a pianist who has visited the park for a decade, told Beijing Daily. “I couldn’t keep up.”

Liang said there was no particular trick to catching the caterpillars, though she found more in less crowded parts of the park and in the shade beneath taller trees. “I brought my own plastic bottles and tweezers, which I found more convenient,” she said.

The winner on the second day, Zhang Hanfang, 18, collected 1.3 kilograms with a six-person team. A taxidermist who runs a studio specializing in insect, reptile, and bird specimens, he made the two-hour drive from neighboring Hebei province with a friend’s family the day after seeing the park’s announcement. The group shares an interest in natural science.

“There’s no secret,” Zhang told Sixth Tone. “Just keep your eyes on the trees and keep at it. It was intense and thrilling. The contest also satisfied our October itch to go bug hunting.”

A video about the contest posted on the lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, known in English as RedNote, received more than 31,000 likes and 1,400 comments. One commenter described the initiative as “crowdsourced debugging,” while a related hashtag on Weibo attracted nearly 3 million views.

In recent weeks, residents across Beijing have reported seeing fall webworm caterpillars — the larvae of an invasive moth native to North America — on sidewalks, balconies, and even people’s shoulders.

The city is experiencing the peak larval period of the pest’s third generation this year, with mature larvae descending from trees in search of sheltered places to pupate and survive the winter.

Yang Zhongqi, chief scientist at the Chinese Academy of Forestry, said the species is a major invasive pest that threatens more than 300 plant species, including forest and fruit trees, flowers, and crops.

“During severe infestations, the caterpillars can strip a tree of every leaf, damaging urban greenery and hindering the tree’s growth,” Yang said. “But they do not kill the tree.”

Beijing had released nearly 700 million parasitic wasps this year before beginning the release of another 400 million on Sept. 28. Harmless to people and pets, the wasps lay their eggs inside fall webworm pupae, preventing adult moths from emerging.

Yang Sihan, head of monitoring and forecasting at the Beijing Gardening and Greening Resources Protection Center, attributed this year’s surge to a cyclical pattern of severe outbreaks, warmer winters, and frequent summer rain that disrupted spraying.

At sites monitored over five consecutive years, the survival rate of overwintering pupae rose from 65.3% in 2023 to 84.2% this year, Yang Sihan said. Heavy rain also left fewer clear days for spraying and washed away pesticides after they were applied. A single female moth can lay 300 to 600 eggs and sometimes as many as 2,000.



Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A participant tries to catch a caterpillar at Beijing Wildlife Park, September 2026. From @北京野生动物园 on Xiaohongshu)

World.title: In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday

World.content:
China’s weeklong National Day holiday began Thursday, extending a travel period that started with the Mid-Autumn Festival less than a week earlier and fueling demand for long-distance trips at home and abroad.

The Mid-Autumn Festival, traditionally an occasion for family reunions, fell on Sept. 25 this year. National Day, which marks the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, followed on Oct. 1 and began a weeklong public holiday. With only three working days between them, people who took those days off could combine the two breaks into a 13-day holiday ending Oct. 7.

Chinese airlines are expected to carry 31.19 million passengers from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7, up 3.6% from the same period last year, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China. Bookings for domestic flights covering more than 2,000 kilometers rose about 14%, according to aviation data provider Umetrip.

International flight bookings for the period were up 22.5% year on year as of Sept. 24, the CAAC said. Flights to Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, and Laos increased by about 20%, while those to Britain, Germany, and Spain rose by about 15%.

Here are snapshots from the extended holiday period across China.

World.title: Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019083/Chinese Olympic Diver’s Mother in Hot Water Over Toxic Parenting
World.content:
Chinese Olympic diving champion Zhang Jiaqi has sparked debate after starring in a popular reality show and revealing years of criticism, little emotional support, and financial control from her mother.

The debate intensified Sunday after Zhang’s mother, Xiao Yingjie, read aloud a letter telling her daughter that, despite not having “performed very well,” she still chose to “trust” and “forgive” her. Xiao had written the letter ahead of the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, where Zhang, then 17, went on to win gold in synchronized diving. Related hashtags later trended on microblogging platform Weibo, drawing tens of millions of views.

The 22-year-old from Beijing retired last year. She now studies sports training at Beijing Sport University and also works as a livestreamer. In late August, she joined the current season of “My Little One,” a reality show that follows female celebrities and their parents at home, inviting guests to provide commentary on family dynamics.

The show revealed that before Zhang retired, all of her earnings, including a prize of 810,000 yuan ($120,000) she had received as a teenager, and three bank cards were managed by her mother.

On “My Little One,” Xiao is seen repeatedly criticizing her daughter, complaining about everything from Zhang letting her cats onto the table to drinking ice water, eating snacks, and leaving the tag on her pajamas. On one occasion, she says to the show’s other guests, “Look how lazy she is.”

Xiao’s private communications to Zhang via the instant messaging platform WeChat — messages critiquing everything from her tone of voice to table manners, as well as forwarded educational videos — were also shown to viewers. Zhang largely responded with silence as they were presented. “It’s so suffocating (to watch),” one highly upvoted comment on the microblogging platform Weibo read.

The show also revealed that Xiao, despite having no other job commitments, rarely visited Zhang once she left home to attend training at age 6.

On the show, Zhang told Xiao that she often felt that her mother didn’t love her and that her parents were not what she “imagined.” She added that she “always hated” Xiao as a child and that she believed she had been raised not by her but by her diving team.

Popular social media comments labeled Xiao as “NPD,” short for narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis that has become an online shorthand in China for controlling, self-centered, or emotionally manipulative people.

One post with nearly 20,000 likes on Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, called Zhang a “survivor of criticism-based parenting,” praising her for expressing her dissatisfaction with her mother on the show and actively distancing herself from her mother’s control. Others questioned Zhang’s father for his apparent absence from the conflict.

Domestic psychologist Li Songwei, appearing as a guest on the show, described the conflict as “delayed adolescence” on Xiao’s part. In a Weibo post, Li later urged people not to vilify Xiao, saying she had since voluntarily signed up for courses on parent-child communication and apologized to her daughter for her mistakes.

“This is a typical mother who is blinded by anxiety,” Li wrote. “In fact, the reason young viewers see so many parental traits in Zhang Jiaqi’s mother that they find ‘annoying’ or even ‘infuriating’ is that they, too, are working through issues from their own adolescence. It is a path every family has to take.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Zhang Jiaqi (right) and her mother on the show “My Little One.” From Weibo)

World.title: Can I survive an action-packed day with the vivo V80 Lite – sans the power bank?
World.content:
Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by vivo and was produced by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the production of this piece.

For a self-proclaimed “Type B” person, I can be a little obsessed with Plan Bs. This is why I love a reliable power bank.

I’m fine with carrying additional weight if it means having peace of mind, especially for someone like me who’s chronically busy (or doing too many side quests). Besides, I had previously used phones that would die on me midday, which would then require me to head to the nearest cafe and pray that they have an available electrical outlet.

Recently, I learned that vivo released a new smartphone in the roster, the vivo V80 Lite, which is specifically engineered for busybodies. Its core asset? The 10,000mAh Long-Lasting BlueVolt battery with 4th-Gen Silicon Anode technology. According to vivo, this device can let you go through two days with just a single charge. I wanted to try it myself for a whole weekend and one weekday with light to moderate use – mostly for taking photos and tinkering with a few of its apps – sans the power bank, of course.

But can we talk about the look first?

For a phone that houses a massive battery capacity, it’s pretty slim to hold. I instantly got captivated by the Afterglow Pink variant, and was amazed at how the color scheme appeared so alive that I instantly likened it to a cotton candy sky. It sometimes looks like a painting, too, thanks to its “moonlight effect”. The texture is an experience in itself – it’s a mix of glossy, satin, and metallic, but not so delicate that you can feel it easily slipping from your hands, especially if you’re on the go.

It’s simply pretty that I didn’t have the urge to think of a good phone case to match it with – except the silicone case that’s included with the unit, for added protection.

Using the different zooms of the vivo V80 Lite, which easily matches my outfit

Apart from good looks, the phone was also built to have military-grade durability, especially its resistance to foreign matter or unwanted liquid. Since the vivo V80 Lite is equipped with flagship-level IP68 & IP69 dust and water resistance (depending on your chosen variant), it felt easy to use even when it suddenly rained during one of my walks to finish an errand, and I was too preoccupied to fish out my umbrella.

There was also a moment when it got so sunny while I was waiting for my ride, but the performance didn’t change. The words on my screen were also still easy to read, thanks to the 1.5-high-brightness OLED display.

Lasting power

I went to a couple of places that varied in atmosphere: a heavily air-conditioned mall, a somewhat humid garden, and restaurants that, of course, contained a lot of steam and smoke in their cooking processes, among others. Apart from testing the quality of its body, it was a great way to test the 10,000mAh Long-Lasting BlueVolt battery – the largest battery capacity vivo has offered so far.

In total, I had a packed schedule during the three days of phone testing: a two-hour gift shopping session, my cousin’s birthday party, a spa appointment, a movie date with my mother, a coffee catch-up with my friends, an almost six-hour writing workshop, a walk in the park, and a lot of travelling from one spot to another, where I took a lot of photos.

Within this timeframe, I also streamed a two-hour movie and doomscrolled through shopping apps to watch livestreams. I also played classic games that were already ready to be downloaded on my vivo V80 Lite like Temple Run and Fruit Cut 3D. I was particularly impressed with the quality of my experience when I played League of Legends: Wild Rift, my favorite MLBB, as I didn’t experience any lag.

After the first day, my battery dropped to only 91%, after using the phone mostly for taking photos and watching videos. On the second day, I had more intensive use, from taking more photos to playing games, and I was left with 83% battery at the end of the day. On the third day, I was left with 61% after watching a movie, playing more games, and taking more photos.

No wonder. Proving its stellar battery life, the vivo V80 Lite recently set a Guinness World Records title, “The Longest Electronic Product Live Stream,” after completing a 32-hour and 37-minute continuous livestream in Thailand.

A phone that supports constant movement

I’m not glued to my phone all the time, given my often hectic daily schedule. But that doesn’t mean I don’t need a durable and reliable one. After all, I mainly use my phone to document moments – big or small – because I enjoy chronicling my life as much as I enjoy actively participating in it.

While it’s easy to get lured in by over-the-top aesthetics and new complex features, I think it’s safe to say that we’ll always care about a gadget’s ability to keep up with our endurance. With the vivo V80 Lite, I feel powered up to take on the next action-packed day, even without the “peace” that comes with a power bank – or frankly, even just a charger.

Pre-order now until October 16 in vivo physical stores or online via the vivo e-store and vivo Store app. Enjoy up to a P1,500 discount, four-year battery warranty, Silver membership exclusive privileges, as well as free limited edition vivo Buds Air3 and 100GB of Google One cloud storage for six months.

Check out the full specs on vivo’s official website. The vivo V80 Lite starts at P24,999. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Put people before platforms,’ Coloma reminds 33rd National PR Congress delegates
World.content:
Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Public Relations Society of the Philippines and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Former Presidential Communications Operations Office Communications Secretary Sonny Coloma reminded public relations professionals of the need to “recover the human being behind the audience.”

In his keynote speech at the 33rd Public Relations Congress organized by the Public Relations Society of the Philippines (PRSP), Coloma said, “In the language of modern communications, people can easily become metrics: reach, engagement, conversion, impressions, click-through rates, sentiment scores, share of voice.”

While acknowledging that metrics are useful, he said communicators must first focus on the person behind every impression, the human being behind every click. “Behind every consumer is somebody trying to make a decision about what to believe and whom to trust. And behind every follower is a human relationship that can either be strengthened of betrayed.”

In the age of artificial intelligence, Coloma said the greatest advantage of the communications professional of the future “may be something profoundly human: the capacity to care, to listen, to understand, to empathize, to distinguish between what is technically possible and what is morally right…to understand that the most powerful communication…is an act of integrity.”

Citing the congress theme, Steward the Story: From Clout to Legacy, he invited participants to foster trust in Philippine society. “We must rebuild a culture where facts matter, where disagreement does not automatically mean hostility, where persuasion does not require deception, where influence is exercised with responsibility, and where technology serves humanity rather than manipulating it.”

Stressing that the communications profession has a civic responsibility, Coloma encouraged over 300 attendees to be “stewards of meaning, custodians of reputation, builders of relationships and guardians of trust” so as to create a positive environment upon which the next generation can build their own future and legacy. – Rappler.com

World.title: With finality: COA affirms disallowance of Sara Duterte’s P73-M confi funds
World.content:
VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte leaves the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on September 5, 2026, after posting bail to the grave threats casefiled against her.

COA's disallowance covers OVP's P69.78-million spending for rewards, and P3.5-million spending for the purchase of tables, chairs, desktops, computers, and printers

MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Audit (COA) affirmed with finality the disallowance of the Office of the Vice President’s P73-million confidential funds under Vice President Sara Duterte.

“WHEREFORE, the Motion for Reconsideration of Vice President Sara Z. Duterte; Ms. Gina F. Acosta, Special Disbursing Officer; and Ms. Julieta L. Villadelrey, Chief Accountant; all of the Office of the Vice President (OVP), is hereby DENIED. Accordingly, Commission on Audit (COA) Decision No. 2026-171 dated April 10, 2026, which affirmed COA Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office Notice of Disallowance No. 2024-002-100 (2022) dated August 8, 2024, on the confidential expenses of the OVP, for the period from December 21 to 31, 2022, in the amount of P73,287,000.00, is AFFIRMED with FINALITY,” read the COA resolution made public on Wednesday, October 7.

COA issued a notice of disallowance to Duterte’s office over P69.78 million in spending for rewards and P3.5 million for the purchase of tables, chairs, desktop computers and printers. These expenses were made from December 21 to 31, 2022.

A notice of disallowance is issued for expenses which are “illegal, irregular, unnecessary, excessive, extravagant, or expenditure.”

The alleged misuse of confidential funds is among the allegations against Duterte in her ongoing impeachment trial. The House prosecution team has finished presenting its evidence on this article and is currently in the middle of discussing Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Video of Baste Duterte calling out Benny Abante dozing off is AI-generated
World.content:
Davao City Mayor Sebastian Duterte did not make the remark; it was impeachment court presiding officer Francis ‘Chiz’ Escudero who noticed that Manila 6th District Representative Benny Abante was dozing off

Claim: Video shows Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte throwing shade at Manila 6th District Representative Benny Abante Jr. who was dozing off during Senate impeachment trial.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The video has already received 130,000 views, 1,100 reactions, 125 shares, and 30 comments as of this posting. It was posted on October 5, days after the mayor attended the impeachment trial as a hostile witness.

Duterte can be seen in the video saying, “May iba sa’tin dito, patulog-tulog lang pero sinusuwelduhan (There are some of us here who just sleep on the job, yet still get paid).”

The video portrays Duterte directly calling out Abante. A clip of the Manila 6th District congressman waking up after the call-out was also attached to the video.

The text on the Facebook reel also reads, “Tulog pa more laki ng sweldo eh nataranta ka atras [Abante] (Keep on sleeping! And yet you earn a huge salary. You panicked, Abante).”

The facts: Duterte did not make the statement. No credible news reports quoted the Davao City mayor making the exact remark. It was the impeachment court presiding officer, Senator Francis “Chiz” Escudero, who noticed that the congressman was dozing off.

“Before calling on Senator Joel Villanueva, may I ask Congressman Defensor, Congressman Barbers to kindly nudge Cong. Benny a bit? It seems he’s tired. He may want to rest somewhere but at least not right behind the witness,” Escudero said.

The call-out also did not happen while Duterte was on the witness stand. Escudero made the statement while senator-judges were asking Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS) Division Chief Rendell Sopeña.

AI-generated: Reverse image search did not show any credible video similar to the post. It only showed real photos of Duterte in the Senate impeachment trial.

Artificial intelligence (AI) detection tools flagged the video as AI-generated. Hive Moderation detected 66.8% likelihood of being deepfake in the video. Decopy AI flagged the screenshot from the video as 60% likely to be AI-generated. In its analysis, it stated that the photo of Duterte was likely manipulated.

“The image mostly suggests a human origin due to natural skin texture and depth of field, but some minor elements like the flat clothing texture and expression rigidity could hint at subtle AI enhancement or smoothing,” it stated.

Duterte: The Davao City mayor appeared before the Senate impeachment court on September 29 as a hostile witness. He was asked about the contracts of the Davao City government with Gencorp, which is linked to the Vice President. Duterte maintained that he had no involvement in the contracts with the company.

Previous fact checks: Rappler has previously fact-checked similar AI-generated videos about public officials:

– Angelee Kaye Abelinde/Rappler.com

Angelee Kaye Abelinde is a student journalist based in Naga City, and an alumna of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: France’s Mistral launches AI model it says outperforms some Chinese rivals
World.content:
MISTRAL. An  for Mistral AI, the French artificial intelligence company, is displayed inside the Grand Central subway station in New York City, USA, on May 21, 2026.

Mistral Large 4 will be made publicly available on October 27

PARIS, France – French AI startup Mistral unveiled a new AI model on Tuesday, October 6, ending a gap of about five months between major releases, and said it outperforms many rival open-weight models.

The three-year-old company, widely viewed as Europe’s strongest AI challenger to US and Chinese competitors, has not released a new model since May. In August, it began offering third-party models to customers, starting with Beijing-based Z.ai’s GLM 5.3.

“The model we’re actually announcing today is actually above the Chinese models on certain aspects, including cyber. So the narrative that Europe cannot compete is something that is not true,” CEO Artur Mensch said at a launch event in Abu Dhabi, without specifying which Chinese models or benchmarks he was referring to.

Mistral said Le Chonk, officially named Mistral Large 4, will be made publicly available on October 27.

Before the release, cybersecurity experts and government authorities will be given access to a version with fewer safety restrictions to test its capabilities, the company said.

Pierre Stock, Mistral’s vice president of science, told Reuters that the model ranks among the strongest open-weight, systems available.

Open-weight means users can download the model from platforms and run it on their own hardware. Many Chinese models are open-weight, while top US models tend to be closed and accessible only through their developers’ infrastructure.

Safety risks contained

Stock told Reuters the model had tried to go beyond its testing environment, but that this was expected and the company was able to prevent it.

OpenAI and Anthropic, whose most advanced models have demonstrated similar behaviour in testing, have restricted access to their most cyber-capable systems.

After executives at US AI companies warned last month that AI could pose an existential threat to humanity, Mensch dismissed such arguments as self-serving.

Mistral, which raised €3 billion ($3.4 billion) in its latest funding round, has positioned itself as a safer, European alternative.

Closing the gap

Mistral said Large 4 is “closing the gap with frontier models” in areas including coding, finance, geospatial analysis, manufacturing and product design.

The company trained the model on its own infrastructure.

Stock said Mistral’s goal was to partner “very deeply” with backers including ASML and new-investor Samsung “across the entire value chain”.

He said Large 4 is capable of designing computer chips, but declined to comment on whether Mistral is currently working with Samsung on chip development. – Rappler.com

World.title: Unemployment eases to 5.3% in August 2026 as agriculture adds jobs
World.content:
Manufacturing continues to weaken as employment in the sector further fell to 3.16 million in August from 3.43 million in July

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ unemployment rate eased to 5.3% in August 2026 as more Filipinos found work, particularly in the agriculture sector.

Around 2.77 million Filipinos were unemployed in August, down from 3.14 million in July, according to preliminary data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA).

The unemployment rate likewise fell from 6% in July, when it hit its highest level in more than four years. However, the August figure is worse than the 3.9% unemployment rate recorded in the same month of 2025.

National Statistician Dennis Mapa said the improvement from July was partly because fewer new entrants joined the labor force after the surge of fresh graduates looking for jobs the previous month.

Around 897,000 Filipinos joined the labor force for the first time in August, down from 1.5 million in July. Of these new entrants, around 470,000 were employed while 427,000 were unemployed, according to Mapa.

Agriculture and forestry accounted for the biggest month-on-month increase in employment, adding around 847,000 workers. Construction added another 390,000 jobs, while wholesale and retail trade gained 227,000.

Mapa said much of the agriculture increase came from rice and sugarcane production.

Manufacturing, however, continued to weaken. Employment in the sector fell to 3.16 million in August from 3.43 million in July and 3.46 million in June. Mapa said the electronics industry was among those affected, citing challenges in the global market, although seasonality may also be a factor.

Underemployment also improved month-on-month, falling to 11.9% in August from 12.9% in July. This meant around 5.9 million employed Filipinos still wanted additional working hours or another job. The rate, however, was higher than the 10.7% recorded in August 2025.

Bad weather also affected the quality of work during the month. Average hours worked fell to 39.2 hours a week from 40.6 hours in July, with millions of workers reporting bad weather as a reason for working fewer hours.

Mapa said shorter working hours could also translate to lower incomes for some workers, particularly the self-employed and those paid according to the amount of time they work.

The PSA expects employment to pick up toward the end of the year as businesses hire more seasonal workers ahead of the Christmas period. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Sets Wheat Export Record as Grain Rail Shipments Rise
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan exported a record 8.87 million tons of wheat from September 2025 to August 2026, as strong demand from Central Asian markets and Afghanistan helped drive shipments to the highest level on record, according to the Grain Union of Kazakhstan.

The figure represents a 16.2% increase from the same period last year, said Yevgeniy Karabanov, head of the union’s Analytics Committee.

The export surge coincided with growing railway shipments of grain. According to the Ministry of Transport, 10.8 million tons of grain were transported across Kazakhstan’s railway network in January–September, up 12% from the same period last year. Export-bound grain shipments reached 8.4 million tons, an increase of 14%.

Central Asia remains the main destination

Central Asian markets accounted for the majority of Kazakhstan’s wheat exports in the 2025/26 marketing year. Kazakhstan shipped nearly seven million tons of wheat to Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Turkmenistan, representing 78.7% of total wheat exports. Uzbekistan alone accounted for 60.8% of all shipments.

Railway data for January–September shows a similar concentration of grain flows toward the region. Kazakhstan transported 5.5 million tons of grain by rail to Central Asian countries, 33% more than a year earlier.

Uzbekistan received 4.11 million tons, up 44%, while shipments to Tajikistan rose 16% to 1.18 million tonnes. Smaller volumes were sent to the Kyrgyz Republic and Turkmenistan. Demand from Afghanistan also remained strong. Wheat exports to the country increased 2.6 times over the marketing year, according to the Grain Union.

The ministry reported that 762,000 tons of grain were transported by rail to Afghanistan in January–September, 4.3 times more than during the same period of 2025.

Kazakhstan expands its export geography

Kazakhstan also recorded sharp increases in wheat shipments to several markets outside its traditional destinations. Exports to Iran increased 617 times, while shipments to Türkiye rose 27 times and those to Russia 12 times. Exports to Uzbekistan increased 42%, Tajikistan 5.7% and the United Kingdom threefold.

Kazakh wheat also entered markets that had not received shipments during the previous marketing year. Around 6,000 tons were exported to France and 23,600 tons to Tunisia.

At the same time, exports to several destinations declined. Shipments to Turkmenistan fell to 28,000 tons, while exports to Azerbaijan decreased to 220,000 tons, Italy to 242,200 tons and Georgia to 39,400 tons.

Exports to China fell more than fourfold to 43,200 tons. Karabanov said the decline was offset by a 1.43 million-ton increase in shipments of feed meal to China, up 65%. Railway data, meanwhile, points to continued growth in grain flows to China, with 750,000 tons transported there in January–September, 54% more than a year earlier.

New harvest drives railway loading

The increase in grain transportation has continued into the new harvesting season. In September, grain loading reached 1.45 million tons, a record monthly figure and 7% above the level recorded in September 2025, according to the ministry.

The ministry attributed the continued growth in grain transportation to preparations for the new harvest and said a special grain headquarters had been established to coordinate railway shipments. The headquarters coordinates participants in the transportation process, monitors the readiness of railway infrastructure and rolling stock, and addresses operational issues that may arise during the harvest season.

According to the ministry, Kazakhstan has 16,900 grain wagons, 17,800 covered freight wagons and more than 2,000 locomotives available for grain transportation. The ministry said the existing rolling stock is sufficient to handle the expected volumes, with additional capacity available if needed.

Strong demand supports export growth

According to Karabanov, the acceleration in wheat exports in August was linked to early harvesting and low wheat stocks in importing countries. Strong demand from Central Asia and Afghanistan persisted throughout the marketing year, helping Kazakhstan expand wheat exports despite weaker shipments to several individual markets.

The record export result also highlights the importance of railway capacity for moving the new harvest to Kazakhstan’s main export destinations, particularly Central Asia, China and Afghanistan.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Oman Sign Investment, Energy Deals, Agree on $150 Million Fund
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Oman agreed to establish a $150 million joint investment fund and expand cooperation in oil and gas, transport and financial connectivity, as Kazakhstan seeks to diversify its investment partnerships and strengthen access to markets across the Gulf, Indian Ocean and beyond.

The agreements were signed during Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said’s state visit to Kazakhstan on Oct. 6, laying the groundwork for a broader economic partnership focused on investment, energy, logistics and access to new markets.

The package covers investment protection, air services, finance, energy, geological exploration and business cooperation. The two leaders also adopted a joint statement outlining the further direction of bilateral relations.

$150 million joint investment fund

Samruk Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund and Oman Investment Authority signed an agreement to establish a joint investment structure. The fund, with planned capital of $150 million, is expected to launch at the Astana International Financial Centre by the end of this year on a parity basis.

The fund will invest in priority projects in Kazakhstan and Oman, creating a dedicated mechanism to finance bilateral investment initiatives. Samruk Kazyna fund also signed an agreement with Oman Investment Authority on the key terms of the Blue City Rixos joint project.

The investment mechanism comes as Kazakhstan seeks to broaden the geographic base of its foreign investment and develop new channels for attracting capital beyond its traditional partners, particularly in sectors where the country is seeking greater value creation.

New framework for oil and gas cooperation

KazMunayGas and OQ Exploration & Production New Ventures signed a strategic cooperation agreement in geological exploration. The framework creates a basis for identifying and assessing potential investment opportunities in the oil and gas sector in Kazakhstan, Oman and other countries.

According to Samruk Kazyna Chairman Nurlan Zhakupov, the agreement is intended to support the joint implementation of oil and gas projects in both countries.

Oman joins Eurasian Development Bank

The Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) and Oman’s Ministry of Finance signed an agreement defining the conditions for the bank’s presence in Oman.

The agreement marks a new stage for the EDB, with Oman set to become its eighth shareholder and the first member state from the Gulf region.

EDB Chairman Nikolai Podguzov said the agreement would strengthen ties between Central Asia and the Gulf region and support cooperation under the bank’s new strategy.

Business council to strengthen direct ties

The Atameken National Chamber of Entrepreneurs and the Oman Chamber of Commerce and Industry agreed to establish the Kazakhstan-Oman Business Council. The council will provide a platform for direct business contacts, B2B meetings, partner searches and promotion of joint projects.

The two sides identified tourism, digitalization and artificial intelligence, agriculture, energy, mining, construction and logistics as promising areas for cooperation. Kazakh businesses also view Oman as a potential gateway to markets in the Gulf, South Asia and East Africa.

Broader economic cooperation

The package also includes an agreement on the promotion and mutual protection of investments, an agreement on air services and a memorandum of understanding between the finance ministries of Kazakhstan and Oman.

The documents signed during the state visit establish new mechanisms for investment and business cooperation and create a framework for expanding economic ties between Kazakhstan and Oman.

For Kazakhstan, the partnership offers an opportunity to combine its resource base, industrial and transport potential with Omani investment and access to markets around the Gulf and Indian Ocean, while creating additional channels for economic diversification and higher-value projects.

World.title: Central Asia’s Water Challenge Deepens as Rivers Decline and Glaciers Melt
World.content:
ASTANA – Central Asia faces growing pressure on its water resources as river flows decline, freshwater reserves remain below normal, and glaciers continue to lose mass, the Eurasian Briefing Telegram channel reported, citing data from the World Meteorological Organization.

The assessment compares recent indicators with data from 2022 and earlier periods. It found significant declines in water inflows to reservoirs in Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Afghanistan. The Aral Sea basin was among the areas where river flows fell below normal levels. Recent years have been among the driest in Central Asia since observations began in 1991.

Glacier loss is another major concern. Central Asia’s glacier mass balance ranked among the three most negative on record, meaning glaciers lost more ice than they accumulated. More than half of the region’s river runoff is generated by snow and ice, making water supplies particularly vulnerable to changes in the cryosphere.

Tajikistan has around 14,000 glaciers. More than 10% of its glacier cover has disappeared, while the total glaciated area has declined by about one-third. Tajik glaciers, including the Fedchenko Glacier, contribute significantly to the Amu Darya flow.

The Kyrgyz Republic has more than 8,000 glaciers, with more than 25% of its glacier cover lost. If the current trend continues, around another third of the country’s glacier mass could disappear by 2040. The Kyrgyz part of the Syr Darya basin depends on meltwater from the Tien Shan glaciers, while declining glacier mass also affects flows in the Naryn River.

Uzbekistan is particularly dependent on transboundary water resources, with more than 80% of its water coming from sources outside the country. Declining glacier contributions to the upper reaches of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya therefore have direct implications for the country’s water security.

Kazakhstan’s southern regions also depend on the Syr Darya. Declining inflows to the Shardara Reservoir have been recorded repeatedly in recent years.

In Turkmenistan, more than 90% of water resources are supplied through the Karakum Canal from the Amu Darya. Changes in the river’s flow therefore directly affect agricultural irrigation and water supplies to populated areas.

Regional water management

Water shortages have been a longstanding challenge for Central Asia. During the Soviet period, the region operated within a unified water and energy system. The Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan used their mountain rivers primarily for hydropower generation, while Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan relied heavily on the same water resources for agricultural irrigation.

After the Soviet Union collapsed, the end of the unified energy system and worsening drought increased pressure on water resources. The Amu Darya and Syr Darya, the region’s two major rivers, became increasingly important to national water and agricultural needs.

The situation is complicated by various priorities between upstream and downstream countries. Tajikistan and the Kyrgyz Republic have significant hydropower interests, while Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan depend heavily on water for agriculture.

The 1998 agreement governing the use of water and energy resources in the Syr Darya basin is also described in the source material as no longer reflecting current consumption patterns and climate conditions. The Eurasian Briefing argues that the existing framework needs to be updated to reflect changing consumption patterns and climate conditions. It points to options including a new multilateral agreement on the Naryn hydropower cascade or financial compensation mechanisms related to reservoir operations.

Kazakhstan focuses on coordination and infrastructure

Kazakhstan is working with neighboring countries to coordinate water releases and ensure supplies during the irrigation season.

In a written response to The Astana Times, the Kazakh Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation said that the heads of water management agencies from Central Asian countries annually approve reservoir operation schedules for the Syr Darya and Amu Darya basins, as well as water withdrawal limits, through meetings of the Interstate Commission for Water Coordination.

In the Kazakhstan-Kyrgyz Republic-Uzbekistan trilateral format, water and energy authorities annually coordinate the operating mode of the Uch-Kurgan hydropower plant, located downstream from the Toktogul Reservoir and serving as the final link in the Lower Naryn cascade.

“This coordination of operating modes makes it possible to ensure stable water supply, taking into account the needs of the countries of the region during the growing season,” the ministry said.

The ministry also noted that Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan coordinate annually on the operating mode of the Bakhri-Tojik Reservoir during the peak vegetation period. The arrangement allows additional water releases through the Dostyk interstate canal, helping supply agricultural land in the Turkistan Region’s Maktaaral and Zhetysai districts and reduce water-scarcity risks during periods of high demand.
