According to an OECD report assessing the situation in 2023-2024, Azerbaijan has made no significant overall progress in combating corruption since 2022. The system for declaring the assets and interests of public officials was not operational, while gaps also remained in declaration forms and procedures for their electronic submission and verification.

In Transparency International’s 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index, Azerbaijan scored 30 out of 100 and ranked 130th out of 182 countries. Despite an eight-point increase compared with the previous year, the score remains low in terms of perceived levels of public-sector corruption.

Arrests of journalists investigating corruption

The authorities’ pledge to protect those who report corruption also contrasts with the situation surrounding the Abzas Media case. On 20 June 2025, seven defendants in the case were sentenced to prison terms ranging from seven years and six months to nine years. They included journalists Ulvi Hasanli, Sevinj Vagifgizi and Hafiz Babali, who had investigated corruption.

The defendants rejected the charges against them. Reporters Without Borders described the sentences as the result of a politically motivated trial aimed at silencing those who expose corruption and injustice.

Against this backdrop, several questions arise: Is a person who reports an alleged demand for a bribe protected from retaliation? Is the alleged offence independently investigated, and are the findings made public? And can a journalist who exposes corruption continue their work without facing the threat of imprisonment?

World.title: Opinion from Yerevan: Baku steps up pressure on Armenia with new tools
World.content:
Opinion on Baku’s tougher rhetoric

Statements by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev should be seen as a “public expression of dissatisfaction with Nikol Pashinyan’s government”, according to political analyst Suren Surenyants.

Speaking at the eighth congress of the ruling New Azerbaijan Party, Aliyev said, among other things, that the blame should not be placed solely on Armenia’s former leadership.

“It is true that Armenia’s former leaders are war criminals and must be punished, but it was Armenia’s current government that made territorial claims against us and insulted the dignity of the Azerbaijani people with inappropriate and uncivilised statements. We must never forget this,” the president stressed.

Political analyst Suren Surenyants analysed what prompted the recent statements by Aliyev and his aide Hikmet Hajiyev, as well as Azerbaijan’s tougher rhetoric more broadly.

“Baku is effectively signalling that it is dissatisfied with the way Pashinyan is fulfilling his commitments and, if necessary, could use his previous positions and statements as an additional means of exerting pressure,” he said.

‘We would like to make peace not only with the Armenian government, but with the Armenian people’

Against the backdrop of Aliyev’s tough statements, the head of the foreign policy department of the Azerbaijani presidential administration also addressed the peace agenda with Armenia. Speaking at the CAMCA Regional Forum in Baku, he said Azerbaijan intended to build a long-term architecture for peace:

“That is why we always say that we want to make this peace not only with the Armenian government and the country’s prime minister. We want to make peace with the Armenian people. And that is why we continue to expect changes to Armenia’s Constitution. Of course, this is an internal matter, and we fully refrain from interfering in this process.

“We are waiting for just one final step – amendments to Armenia’s Constitution concerning territorial claims against Azerbaijan. After that, I think the final peace agreement will become a reality.”

Baku is demanding amendments to Armenia’s Constitution as a precondition for signing a peace treaty. Azerbaijan argues that the document contains territorial claims. The Constitution itself contains no wording that could give rise to such concerns. However, it refers to the Declaration of Independence, which mentions the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. A draft of Armenia’s new Constitution is currently under discussion. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that it should not contain a reference to the Declaration of Independence. At the same time, he insists that constitutional change is something Armenia itself needs.

Expert commentary

Political analyst Suren Surenyants notes that Armenia is building its entire policy around the peace agenda with Azerbaijan, while Azerbaijan, far from softening its rhetoric, has been toughening it in recent months:

“One possible explanation is that Azerbaijan is seeking to consolidate as quickly as possible the political gains resulting from the military advantage it achieved through the war, recognising that the current balance of power will not last forever.”

In his view, this interpretation is also supported by statements from the Azerbaijani president’s aide. In particular, he points to Hikmet Hajiyev’s remarks that a peace treaty will only be signed after Armenia changes its Constitution, despite peace having already been established:

“This is not a contradiction, but a division of labour. One formulation is intended for an international audience, while the other is addressed to Yerevan, reminding it of the need to fulfil its commitments.”

Surenyants also considers the statement about seeking peace not only with the Armenian government but also with the Armenian people noteworthy.

According to him, this means Azerbaijan wants changes in Armenia to acquire “legitimacy enshrined through a referendum and to be made as irreversible as possible”.

The political analyst suggests Baku is in a hurry because the regional balance of power could change, primarily due to the growing Iranian factor:

“If Iran is able to capitalise on its regional influence, a shift in the balance of power in the South Caucasus could limit Baku’s ability to exert pressure on Armenia.”

Surenyants notes that:

Tehran has repeatedly said that any violation of Armenia’s territorial integrity, changes to international borders or alteration of the geopolitical status quo in the region constitute “red lines” for Iran;

Iran is particularly sensitive to the development of transport links through Armenia, viewing them through the prism of its own security and regional influence.

Surenyants argues that the demand for changes to Armenia’s Constitution is taking on additional significance and cannot be seen simply as a “mechanical precondition” for signing a peace treaty.

“Azerbaijan is seeking to achieve its desired outcome within Armenia at both the legal and political levels. And that outcome will not be limited to removing the reference to the Declaration of Independence,” he argues.

The analyst notes that discussions have intensified again in Baku, in particular about the return of Azerbaijanis to “Western Azerbaijan”, by which they mean virtually the entire territory of Armenia. He believes these developments will not end with changes to Armenia’s Constitution and is convinced that Azerbaijan will then present Armenia with a new list of demands:

“Does all this mean that Azerbaijan is preparing for a new military escalation? At present, there is not enough publicly available evidence to draw such a definitive conclusion.”

The political analyst believes Baku has not yet obtained everything it wants from Armenia and is therefore stepping up political pressure. In his assessment, this is driven by concerns that it may become more difficult to secure all its demands in the future:

“And Baku is rushing to get everything it wants while there is a government in Yerevan that regards Baku’s demand for constitutional amendments as part of its own agenda, and before regional developments close the ‘window of opportunity’ for exerting unilateral pressure on Armenia.”

World.title: Russian court fines Abkhaz journalist Nizfa Arshba for violating foreign agent law
World.content:
A court in Vladikavkaz, North Ossetia, Russia, has fined Abkhaz journalist Nizfa Arshba for violating Russia’s foreign agent law. However, no one notified her about the fine. Authorities allegedly sent the notice to an address in Russia where she has never lived.

The court imposed a 30,000 rouble fine [about $353] on 31 August 2026. It ruled that Arshba had “posted material on the social network Facebook without indicating that the material was produced or distributed by a foreign agent, or that it concerned the activities of a foreign agent.”

Nizfa Arshba

Arshba learned about the fine by chance after coming across the information online. The journalist said no one had officially notified her about it.

Opposition journalist Nizfa Arshba, who runs the Telegram channel Aiashara, was added to Russia’s foreign agent register by the Russian Justice Ministry in March 2025, shortly after Abkhazia’s presidential election.

Unlike another Abkhaz journalist, Izida Chania, who also appears on the sanctions list and holds dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, Arshba has only one citizenship — Abkhaz. She has never lived in Russia and has no ties to the country at all.

Under the procedure, Russian citizens, including those listed in the foreign agent register, receive notifications about fines through their personal accounts on the Gosuslugi public services portal. But Nizfa Arshba is neither a Russian citizen nor a resident, so she is not registered on the portal and could not have received notification of the Vladikavkaz court’s decision.

The court’s decision also says that Arshba did not attend the hearing and did not explain why she was absent. At the same time, the court claims that it notified Arshba of the time and place where officials drew up the administrative offence report, as well as the time and place of the hearing. It says authorities sent the notice to her last known place of residence in Russia.

“I would like to know how and by whom my place of residence in Vladikavkaz was assigned to me, given that I have never lived in Russia, never held Russian citizenship and never assumed any obligation to comply with the laws of any foreign state,” Nizfa Arshba wrote on her Telegram channel.

The journalist says she does not intend to pay the fine.

Nizfa Arshba has actively opposed draft laws and Russian-Abkhaz agreements that she believes run counter to Abkhazia’s interests. One example is the controversial bill that would have allowed Russian citizens to build, sell and buy apartments in Abkhazia.

Because of similar positions, two Abkhaz politicians, Kan Kvarчия and Leuan Mikaa, lost their Russian citizenship, while three journalists, including Nizfa Arshba, were added to the foreign agent register.

For Abkhazia’s residents, this label also makes it extremely difficult to travel abroad. Russia remains the most accessible foreign destination for them, and they also have to travel through Russia to reach the wider world. But those labelled foreign agents fear travelling to Russia.

If Arshba violates the foreign agent law again, she could face criminal charges. The local authorities in Abkhazia do not pose any threat to her.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nizfa Arshba fined by Russian court

World.title: All four German political foundations halt work in Georgia; ALDE calls for EU sanctions
World.content:
German foundations close in Georgia

German Ambassador to Georgia Barbara Voss said all four German political foundations that had operated in the country for many years have been forced to close because of restrictions introduced by new legislation, including the Law on Grants.

According to the ambassador, worsening relations between Georgia and Germany have put years of cooperation at risk, including ties in education.

Against this backdrop, the European Liberal, Democrat and Reform Party (ALDE) sent a letter to EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas, calling on the European Union to respond with concrete action.

On 30 September, the Konrad Adenauer Foundation closed its office in Tbilisi. The Georgian office of the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which had worked in the country for 20 years, followed. The Heinrich Böll Foundation and Friedrich Ebert Foundation have also closed their offices.

What the German ambassador said

Barbara Voss, who replaced Peter Fischer as Germany’s ambassador to Georgia in August 2026, said that years of cooperation between the two countries had been seriously damaged.

“All four of our political foundations, which have supported Georgia and its people for decades on their path towards European integration, have been forced to suspend their work following a decision by the Georgian government. Two of the four foundations were forced to close their offices just two days ago,” the ambassador said.

Voss also highlighted Ilia State University, which has long-standing academic ties with Germany and is, according to the ambassador, one of Georgia’s most internationally recognised universities.

She said the university is now at risk of closure.

“These developments are also worsening relations between Georgia and the EU. In the coming years, I personally, as ambassador, will work to preserve what can still be preserved,” Voss said.

The diplomat said Germany would continue to meet its commitments in certain areas, including support for civil society, environmental protection and conservation of natural resources.

The German ambassador also spoke about security cooperation between the two countries. She stressed that Berlin and Tbilisi share common interests and face common challenges in this area.

“Russia is trying to destabilise Europe and divide people through disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression,” Voss said.

She said the Georgian population was well aware of the consequences of Russian military aggression. The ambassador noted that 20% of Georgia’s territory is occupied by Russia and said Moscow’s goal was not to maintain a balance of power but to establish dominance.

According to Voss, Germany continues to support Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as its right to determine its own security policy.

“In this context, we will support cooperation with the Georgian Defence Forces within the NATO framework to further strengthen their defence capabilities against potential aggression and contribute to the security of the South Caucasus and Europe,” the German ambassador said.

“Enough! The Georgian Dream regime is silencing independent voices”

“Enough is enough! The Georgian Dream regime is squeezing out independent voices and pushing Georgia further away from Europe.

After more than 20 years in the country, Friedrich-Naumann-Stiftung für die Freiheit has been forced to close its Tbilisi office because it could no longer operate independently.

ALDE Party President Svenja Hahn and European Liberal Forum President Jan-Christoph Oetjen are calling on the EU to act.

Targeted sanctions against those responsible for repression and the systematic undermining of democracy. No more looking the other way. Our joint letter to Kaja Kallas and Marta Kos,” ALDE said in a social media post.

The letter says the Friedrich Naumann Foundation for Freedom was forced to close its Tbilisi office, which had operated in the country for more than two decades, after the Georgian authorities rejected its application for foreign funding.

“The Georgian authorities made it clear that the foundation’s activities would only be permitted if they were aligned with their priorities. Under these conditions, FNF concluded that it could no longer carry out its mission as an independent political foundation,” the letter says.

The letter describes this as “another clear example of the growing restrictions on independent civil society and the wider repression of protesters, opposition figures, journalists and independent voices.”

“These developments show how far the Georgian Dream government is moving away from the standards expected of an EU candidate country and send a worrying signal to all those with European aspirations.

What is happening in Georgia matters not only to its citizens, but also to the credibility of the EU’s enlargement policy and its commitment to democracy and fundamental rights,” the letter says.

The authors again called on the EU to “respond with targeted sanctions against those responsible for the repression and systematic undermining of democracy and fundamental freedoms in Georgia”.

“The EU must ensure that those defending democracy and fundamental freedoms are not left without support,” ALDE said.

“We are not concerned about unfair sanctions” – ruling party representative

“We are not particularly concerned about their [the EU’s] incompetent and completely unfounded sanctions packages, introduced year after year or month after month,” parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtchkhalia said in response to ALDE’s call.

“We should not be surprised by such statements from ALDE or the EU’s political establishment. For years, our country has been subjected to direct and unfair attacks from them.

No package of sanctions can force us to abandon the course chosen at the request of our society. That course is peaceful development, progress and prosperity for every citizen and, above all, the peaceful reunification of our country,” Kirtchkhalia said.

News in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan calls IPU key platform for strengthening parliaments (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. The Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU) provides a vital platform for exchanging experiences, mutual learning, and strengthening the role of parliaments in building institutions that are more open, inclusive, and trusted, Azerbaijani Parliament Speaker Sahiba Gafarova said in her address to the 153rd Assembly of the IPU in Arusha, during her working visit to Tanzania.

This was reported by the Press and Public Relations Department of the Milli Majlis (Azerbaijani Parliament).

The speaker noted that public hearings and public discussions are crucial mechanisms for ensuring citizen participation. Representatives of state institutions, experts, civil society organizations, and members of the public can take part in discussions regarding draft laws and issues of public interest. These mechanisms enable the parliament to hear diverse professional and public opinions and to strengthen its engagement with society.

Speaking during the general debate on the topic "Strengthening good governance and empowering communities through inclusivity, trust, and opportunities for all," Gafarova said that effective governance depends not only on efficient institutions but also on whether people trust those institutions, can participate in decision-making, and have fair opportunities to contribute to society.

The speaker noted that digitalization makes state institutions more accessible and transparent, thereby supporting this process by creating new avenues for communication and participation. She also emphasized that trust is further strengthened when institutions are open, citizens' voices are heard, and people see that their participation can make a difference.

Highlighting the vital role of parliaments in this process, Gafarova remarked that, as institutions representing the people, parliaments bridge the gap between public expectations and state decision-making. Through legislation, oversight, and dialogue with society, they help make governance more transparent, accountable, and inclusive.

Highlighting the consistent steps taken in Azerbaijan to improve public administration, expand digital solutions, enhance the accessibility of public services, and create broader opportunities for citizen participation, the speaker noted that the Azerbaijani parliament contributes to these efforts.

According to her, modern technologies in this field facilitate greater interaction with citizens and ensure wider access to information regarding parliamentary activities. At the same time, Azerbaijan has established legal and institutional mechanisms that enable citizens and civil society to participate directly in the legislative process. She cited the right of legislative initiative as a significant example of this.

Gafarova also briefed on other digital tools utilized by the Azerbaijani parliament. Attention was also drawn to the work undertaken by the parliament to ensure inclusivity. In this regard, information was provided on the special attention the Azerbaijani parliament pays to the participation and rights of women, youth, and persons with disabilities, as well as the development of relevant legislation in this area.

Concluding her remarks, the speaker said that the IPU offers a vital platform for exchanging experiences, mutual learning, and strengthening the role of parliaments in establishing institutions that are more open, inclusive, and trusted. She pointed out that by enhancing participation and ensuring every voice is heard, it is possible to empower communities and contribute to the creation of more resilient, peaceful, and sustainable societies.

World.title: Shavkat Mirziyoyev to attend Central Asia, CIS summits in Turkmenistan
World.content:
Photo: The Press service of the President of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev will visit Turkmenistan on Oct. 7–9 at the invitation of Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov to participate in regional and multilateral summits.

This was reflected in the statement by the press service of the Uzbek president.

During the working visit, Mirziyoyev will attend the eighth Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan and the next summit of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) in the Avaza National Tourist Zone.

The Consultative Meeting will focus on strengthening political and diplomatic cooperation, expanding trade and economic ties and developing cooperation in energy, according to the press service.

The agenda also includes joint measures to protect the environment and adapt to climate change, as well as expanding cultural, educational and scientific ties and youth exchanges.

The leaders are expected to exchange views on regional and international issues, including efforts to maintain peace, stability and security.

“Particular attention will be paid to strengthening political and diplomatic interaction, deepening trade and economic ties and expanding cooperation in the energy sector,” the press service said.

At the CIS Council of Heads of State meeting, the leaders will review the results of multilateral cooperation within the organization and discuss prospects for its further development. The 35th anniversary of the CIS will also receive particular attention.

A package of joint documents is expected to be adopted following the meetings.

Mirziyoyev’s program in Turkmenistan will also include a series of bilateral meetings with foreign leaders, according to the press service.

The visit comes as Central Asian countries continue to strengthen regional coordination on economic cooperation, energy, environmental issues and other areas of common interest.

World.title: Azerbaijan urges efforts to investigate fate of missing persons
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. The parties to the armed conflict must take all necessary measures to investigate the fate of missing persons, record and share the information in their possession, search for the deceased, and treat their remains with respect, Azerbaijan’s Deputy Foreign Minister Fariz Rzayev said at the 4th international conference on the theme "Strengthening trust and developing effective mechanisms to resolve the issue of missing persons" held within the framework of the Baku Dialogue on Missing Persons on Wednesday, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

He noted that for the family of a missing person, that individual is never merely a statistic or a registration number.

"This uncertainty shapes the future decisions of their loved ones, whether spouse, child, or parent. It remains unknown whether there will be a grave they can visit and where they can mourn. More than 4,000 Azerbaijani citizens are missing, and their fates remain unknown. Thousands of families endure this suffering amid uncertainty for years, or even decades.

Following the liberation of Azerbaijani territories, we discovered numerous mass grave sites containing human remains. The remains were examined, identities were established, and dignified burials were arranged. However, the fate of the vast majority remains unknown," he explained.

Rzayev added that mines and unexploded ordnance continue to make search operations in the area dangerous.

"I once again call upon all parties to share all information in their possession that could help clarify the fate and whereabouts of thousands of missing Azerbaijanis and other persons.

Azerbaijan hasn’t limited its commitment to humanitarian obligations solely to cases involving its own citizens. Since November 2020, it has continued search operations despite security challenges and the risk of mines.

This demonstrates our commitment to a responsible humanitarian approach and the value we place on human dignity, regardless of whose remains are involved," he emphasized.

The 4th international conference on the theme "Strengthening trust and developing effective mechanisms to resolve the issue of missing persons", organized by the State Commission on Prisoners of War, Hostages and Missing Persons, is being held in Gulustan Palace within the framework of the Baku Dialogue on Missing Persons.

The event is attended by former heads of state and government, high-ranking representatives of international organizations and foreign countries, heads of agencies dealing with missing persons, experts, representatives of non-governmental organizations, and human rights specialists, as well as ambassadors and military attachés of foreign countries accredited in Azerbaijan and other officials.

One of the main directions of this year's discussions is the formation and strengthening of trust between the parties.

The purpose of the conference is not to be satisfied with discussions, but to contribute to the formation of practical and sustainable mechanisms that strengthen trust and cooperation, serve to ensure families' right to know the truth, facilitate information exchange, and expand the application of modern forensic, DNA and technological capabilities. The event will continue until October 10.

World.title: Kazakhstan, EIB discuss energy projects, investment
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Kazakhstan and the European Investment Bank (EIB) discussed energy projects, investment and infrastructure development during a meeting in Astana, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy said.

Kazakhstan Energy Vice Minister Yerzhan Yertayev and EIB Vice President Marek Mora discussed cooperation in energy security, infrastructure development and modernization, the energy transition and the wider use of renewable energy sources.

Particular attention was paid to prospects for implementing joint energy projects, attracting investment and receiving technical and expert support from the EIB, the ministry said.

The sides also exchanged views on regional energy cooperation and the implementation of major infrastructure projects aimed at supporting the sustainable development of Kazakhstan’s energy sector.

They highlighted the importance of further cooperation with international financial institutions and European partners to attract financing, exchange expertise and introduce modern approaches in the energy sector.

Following the meeting, the sides confirmed their interest in continuing dialogue and developing cooperation in the energy sector.

The energy talks are part of a broader visit. On October 6, the European Union Delegation to Kazakhstan said that EIB Vice President Marek Mora is visiting Kazakhstan on October 7–8, with a focus on strengthening cooperation between Kazakhstan and the EIB, advancing key investment projects, deepening Kazakhstan–EU cooperation and supporting the development of the Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Japan discuss 2025 summit projects, new cooperation
World.content:
Photo: The Ministry of Economy and Finance of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Uzbekistan and Japan discussed expanding cooperation in trade, infrastructure and innovation, as well as preparations to implement initiatives from the first "Central Asia + Japan" Summit in 2025, during talks between Uzbek First Deputy Economy and Finance Minister Ilkhom Norkulov and Japanese Prime Minister’s Special Adviser Yoshimasa Uno in Tashkent on Oct. 6.

This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Economy and Finance of Uzbekistan.

The meeting was also attended by Japanese Ambassador to Uzbekistan Kenji Hirata and other representatives, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Economy and Finance.

The sides reviewed prospects for expanding bilateral trade and economic cooperation, developing infrastructure and advancing innovation, while also exploring new areas of mutually beneficial partnership.

They discussed initiatives put forward at the first "Central Asia + Japan" Summit, held in Tokyo in December 2025, as well as progress in implementing agreements reached following the high-level visit. The summit brought together the leaders of Japan and the five Central Asian countries, including Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.

Moreover, the Japanese side presented its updated "Free and Open Indo-Pacific" (FOIP) concept, which was announced by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi in May 2026.

"Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi announced its updated version, FOIP 3.0," the ministry said.

Against this backdrop, the meeting also covered prospects for implementing projects in green energy, energy efficiency and water-saving technologies.

The discussions are part of broader efforts to translate the outcomes of the 2025 summit and bilateral agreements into practical projects and cooperation.

At the conclusion of the meeting, the parties expressed readiness to continue cooperation in priority areas of mutual interest and further expand practical engagement between Uzbekistan and Japan.

World.title: Azerbaijan rejects reports linking it to August Hanning probe (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Reports circulating in various foreign media outlets that link Azerbaijan to the investigation concerning the former head of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service (BND), August Hanning, are disinformation and are viewed as part of the intensive smear campaign recently waged against Azerbaijan.

This was stated by the Media and Broadcasting Council of Azerbaijan.

According to the statement, the presentation of baseless allegations, linking Azerbaijan to the investigation in question, to a wide audience as fact is a matter of serious concern; these claims originated with the German publication Der Spiegel and were subsequently circulated by Reuters, AFP, France 24, The Times, The Telegraph, and other international media outlets. The spread of such material without citing official sources is considered unacceptable information manipulation.

"The malicious intent of the forces behind this disinformation operation is to undermine the Azerbaijan-Germany relations that have been further developing in recent times.

The Media and Broadcasting Council of Azerbaijan strongly condemns such disinformation campaigns aimed at baselessly portraying Azerbaijan in a negative light within the international information space; it calls upon international media entities to strictly adhere to the fundamental principles of professional journalism, including accuracy, objectivity, reliance on reliable sources, and fact-checking, and to refrain from disseminating false information or manipulating public opinion," the Council's statement added.

World.title: Azerbaijan urges action on missing persons for lasting peace with Armenia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Determining the fate of the missing persons is a crucial condition for lasting peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia, Chairman of the Azerbaijani State Commission on Prisoners of War, Hostages and Missing Persons, Ali Naghiyev, said at the 4th international conference on the theme "Strengthening trust and developing effective mechanisms to resolve the issue of missing persons," being held in Baku within the framework of the Baku Dialogue on Missing Persons, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

“Determining the fate of the missing is our humanitarian responsibility, our moral obligation to their families, and a crucial condition for lasting peace,” he noted.

The official pointed out that the goal of the Baku Dialogue, now held for the fourth time, is to bring together the expertise of states, international organizations, and specialists, and to develop cooperation mechanisms that accelerate search efforts and help families find answers.

"Azerbaijan is one of the countries suffering from the issue of missing persons. In the past, Armenia's unfounded claims and policy of occupation resulted in grave humanitarian consequences for our people. Although the war has ended, the period of waiting continues for families who remain unaware of their loved ones' fates.

The state commission has registered 4,010 persons who went missing as a result of military aggression. Of these, 4,004 went missing during the First Karabakh War, and six during the 44-day Patriotic War of 2020. Among the missing, 3,228 were military personnel and 782 were civilians. The civilians include 71 children, 288 women, and 319 elderly individuals. These figures illustrate the scale of the tragedy," he said.

Naghiyev added that the State Commission, in collaboration with relevant agencies, has expanded efforts regarding the identification of burial sites, excavation and exhumation, and the identification of remains.

"Biological samples have been collected and cataloged from a total of 11,566 donors who are close relatives of the missing persons. This data serves as a crucial foundation for scientifically based identification. As of October 1, 2026, human remains believed to belong to 913 missing persons have been discovered and recovered, and remains presumed to belong to 253 individuals have been exhumed from 32 mass graves found in the liberated territories," he emphasized.

The 4th international conference on the theme "Strengthening trust and developing effective mechanisms to resolve the issue of missing persons", organized by the State Commission on Prisoners of War, Hostages and Missing Persons, is being held in Gulustan Palace within the framework of the Baku Dialogue on Missing Persons.

The event is attended by former heads of state and government, high-ranking representatives of international organizations and foreign countries, heads of agencies dealing with missing persons, experts, representatives of non-governmental organizations, and human rights specialists, as well as ambassadors and military attachés of foreign countries accredited in Azerbaijan and other officials.

One of the main directions of this year's discussions is the formation and strengthening of trust between the parties.

The purpose of the conference is not to be satisfied with discussions, but to contribute to the formation of practical and sustainable mechanisms that strengthen trust and cooperation, serve to ensure families' right to know the truth, facilitate information exchange, and expand the application of modern forensic, DNA and technological capabilities.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s renewable power output rises 20% in nine months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Kazakhstan’s renewable energy facilities generated 7.8 billion kWh of electricity from January through September 2026, up 20% year-on-year, the country’s Ministry of Energy said.

“Wind power plants accounted for the largest share of renewable generation at 4.9 billion kWh, while solar power plants generated 1.9 billion kWh and small hydropower plants produced 993 million kWh,” the ministry said.

The share of renewables in Kazakhstan’s total electricity generation reached 8.5% in January-September 2026, up from 8.08% in the first half of the year.

According to the ministry, the country’s installed renewable energy capacity reached about 3.7 GW. Wind power accounted for 2 GW of the total, followed by solar power at 1.3 GW and small hydropower plants at 313 MW.

Kazakhstan plans to commission 10 renewable energy facilities with a combined capacity of 245 MW in 2026, including four wind farms, five solar power plants and one hydropower plant, the ministry previously said.

Renewable electricity generation is expected to reach 8.8 billion kWh by the end of 2026.

In 2025, Kazakhstan’s renewable energy facilities generated 8.6 billion kWh of electricity. Nine new renewable energy facilities with a combined capacity of more than 500 MW were commissioned during the year.

World.title: Is a waterfront city stadium actually on the cards for Canberra?
World.content:
After it was all but ruled out by the ACT government, a fresh pitch for a city stadium in Canberra has been floated.

The proposal has been met with positive but cautious responses from lawmakers, and although it is likely to be popular among Canberrans, it does not yet have the required land, an owner or a builder.

Here's what's known about the latest pitch for a city stadium.

What is the proposal?

A new city stadium is being suggested, based on the model of the Te Kaha Stadium in Christchurch — a rectangular stadium with a roof that holds 25,000 fans for sports events and 35,000 for concerts.

That stadium cost about half a billion Australian dollars to deliver.

Canberra's current rectangular stadium in the suburb of Bruce sits in the same precinct as the Australian Institute of Sport, but has drawn criticism in recent years due to its aging infrastructure and location, which means patrons cannot easily stream out to bars and restaurants or public transport.

Where would the stadium be built?

The proposed site of a new city stadium in Canberra is partially occupied by the Archbishop's House. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The proposed stadium would be waterfront, sitting on the north shore of Lake Burley Griffin near Regatta Place.

The area is a block of Commonwealth land that includes the Catholic Archbishop's house and the car parking next to it.

Crucially, it would be near the next stage of light rail, with construction to take the trams to the lake's edge already underway.

And the proximity to the city would give people the option to walk to Canberra's nightlife after an event.

Who's behind the idea?

A consortium of Canberra business heavy-hitters is behind the pitch, including Canberra Airport boss Stephen Byron, the founder of Canberra Data Centres, Greg Boorer, and other corporates.

However, Mr Byron has clarified that the consortium does not want to build the stadium or own it.

So, who will build it?

That's not yet clear.

The consortium is in discussions with the Catholic Archdiocese to buy the land, and said they would then hand it over for free to whoever runs the project.

That would be either the Commonwealth government, a combination of the Commonwealth and ACT governments, or potentially a private company tasked with developing the stadium.

When would it be built by?

An artist's rendering of an all-event stadium in Canberra's city (Supplied: Canberra Airport)

The business owners are optimistic the stadium could be complete by 2030.

Their plan is to take six months to get the architect designs finished.

That would then give the ACT government six to 12 months to consider the development and then, if approved, estimate it would take 2.5 years to build.

How would parking work at the stadium?

Canberra's rectangular stadium in Bruce is criticised for its location and age. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The new tram stop would be 80 metres from the proposed stadium.

Mr Byron also said he estimated there were already 7,000 car spaces north and south of the lake, while he said the current Bruce stadium "has about 1,700 car spaces".

He also said he believed that if the lake could fit 120,000 people for Canberra's Skyfire fireworks show, then a live music concert with 35,000 fans, for example, should be fine.

What does the government say?

ACT Senator Katy Gallagher did not disagree with the idea of a lakefront stadium. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

ACT Senator Katy Gallagher said the idea was "potentially very exciting" and that the purchase of the Catholic Archbishop's land would be significant.

ACT Treasurer Chris Steel said: "We certainly wouldn't rule out considering this proposal at this stage, we'll see what comes through this new study that's being proposed."

However, he did raise questions about transport to the site, parking and game-day access.

What about the pool?

The ACT government has proposed a new pool be built at Commonwealth Park to replace Civic Pool. This is because the previous pool's site is slated for a new National Convention Centre.

Mr Byron suggested the pool could be built next to the new stadium or at another site.

The federal government will have a big say in the decisions because both proposals involve the use of Commonwealth land.

So, Senator Gallagher said the government would have to weigh up the stadium proposal alongside plans for the convention centre and pool.

World.title: Mother sentenced after 'negligence' causes son's death
World.content:
For Andrew O'Sullivan, there is no justice for his young son.

The actions of his former partner, the mother of four-year-old Tarrin, still haunt him.

Tarrin O'Sullivan was found unresponsive in the family's unused pool on August 29, 2021, in Munbura, south of Mackay in north Queensland.

He was pronounced dead later that night after being taken to Mackay Base Hospital.

Tara Maree Richardson, 49, was yesterday freed from jail, having been given a five-year suspended sentence for her guilty plea on a charge of domestic violence manslaughter, by way of negligence.

She had spent more than 1,000 days on remand.

Richardson appeared in the Supreme Court in Mackay yesterday via video link from a Townsville prison.

With her head down, Richardson wrote in her notebook as Mr O'Sullivan detailed the impact of their son's death.

Outside court, Mr O'Sullivan said the court process had provided his family with "no answers".

Tarrin O'Sullivan's aunt Lana Mason and father Andrew O'Sullivan. (ABC Tropical North: Liam McNally)

Tarrin's last day

There is still some uncertainty surrounding Tarrin's death.

An autopsy report disclosed findings "consistent with immersion" however "classical" signs of drowning were not present, and a definitive cause of death was never identified.

Justice Christopher Johntsone said Richardson had been inconsistent in her interviews detailing the events on the day Tarrin died, but to the best of the court's knowledge, the afternoon began with him playing while Richardson cleaned the house.

The court heard the pair was alone in the house from noon.

Tarrin moved in and out of the house playing with his bike and in his sandpit and somewhere between about 2 and 2:45pm he came inside for a drink.

By 4:25pm, the court heard Tarrin did not respond to Richardson's call, and she began searching her own and the neighbour's property.

Half an hour later, her then-partner Jason Richardson came home to help the search. He found unresponsive Tarrin in the property's unused pool.

Just after 7pm, Tarrin was declared dead at the Mackay Base Hospital.

The house at Munbura where the boy died in August 2021. (ABC Tropical North: Tobi Loftus)

'Pattern' of neglect

The court heard Richardson had said she felt "smothered" by her non-verbal, autistic son.

The court heard that in the month before Tarrin's death, Department of Child Safety officers visited Richardson's home and raised concerns after seeing the boy only wearing a nappy, about his erratic behaviour, and the cleanliness and safety of the house.

The property's unused "dirty" pool had a fence, but it was not safety compliant and there were toys and items around that could have been used to climb, and Tarrin was known to be able to climb fences.

In a victim impact statement, Richardson's adult daughter, Tayla Richardson, said caring for her children was never her mother's priority.

"It is about a pattern I experienced throughout my life, where my mother's own priorities appeared to come before the safety, wellbeing and needs of her own children."

Justice Johnstone said while the exact mechanism of death was uncertain, "a consistent lack of supervision" contributed.

"You were overwhelmed as a parent, you were not responding appropriately as a parent and you were not doing all that you were required to do as a mother of a highly vulnerable child," he said.

Richardson's barrister Anna Cappellano said mitigating factors in her client's offending included her bipolar disorder diagnosis and having no criminal history.

Tarrin O'Sullivan died in 2021. (ABC News: Tegan Philpott)

Charge change

Richardson was arrested more than two years after Tarrin's death and originally charged with murder.

Before her sentencing yesterday, her charge was downgraded and she subsequently pleaded guilty to manslaughter.

In his victim impact statement, Mr O'Sullivan, who was living separately to Richardson at the time of their son's death, said the lower charge was an "insult" to his child's memory.

"The one person that I believe gave up on my son that day was his mother, and it still haunts me and gives me heartache to know that," he said.

"I felt there was no justice for my son should Tara Richardson walk free today or in the near future.

"She gets to go home and my son will never do that again."

Justice Johnstone criticised the impact statement for questioning the way justice was administered.

He later said Richardson was sentenced on the basis that Tarrin's death was a result of neglect "as opposed to something more sinister".

After the sentencing, Mr O'Sullivan said he would pursue a coronial inquest to try to find more information about his son's death.

World.title: Football Queensland clubs push back on governing body's fee changes
World.content:
More than 100 Queensland football clubs have called on the state's governing body to be more transparent regarding major decisions about player registration fees.

In a group statement, the clubs called on Football Queensland (FQ) to pause its new Competition Access Fee (CAF), saying an increase in fees could make the sport unaffordable for families.

Football Queensland is disputing the clubs' claims that player fees have dramatically increased, adding it has the lowest fees in the country.

"FQ's illustrative modelling shows that, where a club passes the CAF through directly, the total paid by a participant is broadly comparable to 2026," a spokesperson from Football Queensland said.

Wynnum Wolves Football Club president Rabieh Krayem penned a letter to Football Queensland petitioning against what he said was an unjustified increase in fees and expressing concern about the effect this could have on participation.

Wynnum Wolves president Rabieh Krayem penned a letter to Football Queensland. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

"The consequences for participation in 2027 may be significant," he said in the letter.

" Families—particularly those registering multiple players or managing cost-of-living pressures—may decide that football is no longer affordable. "

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli urged all sporting governing bodies to lower costs for families.

"We want to see more kids in sport and anything that administrations can do to follow suit and lower costs is something that we should be backing," he said.

'Serious shock to clubs'

Mr Krayem sent the letter on behalf of 71 football clubs.

"The scale of the increase introduced through the 2027 CAF model was therefore unexpected and has come as a serious shock to clubs across Queensland," he wrote.

Mr Krayem applied Football Queensland's new fees to his club in Wynnum and determined charges from the governing body would increase by 64.6 per cent for 2027.

Hidden cost of kids' sport Research finds families spend thousands more than just registration fees.

"An increase of this magnitude cannot reasonably be treated as routine without a detailed cost justification," he said.

"Clubs do not have the financial capacity to absorb an increase of this scale, and the additional FQ cost will therefore be passed on to players and parents through higher registration fees."

In a statement, Football Queensland said the "inflation adjusted changes" within the CAF reflect less than a $10 per person increase.

The governing body provided its own modelling that shows in 2026, a senior player would pay a total of $1,417.26 in total fees to play. For 2027, after all fees are consolidated into the new CAF, a senior player would be charged $1,415.88.

"We note that between 90 per cent and 97 per cent of fees paid by participants are received by clubs and not Football Queensland," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added the new fee structure "will provide a reduction in administrative complexity and a significant lowering of administrative transaction volumes across the ecosystem".

World.title: Man charged over damage to Tasmania's Parliament House, Hobart casino
World.content:
A 44-year-old man has been charged after allegedly breaking several windows and two glass doors at Parliament House in Hobart on Saturday night.

Police were called about 11.20pm after 10 windows and two glass doors were damaged, including the front door to Parliament House.

Police say the damage to Tasmania's Parliament House occurred late on Saturday night. (ABC News: Meg Whitfield)

No entry was gained to the building.

Police allege the Dover man was also involved in breaking 26 glass panels at the Wrest Point Convention and Entertainment Centre in the early hours of Monday morning, in the Hobart suburb of Sandy Bay.

"Significant repairs and replacement costs are expected in both incidents," Tasmania Police said in a statement.

"Following investigations, police obtained a warrant for the man's arrest.

"He was located and arrested in Hobart on Tuesday, 6 October, before being taken to Hobart Police Station."

No entry was gained to the parliament building. (ABC News: Meg Whitfield)

Police say 10 windows were smashed. (ABC News: Meg Whitfield)

The man was charged with offences relating to the destruction of property and will next appear in the Hobart Magistrates Court in January.

Repairs on the damaged windows at Parliament House began on Sunday morning.

World.title: Lawyers for man who stabbed wife to death say no evidence he'd be violent again
World.content:
Lawyers for an elderly man who stabbed his wife to death in their home in Canberra's south have said there is no evidence to suggest he would act violently again.

Police found the body of Wanda Uhle, 78, on the floor of the couple's Gordon property, covered by a doona in June 2024.

Manfred Uhle was taken into custody at the home of a family member in Fadden a short time later and charged with murder.

He had told family members that he had fought with Mrs Uhle, believing she had had an affair with their neighbour, something the ACT Supreme Court found there was no evidence of.

Now 88 years old, and with a likely diagnosis of dementia, he was found unfit to plead earlier this year.

It meant that rather than a trial, the case proceeded by way of a special hearing.

Last month, Justice Andrew Muller ruled he was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt the elements for the offence of murder had been met.

The court will set a nominal sentence, but the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal will determine how Uhle is cared for in future.

'Degree of malice': prosecution

Police outside the Gordon home where 78-year-old woman Wanda Dorothy Uhle was killed in 2024. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

Today, prosecutor Sam McLaughlin said there was currently no other option than jail for accommodating Uhle.

And he argued the nominal sentence must reflect the seriousness of the crime, regardless of Uhle's condition at the time of the killing.

"Clearly the offender's reduced moral culpability cannot overwhelm the sentencing exercise," Mr McLaughlin said.

"The irresistible finding of the court must be, particularly given the admissions made by Mr Uhle later in the day, that the accused must have intended to cause the death of the deceased.

"The victim was, of course, significantly vulnerable, not only because of her advanced age but because at the commission of the offence she was asleep in bed.

"It is not without a degree of malice."

Mr McLaughlin told the court Uhle's "prognosis is poor" and his conditions were likely to worsen, presenting a risk to the community.

"The predictor of the future is the past," he said.

Case 'fairly unique': defence

Defence lawyer Jan de Bruin said no alternative to jail had yet been found to accommodate his client.

But he argued there had been no allegations of Uhle acting violently during his time in custody, including while being treated in hospital, and said he would present very limited risks if accommodated in a suitable aged care facility.

"This is a fairly unique type of case … there is nothing similar to this case I could find searching through case law," Dr de Bruin said.

" General deterrence and specific deterrence have little weight here. "

The court reserved its decision for a later date.

Uhle remains in custody in Canberra's jail.

World.title: Inquiry hears delegate felt he 'brought danger' to his family after CFMEU comments
World.content:
An organiser with the Australian Workers Union has recounted the moment a CFMEU member allegedly made sinister comments about his young family during a confrontation near a Brisbane work site.

James Downie told the Queensland inquiry into the CFMEU the comments came during a sustained campaign of harassment and intimidation by the CFMEU against members of the rival union during visits to work sites.

In mid-2023, Mr Downie and a colleague went to visit the Cross River Rail development in Woolloongabba when they were set upon by a large group of CFMEU members.

James Downie told the inquiry a CFMEU member made sinister comments about his young family. (ABC News)

The CFMEU men allegedly screamed insults at them as they tried to exit the site, ripped at Mr Downie's backpack, and started shoving him as he tried to cross Stanley Street and into the safety of a nearby shopping centre.

As he crossed, he said he was nearly pushed into traffic.

"They charged at me with such force that I was bumped off the pedestrian walkway and there was a large truck … coming at me," he said.

"I had to throw my body back at the pedestrian crossing to get back onto the street, because if I hadn't, I would've been hit by the truck."

Loading...

He said the truck was so close he felt the wind on his backpack.

"After that I just started running," he said.

Mr Downie told the inquiry the CFMEU mob cornered the two AWU representatives at the stairs leading into the shopping centre. The moment was captured on CCTV and played to the hearing.

During this interaction, Mr Downie said the CFMEU men were trying to goad him into fighting them.

Loading...

When he refused, Mr Downie said they asked: "Is that what you teach your kids?"

He said he told the men he had no kids, to which he says one replied, "we know you have two sons".

"Then they gave the name of my sons and where they went to school, and to daycare, and my patterns and what I did in my personal life."

Counsel assisting the inquiry asked Mr Downie what he was thinking at that moment.

"That my job had crossed over to my personal life, and I'd brought danger to my family," he responded.

Mr Downie said another member of the CFMEU then told the others the "message has been sent" and they dispersed.

Delegates blocked from visiting members

The inquiry heard about several hostile interactions between the CFMEU and AWU around this time.

CFMEU inquiry hears Dutton Park brawl details A commission of inquiry into the Queensland branch of the CFMEU has heard a group of workers were attacked by union members at a Cross River Rail site in Dutton Park.

On several occasions CFMEU members physically blocked AWU delegates from entering sites to visit their members.

Some of these interactions were captured on phone footage and played to the hearing.

During these incidents, large groups of CFMEU members can be heard yelling insults at the AWU delegates and daring them to try and push past their blockades.

Mr Downie said on one occasion, out the front of the Cultural Centre bus stop upgrade, he was told "take a step forward, you're not getting through, I'm a boxing champion, I'll put you out straight away".

Fearing for their safety, Mr Downie said they decided to leave without visiting members.

World.title: Australia among top picks for Chinese tourists during Golden Week holiday
World.content:
When Fei Chang and her husband landed in the Whitsundays for their holiday, they were shocked to find it filled with Chinese tourists.

"At some tourist spots, it felt like I could almost speak Mandarin to everyone," she said.

Ms Chang and her husband were among the Chinese tourists who visited Australia over the past week, during China's week-long national day holiday that ends today.

This year, the timing of the three-day Mid-Autumn Festival public holiday together with Golden Week from October 1 to 7 gave people 13 days off.

Fei Chang and her husband enjoyed visiting beaches in Sydney. (Supplied: Fei Chang)

Australia was one of the most sought-after destinations for Chinese travellers, according to one of China's popular travel booking platforms Trip.com.

The company said people were also taking "longer and further trips beyond the region" this year.

International Air Transport Association (IATA) data showed that flight bookings from China to Australia for October 2026 were up 19 per cent compared to October 2025.

There were also more than 2.2 million inbound and outbound passengers during the Mid-August Festival, according to China's official immigration data, a 16.8 per cent increase compared to the same holiday last year.

Zhang Cheng, a Melbourne travel agent and owner of Great Wall Travel Services, told the ABC that she had received a surge in bookings over the past week.

Her agency takes bookings primarily from Chinese-speaking tourists.

The number of Chinese tourists in Australia is yet to return to pre-COVID highs. (Supplied: Fei Chang)

However, Ms Zhang was not sure how many of those tourists were from overseas and how many were from the Chinese-speaking community in Australia.

"We are fully booked with two-day tours to the Great Ocean Road," she said.

This week, Ms Zhang is taking a group of Chinese-speaking tourists to Canberra for one of the biggest horticultural shows in the Southern Hemisphere.

Tourists prefer 'quality trips'

Ms Chang says she was shocked to see so many Chinese tourists in Australia. (Reuters: David Gray, file)

China was Australia's second-largest inbound tourist market in 2025, according to Tourism Research Australia.

In 2025, Australia saw 1.04 million visitors from China, a 17 per cent increase year-on-year.

However, this was still below the 1.4 million visitors from China pre-COVID, in 2019.

Ms Zhang said before the pandemic, people tended to travel in big groups.

But they now prefer "quality trips" in small groups or going on road trip by themselves, she said.

Chinese guided-tour groups sometimes operate under the Approved Destination Status (ADS) scheme, which is a bilateral agreement that facilitates group tours from China to Australia, organised by approved agencies.

The program was paused during COVID and resumed in 2023.

More than 300,000 tourists reportedly joined an ADS group tour in 2019 financial year, according to Austrade data.

In the 2026 financial year, the number of visitors on ADS group trips dropped to 70,205.

World.title: Tensions escalate in Middle East as Houthis target airports
World.content:
The Iran-backed Houthi rebels are continuing to intensify their assaults in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

Yemen's Transport Ministry said the rebels attacked Aden International Airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones early on Wednesday, local time.

The ministry said one missile landed near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land. Authorities diverted the aircraft to Jeddah.

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis.

The Yemeni capital Sanaa is under Houthi control. (AP: Osamah Abdulrahman)

Aden International Airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital, Riyadh.

It said it was tracking the launch platform over the Houthi-controlled city of Sanaa and would destroy the missile, but gave no details of casualties or damage.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones.

There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of an attack on the airport.

Fighting intensifies

The attacks came as fighting intensified on several fronts in Yemen after Saudi-backed government forces launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis, who have made territorial gains along the country's Red Sea coast in recent weeks.

Yemeni government forces, with Saudi-led coalition air support, launched a lightning offensive this week to retake the Red Sea coast around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the city of Mocha, pushing the Houthis out of areas they had seized last month.

Earlier on Wednesday the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards the south-western Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, Saudi state television reported.

More than 184,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the fighting started. (AP: Abdulnasser Alseddik)

In a separate statement, Yahya Saree said the Houthis had attacked Abha International Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait with ballistic missiles and drones.

It was not immediately clear whether this was linked to the missile the coalition said it had intercepted near Khamis Mushait.

Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm an attack on Abha airport.

Reuters

World.title: ‘The system is a farce’: Constitutional expert Anne Twomey slams Albanese golf grant as ‘grey corruption’
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalGovernment grants ‘The system is a farce’: Constitutional expert Anne Twomey slams Albanese golf grant as ‘grey corruption’ Rob Harris October 7, 2026 — 6:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One of Australia’s leading constitutional experts has accused the Albanese government of “grey corruption” over a $6 million grant handed to the prime minister’s local golf club, declaring its grants system a “farce” that dressed up political favours as sound public policy. University of Sydney professor emerita Anne Twomey delivered a blistering assessment of the scheme, warning that politicians should take “lessons in both federalism and integrity” before promising taxpayers’ money to local projects. A golf course in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s electorate was a beneficiary of the grant. AP Twomey told a parliamentary inquiry that that Marrickville Golf Club, in Anthony Albanese’s electorate of Grayndler, had already received five federal grants totalling almost $58,000 before Albanese promised it the $6 million during the 2025 election campaign. The earlier grants were made through programs where local MPs could nominate organisations for funding and were classified as “closed, non-competitive”. Twomey said this meant there was no meaningful comparison with other projects to establish whether the club had the greatest need for taxpayers’ money.



“They were effectively gifts of political largesse, funded by taxpayers,” she wrote in a submission to the senate inquiry into the scheme. The probe was sparked after the Centre for Public Integrity released an investigation in September which found nearly three-quarters of the Albanese government’s $560.9 million Major and Local Community Infrastructure Program was allocated to notionally Labor-held or competitive seats. “They were effectively gifts of political largesse, funded by taxpayers.” Constitutional expert Anne Twomey Twomey said the original design of the program was itself constitutionally invalid because the Commonwealth did not have a general power to directly fund local sporting and community facilities. The scheme was subsequently changed, so grants could flow through state or local government bodies under section 96 of the Constitution. Twomey said that alteration appeared to make the Marrickville grant constitutionally valid. But she warned the government still had to comply with laws requiring public money to be spent efficiently, effectively, economically and ethically.



Related Article Government grants ‘Crime only happens in Labor seats’: Coalition claims Labor rorting crime grants “The system is a farce, with the paperwork drafted to justify decisions already made without any consideration of merit, need, value for money or the public interest,” she wrote. She said the grant rules had effectively been constructed to give the public appearance of integrity while allowing politicians to deliver promises already made. Twomey pointed to the Marrickville club’s history of federal funding, including grants for clubhouse toilets and lockers, computer upgrades, energy-saving lights and benches around the course. Some were awarded while the Coalition was in government. But Twomey noted Albanese was the local member throughout the period and had the power to nominate organisations under the relevant programs.



Albanese announced the $6.05 million commitment in April 2025, promising to “secure the future” of the club. The NSW government separately provided $269,500 in 2025 to connect the clubhouse to the sewer system and prevent reliance on septic tanks that could overflow during floods. Marrickville Golf Club has received $6 million for upgrades from the federal government in a controversial “invite-only” grants program. Janie Barrett The announcement came without reference to his honorary membership of the club, which was later revealed by the ABC. Albanese said he did not know he held the honorary membership and had not visited the clubhouse “for many, many years”. Twomey invoked the Productivity Commission’s description of politically driven grants as “grey corruption” – a term used by commissioner Danielle Wood for government decisions that favour private or political interests over the national interest.



“Federal politicians should not be making election promises about specific local projects and should not be making promises for the spending of public money based on political self interest rather than the public interest,” she wrote. Related Article Opinion

Political leadership It’s not an ABC journalist who should do better. It’s the prime minister himself Rob Harris National correspondent Twomey also cited research by Labor MP Andrew Leigh, then an academic, into the Coalition’s sports grants scandal, arguing politically directed grants did not necessarily deliver electoral rewards. “No, this is not about ‘being a good local member’,” she wrote. “It is about indulging in grey corruption and the misuse of public money at the public’s expense.” Federal Infrastructure Minister Catherine King has defended the program as in line with longstanding practice and with updated rules and principles for grants. World.title: Exporting coal, owning the damage: a legal reckoning arrives for Australian mining
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeClimate policy Exporting coal, owning the damage: a legal reckoning arrives for Australian mining Nick O'Malley October 7, 2026 — 6:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The decision by the High Court that NSW coal mines must account for the emissions caused by the product when burnt overseas is “a game changer” for coal production across the country, says Professor Jacqueline Peel, an international climate law expert with the University of Melbourne. Emissions from coal mining are under growing legal threat. AP At first blush, the ruling is far more narrow than that. The court found that under NSW planning law, miners have to account for the climate damage done by their pollution. In the past, this has been interpreted to focus on what are known as “scope one” emissions – that is, pollution created in NSW in the process of digging the stuff up. Now the High Court has found that under NSW planning law, miners must also account for “scope three” emissions – the pollution created when the coal is burnt by their overseas customers – and decision-makers have to consider whether measures are needed to mitigate these emissions. If this is the case, then mines in other states should not be affected. So far. But as Sue Higginson, a NSW Greens MP and veteran environment lawyer, says you can bet that there are climate activists closely reading planning rules in other states to see if they can take down polluting mines around the country.



Of course, governments can legislate to change their planning laws and regulations to protect the industry, but over time this will come at increasing political cost. Related Article Climate policy Fire, cyclones, extreme heat: Albanese’s hellish summer forecast “The High Court is the High Court,” says Higginson. “It surpasses any environment courts, any tribunals and, of course, any of the states’ supreme courts. “When governments do things like that, and act outside and above the environmental rule of law when it’s been dictated and determined by the High Court, that is significant risk to democracy.” Nonetheless, governments have done this in the past, and it is hard to imagine an Australian government would allow a court decision to kill off a major industry. The federal opposition and mining groups are already calling for the NSW and federal governments to introduce legislation to protect it from what the industry calls “lawfare”.



But this case does not come in isolation. Last year the International Court of Justice issued a landmark advisory opinion establishing that governments have a legal duty under international and human rights law to protect the climate system. According to Peel, there are more than 3600 climate cases either already adjudicated or pending in various jurisdictions around the world. Many of them, including the case just decided by the High Court, make reference to the ICJ opinion. Related Article High Court of Australia ‘Groundbreaking’: High Court quashes coal mine expansion over climate emissions The US Supreme Court is now hearing arguments in another blockbuster climate case. There, Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing a case brought by local officials demanding that they be forced to help pay for climate damage. Higginson believes the High Court decision could have an immediate impact on the NSW Independent Planning Commission’s approval last month of the Hunter Valley Operations Continuation Project to extend the life of the HVO North and HVO South coal mines, which could create 793.8 million tonnes of scope three emissions. This surge of litigation is no coincidence, but a reflection of a set of facts that is becoming harder to ignore. The cost and human toll of climate change is no longer a future fear but an immediate fact confronting communities and nations around the world.



At the same time attribution science – experts’ ability to attribute climate disasters to carbon pollution from specific fossil fuel projects – is rapidly improving. Just last month the University of NSW launched a new open-source climate tool – the Carbon Impacts Tracer – to do just that. It harnessed research published by experts from six universities in Australia and the United Kingdom on the damage that corresponds with emissions from the newly approved Scarborough gas project in Western Australia. Related Article Updated

Mining Largest coal mining proposal in state’s history wins approval It found that 876 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions from the Scarborough project would expose an extra 516,000 people worldwide to unprecedented heat, resulting in 484 heat-related deaths in Europe by 2100 and destroying millions more coral colonies during every future mass bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef. The Mount Pleasant coal mine expansion case decided by the High Court of Australia involved an estimated 859 million tonnes of scope three emissions.



Even if the NSW or federal government steps in to change laws to protect the Mount Pleasant mine, or mining in Australia more broadly, the cases are going to keep coming as climate damage becomes more lethal and costly, and the science proving the impacts steadily improves. Given that our legal system is based on the notion that those injured should be able to seek remedy from those who injure, industries and governments causing climate damage cannot expect that they will be allowed to endlessly duck responsibility. “Eventually, if there’s lots of these cases coming at different angles, then they may overwhelm the efforts trying to shut them down through legislation,” says Peel. Higginson believes we are at a crossroads. “We are literally at the confluence of law, science, community expectation, morality, and survival – we’re here.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Cryptic billboards have Powderfinger fans in a whirl of wonder
World.content:
NationalQueenslandEntertainment Cryptic billboards have Powderfinger fans in a whirl of wonder Dominique Tassell and Courtney Kruk October 7, 2026 — 5:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cryptic billboards in three of Australia’s major cities have prompted rumours that iconic homegrown band Powderfinger is set to reunite, 16 years on from their break-up, and almost a decade from their last performance. Photos of billboards in Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney have been shared to an Instagram account called The Return of the Electric Horsemen, which could be a reference to the band’s song (Return of) The Electric Horseman from their 1996 album Double Allergic. Brisbane’s billboard was located on the corner of James and Ann streets in Fortitude Valley. The billboard on the corner of James and Ann streets hints at a Powderfinger reunion. The Return of the Electric Horsemen The account’s most recent post is a video with “Melbourne, do you see the signs on the street now?” written over it.



“I’ll watch from the other side of the road,” the caption reads. The caption could be a reference to the opening line of the song My Happiness: “I see your shadow on the street now.” Brisbane band Powderfinger broke up in 2010 and last performed together in 2017. The Return of the Electric Horsemen account does not follow anyone, but the official Powderfinger account does follow them. Powderfinger, made up of Bernard Fanning, Darren Middleton, Ian Haug, Jon Coghill and John Collins, formed in 1989 and broke up in 2010.



Fanning went on to have a successful solo career, and last released music in 2024. Middleton last toured in 2016 for a solo project; the official Powderfinger Instagram account was spruiking a new album by Haug’s band, The Church, just two weeks ago; and Coghill studied at Griffith University after the band broke up before working as a journalist for the ABC. Collins is currently Queensland’s first Night-Life Economy Commissioner, a role to which he was appointed in 2024. The last time the band performed was in 2017.



In the dying minutes of his solo set at Splendour in the Grass in 2017, former Powderfinger lead singer Bernard Fanning made an announcement that sparked an eruption of excitement from hundreds of unsuspecting festival goers. Related Article Queensland government Night-life tsar hands over plan to incentivise live music “It’s been 10 years since Powderfinger played Splendour, so let’s have a little anniversary,” Fanning said. Fans perched above the Amphitheatre leapt to their feet and screamed with approval as Fanning’s former bandmates – Middleton, Haug and Collins – readied their instruments. Drummer Coghill was the only absent member. For about 15 brief but glorious minutes, punters were transported back to the 2000s to relish in two of the Brisbane rockers’ most iconic hits: (Baby I’ve Got You) On My Mind and These Days.



So, could it be coming ’round again? Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.
