World.title: The biggest media deal in history has all the hallmarks of Trump’s America
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing The biggest media deal in history has all the hallmarks of Trump’s America Calum Jaspan October 7, 2026 — 5:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two of Hollywood’s five top film studios have officially merged, capping two years of disruption to the world’s traditional media industry in a deal spearheaded by the son of a major Trump ally who also happens to be the world’s eighth-richest man. Paramount’s buyout of Warner Bros Discovery valued the latter at $159 billion, making it the biggest media deal in history. And the creation of the new merged entity, dubbed Skydance, has all the hallmarks of Trump’s America. The merger of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery has created the biggest media player in the world. Bloomberg Bankrolled by Skydance boss David Ellison’s father – Oracle founder and tech oligarch Larry Ellison – with a little help from private equity and three Middle Eastern sovereign funds, the deal has had its fair share of critics. But with it now set in stone, David Ellison holds the keys to an entertainment and news business juggernaut, and that could change how you and I watch our favourite shows in the future. Given it is one of the biggest disruptors to global media in the 21st century, the marriage of Paramount and Warner Bros has understandably received widespread condemnation for how it will affect the livelihoods of thousands of workers in the entertainment and media industries.



More than 1400 members of the entertainment industry, including the likes of actors Javier Bardem and Ben Stiller, signed an open letter this year opposing the deal, arguing it would result in a reduced industry. Related Article Opinion

Film & TV production As media moguls show Warner Bros the money, keep an eye on CNN – and US democracy Bill Wyman Contributor Hollywood actor Mark Ruffalo, who starred in HBO show Task last year, has been one of the most outspoken critics, arguing last week that the deal will stifle creativity, weaken free speech and cost jobs. Coveted prize comes with baggage David Ellison – the man heading up the combined company – has plans to use technology to cut costs and transform Skydance into a media machine that can go toe to toe with the likes of Netflix and others that turned traditional media on its head.



Netflix almost picked up the Warner Bros film studio and home of “prestige TV” HBO in a bidding war with Ellison earlier this year. But Ellison, who had his eyes set on Warner Bros even before he took control of Paramount last year, managed to beat Netflix to the prize with a godfather offer, which does come with some hefty baggage. Skydance boss David Ellison has paid a very hefty price to get his hands on his prize. Bloomberg Newly minted Skydance now has more than $100 billion in debt to deal with, on top of a host of legacy media headaches which Netflix decided weren’t worth breaking the bank on. “Congratulations on saying the biggest number, you f---ing morons,” one of HBO’s most famous characters, Logan Roy, told his kids in the smash hit Succession. Ellison now owns the rights to that show, and it looks like his tycoon father didn’t quite have the same advice when it comes to overpaying for a prize simply because you have to have it. The Oracle founder personally stumped up $57 billion to guarantee his son’s deal went through.



What does it mean for Australian consumers? While this might all seem like problems for our friends across the Pacific to deal with, it does have local implications. Australians spend more time watching TV shows and movies on paid streaming services than they do any other way, be that live free-to-air TV, catch-up or on social media, according to the Australian Communications and Media Authority. Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump Hail to the king: Trump will steer battle for the future of Hollywood Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Our culture is increasingly shaped by global, US-dominated programming. Occasionally, there is a homemade hit. But more and more, the content that defines “water cooler” conversations is produced and paid for by companies overseas – except for live sport. Most people will have crossed paths with content produced by either of the film studios in the merger, in the past weeks, months or years. WBD produced mega hits such as Barbie, One Battle After Another, the series, Sinners and F1. Recent Paramount movies include Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning and Gladiator II.



And most will have seen some of HBO’s famous back catalogue, such as Veep, The Wire and The Sopranos, or ongoing programming like The White Lotus and House of the Dragon. Paramount has its own hits, such as Yellowstone, Landman and The Agency. Many of these productions will end up on a newly merged service, with Skydance planning to combine HBO Max and Paramount+. Under what name is unknown, and we also don’t know what it will cost. Skydance signage in Times Square, New York, this week. Bloomberg Part of the rationale for the deal includes the thesis that by bringing HBO Max and Paramount+ together, a combined service with a greater back catalogue and pipeline of programming will be able to compete with Netflix more effectively. But for consumers, this will probably eventually mean greater costs, particularly when the company adjusts its price point to reflect what used to be two different products. Skydance also owns news services CBS and CNN and a slew of television stations, including Network 10 locally.



The mega-deal poses new challenges for the global entertainment industry, politics and for consumers of all that the industry produces. The company has appointed a new co-CEO, Ynon Kreiz from toy giant Mattel, whose central task will be finding more than $8.5 billion in cost savings over the next three years. Kreiz cut thousands of jobs during his eight years at Mattel. David Ellison has sought to sell the deal as a positive for the public, by placing new technology, the sector in which his father made his billions, at the centre of the transformation. Expect greater innovation, he says. The most immediate impact on Australia’s third commercial network could be the trickle down of those cost cuts. If you’re expecting to see some of HBO’s biggest shows, like Game of Thrones, on free-to-air as part of this deal, don’t hold your breath. ‘Terrific people’ for Trump Skydance has already made some executive and board decisions, such as appointing Kreiz, ditching the WBD studio heads and appointing former British prime minister Tony Blair as an adviser to its board.



Larry Ellison has donated hundreds of millions to the Tony Blair institute. Ellison is also a major Trump donor. Donald Trump praised both Ellisons after the deal’s closure. Larry Ellison has a close relationship with US President Donald Trump. Bloomberg “They’re terrific people, and it’s going to be a great company,” the US president said, though the younger Ellison has since sought to distance himself from Trump. “We want to speak to everybody,” Ellison said. “We do not want to politicise the company.” But political interference has become a hallmark of Ellison’s initial takeover of Paramount a year ago. He installed a news chief at CBS, Bari Weiss, who is considered friendly to Trump and Israel. Larry Ellison has donated heavily to Israeli causes over the years. Part of the WBD deal includes a measure to implement a standalone board to protect CNN’s editorial independence. CNN staff had feared David Ellison would bring the network under Weiss as well.



But CNN’s existing chief executive, Mark Thompson, looks as if he is sticking around for now, with Ellison telling staff after the deal closed that “we believe in complete editorial independence”. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America ‘Fake news’ v faker-in-chief: Why Trump’s media war is backfiring Bruce Wolpe Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer He also plans to keep CNN and CBS separate, for now, and said he backs CNN’s legal fight against Trump after the president banned the outlet from the White House. With the deal done, Ellison’s Skydance is the new king of the castle. Hollywood and the golden age of prestige television are in for a change. Whether it’s for the better remains to be seen. World.content:
Just returning to Liberal senator Dave Sharma on ABC News for a moment, and he was also asked about today being the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks in Israel.

Sharma, a former ambassador to Israel, said he reflected on the day “with incredible sadness”.

People mark the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel at the site of the Nova music festival in Israel. AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg

“It unleashed terrible conflict in the Middle East costing tens of thousands of lives … [but] most concerning for me [was] the mood that was allowed to take hold after October 7, that sought to hold Jewish Australian accountable for the actions of a foreign state,” he said.

Sharma said what followed Hamas’ attacks and Israel’s response in Gaza was “the worst uprising of antisemitism in Australia’s history”, which “led very directly to the horrific, the worst terror attack in Bondi”.

World.title: Final pieces falling into place for Everest field to tackle champion
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Final pieces falling into place for Everest field to tackle champion Craig Kerry October 7, 2026 — 5:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Only two, or maybe three, slots are left to fill in the $20 million Everest after a busy 24 hours of announcements. As expected, premier trainer Chris Waller and his partners confirmed Joliestar would represent them for a third consecutive year in the race on October 17 at Randwick. James McDonald and Joliestar win the Canterbury Stakes. Getty Images Later on Wednesday, Coolmore announced seven-year-old Giga Kick would take its slot, after the breeding giant’s $30 million colt and likely selection Guest House was ruled out for the spring with a hamstring injury on Saturday. The confirmations followed news late on Tuesday from Jimmysstar’s managing owner Ozzie Kheir on SEN that the Ciaron Maher-trained galloper, which was third in the race last year, would run again. Kheir said Nash Rawiller would ride Jimmysstar, and a deal would be finalised within 24 hours. Jimmysstar ran in the TAB slot last year and it was expected they would combine again, but no confirmation had come late on Wednesday afternoon.



If a deal is done, it would leave just bloodstock agent James Harron and racing heavyweights Yulong left to confirm their runners to round out the 12-horse field. Angel Capital, which ran in the Coolmore slot last year, was expected to get owner Yulong’s position. Ninja (Fairway Thoroughbred), Headwall (Neil Werrett and partners), Tempted (Godolphin), Blue Door (Newgate-GPI Racing), Savvy Hallie (Mulberry Racing) and Spicy Martini (Inglis) were the others confirmed to take on defending champion and $1.30 favourite Ka Ying Rising, which races in the Hong Kong Jockey Club slot leased from the Australian Turf Club. Everest favourite Ka Ying Rising. Getty Images Clayton Douglas-trained Giga Kick, which won the Everest in 2022 then was second in 2024 to Bella Nipotina, was perhaps the most surprising after the seven-year-old finished four lengths away eighth in the Manikato Stakes last start. Sydney jockey Dylan Gibbons, fresh from his group 1 Flight Stakes win on Global Goal, gained the ride. He was eighth aboard Matt Smith-trained Buenos Noches with his only ride in the race, in 2023.



“It’s a nice little pick up,” Gibbons said. “Obviously, Global Goal’s been a bit of a help there. I was fortunate enough they picked me after Mark [Zahra] would have been committed to Half Yours [in the Caulfield Cup]. Giga Kick winning the 2022 Everest. Getty Images “There’s only 12 in it, so you need to be going all right to find a ride in that race. “His picture’s there on the wall [at Randwick], and he’s run second in it before, so he loves the race and any rain around is going to be a positive, so hopefully we can get a few favours. I’m pretty sure he’s going to have the blinkers on, too.” Joliestar, now six-year-old, was fifth last year in the Everest and seventh in 2024. She looked on track for another shot after a strong finish to come a close second in The Shorts (1100m) on September 19. It was Australia’s champion sprinter of last season’s first run back from her UK trip, where she was third in the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee at Ascot.

Twomey invoked the Productivity Commission’s description of politically driven grants as “grey corruption” – a term used by commissioner Danielle Wood for government decisions that favour private or political interests over the national interest.



“Federal politicians should not be making election promises about specific local projects and should not be making promises for the spending of public money based on political self interest rather than the public interest,” she wrote. Related Article Opinion

Political leadership It’s not an ABC journalist who should do better. It’s the prime minister himself Rob Harris National correspondent Twomey also cited research by Labor MP Andrew Leigh, then an academic, into the Coalition’s sports grants scandal, arguing politically directed grants did not necessarily deliver electoral rewards. “No, this is not about ‘being a good local member’,” she wrote. “It is about indulging in grey corruption and the misuse of public money at the public’s expense.” Federal Infrastructure Minister Catherine King has defended the program as in line with longstanding practice and with updated rules and principles for grants. World.title: Exporting coal, owning the damage: a legal reckoning arrives for Australian mining
World.content:
EnvironmentClimate changeClimate policy Exporting coal, owning the damage: a legal reckoning arrives for Australian mining Nick O'Malley October 7, 2026 — 6:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The decision by the High Court that NSW coal mines must account for the emissions caused by the product when burnt overseas is “a game changer” for coal production across the country, says Professor Jacqueline Peel, an international climate law expert with the University of Melbourne. Emissions from coal mining are under growing legal threat. AP At first blush, the ruling is far more narrow than that. The court found that under NSW planning law, miners have to account for the climate damage done by their pollution. In the past, this has been interpreted to focus on what are known as “scope one” emissions – that is, pollution created in NSW in the process of digging the stuff up. Now the High Court has found that under NSW planning law, miners must also account for “scope three” emissions – the pollution created when the coal is burnt by their overseas customers – and decision-makers have to consider whether measures are needed to mitigate these emissions. If this is the case, then mines in other states should not be affected. So far. But as Sue Higginson, a NSW Greens MP and veteran environment lawyer, says you can bet that there are climate activists closely reading planning rules in other states to see if they can take down polluting mines around the country.



Of course, governments can legislate to change their planning laws and regulations to protect the industry, but over time this will come at increasing political cost. Related Article Climate policy Fire, cyclones, extreme heat: Albanese’s hellish summer forecast “The High Court is the High Court,” says Higginson. “It surpasses any environment courts, any tribunals and, of course, any of the states’ supreme courts. “When governments do things like that, and act outside and above the environmental rule of law when it’s been dictated and determined by the High Court, that is significant risk to democracy.” Nonetheless, governments have done this in the past, and it is hard to imagine an Australian government would allow a court decision to kill off a major industry. The federal opposition and mining groups are already calling for the NSW and federal governments to introduce legislation to protect it from what the industry calls “lawfare”.



But this case does not come in isolation. Last year the International Court of Justice issued a landmark advisory opinion establishing that governments have a legal duty under international and human rights law to protect the climate system. According to Peel, there are more than 3600 climate cases either already adjudicated or pending in various jurisdictions around the world. Many of them, including the case just decided by the High Court, make reference to the ICJ opinion. Related Article High Court of Australia ‘Groundbreaking’: High Court quashes coal mine expansion over climate emissions The US Supreme Court is now hearing arguments in another blockbuster climate case. There, Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing a case brought by local officials demanding that they be forced to help pay for climate damage. Higginson believes the High Court decision could have an immediate impact on the NSW Independent Planning Commission’s approval last month of the Hunter Valley Operations Continuation Project to extend the life of the HVO North and HVO South coal mines, which could create 793.8 million tonnes of scope three emissions. This surge of litigation is no coincidence, but a reflection of a set of facts that is becoming harder to ignore. The cost and human toll of climate change is no longer a future fear but an immediate fact confronting communities and nations around the world.



At the same time attribution science – experts’ ability to attribute climate disasters to carbon pollution from specific fossil fuel projects – is rapidly improving. Just last month the University of NSW launched a new open-source climate tool – the Carbon Impacts Tracer – to do just that. It harnessed research published by experts from six universities in Australia and the United Kingdom on the damage that corresponds with emissions from the newly approved Scarborough gas project in Western Australia. Related Article Updated

Mining Largest coal mining proposal in state’s history wins approval It found that 876 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions from the Scarborough project would expose an extra 516,000 people worldwide to unprecedented heat, resulting in 484 heat-related deaths in Europe by 2100 and destroying millions more coral colonies during every future mass bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef. The Mount Pleasant coal mine expansion case decided by the High Court of Australia involved an estimated 859 million tonnes of scope three emissions.



Even if the NSW or federal government steps in to change laws to protect the Mount Pleasant mine, or mining in Australia more broadly, the cases are going to keep coming as climate damage becomes more lethal and costly, and the science proving the impacts steadily improves. Given that our legal system is based on the notion that those injured should be able to seek remedy from those who injure, industries and governments causing climate damage cannot expect that they will be allowed to endlessly duck responsibility. “Eventually, if there’s lots of these cases coming at different angles, then they may overwhelm the efforts trying to shut them down through legislation,” says Peel. Higginson believes we are at a crossroads. “We are literally at the confluence of law, science, community expectation, morality, and survival – we’re here.” Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Cryptic billboards have Powderfinger fans in a whirl of wonder
World.content:
NationalQueenslandEntertainment Cryptic billboards have Powderfinger fans in a whirl of wonder Dominique Tassell and Courtney Kruk October 7, 2026 — 5:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cryptic billboards in three of Australia’s major cities have prompted rumours that iconic homegrown band Powderfinger is set to reunite, 16 years on from their break-up, and almost a decade from their last performance. Photos of billboards in Brisbane, Melbourne and Sydney have been shared to an Instagram account called The Return of the Electric Horsemen, which could be a reference to the band’s song (Return of) The Electric Horseman from their 1996 album Double Allergic. Brisbane’s billboard was located on the corner of James and Ann streets in Fortitude Valley. The billboard on the corner of James and Ann streets hints at a Powderfinger reunion. The Return of the Electric Horsemen The account’s most recent post is a video with “Melbourne, do you see the signs on the street now?” written over it.



“I’ll watch from the other side of the road,” the caption reads. The caption could be a reference to the opening line of the song My Happiness: “I see your shadow on the street now.” Brisbane band Powderfinger broke up in 2010 and last performed together in 2017. The Return of the Electric Horsemen account does not follow anyone, but the official Powderfinger account does follow them. Powderfinger, made up of Bernard Fanning, Darren Middleton, Ian Haug, Jon Coghill and John Collins, formed in 1989 and broke up in 2010.



Fanning went on to have a successful solo career, and last released music in 2024. Middleton last toured in 2016 for a solo project; the official Powderfinger Instagram account was spruiking a new album by Haug’s band, The Church, just two weeks ago; and Coghill studied at Griffith University after the band broke up before working as a journalist for the ABC. Collins is currently Queensland’s first Night-Life Economy Commissioner, a role to which he was appointed in 2024. The last time the band performed was in 2017.



In the dying minutes of his solo set at Splendour in the Grass in 2017, former Powderfinger lead singer Bernard Fanning made an announcement that sparked an eruption of excitement from hundreds of unsuspecting festival goers. Related Article Queensland government Night-life tsar hands over plan to incentivise live music “It’s been 10 years since Powderfinger played Splendour, so let’s have a little anniversary,” Fanning said. Fans perched above the Amphitheatre leapt to their feet and screamed with approval as Fanning’s former bandmates – Middleton, Haug and Collins – readied their instruments. Drummer Coghill was the only absent member. For about 15 brief but glorious minutes, punters were transported back to the 2000s to relish in two of the Brisbane rockers’ most iconic hits: (Baby I’ve Got You) On My Mind and These Days.



So, could it be coming ’round again? Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The biggest media deal in history has all the hallmarks of Trump’s America
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing The biggest media deal in history has all the hallmarks of Trump’s America Calum Jaspan October 7, 2026 — 5:40pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two of Hollywood’s five top film studios have officially merged, capping two years of disruption to the world’s traditional media industry in a deal spearheaded by the son of a major Trump ally who also happens to be the world’s eighth-richest man. Paramount’s buyout of Warner Bros Discovery valued the latter at $159 billion, making it the biggest media deal in history. And the creation of the new merged entity, dubbed Skydance, has all the hallmarks of Trump’s America. The merger of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery has created the biggest media player in the world. Bloomberg Bankrolled by Skydance boss David Ellison’s father – Oracle founder and tech oligarch Larry Ellison – with a little help from private equity and three Middle Eastern sovereign funds, the deal has had its fair share of critics. But with it now set in stone, David Ellison holds the keys to an entertainment and news business juggernaut, and that could change how you and I watch our favourite shows in the future. Given it is one of the biggest disruptors to global media in the 21st century, the marriage of Paramount and Warner Bros has understandably received widespread condemnation for how it will affect the livelihoods of thousands of workers in the entertainment and media industries.



More than 1400 members of the entertainment industry, including the likes of actors Javier Bardem and Ben Stiller, signed an open letter this year opposing the deal, arguing it would result in a reduced industry. Related Article Opinion

Film & TV production As media moguls show Warner Bros the money, keep an eye on CNN – and US democracy Bill Wyman Contributor Hollywood actor Mark Ruffalo, who starred in HBO show Task last year, has been one of the most outspoken critics, arguing last week that the deal will stifle creativity, weaken free speech and cost jobs. Coveted prize comes with baggage David Ellison – the man heading up the combined company – has plans to use technology to cut costs and transform Skydance into a media machine that can go toe to toe with the likes of Netflix and others that turned traditional media on its head.



Netflix almost picked up the Warner Bros film studio and home of “prestige TV” HBO in a bidding war with Ellison earlier this year. But Ellison, who had his eyes set on Warner Bros even before he took control of Paramount last year, managed to beat Netflix to the prize with a godfather offer, which does come with some hefty baggage. Skydance boss David Ellison has paid a very hefty price to get his hands on his prize. Bloomberg Newly minted Skydance now has more than $100 billion in debt to deal with, on top of a host of legacy media headaches which Netflix decided weren’t worth breaking the bank on. “Congratulations on saying the biggest number, you f---ing morons,” one of HBO’s most famous characters, Logan Roy, told his kids in the smash hit Succession. Ellison now owns the rights to that show, and it looks like his tycoon father didn’t quite have the same advice when it comes to overpaying for a prize simply because you have to have it. The Oracle founder personally stumped up $57 billion to guarantee his son’s deal went through.



What does it mean for Australian consumers? While this might all seem like problems for our friends across the Pacific to deal with, it does have local implications. Australians spend more time watching TV shows and movies on paid streaming services than they do any other way, be that live free-to-air TV, catch-up or on social media, according to the Australian Communications and Media Authority. Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump Hail to the king: Trump will steer battle for the future of Hollywood Elizabeth Knight Business columnist Our culture is increasingly shaped by global, US-dominated programming. Occasionally, there is a homemade hit. But more and more, the content that defines “water cooler” conversations is produced and paid for by companies overseas – except for live sport. Most people will have crossed paths with content produced by either of the film studios in the merger, in the past weeks, months or years. WBD produced mega hits such as Barbie, One Battle After Another, the series, Sinners and F1. Recent Paramount movies include Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning and Gladiator II.



And most will have seen some of HBO’s famous back catalogue, such as Veep, The Wire and The Sopranos, or ongoing programming like The White Lotus and House of the Dragon. Paramount has its own hits, such as Yellowstone, Landman and The Agency. Many of these productions will end up on a newly merged service, with Skydance planning to combine HBO Max and Paramount+. Under what name is unknown, and we also don’t know what it will cost. Skydance signage in Times Square, New York, this week. Bloomberg Part of the rationale for the deal includes the thesis that by bringing HBO Max and Paramount+ together, a combined service with a greater back catalogue and pipeline of programming will be able to compete with Netflix more effectively. But for consumers, this will probably eventually mean greater costs, particularly when the company adjusts its price point to reflect what used to be two different products. Skydance also owns news services CBS and CNN and a slew of television stations, including Network 10 locally.



The mega-deal poses new challenges for the global entertainment industry, politics and for consumers of all that the industry produces. The company has appointed a new co-CEO, Ynon Kreiz from toy giant Mattel, whose central task will be finding more than $8.5 billion in cost savings over the next three years. Kreiz cut thousands of jobs during his eight years at Mattel. David Ellison has sought to sell the deal as a positive for the public, by placing new technology, the sector in which his father made his billions, at the centre of the transformation. Expect greater innovation, he says. The most immediate impact on Australia’s third commercial network could be the trickle down of those cost cuts. If you’re expecting to see some of HBO’s biggest shows, like Game of Thrones, on free-to-air as part of this deal, don’t hold your breath. ‘Terrific people’ for Trump Skydance has already made some executive and board decisions, such as appointing Kreiz, ditching the WBD studio heads and appointing former British prime minister Tony Blair as an adviser to its board.



Larry Ellison has donated hundreds of millions to the Tony Blair institute. Ellison is also a major Trump donor. Donald Trump praised both Ellisons after the deal’s closure. Larry Ellison has a close relationship with US President Donald Trump. Bloomberg “They’re terrific people, and it’s going to be a great company,” the US president said, though the younger Ellison has since sought to distance himself from Trump. “We want to speak to everybody,” Ellison said. “We do not want to politicise the company.” But political interference has become a hallmark of Ellison’s initial takeover of Paramount a year ago. He installed a news chief at CBS, Bari Weiss, who is considered friendly to Trump and Israel. Larry Ellison has donated heavily to Israeli causes over the years. Part of the WBD deal includes a measure to implement a standalone board to protect CNN’s editorial independence. CNN staff had feared David Ellison would bring the network under Weiss as well.



But CNN’s existing chief executive, Mark Thompson, looks as if he is sticking around for now, with Ellison telling staff after the deal closed that “we believe in complete editorial independence”. Related Article Opinion

Trump's America ‘Fake news’ v faker-in-chief: Why Trump’s media war is backfiring Bruce Wolpe Senior fellow at the US Studies Centre and former political staffer He also plans to keep CNN and CBS separate, for now, and said he backs CNN’s legal fight against Trump after the president banned the outlet from the White House. With the deal done, Ellison’s Skydance is the new king of the castle. Hollywood and the golden age of prestige television are in for a change. Whether it’s for the better remains to be seen. World.title: Final pieces falling into place for Everest field to tackle champion
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Final pieces falling into place for Everest field to tackle champion Craig Kerry October 7, 2026 — 5:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Only two, or maybe three, slots are left to fill in the $20 million Everest after a busy 24 hours of announcements. As expected, premier trainer Chris Waller and his partners confirmed Joliestar would represent them for a third consecutive year in the race on October 17 at Randwick. James McDonald and Joliestar win the Canterbury Stakes. Getty Images Later on Wednesday, Coolmore announced seven-year-old Giga Kick would take its slot, after the breeding giant’s $30 million colt and likely selection Guest House was ruled out for the spring with a hamstring injury on Saturday. The confirmations followed news late on Tuesday from Jimmysstar’s managing owner Ozzie Kheir on SEN that the Ciaron Maher-trained galloper, which was third in the race last year, would run again. Kheir said Nash Rawiller would ride Jimmysstar, and a deal would be finalised within 24 hours. Jimmysstar ran in the TAB slot last year and it was expected they would combine again, but no confirmation had come late on Wednesday afternoon.



If a deal is done, it would leave just bloodstock agent James Harron and racing heavyweights Yulong left to confirm their runners to round out the 12-horse field. Angel Capital, which ran in the Coolmore slot last year, was expected to get owner Yulong’s position. Ninja (Fairway Thoroughbred), Headwall (Neil Werrett and partners), Tempted (Godolphin), Blue Door (Newgate-GPI Racing), Savvy Hallie (Mulberry Racing) and Spicy Martini (Inglis) were the others confirmed to take on defending champion and $1.30 favourite Ka Ying Rising, which races in the Hong Kong Jockey Club slot leased from the Australian Turf Club. Everest favourite Ka Ying Rising. Getty Images Clayton Douglas-trained Giga Kick, which won the Everest in 2022 then was second in 2024 to Bella Nipotina, was perhaps the most surprising after the seven-year-old finished four lengths away eighth in the Manikato Stakes last start. Sydney jockey Dylan Gibbons, fresh from his group 1 Flight Stakes win on Global Goal, gained the ride. He was eighth aboard Matt Smith-trained Buenos Noches with his only ride in the race, in 2023.



“It’s a nice little pick up,” Gibbons said. “Obviously, Global Goal’s been a bit of a help there. I was fortunate enough they picked me after Mark [Zahra] would have been committed to Half Yours [in the Caulfield Cup]. Giga Kick winning the 2022 Everest. Getty Images “There’s only 12 in it, so you need to be going all right to find a ride in that race. “His picture’s there on the wall [at Randwick], and he’s run second in it before, so he loves the race and any rain around is going to be a positive, so hopefully we can get a few favours. I’m pretty sure he’s going to have the blinkers on, too.” Joliestar, now six-year-old, was fifth last year in the Everest and seventh in 2024. She looked on track for another shot after a strong finish to come a close second in The Shorts (1100m) on September 19. It was Australia’s champion sprinter of last season’s first run back from her UK trip, where she was third in the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee at Ascot.

World.title: RNZ board member Richard Dellabarca steps in following unexpected resignation of CFO
World.content:
RNZ has taken the step of appointing a board member to complete its end of year accounts after the unexpected resignation of its Chief Financial Officer.

The public broadcaster told staff earlier this week that CFO Hilary Parker had resigned.

"We wish Hilary well," said a spokesperson in a statement.

RNZ said board member Richard Dellabarca, a chartered accountant, is now acting as Chief Financial Officer.

A spokesperson said Dellabarca's appointment would ensure financial leadership during the annual reporting period.

RNZ said it expected to meet the timeframe for reporting its accounts. Last year, the annual report was signed on September 30 and published on October 21.

"As is standard, the accounts are subject to audit before they are finalised."

A spokesperson said all RNZ's key stakeholders had been informed.

A spokesperson for Broadcasting Minister Paul Goldsmith confirmed his office had been notified of the CFO's departure under the no surprises convention.

The change in CFO comes six months after the government spelled out financial expectations for the organisation.

Goldsmith highlighted the public broadcaster's financial performance as the top item in the Letter of Expectation to the Board on March 18, 2026. Improving audience reach and growing trust levels were the other main items.

The Letter noted: "It is a vital, ongoing expectation that RNZ delivers improved performance and represents a value-for-money investment for the Crown as owner. This includes right-sizing operations and increasing efficiency to mitigate reliance on cash reserves and the sale of land to fund operations."

Dellabarca, a Chartered Accountant with a Bachelor of Laws, is currently working out of the RNZ Auckland offices it shares with TVNZ.

Dellabarca is a director of RNZ, North Harbour Rugby Union and commercial vehicle group Keith Andrews, and chair of bio-technology distributor Epic Char.

World.title: Large bush fire burns through 1400 hectares in high country above Lake Whakatipu
World.content:
Audio player for " Latest from scene of fire near Queenstown " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/emergencies_local/1774948%2Flarge-bush-fire-burns-through-1400-hectares-in-high-country-above-lake-whakatipu

Latest from scene of fire near Queenstown Midday Report Download MP3 3m

Firefighters will work until dusk this evening as they continue to tackle a large bush blaze burning in the high country above Lake Whakatipu.

The fire is estimated to have burnt 1400 hectares of mainly tussock and scrub, with areas of trees, Fire and Emergency NZ said.

It was not yet controlled or contained.

The fire had spread from Walter Peak station along the McKinley's Creek area and had also affected parts of adjoining conservation estate and Cecil Peak station.

No homes or buildings were damaged, and there were no structures or livestock at immediate risk

Five helicopters with monsoon buckets had been dropping water on the fire, targeting the most active fire edges, FENZ said.

"Ground crews are continuing structure protection work around the homestead, creating defensible space and strengthening containment lines. An Incident Management Team is directing operations and planning further ahead.

"Firefighting operations will be suspended overnight for safety, with helicopters standing down at last light. A ground crew will remain at Walter Peak to monitor the fire and maintain readiness, enabling crews to resume operations at first light tomorrow," FENZ said.

District Commander Blair Kiely said the fire's behaviour continued to be influenced by steep terrain, the vegetation and changing wind conditions.

There would be five aircraft supporting 23 firefighters, with incident management and support personnel all active on Thursday.

Crews from the Department of Conservation (DOC) were working alongside Fire and Emergency volunteer firefighters.

The fire at Lake Wakatipu as seen on Wednesday morning. SUPPLIED

Earlier, Kiely said today's efforts were focused on extending the contained area and protecting livestock in the vicinity, while maintaining the ability to protect the Walter Peak homestead and associated buildings if wind changes drove the fire nearer.

He said forecast rain could assist suppression efforts but could also create additional operational challenges.

Drifting smoke would continue to be seen and smelled in a wide area, with exact locations changing as the wind shifts, Kiely said.

Air quality around affected areas might be impacted by smoke. Health NZ encouraged at-risk people to:

Keep windows and doors closed.

Set air conditioning systems to recirculate or turn them off.

Air out homes once smoke conditions have improved.

Check on children, older people, and others who may be more vulnerable to smoke.

Keep pets indoors where possible and ensure they have access to clean water and food.

The fire on Tuesday. FENZ

Walter Peak tour operator RealNZ said it would be working with fire investigators to determine how a controlled burn on its land reignited.

Chief executive Dave Beeche said he had been on site today talking to fire crews.

"We had a controlled burn last Wednesday and had an appropriate plan, and FENZ were on site and that all was successful and went well at the time. FENZ believes that that has somehow reignited - so we'll obviously work closely with them to understand how that might have happened," he said.

The fire came within 300 metres of the historic Walter Peak homestead yesterday, prompting the evacuation of 350 guests and staff, he said.

It had since moved up towards the McKinlays Creek area, but there had been no stock or property damage on RealNZ's land, he said.

"There's no further immediate risk to property at our station at the moment," he said.

Beeche said he was grateful for the "hard tireless work" of fire crews and pilots.

Barring any changes overnight, he said RealNZ was hoping to resume tours tomorrow.

Queenstown's mayor John Glover said the blaze was "confronting".

"It's very large, very visible, and the fact that we haven't been able to contain it is top of mind for everyone involved in the response."

Glover said it was normal for high country stations in the area to have burns this time of year to renew land for Spring - but these could get out of control.

"It's a real stark reminder of the fact that our hillsides can be dry and if we get a wild fire it can spread quite easily."

Glover understood the historic Walter Peak homestead had not been damaged, which he was relieved about.

He advised locals to keep boats away from the area, which was across the lake from the central city.

Members of the public on the lake are reminded to stay at least 500 metres offshore to keep clear of where our helicopters are operating.

Kevin Pilbrow

This exclusion zone would be monitored by the Harbourmaster and Coastguard throughout the day to ensure public and firefighter safety, FENZ said.

Queenstown locals and visitors flocked to the lakeside to watch as the fire smoulders.

There was a steady stream of people coming by with their binoculars and cameras.

Thomas Ah Chee said it was sad to see how much land had been blackened by the blaze.

"[It's] pretty devastating to watch and quite a spectacle at night last night. It was glowing red and you could see the fires clear as day," he said.

Demi-Ann Klocek, who was visiting from Brisbane, was surprised to see the scale of the fire while driving towards Glenorchy on Wednesday morning.

"I wasn't expecting to experience bush fires here in Queenstown," she said.

World.title: Loafers Lodge fire trial: Charred remnants of building shown to jury
World.content:
The jury for the Loafers Lodge manslaughter trial have viewed the remnants of the budget accommodation building on Wellington's Adelaide Road.

Five people died when a fire lit by Esarona Lologa tore through the building - with nearly 100 hundred residents inside - in May 2023.

The manslaughter trial of Gregory Bruce Mein, Barry Charles Collins, Glenn Brendan McAllister, and Marie Louise Murphy, for their roles in the maintenance and operation of the building, is in its third day in the High Court at Wellington.

During the tour on Wednesday, court staff pointed out to the jury parts of the building in relation to how they were described in evidential documents.

More than three years on from the fatal fire, the site is boarded up with plywood, spattered with graffiti and in varying states of decay.

Through the building's upper windows, the sky is visible where the fourth floor mezzanine once was.

Here was where victims of the fire; Michael Wahrlich, Melvin Parun, Peter O'Sullivan, Kenneth Barnard and Liam Hockings all lived.

Outdated floor plans hamper rescue attempts

Back in the High Court, Fire and Emergency senior station officer Clark Townsley said he was the first senior officer to arrive at the fire and co-ordinated the initial response.

He told the court that, prior to the fire, firefighters' discussions on how best to approach fires in dense, low socio-economic housing in Wellington used the Loafers Lodge site as an example.

On the night of the fire, Townsley and his crew were alerted to "smoke logging in a building" at 12:26am.

They left the Newtown Fire station about a minute and a half later.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Townsley said they could see smoke, but no flames, when they arrived at the scene at 12:30am.

He said he expected there were many people inside, and he called for more support.

Fire crews jostled by panicked residents

While fire-fighters were setting up breathing equipment, Townsley said he saw people streaming out of the entrance on the northern side of the building.

Panicked residents "abused, jostled and accosted" firefighters telling them the fire was on the third floor and there were people still inside.

Townsley called for police to help with the growing number of agitated people gathering outside the building.

Once inside, Townsley said he did not hear any main alarms and other fire-fighters commented as to how quiet it was on the top floors.

Heading up to the third floor, Townsley told the court he saw thick black smoke and determined that survivability for people on the level was "low but not impossible".

He made the decision to attack the fire on that level "to give those residents the best chance".

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Back on the street, he encountered a man who said he had responsibilities relating to the building, he had access keys and warned him there could be up to 148 people staying in the hostel. That man would turn out to be accused, Glen McAllister.

"He wanted to go back in the building. I said 'no way' but I do need your keys," Townsley said.

He told the jury the building's alarm panels indicated fire was present in multiple areas that, in hindsight, were every where but where the fire actually was.

Another light indicated a potential defect in the system.

Firefighters unaware of the addition of mezzanine level to the building

Shortly before 1am, Townsley received a report that someone was trapped on the mezzanine level but said his crews didn't know where that level was, or how to get there.

Soon after, he was told a person had jumped from the building and had landed on the roof of Zip Electrical next door, suffering a broken leg.

He said he assigned an aerial unit to reach people on the building's roof and, seeing a person signalling from with a flashing light, directed crews to their location as well.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"I was still receiving radio messages from the comms centre that people were trapped in the building and making calls to 111," he said.

Crews inside reported deteriorating conditions and the potential for flashover and withdrew from the building.

"Flashover refers to the heat in area reaching such a temperature that all combustible materials can spontaneously combust. The heat could've been upwards of 1000 degrees. The survivability in these sorts of conditions is very low. Within a matter of seconds it can be fatal for even a fully kitted fire-fighter," Townsley said.

He said a firefighter on the ladder of an aerial appliance reported "intense fire and structural collapse" inside the building.

Having avoided the flashover, fire-fighters targeted the blaze from outside - attempting to cool the building until a crew could be prepped to re-enter the structure to assess conditions.

On re-entering, a team of four firefighters found three bodies on the third floor.

Under cross examination from counsel for Greg Mein, Christopher Stevenson KC, Townsley acknowledged that the plans firefighters could see on their systems were actually from 2005 and contained no indication of the mezzanine floor.

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

This lead to confusion when residents told 111 dispatchers they were stuck in that part of the building.

"If you had accurate plans showing the mezzanine and how you get up to it, that would've assisted you but you just didn't have that info," Stevenson said.

Stevenson said three people had broken through the mezzanine level's skylight windows to escape the fire, while Liam Hockings had been trapped in a room on the mezzanine.

Stevenson put to Townsley that had firefighters known where the trapped people were, they would have attempted to rescue those people.

"If I had known they were there? Absolutely," Townsley said.

Only centimetres on clear air on the fire floor

Senior firefighter Brady Cutting and firefighter Noel Wellington were tasked with fighting the fire at its source on level three.

Cutting said he had to crawl along the floor towards the fire source due to the low, hot smoke which burnt his ears through his protective equipment when he tried to stand.

Cutting said there was only a matter of about three centimetres of clear air above the floor.

"It was as if you were blind folded. Everything's done by touch," he said.

He said he received reports through his radio that there were people trapped in the building but did not know how to find them.

"Immediately after that an orange flame pulsed through the air behind us.

"The conditions were changing rapidly. The heat was unbearable we were lying on the floor simply to protect ourselves."

As debris began to fall about them, they withdrew from the floor and told other firefighters not to enter.

Appearing by video link, Noel Wellington told the court he had attended a callout at Loafers Lodge before the fatal fire.

Having seen the nature of the building and its tenancy, Wellington told the court he was expecting a "worst case scenario" as his crew travelled towards the blaze.

World.title: Slink skin factory manager takes on regional council in the Environment Court
World.content:
A Southland slink skin factory manager facing environmental charges has taken on the regional council in the Environment Court, arguing restrictions on his business are unjustified.

Da Cheng "Eddie" Zhi and his Tuturau business NZAgri Development are facing six charges brought by the Southland Regional Council over discharges of blood, leachate and/or contaminants to land in circumstances where they could enter water.

A seventh charge alleges they failed to comply with abatement notices issued in August and September 2025.

The Environment Court granted interim enforcement orders on 9 September that meant the business could not receive or process carcasses.

Neighbours had complained about offensive smells and piles of carcasses in NZAgri Development's yard.

Representing himself and his company before Judge Kelvin Reid on Wednesday, Zhi argued the business was being unfairly restricted and wanted the court to revoke the enforcement orders.

The regional council maintained regulatory action was necessary to prevent ongoing environmental harm.

During cross-examination, Zhi intensely questioned several council staff members about their qualifications, scientific training and experience collecting environmental samples.

He sought to introduce his own water samples as evidence and at one point asked a witness to test a glass of water in court.

At times Zhi became visibly frustrated.

"We are facing a bunch of people who have never been trained scientifically, who have no idea how to take samples," he told the court.

"We have never, ever discharged any single drop of wastewater to the creek, to the environment."

Judge Reid repeatedly interrupted, saying parts of Zhi's questioning were irrelevant to the issues before the court.

"The court has in front of it affidavit evidence from various council staff, some of whom have taken samples that have been analysed, and there's evidence about what the analysis means and what the discharges that were occurring on the site are doing to the environment," he said.

"The council is not relying on some other samples that you have."

Following the court action in September, Zhi staged protests outside the Southland Regional Council's office, including carrying dead lambs to the council car park.

The company is also facing legal action from the Southland District Council which holds interim enforcement orders.

In a separate application before the Environment Court the district council is seeking to revoke the factory's resource consent.

World.title: Race for vaccine to save hoiho/yellow eyed penguin
World.content:
The hoiho/yellow eyed penguin could be extinct in less than a decade as a respiratory disease continues to wipe out a significant proportion of the chick population on the mainland.

The hunt is on for a vaccine for the disease, and with fewer than 115 hoiho breeding pairs on mainland New Zealand and Rakiura/Stewart Island, it is a race against time to save the birds.

Scientists have recently discovered there are three "deeply distinct" subspecies of the penguin, and that could have major implications for conservation efforts.

Evolutionary virologist professor Jemma Geoghan told Checkpoint that every year for the past three years, about a quarter or a third of the chicks that hatch on the mainland have died from respiratory distress syndrome (RDS).

"And this is really compounded by everything else that they are dealing with, other factors such as fisheries and climate change and predation and things like that, so it's had a really significant impact on the population."

After studying the disease for a number of years and trying to understand its origins, Geoghan and her team discovered a virus that might be responsible for causing the disease.

"Now what is puzzling about this virus is that sometimes chicks can be infected with this virus without disease and sometimes they can be infected with the virus and it causes this really severe disease and death... If they develop symptoms or clinical signs that they have this respiratory disease then most of the time they end up dying within a really short timeframe - 24 hours of showing symptoms.

"So it's a puzzle, that's why we've taken the past couple of years to better understand whether or not this virus is causing the disease."

The scientists also discovered something interesting about the birds themselves.

They found the different populations - the northern ones found around Banks Peninsula and down to Rakiura, and the two southern populations living on sub-Antarctic islands - have actually been not breeding or mixing for thousands of years, with this divergence between their genome suggesting that they were actually sub-species.

"They have the virus in the sub-Antarctic, but don't seem to have the disease, so we're really interested in whether or not the northern population was somehow predisposed to this disease genetically," Geoghan said.

They need to be thought of as sub-species with different lineages that are genetically diverse, Geoghan said.

Understanding more about the northern population and its critical decline in numbers is important so the focus can be on its conservation, she said.

After sequencing the genome of the hoiho from the north and south, they found some genetic markers on the northern birds that were predisposing these hoiho to contract the disease.

Geoghan said they were hopeful this would lead to a vaccine, but time was running out.

World.title: Free mental health support launched for sextortion victims as cases reach record high
World.content:
Audio player for " Netsafe offers free counselling as sextortion at highest level ever " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/crime-and-justice/1783883%2Ffree-mental-health-support-launched-for-sextortion-victims-as-cases-reach-record-high

Netsafe offers free counselling as sextortion at highest level ever Checkpoint Download MP3 5m

Online safety organisation Netsafe says sextortion is at its highest ever level in Aotearoa, and the number of people falling victim to the online harm is rising rapidly.

Sextortion is a form of blackmail in which someone is tricked or pressured into sharing intimate images, then threatened with having them posted online unless they pay a ransom or send more.

Netsafe said cases have gone up nearly 25 percent in the last year, but many aren't reported.

From today, they have partnered with counselling service Ignite, to offer free support to victims.

For many people what may have begun as a friend request online, or a message from a friendly stranger, quickly spiralled into something much more sinister.

Netsafe CEO Brent Carey said sextortion is a rapidly growing issue, with nearly one in ten people having reported it to them.

"Netsafe's been getting on average 50 sextortion reports a week, and it's growing. And we've taken more than 16,000 reports of this harm type."

While the harmful practice is rapidly making its way to our shores, Carey said it is a global phenomenon.

All the way in Michigan, John DeMay's 17-year-old son Jordan fell victim to one of those scams, and in 2022 and took his own life hours after a sextortion scam rapidly escalated.

"He just checked his phone, saw the Instagram message come in, accepted the friend request and started having the conversation with her. He was having this conversation casually with Dani Roberts, and that conversation started to turn a little bit sexual.

"She ended up sending him nude images of herself and enticed him to do the same, and he eventually caved."

Netsafe CEO Brent Carey. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

DeMay said that within about 15 minutes "the switch was flipped", with Roberts demanding money, and threatening to send his nude image to everyone he knew.

But Roberts wasn't a teenage girl like she claimed, Jordan was talking to an organised crime group in Nigeria.

In 2023, a Christchurch teen took his own life just hours after he was sexually extorted online, in very similar circumstances.

Despite his reluctance, he exchanged intimate images with a woman on Facebook, who he thought was from Timaru.

After doing so, she demanded he pay $5000 or she would share the images to his contacts.

In reality, she didn't exist, and the account was also traced back to West Africa.

Carey said people in Aotearoa are being targeted from all over the world.

"In terms of blackmail and extortion, we know that there's organised crime targeting New Zealanders, and they're using social media accounts to socially engineer us and target us.

"But we also know [it's happening] through school communities, we know that there also can be a personal relationship to sextortion, and some people know who the perpetrator of this is."

While victims can report the online harm to Netsafe, Carey said they have been lacking services which provide ongoing support.

Today, Netsafe, alongside counselling service Ignite, have begun offering three free counselling sessions for people affected by sextortion.

Director of Ignite, Sarina Finucane said the stigma around sextortion often makes it difficult for victims to find the help they need.

Ignite director Sarina Finucane. Supplied

"Sometimes going locally for support can be a real challenge. There can be stigma and embarrassment attached to this. You might go into your GP to access some primary mental health support, and the GP may not even recognise what image-based abuse or sextortion is.

"This is why it's been really important to have that recovery pathway direct from Netsafe and to support providers that understand the impact of online harm."

Finucane said that mental health services needed to keep up with the rapidly evolving digital landscape.

"I think there's actually a real need for mental health services in New Zealand to meet the need of the modern problems that are arising for Kiwis. Sextortion is a huge issue, online harm is a huge issue, not just for young people, as we tend to think, but for a lot of New Zealanders and adults as well experiencing this."

Carey said they had seen the issue affecting people as young as eight, and as old at 80.

While counselling is key for victims to move forward, Carey said much more needs to be done to tackle the issue, starting with a review to the Harmful Digital Communications Act.

"We want to keep sextortion a live issue to try and tackle it. It's going to take banks, it's going to take platforms, civil society. therapy providers all working together to tackle this. We'd love for the government to review the act. That's a bottom line, and we also want to make sure that it's staying relevant for new harms."

Carey and Finucane said they hope to expand the pilot programme to offer more counselling sessions in the future.

Anyone who has been a victim of sextortion should report the offending to police on 105 (non-emergency) or 111 (emergency), and Netsafe by calling on 0508 NETSAFE (0508 638 723), or reporting online at netsafe.org.nz/report.

Where to get help:

If it is an emergency and you feel like you or someone else is at risk, call 111.

World.title: Auckland bin collectors dumped, offered chance to buy their own rubbish trucks
World.content:
Almost two dozen rubbish truck drivers in east and south Auckland have been dumped, with some offered the option to buy their own trucks and become contractors instead.

A restructure at Waste Management - the private company contracted by Auckland Council for kerbside rubbish collection in east and south Auckland - would make 23 drivers redundant in favour of independent contractors.

Workers First Union called the restructure a "predatory scam" and warned that the cost of buying the trucks could put workers in "hundreds of thousands of dollars" of debt.

"Drivers will be individually responsible for maintaining, repairing and upgrading their rubbish truck under the false pretence that they can use it for other business," union organiser Justin Wallace said.

"In reality, drivers will be working solely for Waste Management and their truck will wear that same brand and logo while they drive the same shifts they always have."

By becoming contractors, Wallace said drivers would lose their right to sick leave, guaranteed hours and collective bargaining.

A spokesperson for Waste Management said while redundant team members were given the opportunity to become contractors, this was not required or even expected.

"Experienced WM drivers routinely have the option to become independent contractors and many choose to do so," the spokesperson said.

"Independent contractors make their own decisions about vehicles and financing. Any finance is arranged independently with their chosen bank or finance provider."

In a statement released by Workers First Union, Manurewa local board member Joseph Allan said he was worried services would suffer.

"It's one thing to have courier vans parked all over our residential streets, but nobody wants a stinky rubbish truck parked outside their house," he said.

"What happens if the driver is sick? A big company might have spare trucks, a workshop, excess drivers. You lose the economy of scale. Redundancies at a large company like this could lead to worse services for council ratepayers."

Waste Management denied that its services would suffer.

"WM remains responsible for making sure the collection services we are contracted to provide are delivered, including having the trucks and resources required to provide those services each day," the spokesperson said.

"Independent contractors already provide collection services in other parts of Auckland, and the model has proven reliable."

Waste Management signed a 10-year contract with Auckland Council in 2020.

The council's general manager of waste solutions Justine Haves said it expected services to continue as they had been.

"Auckland Council expects Waste Management to continue to meet its contractual obligations and provide reliable kerbside collection services," she said.

"Waste Management remains responsible for ensuring the necessary trucks and resources are available to maintain service continuity."

The Waste Management spokesperson said Auckland Council was consulted on the restructure before it went ahead.

"Auckland Council was aware of and approved the change to the independent contractor model," they said.

World.title: 'One of the greats' signs off after fourth Roosters premiership
World.content:
Sydney Roosters coach Trent Robinson has hailed Daniel Tupou as one of the NRL club's all-time greats after the four-time premiership-winning winger announced his retirement.

Tupou is ending his 15-year career on a high after helping the Roosters win Sunday's grand final against Newcastle.

The 35-year-old, who had been coy about his future all season, became just the sixth player in Roosters history to win four premierships with the club.

Across a 307-game, one-club career, the winger scored 198 tries, the third most of any player in premiership history behind Ken Irvine and Alex Johnston.

"When you look at what Daniel Tupou has achieved over 15 seasons, he will stand as one of the greats," Robinson said in a statement.

"But those numbers only tell part of the story of Toops and what he means to this club.

Tupou a Roosters grand final specialist Daniel Tupou is edging closer to becoming the first Roosters player in more than 80 years to win four premierships because he always finds his best on the biggest day of the season.

"Since he made his debut, he has represented what we want a Rooster to be.

"He has been incredibly consistent, selfless and dependable, and whenever there has been a big moment or a tough moment, he has been present.

"Toops revolutionised the aerial game at the Sydney Roosters and became the greatest high-ball specialist of all time."

Tupou's exit comes as the Roosters prepare for a big off-season exodus over the coming weeks.

Fellow winger Mark Nawaqanitawase and second rower Angus Crichton are moving to rugby union, playmaker Daly Cherry-Evans is heading to Super League side Hull FC, and Connor Watson is joining St George Illawarra.

But none of them gets close to having the impact the towering winger has had on the Roosters since his NRL debut in 2012.

As well as four premierships (2013, 2018, 2019, 2026), Tupou has won three World Club Challenges and played Test matches for both Tonga and Australia.

He was part of the Tongan side that defeated the Kangaroos in 2019 in one of the biggest upsets in international rugby league history.

Tupou played 10 times for NSW at State of Origin level between 2014 and 2022.

"We love Toops, we're incredibly proud of him, and his name will always hold a very special place in the history of the Sydney Roosters," Robinson said.

Tupou retires as the greatest try-scorer in Roosters history after surpassing Anthony Minichiello in 2023.

World.title: Lionel Messi scores final goal in emotional farewell to Argentina
World.content:
Lionel Messi has delivered one last masterclass in blue and white as Argentina's captain brought the curtain down on his extraordinary 21-year international ​career by scoring a goal and setting up two others in a 3-0 friendly win over Benin.

The 39-year-old's final bow in front of more than 85,000 fans at a packed Monumental Stadium was less about football ​and more a national ‌celebration of Messi's service to Argentina.

Landmarks across the capital glowed with the team's sky blue and white colours, while fireworks lit up the skies above the heaving stadium as fans ‌poured their hearts into a rendition of Argentina's national anthem.

Messi's family watched proudly ⁠from the stands alongside some of Argentina's World Cup winners of ‌1978, 1986 and 2022.

"Even through the worst moments we went through, I never stopped fighting, battling, giving everything I had, wanting to always be here," Messi told the crowd after full-time.

Lionel Messi was emotional as he signed off from international duty. (Getty Images: Marcos Brindicci)

"I love all of you, and I will miss all of you. I am proud to be Argentine."

Hours earlier, a ​massive number 10 shirt ‌emblazoned with "Gracias" was unfurled at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, Messi's home town.

As the team bus travelled from the training centre bearing his name, Messi wiped away tears as thousands lined the route.

When the teams took the pitch, Benin captain Sessi D'Almeida looked lost ​for ‌words as he handed Messi a gift and letter during the pre-match handshake.

The crowd rose for applause and more fireworks erupted in the stadium as the clock ticked past the 10th minute of the match.

After a goalless first half, Messi supplied the assist for Nicolas Otamendi to tap home ⁠Argentina's opener.

Otamendi shared 17 years with ‌Messi in the national team, including ‌four World Cups, and was also ending his international career.

Messi then set up Nico Paz, one ‌of the players seen as a potential successor for Argentina's number 10 shirt, to score the second goal.

In a fairytale ending, Messi converted ‌a penalty ​for 3-0, his 126th ⁠international goal, prompting another round of "Messi, Messi" chants from the crowd.

At the final whistle, teammates, opponents and the referee gathered around Messi for embraces before a drone show lit up the sky to mark the end of his magnificent ⁠Argentina career.

Messi leaves as the country's most-capped player (208) and record scorer, having transformed years of frustration on the international ‌stage into a ‌story of World Cup and Copa America triumphs.

For years, Argentina asked ​Messi to deliver. On Tuesday, it simply came to say thank you.

Reuters

World.title: Are Test cricket batters getting worse? The stats say yes
World.content:
Australia's men's head cricket selector, George Bailey, pointed out some home truths recently when questioned on the woes of Test number three Marnus Labuschagne.

"Our batting group in its entirety, not just Marn, probably hasn't been functioning as successfully as we would like," Bailey said, and he's not wrong.

With the first of three Tests against South Africa beginning on Friday ahead of a mammoth run of matches against New Zealand, India and England, Australia's batting line-up will be scrutinised like never before.

Marnus Labuschagne picked a good time to score a century ahead of the first Test against South Africa. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone, file photo)

Since the beginning of the Border–Gavaskar Trophy at home in 2024, Australia has played 18 Tests with only three batters averaging more than 40: Steve Smith (49.4), Travis Head (46.25), and Alex Carey (40.3).

Beau Webster (33.5) and Cameron Green (30.16) are the only other batters averaging over 30 during the period.

Australia's bowlers have repeatedly dug the batters out of a hole, with the team winning 13 of those 18 matches.

Darren Lehmann sees clear reasons for the decline in Test batting, with serious consequences for the game (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

But Australia's batters aren't alone: Across all 12 Test-playing nations, the game has undergone a huge transition with batters fading and bowlers dominating.

The rise of T20 cricket, better balls and seaming wickets have all played a part.

ABC Sport has done an analysis of all Test batters over the past 40 years with the help of ABC radio cricket statistician, Ric Finlay.

Steve Smith, Travis Head and Alex Carey have all averaged more than 40 over the past 18 Tests. Marnus Labuschagne is in the 20s. (Getty Images: Phillip Brown)

We've looked at batters from one to seven and found the same patterns across all positions.

We could list a table of 40 years but to make things easy, we've broken it down to five-year periods that include every test played from the beginning of 1987 to the most recent Test between England and Pakistan.

To see the patterns, we're narrowing the numbers down to batting averages, run rates and average balls per wicket.

Looking at these figures, you can see that the average of all batters in positions one to seven peaked in the period between 2002 and 2016 before dropping back to the low 30s.

It's easier to visualise with a chart that shows the year-by-year average as well as a rolling five-year average to even out the yearly variations.

The period between roughly 2003 and 2014 is when averages were highest.

This coincides with a golden period for world-class test batsmen when the likes of Sri Lanka's Kumar Sangakkara, Australia's Ricky Ponting, South Africa's Jacques Kallis, England's Kevin Pietersen, India's Virender Sehwag and the West Indies' Shivnarine Chanderpaul, to name just a few, were at their peak.

Ricky Ponting was at his peak in the early 2000s. (ABC News)

The rolling five-year average is now at a 40-year low, but that only tells part of the story.

To understand more about the decline of Test cricket batting, two other charts fill in the picture.

The first is strike rate: how many runs batters score per 100 balls.

Batters' strike rates have increased across the board from 41.34 to 58.13: that's almost 17 runs per 100 balls, which is the equivalent of an extra run per over.

But while batters are scoring much faster, they're also getting far out more quickly.

Bowlers are now taking wickets faster than at any time in the past 40 years.

In 1989, top-order batters were lasting more than 85 balls between wickets in the rolling five-year average, while as of this year, wickets are falling every 58 balls — an all-time low.

From the peak to the current trough that's a fall of more than 32 per cent.

It's no accident that we're seeing so many shortened Test matches, like the two-day match in McKay against Bangladesh in August.

The overall figures are mirrored in virtually every individual batting position with averages on the whole going down.

In other words, we have seen a fundamental shift in the battle between the bat and ball playing out over the past four decades and right now, while batters are scoring more quickly, the bowlers are on top.

The same is true for Australia's one to seven batters.

Again we see the early 2000s peak in averages when Ricky Ponting, Matthew Hayden, Justin Langer, Damien Martyn and Adam Gilchrist were in their pomp.

The combined batting rolling average for positions one to seven is now at a 40-year low.

The strike rate rolling average is at an all-time high, although only marginally ahead of that early 2000s era.

But the balls per wicket figure rolling five-year average has dropped alarmingly from its starting high of 98.33 to its current all-time low of 54.26

That's a fall of almost 45 per cent.

To put it another way, opposition bowlers are taking Australian wickets almost twice as quickly as they were 40 years ago.

So, why is this happening?

Former Australia coach and batter, Darren Lehmann, who's currently coaching English country side Northamptonshire, highlights four major changes in cricket that are all linked.

Darren Lehmann (right) as coach of Australia in 2014, with the current head of selectors, George Bailey, and the late Rod Marsh. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour)

The first is the rise and rise of T20 cricket.

"Now they [batters] just don't leave balls," he told ABC sport.

"They have to score off more, so they play more shots to more risky balls in Test cricket,"

"Hence they go at balls they shouldn't go at, which they normally wouldn't have 20 years ago."

The second reason, Lehmann said, was the state of Test wickets around the globe, which he said were spinning and seaming more and earlier.

"They've got more in them and that is a by-product of making sure you get results," he said.

Lehmann said the balls used in Test Cricket, the Kookaburra and Duke, had added an extra layer of lacquer, which meant they stayed harder and the seam stayed prouder for longer, creating more movement.

"Blokes are playing shots to balls they shouldn't because they're trying to score before they get one that gets them out," Lehmann said.

The fourth reason bowlers are on top of batters is the one that ties it all together: data analytics.

"You're honing in on the weakness of players better than you did in the past and you're relentless with that.

"So, if a bloke can't cover drive or doesn't play well off the front foot, you now target that area with more balls, and you don't go away from that."

Mitchell Starc can be relied on to take wickets. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

"If a bloke gets out to a left-armer all the time, well you get Mitchell Starc straight on."

Sooner or later, the batter's lack of patience, the moving ball and seaming wicket combined with the bowler's knowledge of their opponent's weakness will result in a wicket.

Cricket's delicate balance between bat and ball has fundamentally shifted and the cost is two-day test matches like the Boxing Day Ashes test, which cost Cricket Australia millions.

Lehmann said wickets needed to get flatter or lacquer taken off balls in order to shift the balance back towards batters.

"There are consequences: two-day games in Test cricket can cost people their jobs."

Failing Test batters can also lose one of the most coveted jobs in Australian sport.
