World.title: Athletes drive to make table tennis a smash at national Special Olympics debut
World.content:
The repetitive click-clack of a small white ball paddling back and forth over a net may seem like a simple game of ping pong, but for these three teammates, it could be their ticket to the world stage.

The Bundaberg athletes are gearing up to compete in the Special Olympics Australia in Melbourne later this month, where table tennis is making its competitive debut.

Oscar Quarrell, 16, is diligently working to perfect his pendulum — a serve with a bit of side and back spin.

Oscar Quarrell (right) talks with coach Ha Bui as he prepares to play in his first Special Olympics. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Oscar is one of three from his regional club, 400 kilometres north of Brisbane, to be selected as part of the 14-strong Queensland table tennis team.

"I love table tennis because it's something that takes my mind off thinking and gives me a break," he said.

"It's also very fun to do with people that actually enjoy hanging around you."

Celebrating 50 years

The Special Olympics is for people with intellectual disabilities, cognitive delays or autism. It is also an organisation that supports community-based clubs and participation.

This year marks the 50th anniversary of the Special Olympics movement in Australia.

Oscar Quarrell, Taylah Sim and Nicholas Jefferson train with coach Ha Bui. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Special Olympics Australia CEO Jamie O'Connor said 850 athletes across 13 sports would compete at the 2026 games.

"Special Olympics provides programs at a grassroots level week in, week out, at a community level," he said.

"But it also has the path that goes through local competitions to state events, to national events, to international events.

"Our Special Olympics is more about participation opportunities than it is about winning gold medals."

Mr O'Connor said that, in addition to the inclusion of table tennis, dance sport would be a demonstration sport for the first time this year.

Oscar Quarrell practises with Taylah Sim. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

"As sport evolves, and the demand for different sports evolves, then we try and provide options for people with intellectual disability and the sports that they want to compete in," he said.

About 60 athletes who are successful in the national games will go on to compete at the Special Olympics World Games in Santiago, Chile, next October.

Trio take on games

As the excitement builds towards the national games alongside his backhand, Oscar was also preparing for a big leap in independence.

"I'm excited to do something different, and it's also the first time I haven't had my parents with me, so they are going to come and watch, but I'm not allowed to speak to them," he said.

Clubmates Taylah and Nicholas will be joining Oscar in Melbourne.

Taylah Sim has been putting in the hours to prepare for her Special Olympics debut. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Taylah has her eyes firmly on the prize, saying she looks forward to winning then going on to compete at the world games.

Nicholas is also hoping to win a medal, having played the game for 13 years.

His mum, Margaret, said table tennis had opened doors for her son and she enjoyed watching the competition.

"They all want to do their best but, at the end of the day, whoever gets first, second or last, they're all rewarded, and they are happy for them," Ms Jefferson said.

"There's cheering, there's no jealousy, they're here to support each other."

Table tennis has opened doors for Nicholas Jefferson. (ABC Wide Bay: Jacqueline Kelly)

Queensland table tennis head coach Kim Hammermeister had high hopes for her Queensland team when they competed at the national level for the first time.

"Bundaberg has always been very strong with their school program for people with an intellectual impairment," she said.

Ms Hammermeister said any Special Olympics sport provided opportunities for friendship.

"People with an intellectual impairment can become very isolated, especially after school," she said.

"Of course, the physical benefits of being active are amazing; you can't put a price on that."

World.title: Bombers call draft 'a priority' after Ridley deal amid Blakey link
World.content:
Essendon has once again headlined the trade period after sending veteran defender Jordan Ridley to Geelong in a bumper deal involving the exchange of four draft picks.

Essendon acquired Jack Bowes, who had requested a move to the club, a 2027 first-round selection and a 2028 second-round selection in exchange for Ridley, a fourth-round selection in this year's draft (currently No.60) and 2028 fourth-round pick.

The move comes as the Bombers and Cats were two of three clubs reported to have canvassed a move for Sydney's Nick Blakey, with St Kilda the third.

Blakey is contracted through 2031 with Sydney and there is no indication thus far that the Swans will agree to a trade this summer.

Nick Blakey could be seeking a move away from Sydney. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

While Essendon may be interested in Blakey, given its Sydney links through Mark McVeigh and John Longmire, the Bombers maintain that "bringing in young talent is the priority". It is unclear how the 26-year-old Blakey would fit into that equation.

Geelong and St Kilda also remain at an impasse over a deal for Saints ruckman Rowan Marshall, who wants to join the Cats for the second straight year.

The Cats will likely have to part ways with players if they are successful in luring Marshall and Blakey, with Gryan Miers's name continuing to be linked with a move away.

Miers's agent, Liam Pickering, said on Wednesday that the 27-year-old will not be joining West Coast, but left the door open to another rival club.

Follow the live blog below for a recap of all of Wednesday's trade action.

World.title: Gauff hits out at racist abuse after China Open incident
World.content:
Coco Gauff says she received an "insane" amount of racial abuse on social media after beating local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open.

The ‌American won 7-5, 6-1 on Monday to reach the fourth round but was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in the first set.

She raised her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board just as Sun was about to put away a winner.

After a video review, the umpire ordered the point to be replayed.

Gauff won the replayed point and held serve ⁠for 5-5 before cruising to victory against her 16-year-old opponent.

De Minaur retires from China Open with injury Alex de Minaur says he did not want his Beijing campaign to end in the way it did, with injury forcing the Australian to retire early in the second set.

The two-time major singles champion said she received a barrage of abusive messages on social media after the match.

"You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist," Gauff wrote on X in reply to a post containing a racial slur.

"The amount of racist comments/direct messages I've received in the last few hours is insane.

"Lastly, I'm not a cheater or a thief."

The WTA has made efforts to ‌tackle ⁠online abuse by introducing an AI-powered system that monitors thousands of players and officials on social media.

A study by the WTA and World Tennis showed players were subjected to over 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, up from 8,000 posts a year earlier.

Gauff explained she was ⁠following the rules when she challenged the point.

Players are allowed to request video reviews of select judgement calls, including claims a distraction may have interfered with play.

Gauff said she spoke to Sun about the ⁠point at the end of the match.

"I apologised for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood," Gauff wrote.

"I didn't like to see ⁠her so emotional as I've been there and I really understand what it's like but this is the beginning of an incredible career.

"It was an honour to share the court in front of her home crowd."

Reuters

World.title: Aussies dealt major injury blow ahead of first South Africa Test
World.content:
Cameron Green has been ruled out of the first Test against South Africa in Durban after succumbing to an abdominal strain.

Australia coach Andrew McDonald said Green failed to overcome the injury, which he suffered in the final one-day international (ODI) played in Potchefstroom last week.

McDonald said it was "highly unlikely" Green would bowl later in the series, should he prove his fitness for the remaining two Tests.

The injury blow is likely to leave Australia with a choice to make between Cooper Connolly or Nic Maddinson at number five in the batting order for the first Test, which begins on Friday night, AEST.

Travis Head is expected to remain as opener, with Alex Carey to bat at six.

Australia calls Maddinson and Harper into Test squad Nic Maddinson is within touching distance of a remarkable return to the Test team, after Cameron Green's abdominal strain left him in doubt for the series opener against South Africa.

Green appeared to be finding some rhythm with the bat, having scored a century against Bangladesh in Darwin in August.

"He is progressing pretty well, all things considered … he is still here for a reason, so there is some light at the end of the tunnel," McDonald said

"It will just be a matter of going through the rehab. He has a pretty demanding week as he reintroduced some activities.

"It's a bit of an unknown, but there is still optimism that he will take part in the series at some stage."

Green had been managing a shoulder injury that stopped him bowling in the white-ball matches against the Proteas.

His planned bowling return in the final ODI was aborted due to the abdominal injury.

"We would be solely focused on getting him to return as a batter. We wouldn't be putting that demand on him to return as a bowler," McDonald said.

"That would be too high-risk, is the information I have."

Maddinson has not played a Test for Australia since 2016 but was a surprise addition to the squad last week when Josh Inglis suffered a fractured finger.

Australia is also weighing up whether a dry Durban surface pushes them towards picking Connolly, with an expectation the Kingsmead wicket will turn later in the match.

Matt Kuhnemann is also on the tour as a second spinner, but it would appear unlikely Australia will opt to play him ahead of one of the three frontline quicks.

Green's injury also increases the chances of Beau Webster holding his spot as a fourth seamer, after he played in the last three Tests batting at number seven.

AAP

World.title: Geelong scores major coup with Matildas-Colombia clash
World.content:
The Matildas will return to Victoria this year, with Geelong's Kardinia Park named as the venue for the second leg of a two-match series against Colombia.

The Victorian government today announced the December 2 fixture, two years after 30,000 fans packed out the regional stadium to see the "Tillies" beat Chinese Taipei 6-0.

The announcement is a major coup for Geelong, which will be the only Victorian city to host the Matildas this year.

The national team last played in Victoria in May 2025.

"This blockbuster clash will drive visitation across the Geelong region, support local businesses and showcase Victoria's unmatched ability to host world-class sporting events," Visit Victoria chief executive Brendan McClements said.

Football Australia deputy chief executive Heather Garriock said Victorians' support of the Matildas was "always outstanding".

"We're delighted to bring the CommBank Matildas back to Victoria for what promises to be a special occasion for football fans, as our FIFA Women's World Cup 2027 preparations intensify," Ms Garriock said.

The first leg of the Colombia series will be played at Canberra Stadium on November 28, with the games expected to serve as a valuable test ahead of the World Cup in Brazil in June.

Both Australia and Colombia have already qualified for the World Cup.

Matildas fans were out in force in 2023, and will be raring to go in Brazil (AAP Image)

The Matildas finished fourth in the 2023 World Cup, and earlier this year were runners up in the AFC Women's Asian Cup.

Ms Garriock, who is also Football Australia's executive director of football, in August said the Colombia series would be an opportunity to give younger talent a chance to impress.

"We sat down with (coach) Joe (Montemurro) some 12 months ago when he started in the Matildas position, and we asked him what his ideal preparation was in the lead-up to the Women's World Cup," Ms Garriock said.

"It was very evident that different styles of play were important to him, but also trying to blood some of the next generation as well.

"We've seen that (younger players getting an opportunity) at the recent World Cup in the US with (Socceroos coach) Tony Popovic as well."

Tech.title: OpenAI drops another batch of mathematical breakthroughs
Tech.content:
is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes.

OpenAI has revealed solutions to a number of long-standing mathematics problems produced by an unreleased frontier model in a batch of 722 manuscripts, covering 372 result families that group related papers. It extends a run of breakthroughs that have both impressed and unsettled parts of the mathematical community while raising questions about research ethics and academic conduct. According to AGMAI, the newly formed independent advisory group of elite mathematicians put together to work on communicating the results responsibly, the release includes solutions to “hundreds” of open questions.

The results have been expected for weeks, although until now OpenAI had not provided details about which problems the model had solved or exactly when they would be published. In September, the company said its model had “resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics.” The released papers and other details also include some summaries of the model’s reasoning, estimates of the compute used, and stats about the number of problems attempted. OpenAI claims the “average result” used the equivalent of three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.

AGMAI, or the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, published its first recommendations in late September, urging AI labs to release mathematical results promptly and through established academic channels where possible, while disclosing details such as the name of the model used, prompts, and compute costs. The group also implored AI companies to “refrain from treating the release of mathematical results as marketing vehicles to promote their models,” a practice they said inflicts significant harm on the mathematical community.

Here’s how OpenAI described its process for this release:

For this release, we’re publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations. We’re continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee’s guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding

The full impact of the results will likely take some time to be felt as mathematicians assess and digest them. They add to a rapidly growing body of mathematical results from OpenAI and rival labs like Anthropic that the field is still processing, including results concerning a Millennium Prize problem, among the most famous open questions in the field. The speed at which AI labs have barreled into the discipline this year — particularly their handling of announcements — has provoked fierce debate over research practices, ethics, and how companies credit the human mathematicians whose work their systems build upon and potentially use to produce results.

Tech.title: Xbox has secured GTA 6 streaming rights
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma told employees that Microsoft is getting ready to do something around Grand Theft Auto VI that “no other platform holder is doing” during an employee all-hands this morning. According to sources familiar with Microsoft’s plans, Sharma’s brief teaser was actually about Xbox managing to land a deal for game streaming rights for Grand Theft Auto VI.

The deal will mean Xbox Cloud Gaming can stream Grand Theft Auto VI to players at launch, but it’s not clear how long the agreement will be in place. Rockstar Games still hasn’t announced a PC version of Grand Theft Auto VI, and a streaming deal would normally also allow Xbox to market its Xbox Cloud Gaming service to PC players who would otherwise need an Xbox Series X / S or PS5 console.

After The Verge originally reported that the deal would be exclusive, Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball revealed on X that Microsoft wouldn’t be streaming Grand Theft Auto VI exclusively, nor to PCs. That suggests the deal is simply for Xbox console streaming, and may mean the web browsers and apps that can usually access Xbox Cloud Gaming will not be able to stream Grand Theft Auto VI.

News of the streaming rights comes around a month after Microsoft announced some major changes to Xbox Cloud Gaming. From November, the same month Grand Theft Auto VI releases, Microsoft is limiting streaming hours to just 15 hours for Xbox Game Pass Ultimate subscribers, 10 hours for Premium subscribers, and just five hours for Game Pass Essential.

Microsoft is also opening up access to Xbox Cloud Gaming with a pay-as-you-go option next month, rather than being limited to Game Pass subscriptions. The pay-as-you-go option is perfectly timed for Grand Theft Auto VI, allowing those who don’t own an Xbox, or who primarily play from a phone, to stream the game by paying for a bundle of hours.

During the Xbox all-hands, Sharma also told employees that Project Helix, the next generation of Xbox hardware, will be a “family of devices” and that Microsoft will partner with others on some of those devices. Sharma first called Helix a family of devices last month in an interview, after Microsoft and AMD announced a “strategic multi-year partnership” last year to work together on “a portfolio of devices,” including Microsoft’s next-generation Xbox console.

Correction, October 6th: Xbox has clarified that its streaming deal isn’t exclusive and Grand Theft Auto VI won’t be streamed to PCs.

Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

All the smart home news, reviews, and gadgets you need to know about

The products will reportedly feature LG branding but integrate with the company’s rumored smart home hub that’s expected to launch during an event on October 13th.

Sources tell Bloomberg that the upcoming line of devices also includes a deadbolt lock, outdoor security camera, and a floodlight camera.

Previous Next

Several of the devices will reportedly come with support for the smart home protocols Thread and Matter amid a “formal reboot” for Apple’s HomeKit platform. Tech.title: Sebastian Maniscalco’s SiriusXM channel is hurting up-and-coming talent, comics say
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Comedian Sebastian Maniscalco is facing backlash from fellow comics who claim his takeover of SiriusXM’s Raw Comedy channel is harming up-and-coming talent, as reported earlier by Deadline. Many established comics, including Patton Oswalt and Margaret Cho, have posted videos online calling on Maniscalco to carry on Raw Comedy’s legacy by highlighting newer comedians on his channel, instead of mostly focusing on well-known ones.

SiriusXM launched Sebastian Maniscalco’s Comedy Radio in April, which is “curated and headlined by Sebastian himself,” according to the satellite radio provider. The move replaced SiriusXM’s long-running Raw Comedy channel featuring uncensored stand-up comedy shows from a range of talent. Now, the channel airs Maniscalco’s own show, alongside a stream of stand-up content that comedian Dan Soder says features “very famous comics who are dead or who don’t necessarily need the money.”

The widespread criticism comes as Stand Up for Standup, a nonprofit organization that provides resources for comedians in need, published a report about the channel’s shift away from emerging talent, who rely not only on the visibility they receive from appearing on the station, but also on the royalties they earn from SiriusXM. The organization says that since March, the spins on Maniscalco’s channels have decreased from a wider net of more than 800 comics to a much narrower pool of 275 artists, largely skewed toward celebrities.

“We believe this shift, both in the overall quantity of artists enjoying plays on Channel 102, and the change in distribution across all spin-getters favoring the top few, is bad for comedians, and bad for the future of comedy,” Stand Up for Standup says.

“There’s a lot of up-and-coming comedians who are depending on the money and the checks that they get from Sirius,” Oswalt says in an Instagram video. “But 500 of them have been booted off of Sirius… You can easily reverse this decision. Get those young comedians back on the Sirius channel. Let them get those checks.” Many other comedians, including Liz Miele, Kyle Kinane, and Michelle Wolf, have called out Maniscalco as well.

In a statement to Deadline, SiriusXM says Maniscalco’s channel “introduced a new creative direction and a regularly evolving programming mix for the channel,” adding that “SiriusXM continues to invest in comedians more than any other audio platform.” Neither SiriusXM nor representatives for Maniscalco immediately responded to The Verge’s request for comment.

Tech.title: Tesla’s Model 3 and Model Y can be a backup battery for your house
Tech.content:
Some Tesla Model 3 and Model Y owners can use their EV battery to keep the lights on longer during a power outage, now that Tesla’s expanding the Powershare Home Backup feature. It was previously only available on the Cybertruck, and also requires owning Tesla’s Powerwall 3. However, support for the Powerwall 2 and Powerwall Plus is “coming soon.” Tesla’s EVs aren’t the first or only ones with bidirectional charging; companies like Kia and GM also offer vehicle-to-home power on their vehicles, while Nissan’s Leaf offered power-to-grid charging years ago.

Tesla says the Model 3 and Model Y can extend home backup power to over two days for Premium and Performance models, which is shorter than the “over three days” Tesla claims you can get from the Cybertruck’s battery.

As Electrek points out, Tesla is only guaranteeing Home Backup will work on Model 3 and Model Y vehicles ordered from October 1st onward because not all older models include the PCS2 Lite inverter required to make it all work. So far, the feature is also only mentioned as available in the US and Puerto Rico, but not Canada, and not for the larger Model S or Model X. Tesla’s Powershare Grid Support feature is also still exclusive to the Cybertruck.

Tech.title: Google’s power-hungry data centers crave nuclear energy
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google announced a new agreement to update six nuclear power plant sites across the US as the tech giant seeks to generate more electricity for its power-hungry data centers.

Google signed the 20-year deal with Constellation, the leading nuclear power plant operator in the US. The power purchase agreement is meant to guarantee the revenue needed to cover the cost of efficiency upgrades at existing nuclear plants and “represents more than $4.3 billion of new investment by Constellation,” according to the press release.

Over the next five years, the companies expect new equipment at each site to collectively lead to 890 megawatts of additional nuclear capacity. That’s roughly equivalent to the amount of electricity one large new nuclear reactor or three small modular reactors might generate, according to Google and Constellation.

PJM has struggled lately to meet growing demand from AI data centers

They plan to modernize 11 reactors at six sites in Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. Each is connected to the PJM Interconnection grid, the largest power grid in the US, which spans 13 states and the District of Columbia — including the nation’s largest hub for data centers in Loudoun County, Virginia.

PJM has struggled lately to meet growing demand from AI data centers. An independent market monitor filed a complaint last year with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) saying that PJM was planning to allow huge data centers to connect to the grid that it could not reliably serve, which could lead to blackouts.

Along with the nuclear power deal, Google also inked a separate, much larger 15-year energy supply agreement with Constellation meant to guarantee continued revenue for other existing power plants Constellation operates within PJM, regardless of fuel type. Nuclear energy made up 70 percent of Constellation’s total generating capacity last year, and another 8 percent came from renewables. Gas and oil made up the remaining 22 percent, according to the company’s latest sustainability report. Gas also accounts for the largest chunk of PJM’s fuel mix. At 2,700MW, the second deal is much larger than the nuclear power purchase agreement.

Data centers are driving a surge in new gas infrastructure projects in the US, moving many tech companies further from their sustainability goals. Google’s carbon emissions rose by 18 percent last year along with a jump in electricity demand of 37 percent, according to the company’s latest sustainability report.

Tech.title: Amazon’s last-gen Kindle Paperwhite is 30 percent off
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Calling something “last-gen” usually means it comes with big compromises compared to the latest version. That’s not as true for the last-gen Kindle Paperwhite as it is with some other tech. The newer version can open books 30 percent faster (not the same as page-turning speed), and its aluminum design is a millimeter thinner — but it costs $50 more.

The 2024 edition has the same fantastic 300ppi screen, an auto-adjusting front light, and waterproof (IPX8) design. And the Signature Edition that’s discounted has no lockscreen ads, twice the storage (32GB) of the base model, plus wireless charging and an ambient light sensor, and it’s down to $169.99 (originally $249.99) at Amazon.

The standard Paperwhite is $149.99 (was $199.99) at Amazon, and while the lower price is nice, I’d suggest only opting for that model if you’re alright with what you’re giving up (which is a lot): it has half the storage, no wireless charging, and lockscreen ads.

Tech.title: How to find out if Amazon thinks you have ‘flat buttocks’
Tech.content:
It shouldn’t come as a surprise that Amazon collects data about you based on what you buy. If you buy a lot of cat litter, Amazon will probably infer that you have cats, or if you buy a lot of anti-acne skin products, then Amazon might guess you’re prone to breakouts. Even if we know that Amazon customizes our shopping experiences based on our purchase history, it still comes as a surprise to see all of these personal details laid out in a convenient list. Especially when those details get uncomfortably intimate.

One Threads user came across this section of her Amazon settings where you can see who the shopping giant thinks you are, and alongside more benign assumptions like “Shops from women’s departments” and “Probably owns a Shark robot vacuum,” she found that Amazon assumes she “has flat buttocks.”

“I stumbled upon a page of assumptions that Amazon has made about me based on my purchases and I’m literally speechless,” an Amazon customer, @fangirlinmegan, wrote on Threads. “I mean it ain’t wrong but damn did you have to call me out like that?”

In less than a day, the post garnered over a million views, including many from users who were curious what their own Amazon profiles might reveal. Here’s how you find out.

On desktop, you can find this page by hovering over where Amazon says “Hello, [your name]” in the upper right corner. Then click “Account” under the “Your Account” section. Under the “Ordering and shopping preferences” section, click “Your Shopping preferences.” From here, you can add in information of your own, like your shoe size, interests, and dietary preferences. But we’re not here to tell Amazon that it should stop selling you beef jerky since you’re a vegetarian. We’re here to see if Amazon thinks you have “flat buttocks.” When you scroll to the bottom of the page, you’ll see a blue hyperlinked option that says “Manage your information.” Once you click that, you’ll see what dirt Amazon has on you.

On the mobile app, you can get here by clicking the hamburger icon from the bottom menu bar, then navigating to Account > Shopping preferences > About you.

For me, Amazon has gleaned that I am someone who “practices photography,” “plays collectible card games,” and is “invested in the Apple ecosystem.” This is all true. Amazon has even flattered me by noting that I “read diverse non-fiction,” to which I say — why yes, I am indeed an open-minded intellectual with a thirst for knowledge. Thank you for noticing.

Other colleagues of mine found that Amazon correctly noted their interests in vinyl records and ceramics, as well as a penchant for “natural materials” in home decor and clothing that “prioritizes comfort.” None of us had anything as affronting as “has flat buttocks,” but the Threads user noted that this was likely because she had purchased “butt scrunch leggings.”

Tech companies know too much about us, and it’s jarring to realize just how closely they’re paying attention to how we use their platforms. We live in a world of alarming surveillance, but at least I know that Amazon doesn’t think my butt is flat.

Tech.title: Apple is reportedly partnering with LG to launch a smart lock, thermostat, and doorbell
Tech.content:
In Brief

Apple is working on a new ecosystem of smart home devices via a partnership with LG, Bloomberg has reported.

The new devices — which include a smart lock, a thermostat, and a doorbell — are designed to integrate with the company’s smart home hub, another upcoming product that will reportedly launch on October 13. That hub is expected to include a 6-inch square display that can be placed on a countertop or mounted on a wall.

The two companies are also working on a slate of security cameras, including models for indoor and outdoor, was well as a floodlight. The LG devices are expected to be announced, if not formally released, next week, too. TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information.

Interestingly, the devices will reportedly carry the LG brand — despite being developed by both companies.

The new products could aptly be read as a swipe at Amazon’s smart home offerings, which currently include a variety of similar products, including its Ring home security cameras.

Apple has sought to push into new territory with its recent hardware releases. One of those new territories is an expanded smart home presence.

Tech.title: Ex-Ramp engineers raise $20M for platform Melius after scrapping their first product
Tech.content:
Melius, an AI platform for generating ad campaigns, images, and videos, announced on Tuesday that it raised a total of $25 million in funding, including a $20 million Series A led by CRV and a $5 million seed round led by General Catalyst.

While the startup claims to have hit more than $1 million in annualized revenue within two months of coming out of stealth in July, co-founder Joowon Kim (pictured on right) admits that Melius didn’t hit it out of the park initially.

When the New York-based company first launched over a year ago, Kim and his co-founders, Young Kim (pictured on left) and Arnav Ramu (pictured center) set out to build an AI-powered performance marketing tool. The three knew each other from working as engineers at Ramp, the corporate spending and finance software company.

More than six months after building the product, the co-founders decided their original idea didn’t “have legs,” Joowon Kim told TechCrunch.

Instead of helping marketers manage and optimize ad spend, the team chose to focus on what it saw as a much larger opportunity: building the tools that generate the creative assets and campaigns themselves.

“We scrapped the entire codebase; we burned all of it,” Kim said. Melius quickly went to work on an entirely new product. Nearly a year after its initial launch, it revealed a platform that it describes as an “agents lab for creative work.”

Melius is far from the only startup helping ad agencies, marketers, and brands generate creative assets and campaigns with AI. Competitors include rapidly growing Higgsfield, which was valued at $5.4 billion in August, as well as other small startups, including Krea and Flora AI.

Kim isn’t concerned about the competition.

He acknowledged that Higgsfield, a three-year-old company that has hit over $700 million in annualized revenue, “is growing like mad,” but according to Kim, the size of the market is so large that it can support multiple competitors.

“There are a lot of players, which is pretty exciting,” he told TechCrunch. “That means there are customers to be won and there is demand in this space.”

As for why former Ramp engineers are building an ad-generation product, Kim, who describes himself as a social media influencer, says he has been passionate about making short videos since elementary school and once dreamed of becoming a famous YouTuber.

“I tried my best to make vlogs,” he said. “My dad was great at using FinalCut Pro, but I wasn’t.”

Those early vlogs never quite took off, but his fascination with making digital media remained.

Now, with Melius, he’s building the tool he always wanted: a platform where anyone, including seasoned creative directors, can turn their ideas into reality using plain language.

Tech.title: Silicon Valley’s AI wunderkind launches Underdog, the most private Instinct/Muse competitor yet
Tech.content:
When self-taught coder Sigil Wen was 17, he moved to Silicon Valley and lived in an AI hacker house with famed AI researcher Andrej Karpathy.

While there, he hacked and coded alongside other people who would become the biggest names in AI, like Perplexity founder Aravind Srinivas and OpenAI researcher Noam Brown. He tested early versions of AI tools that would later become well known, including a chatbot shared by Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann that would become Claude, an image generator from David Holz that would become Midjourney, and what would become OpenAI’s GPT-3 and the image generator Stable Diffusion. Prominent investor and entrepreneur Naval Ravikant hired him for Airchat, Ravikant’s now-defunct rival to the Clubhouse social network.

For fun, he figured out how to get GPT-2 running on his Apple Watch. “It was a magical time,” Wen told TechCrunch.

Now a Thiel Fellow — the program from investor Peter Thiel that invites young founders to pursue projects instead of college — Wen on Monday launched an invite-only beta of Underdog, one of the most private AI assistants Silicon Valley has yet to offer. The model runs wholly on-device, meaning the user’s data remains on devices they already own, currently Macs and Windows PCs, with Linux, iPhone, and Android versions coming soon.

Underdog is powered by Husky, the inference engine Wen built to run AI models quickly on a user’s own hardware. Wen says it moves less data between a computer’s main chip and its graphics chip than rival on-device engines.

Underdog has other security features baked in, too, like encrypting the keys to the email and other accounts that users authorize Underdog to access.

Underdog is, however, using much smaller models than today’s state-of-the-art ones hosted in data centers. It currently uses a 27-billion parameter reasoning model fine-tuned from Qwen3.8-27B.

Wen argues that this model compares favorably with Claude Opus 4.6 in some benchmarks, or what was considered top performance six months ago. He says that means it can handle the everyday tasks that people want an AI assistant to do, like shopping research or answering math homework questions.

“You don’t need to sacrifice your privacy for the capability because they’re just as capable,” Wen says. He adds that small on-device models will continue to grow more capable over time.

Perhaps the most interesting thing about Underdog is its early business model. The app will be free at first and never ad-supported. Since the AI runs on users’ machines, Underdog doesn’t have the giant overhead of paying a provider for inference. “I don’t have to charge you a subscription to run this because my costs are so super low,” he said.

Instead, with Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison as one of his angel investors, he’s borrowing a play from the fintech era. Underdog will take a tiny percentage of payment transactions that the AI assistant makes using Stripe’s secure payment rails, something like an interchange fee. In this way, the AI assistant never has to mine your data. It is as aligned with you as your bank or credit card providers.

This runs contrary to the business motivations of many of the other players in AI assistants, whose privacy policies allow them to collect data on users that they may sell to advertisers or other third parties, or use to train other models.

That kind of data collection could be a particularly treacherous trade-off for users of an AI assistant, which may need access to the most intimate details about you in order to be useful, from medical conditions to financial data to data on your kids.

As Wen wrote in what he calls his AI manifesto, “Why should using AI require surrendering your private information?”

He tells TechCrunch: “I honestly want to build Underdog for myself. I’m building a product that I would be proud for my future children to use.”

The startup behind Underdog is named Conway Research, and Collison isn’t its only big-name investor. Conway is backed by Andreessen Horowitz via partner Chris Dixon, as well as Khosla Ventures, Hummingbird, SV Angel, the Anthology Fund (the partnership fund between Menlo Ventures and Anthropic), and a prominent list of angel investors that includes Vercel founder Guillermo Rauch, Noam Brown, and Deedy Das, among others.

Tech.title: How AI decision models could change content moderation
Tech.content:
As decision models spread across the industry, a company called Musubi has a new idea for how to put them to work: moderating content. On Tuesday, Musubi announced a lightweight decision model made for real-time moderation called PolicyLM-1.7B, released with open weights.

The idea is to take a content policy written in plain English and apply it to messages in under 50 milliseconds. Musubi’s model is designed to be similar in cost and speed to the AI classifier systems that power moderation on most social platforms — but because it has the flexibility of a modern LLM, it can apply complex policies without special training. Even more important, the model won’t need new training when the policy changes, allowing for human policy-setters to iterate as much as they need.

As Musubi co-founder and chief AI officer Filip Jankovic sees it, it gives platform managers a way to label content proactively.

“Product teams just want a better understanding of what’s happening on their platform, especially as the amount of content is exponentially increasing,” Jankovic says. “Being able to label all of that in a very scalable, customizable way is extremely useful.”

Decision models have become a hot topic in the AI world since the release of TypeSafe AI’s Jev in September, which was shortly followed by competing decision models from OpenAI and Amazon. Instead of outputting text, a decision model outputs outcome probabilities, though in this case the model outputs a binary judgement: Either the content is in the category or it isn’t. By limiting the model’s output to a set of predetermined choices, decision models are able to run faster and cheaper than large language models, while still maintaining the flexibility of the transformer architecture.

One early use case is reining in misbehavior by AI agents — so it’s only natural to apply the same technology to human misbehavior.

Notably, Jankovic says his interest in decision models predates Jev, tracing it back to a 2024 project called GLiNER (Generalist Model for Named Entity Recognition) that deployed many of the same techniques.

Still, Musubi isn’t wary of the comparison. If anything, the company is eager to use the new interest in decision models to shine a light on content moderation. “If Jev caught your eye, PolicyLM-1.7B is the same kind of model, trained specifically for content moderation, that you can run yourself,” the product announcement reads.

Tech.title: AI computing startup Lambda to raise $4B ahead of planned IPO
Tech.content:
In Brief

Cloud provider Lambda is raising up to $4 billion at a $14.5 billion pre-money valuation, marking what could be its last private round before a planned 2027 IPO, according to The Wall Street Journal. Coatue Management and Blackstone are leading the round.

A letter to investors reviewed by the Journal shows Lambda’s backlog grew from $15 billion in June to $50 billion in September. While that might look like a hearty increase in demand, much of that increase appears to be driven by a $35 billion commitment from one company: Anthropic, which signed a deal with Lambda in late August.

That means Lambda’s valuation, which has climbed significantly since its 2025 funding round, could be leaning heavily on Anthropic’s ability to keep paying. Still, with reliable GPU capacity so scarce, investors are clearly still willing to bet on companies that provide it, especially ones with large contracts with a major AI lab.

For neoclouds like Lambda, demand isn’t so much the problem as is the cost of meeting it. Data center buildouts are largely funded by debt — of which Lambda just raised an additional $1 billion last week — and lenders are getting choosier about who they offer cash to and under what circumstances. Lambda’s decision to raise more now not only sets the tone for its IPO pricing, but also gives it access to more capital before the scrutiny of public markets arrives.

If and when Lambda does IPO — the company was reportedly meant to debut this year, but has pushed that back amid market uncertainty — it will join other Nvidia-backed neoclouds, like CoreWeave and Nebius, that now depend on the health of their stock to fund their data center buildouts. British neocloud Nscale filed for an IPO last month and is expected to begin trading soon.

Lambda, Coatue, and Blackstone did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: The next hurdle for AI agents: getting websites to let them in
Tech.content:
Personal AI agents, like Meta’s Muse, Instinct, ChatGPT’s Dots, and others, are kicking off a new wave of consumer AI that involves more than just responding to queries. These AI agents can actually get things done on users’ behalf, like booking flights, making dinner reservations, ordering groceries, and more, all without having to be technical enough to set up OpenClaw or some other agent on your own computer.

But consumers adopting these agents are often running into issues when the website on the other end of their request blocks the AI from completing the job.

Most recently, Amazon began blocking Meta’s Muse AI agent from its retail site, meaning that the agent could no longer browse or make purchases from its product catalog.

However, the problem is not limited to Amazon or Muse. User complaints across social media indicate their agents are often running into similar blocks. Some of these are intentional, like Amazon’s, while others are the result of websites’ traditional anti-bot measures designed to protect against spam and malicious activity.

What’s not clear to the end user is whether or not the block is accidental on the website owner’s part, which leaves them frustrated with both the service provider or retailer and the agent trying to facilitate the transaction.

For instance, TechCrunch has seen a handful of complaints on social media claiming that Muse couldn’t complete a purchase on Walmart’s retail website. (NBC also reported that this was a problem Walmart had faced in its tests of the AI agent.)

But a spokesperson for Walmart told us these weren’t intentional. In fact, Walmart is partnered with Muse, as was announced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September. The company said it wants to be where its customers are, and that now includes being available through AI agent experiences.

The issue that Walmart customers often appear to be running into (see below) is that the website presents a button that has to be clicked to verify the visitor is human. If that experience is interrupted, the check could fail, and the agent gets booted out.

It’s an indication that the current technology we use to verify humans and keep websites safe from spam and bots may not be the best fit for the agent-first era of the web we’re now moving into.

To address this problem, industry partners including Meta, Walmart, Stripe, Sierra, Genesys, Rocket, NiCE, and Decagon have begun working on an open standard that would dictate how AI agents can communicate with businesses, helping to separate the good bots acting on behalf of the user and the bad. This protocol will be specifically focused on agent-to-agent communication for the purposes of online commerce, Meta said in a blog post.

This is frustrating. @Walmart in their attempt to stop agent from making purchases has gone too far and is essentially blocking actual human from making purchase on their website. I tried to purchase something directly and I can't even sign in. pic.twitter.com/CRAgkrCCa0 — Kevin Wang (@buzaza) October 5, 2026

In the meantime, consumer confusion abounds.

Although Walmart is at least trying to be accessible via AI agents, other companies aren’t so keen on the idea or haven’t fully embraced the technology.

For example, flight booking is currently one of the main use cases being positioned for agents, but many people have reported issues with airlines rejecting their agents’ requests.

Delta, for instance, told us that the company is taking steps to protect customers from unauthorized automated activity, and that if it were to open up to AI agents, it would have to be done with “security and the customer experience in mind.”

“While Delta does not currently have a partnership or integration that enables a third-party AI agent to shop for or book Delta flights on a customer’s behalf on our digital platforms, we’re continuing to evaluate how new technology, including external AI agents, could enhance the way customers engage with Delta,” said Delta’s general manager of Global Communications, Heena Chavda, in response to our questions about whether or not it was blocking agents, as some users complained.

United was not quite as direct as Delta, but a spokesperson pointed us to the part of its Terms of Use policy, which says that the user agrees “not to use any robot, spider, other automatic device, or manual process to monitor or copy this website or the content contained therein or for any other unauthorized purpose without United’s prior written permission.” (United didn’t respond to a follow-up question about whether it was blocking specific personal AI agents, like Muse.)

Early adopters’ complaints across social media have referenced a number of brands that are reportedly blocking AI agents, including Yelp, eBay, Zillow, Pizza Hut, Adidas, and various airlines. Some believe that the blocking activity seems to have recently increased.

A couple of people even said eBay suspended their accounts because of their use of agentic AI. Another complained that Google kicked out Instinct while it was cleaning up their Gmail inbox for them.

Looks like @adidas won't get my business tonight 😪 pic.twitter.com/DXcPYE5S6O — Martin Kessler (@kesslerIO) September 28, 2026

Despite the push to have agents book tables at restaurants and other tedious tasks, Yelp told us that it doesn’t permit non-human traffic on its platform unless the agent has paid to access Yelp’s content and data through its data licensing program. That means agents trying to use its site to get a quote, add a user to a waitlist, or book them a table will likely fail if they don’t have a formal partnership with Yelp.

eBay told TechCrunch that its approach is not to prohibit all third-party shopping agents from completing purchases. Instead, its policies restrict unauthorized agents and actions, like automated scraping and model training.

Adidas, Zillow, and Pizza Hut either didn’t respond or declined to provide a comment by the time of publication.

One major company involved in this space is Cloudflare, which offers sites protection from AI agents that could be training on its data and managing other automated activity. Some suspect that Cloudflare and other content delivery networks (CDNs) like it are currently disrupting Muse traffic. This is attributed to a change to crawler defaults on September 15, which allows site owners to block AI training while allowing other types of bots. Existing sites that were previously set to block AI bots for security reasons were then shifted to block AI agents on any pages that had ads.

However, when we asked if Cloudflare had any insight into what was happening with the blocking of these personal AI agents, like Muse and others, the company said it didn’t have any specific data to share at this time. It pointed us instead to its free public data hub, Cloudflare Radar. The site shows the increase in bot activity (which Cloudflare has also commented on previously), but it doesn’t help differentiate between the good bots and the bad ones.

Cloudflare also has a vested interest in mitigating AI traffic to websites, as it now runs a marketplace where AI bots have to pay for the data they access. It recently began testing a new web browser built specifically for AI agents.

Given the rapidly evolving space, Meta’s decision to form specific brand partnerships for Muse access seems to be the right way to go, as is its decision to focus on new standards. In doing so, it assures its customers that its agent, at least, is welcome at these partners’ sites — so any issues with access would be reportable bugs.

Meta also maintains a list of “connectors” (a.k.a. partners) inside the Muse app, which continues to grow. Many of Meta’s newly announced partners haven’t yet shown up in this list. But given Muse’s rapid expansion, which now includes partnered tools for small businesses, a bigger reorganization of Muse’s connector list is likely soon to be underway.

“Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it. We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer,” Meta said in its announcement about the newly announced plans to develop a standard. “There is a path that is good for users and good for businesses. It starts with clear norms, gives businesses more predictable control, and evolves toward a more efficient way for agents to work together.”

Tech.title: Hark releases an AI personal assistant with a focus on privacy
Tech.content:
From Muse to Instinct to Dots, tech firms are hunting for the user experience that will make an AI personal assistant a must-have product.

Hark, a startup founded less than a year ago by serial founder Brett Adcock, is throwing its hat in the ring today with the wide release of Hark Pro. Users can access the service for free, with a subscription tier for heavy users.

The company sees its mission as building a user interface for AI, not creating AGI or curing cancer. The foundation is a model trained specifically for computer use, and that’s what Hark Pro does — it uses your computer for you.

That’s perhaps a less ambitious claim than some frontier labs are making, but a little humility goes a long way in winning over users. And rather than an app, Hark’s goal is to create an operating system for the AI computers of our future.

Hark Pro is a full-screen experience with a kind of homepage, featuring a central chat dialog and a feed populated by prompts for actions you might need it to take and visualizations the company calls “panels” that offer mini-dashboards for things you’re interested in. The background is a piece of custom imagery tailored to the weather and time where you are.

Like other AI assistants, users configure it to access their digital life — email, calendar, hard drive, credit cards, etc. Then, it can take on digital tasks as well as fielding classic chatbot questions.

Abidur Chowdhury, a former Apple staffer who leads design at Hark, demoed the product for me. It proactively asked him about expenses he needed to approve, emails he needed to respond to, a meeting with this reporter, and, of course, pointed out that he needed to book a flight for a trip and offered to take care of it. (“I know the flight thing is put to death,” he admits, grinning.)

That does get at the challenge with these apps: One of the harder things for users is actually coming up with useful tasks they are capable of accomplishing. Chowdhury says he was impressed when the AI assistant recently recognized that one of his colleagues needed to renew their car registration at the California DMV, and handled it through the agency’s website.

One notable UX choice that Hark makes is showing the user how the agent navigates the web in a small window, an action most AI assistants perform without it surfacing in the app, which Chowdhury says is intended to build trust with users that the agent is doing the right thing.

That matters because part of Hark’s pitch is that they are not Meta or OpenAI — “we’re not here to like sell you ads and steal your data,” Chowdhury says. To truly leverage these models, users will need to share their entire digital lives. Beyond very real cybersecurity concerns, will users be comfortable with a company like Meta having its products create detailed profiles of their friends and family?

Asked about that kind of profiling, Chowdhury says that “we are doing work to understand you, and be helpful for what you need, but it’s really like task-related — it’s really about how Hark can help take something off your plate and be useful.”

What sets Hark Pro apart from its competitors, Chowdhury says, is its effort to fully subsitute for your computer, but also his belief that it just works better.

“Please compare it to the others, be critical,” he says. “It might not be faster than Muse, but it will give you a better result, and it will work end-to-end instead of asking you to take over at a point.”

One open question is what kind of model best suits the AI personal assistant. Hark’s is explicitly trained for computer use, which makes it faster and cheaper at those tasks, but it’s not clear how much it is trading away the broader knowledge and capability of a frontier LLM.

This software is only half the promise of Hark; Chowdhury made his name designing devices at Apple and Hark promises to release an AI-native device to support its software in 2027.

They’re still cagey about the form it will take, with Chowdhury bemoaning the “creep factor” of wearable cameras. “I will give you this: The first product that we’re building is a product that’s never ever existed before,” he says. We’ll have to wait and see if this is mere hype and Hark puts out some retread tech instead of a truly novel product.

“It’s so hilarious to me that you have AI now, you have a chatbot, and you type stuff in with a keyboard,” Chowdhury says. “Fifty years later and the future of computing is still a terminal.”

Tech.title: Jaguar Finally Reveals Its Biggest Gamble: the Type 01
Tech.content:
“A bold grand tourer that never arrives unnoticed, like all the best Jaguars of the past,” Jaguar’s press material says. This is most certainly true: you will see this thing coming. The low roofline, short front and extended rear overhangs, long hood, and huge 23-inch wheels all remain from the prototype, just as promised. The cab-rear design hides a 50–50 weight distribution, and the huge surfaces make it hard to square the fact that this is the most aerodynamic Jag ever, with active vanes, a deployable spoiler, and airflow trickery delivering a drag coefficient of 0.23 Cd.

Crucially, the production model’s extra doors make more sense of the design, shifting the Type 01’s look away from Thunderbirds territory to more familiar ground. The front has been softened ever so slightly as well, which again is preferable to the prototype’s exceedingly bluff nose. The rear, however, is where the exterior design really shines with hidden-until-lit, full-width lights embedded in horizontal strikethroughs.

Let’s get the specs out of the way: the Type 01 is the most powerful Jaguar road car, with up to 1,030 Pferdestärke (PS) and 1,365 Newton-meters. It goes from standstill to 62 mph in 3.2 seconds. Justifying the tagline of “power in reserve,” the car can rocket from 62 to 112 mph in a further 4 seconds. I’ve been driven in it, and it feels like the acceleration never ends thanks to the tri-motor setup of a 260-kilowatt (kW) front motor paired with twin 310-kW rear motors.

It stands 5,235 mm long and 1,403 mm tall, but all-wheel steering makes it feel much smaller on the road. The 850-volt bespoke Jaguar architecture and 118-kilowatt-hour usable battery supposedly deliver an EPA range of up to 400 miles (450 miles on WLTP), with a “sustained highway speed” range of up to 320 miles. Drivers can add up to 200 miles of range in 13 minutes using 350 kW rapid DC charging. So the TL;DR? It’s huge, fast, aerodynamic, powerful, and, most definitely, unique.

Inside, a dramatic central spine runs the full length of the cabin, creating a zone for each occupant. Lots of “brass-inspired” finishes are intended to underline the luxury message. A panoramic glass roof with adjustable virtual blinds brings in the light, but there’s no rear windscreen. Instead, a digital “ClearSight” rearview display is embedded centrally in the full-width panoramic soundbar at the base of the windscreen to show what’s behind. Cleverly, the feed from this rear-facing camera is positioned at the same height as the door mirrors, supposedly reducing the annoying focal adjustment these systems usually demand.

Tech.title: You Probably Aren’t Going to Get the Plague
Tech.content:
A mysterious death of a woman in Russia following a lab accident has stoked fears about plague spreading. But the odds of that actually happening remain very low, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention saying on X Tuesday afternoon that the circumstances of the case remain unconfirmed and that there is “no indication of a broader threat to the United States” at this time.

“We are working across the US government to assess developments as additional information becomes available,” the agency said. “CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely.”

Last week, a young researcher died from severe pneumonia of “unknown” origin after reportedly breaking a test tube at her workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute in Siberia. The hospital that treated her before her death was placed under quarantine, and her coworkers at the lab were isolated, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty.

Christian Lindmeier, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization, told reporters in Geneva on Tuesday that the group has been in touch with Russian authorities. Based on currently available information, WHO says the ​public health risk to the general population is very low.

“I think that’s the correct assessment,” says Gigi Gronvall, an immunologist and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. “We don’t know anything about anything right now.”

Russian authorities have said contact tracing hasn’t yielded any signs of dangerous pathogens spreading, according to the Associated Press. Infamous for causing millions of deaths in Europe during the Middle Ages, plague is rare today. It is caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis, which is found in wild rodents and their fleas in many parts of the world. It’s spread to humans through the bite of an infected flea and occasionally through direct contact with an infected animal. Antibiotics can cure plague, but they must be started as soon as an infection is suspected.

Pneumonic plague occurs when a person inhales infectious droplets that contain the bacteria. In July 2025, an Arizona man died from pneumonic plague after exposure to infected cats. It can also spread from person to person through respiratory droplets during close contact. But human-to-human transmission is rare, with the last reported occurrence happening in 1924 in Los Angeles. The possibility, though, is why the CDC says it’s important to rapidly identify cases and treat them.

“Once you know that somebody has been exposed to it, and even if you have a doubt that somebody has been exposed to it, you can immediately start antibiotics to prevent the person getting afflicted with the disease and to avoid the continuous spread of the disease,” says Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
